title: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline
content_c:
Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline
- Published
Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher.
The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war.
The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen.
New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week.
The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks.
It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping.
The price of a barrel of oil has surged since Saudi Arabia said on Friday it was closing the pipeline as a precaution. Brent crude was trading as high as $108 (£80) a barrel on Tuesday, down slightly from $109.80 on Monday.
Experts from trade intelligence firm Kpler said the pipeline's closure could reduce oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day - or about 3.6% of global demand.
"Based on new information we've received, damage to the pipeline could take four to six weeks to resolve, given spare-parts availability and impaired supply chains," said Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis.
Anne-Sophie Corbeau, from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said pipelines are "like sitting ducks" and recent strikes are a "very important signal" indicating workarounds being used to avoid the Strait of Hormuz "may not be super useful because they can be destroyed".
The Houthis have targeted other Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles which has led to some operations being suspended.
There have also been attacks on military bases. New satellite images captured on Monday show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait which the Houthis said they had targeted with ballistic missiles and drones last week after it was used to carry out air strikes on Yemen.
At least three aircraft hangars or shelters appear to have been damaged at the Royal Saudi Air Force facility where US-made F-15 fighter jets are based.
The Saudi-led anti-Houthi military coalition of Arab states said on Tuesday that a Houthi missile and drone attack had injured 13 people in attacks on what the coalition said were "civilian objects".
The Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out with more than 50 strikes in western Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
The UN Refugee Agency has said that more than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed conflict.
Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler and Benedict Garman
Graphics by Tom Shiel
description: Experts tell BBC Verify the pipeline's closure could cut oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day.

title: Police boss cancels 'ridiculous' theatre tour
content_c:
Police boss cancels 'ridiculous' theatre tour
- Published
An under-fire £79,000-a-year police commissioner said he had cancelled heavily criticised plans to take part in a 127-date national theatre tour.
Opposition parties had questioned how Reform UK's Colin Sutton would be able to oversee Norfolk Police while also presenting a live true crime stage show across the UK.
Sutton told a council meeting that the number of dates was "ridiculous" and that he had pulled out of the "Makings of a Murderer" tour after being contacted by residents.
Conservative Matthew Taylor, who stood against Sutton in the police and crime commissioner election in July, said it had been "a sorry saga".
A high profile former detective who led the investigation to catch Levi Bellfield, the murderer of Milly Dowler, Marsha McDonnell and Amelie Delagrange, Sutton comfortably won the election to become Norfolk's commissioner two months ago.
A regular on TV documentaries, he has previously carried out a long national theatre tour talking about his career.
Last week, promoters announced his follow-up series of shows would take place next year and Sutton initially said it "wouldn't impinge" on his day job.
But on Tuesday, he admitted to the BBC that he was considering cancelling the tour and on Wednesday he told councillors he had now scrapped it.
"What surprised me and what made me reflect and think again was the reaction that I got personally from a number of residents," he told North Norfolk District Council's scrutiny committee.
"I'm not sure I could do 127 dates because it was ridiculous, but I could have done some. What I don't want to do is to give the impression to anybody that I don't take this role seriously and I'm not going to do a good job on this.
"So that's why my decision has been: OK, I'm not legally obliged to do this, I'm not going to do it."
Taylor, a county councillor who came second to Sutton in the commissioner election, said it had "been a sorry saga, one that erodes public confidence in those who are supposed to represent them".
"I know many people across Norfolk have been deeply disappointed by this episode," he added.
South Norfolk Labour MP Ben Goldsborough also said it was "good" that Sutton had pulled out.
"But the fact it took a huge public backlash to make him realise that being Norfolk's police and crime commissioner should come before his career as a touring personality tells its own story," he said.
In a statement, the promoters of the show, Entertainers, said Sutton had been invited back to The Makings of a Murderer due to "popular demand".
"Through our recent discussions with Colin, it has become clear that he had underestimated the overall demands of the forthcoming tour alongside his other professional commitments.
"What has also been abundantly clear throughout those conversations is how seriously Colin takes his responsibilities to the people of Norfolk, and how deeply committed he is to serving them.
"We are now working closely with Colin to find a route forward and those discussions are ongoing."

title: Would you buy branded clothing from your favourite tech firm?
content_c:
Would you buy branded clothing from your favourite tech firm?
- Published
For Natalie Fratto, putting on her dark green jumper from US microchip giant Nvidia is like wearing the kit from a favourite sports team.
On the front of the $178 (£132) woollen garment is a cartoonish image of the tech company's boss Jensen Huang.
Fratto doesn't work for Nvidia. Instead, she's a fan of the company.
"I have a New Zealand All Blacks rugby jersey, and I think of my Jensen sweater in kind of the same way," says New York-based Fratto, who runs a tech start-up.
She explains that it's a representation of a team and ethos "that I am impressed by and root for", and she proudly wears the jumper in videos she posts on social media., external
Nvidia certainly plays in the top league of global tech firms. Under Huang's leadership, it has capitalised on the AI boom to become one of the world's most valuable companies.
While it sells tens of millions of its chips per year, its clothing is far more exclusive. The lines, which also include t-shirts, hoodies and hats, are typically only available to buy from pop-up stalls at its conferences, and for very limited periods or "drops" via an online store and sell out very quickly.
And while it might seem odd that such a tech company is selling clothing, others are getting in on the act too – and also focusing on exclusivity.
OpenAI, the operator of ChatGPT, usually only offers its branded fashion to employees, but occasionally it goes on general sale for a few days via its website.
Meanwhile, Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, last year opened a temporary, pop-up coffee shop in Manhattan's West Village. For just one week it gave away free baseball hats with the word "thinking" embroidered on the front.
Professor Hazel Clark, who teaches fashion at Parsons School of Design in New York, says that by limiting availability, tech firms have taken inspiration from the world of fashion. "It's a very common strategy for brands to use. It elevates the desirability," she says.
But why are such companies selling clothing in the first place? It is not as if they need the supplementary income streams.
Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic all declined to comment, but it appears to be about brand promotion and reputation management.
Take US software firm Palantir Technologies, which has faced criticism due to it work for the military and police, both in the US and overseas. Since launching its own clothing range last year, Palantir now calls itself a "lifestyle brand".
Eliano Younes, Palantir's head of strategic engagement, says: "A lifestyle brand isn't defined by what you sell, it's defined by what you stand for and whether people want to affiliate with it. I believe that the store's success and the enthusiasm from our community proves this."
Younes adds that "investors, customers, employees, and everyday people" in more than 60 countries have bought Palantir's gear, which includes a cotton jacket.
One US buyer of Palantir clothing, who didn't want to be named, says it was attracted by the controversy and "amount of people talking about it". He adds: "It's the purest form of anti-fashion…and that is what makes it so interesting and unique."
Critics suggest companies like Palantir are using stylish merch "to get their name into a more positive conversations", as Clark puts it.
Younes says: "Our clothing, like our software, is not political. It's designed for all people who support Palantir and what it stands for."
Some other companies are being more overtly political with their clothing, such as US defence firm Anduril, which makes military drones. It sells a hoodie emblazoned with the words "Rebuild the Arsenal", reflecting its aim of seeing more US defence spending and manufacturing.
Jonathan Sargent, a legal assistant in Albuquerque, New Mexico, has bought clothing from both Palantir and Anduril. "A lot of apparel today, whether it's Nike or other large brands, can feel disconnected from anything tangible," he says.
"But Palantir and Anduril are companies that people associate with building things that have a visible impact, whether that's defence, AI, infrastructure, or decision-making systems," he adds.
Back at Nvidia, the popularity of its founder Huang may be driving the sale of its clothing. He has been known to attract crowds of adoring fans, competing for autographs or selfies with the 63-year-old who is known for his trademark leather jacket.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described Huang as "Taylor Swift, but for tech".
Prof Gianpaolo Vignali of the Manchester Fashion Institute says: "People look at them [such big tech bosses] as role models. They want to aspire to them."
For Greg Epstein, author of the book Tech Agnostic, who describes the tech industry as a cult or new global religion, wearing tech merch is "a way of symbolising that you're one of the prophetic elite". This can particularly appeal to Silicon Valley insiders who are often "searching for a sense of identity, a sense of purpose, a sense of community".
Epstein, who is the humanist chaplain at both Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, adds: "When tech bros put themselves on sweaters, it's more than just a cutesy phenomenon, it's an attempt to sell a cult whose goal is to radically alter the human condition."
Whether or not you choose to buy your next shirt or hat from a tech or defence firm, Vignali argues that all clothing choices are loaded with meaning. "The subtle colour of a tie or hair bobble… all of these are signals that allow the wearer to symbolically share their cultural and ideological positions," he says.
While tech and defence fashion seems to draw both ardent fans and fierce critics, not everyone takes it so seriously.
"It's a unique moment in our collective zeitgeist for sure," says Fratto, but she also thinks that Nvidia's decision to put Jensen Huang on the front of its official merch is also "kind of funny".

title: Record fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firms
content_c:
European governments have discussed imposing a bloc-wide windfall tax on energy companies, as near-record fuel and gas prices pile pressure on leaders desperate to contain mounting public discontent and the challenge of the far right.
With elections due next year in eight EU countries including France, Italy, Spain and Poland, leaders are scrambling to head off the potential fallout from what analysts have warned could be one of the continent’s biggest energy shocks in decades.
Germany’s finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, called on the European Commission at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday to propose possible ways to tax what he described as the excessive profits of oil companies.
“Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil said, demanding proposals by next month. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.”
Oil futures have climbed back above $100 a barrel, about 50% higher than before the Iran war, as escalating attacks across the Middle East threaten more supply routes. Derivatives markets suggest traders do not expect a near-term drop in prices.
Pump prices have already reached all-time highs across Europe. In Germany, diesel prices surged to a record average of €2.45 a litre on Wednesday, while petrol hit a fresh high of €2.31 a litre, according to Europe’s largest motoring association, ADAC.
Prices are even higher in the Netherlands, where petrol eclipsed last week’s record high to reach €2.73 a litre on Wednesday, with diesel at an average €2.78 a litre. Prices have risen higher still for petrol in Denmark and for diesel in Finland.
Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% higher than a year earlier, while diesel is up 38% and jet fuel costs more than 100% more. Benchmark gas is trading at €81 a megawatt hour, up 150% on a year earlier, with analysts suggesting it could hit €100.
The EU’s economic commissioner, Valdis Dombrovskis, has said the commission has no plans “at this stage” for an EU-wide taxing mechanism, but stressed it was “ready to engage in discussion” and member states were free to impose their own taxes.
Sky-high fuel prices are already a major domestic political issue in France and Italy, both of which next year face crunch elections in which voters’ concerns are likely to be dominated by the soaring cost of living, driven largely by high energy prices.
In Italy, Giorgia Meloni’s ruling rightwing coalition, trailing rivals in the polls, said this week it would scrap road tax for 14.5m cars and motorbikes from next year at a cost of over €2bn, on top of a cut to diesel duty that has already cost €2.8bn.
“We have chosen to redirect a portion of the resources used to address rising fuel prices into a simple, structural measure designed especially for those who use cars and motorcycles every day to work, take their children, or get around,” Meloni said.
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, told ministers he wanted the government’s “full mobilisation” on fuel supply and prices, including efforts to secure supplies internationally by working toward the “peaceful reopening” of the strait of Hormuz.
In the latest of a wave of protests, French fishers blocked access to two ports and a fuel depot in southern France on Thursday over soaring diesel prices that this week rose to €2.37 a litre, just below their record of €2.38.
The fisheries minister, Catherine Chabaud, said the fishers had agreed after six hours of talks to lift the blockades after a promise that those with cashflow issues would be granted zero-interest loans and support measures would to be tied to fuel price changes.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, this week extended emergency fuel subsidies until the end of the year for the agriculture, fishing and construction sectors. But the government is reluctant to step in to cut fuel prices for all.
“Blanket measures that affect everyone – including those who don’t need them – are a false economy,” the country’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, told journalists earlier in the week. “Why? Because ultimately, we’ll have to fund them.”
In August, Spain doubled its diesel tax discount to €0.20 a litre from 1 September after diesel prices jumped by 15.7% in July, while in Germany, the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has promised action “soon” to ease the impact of record fuel prices.
Berlin cut fuel taxes for two months in May, but that lapsed just as renewed clashes in the Middle East began further pushed up oil prices. Merz’s centre-right CDU was this month heavily defeated in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt by the far-right AfD.
Two more state elections this weekend are likely to bring further gains for the far-right party, which has campaigned on a platform of a return to the cheap Russian gas imports Europe largely abandoned after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
author: Jon Henley Europe correspondent and Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent

title: Organized crime and drug-related deaths rise Germany
content_c:
Organized crime and drug-related deaths rise Germany
September 18, 2026
"We are experiencing a flood of cocaine in Germany," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, from the Christian Democrats (CDU), said earlier this week as a new police report was presented. "We are experiencing a record number of drug-related deaths. We are seeing children being exploited as criminals."
Standing alongside Dobrindt, Holger Münch, the president of the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), and Hendrik Streeck, the German government's drug and addiction commissioner, presented findings described as alarming.
Last year, 10 tons of cocaine were seized, two thirds of that amount in German ports. And 2,150 people lost their lives because of drug use, 13 more than in 2024.
Profits generated from drugs by international organized crime networks are often invested in real estate to conceal their origin. Münch said that 195 cases of money laundering, amounting to almost €1.4 billion (ca. $1.6 billion) had been investigated in 2025.
"They [the criminals] use their considerable financial clout to bribe and to exert influence," he said. "And they launder the money and funnel it into the legal economic system."
He added that the most widely used drug was cocaine and that it posed a threat to the state, the economy and society as a whole.
'There is blood on every gram of cocaine consumed for pleasure'
"It is not only the state that is being damaged," said Streeck. "Above all, it is people who are being damaged."
About 83% of the drug-related deaths concerned men, whose average age was 41.
"They are all customers of a market that deals in deadly substances and is driven by violence, environmental destruction, extortion and exploitation," said Streeck, who trained as a doctor.
He insisted that there should be zero tolerance for those who profited from addiction and zero indifference to those suffering from it. His focus is on preventative measures, which include a public awareness campaign about the impact on health and the environment.
He explained that in some countries, rainforests were being cleared to make way for cocaine production. Streek pointed out that toxic substances used for processing the drug, such as kerosene or battery acid, ended up in the soil and water. Farmers and their families were blackmailed. He lamented the fact that cocaine had become more popular in Germany.
"There is blood on every gram of cocaine consumed for pleasure," the drug and addiction commissioner stated.
Digitalization of drugs trade
Streeck added that the situation had changed significantly in recent years and the market had gone digital.
"Dealers are no longer on the street corner; they're on the phone. For example, people can order so-called 'cocaine taxis' [cars that deliver drugs to any location] via QR code," he said.
"What is particularly alarming is that criminal groups are recruiting minors through social media or gaming platforms," he added. "Organized criminals look for recruits in the places where young people spend their free time."
Münch noted that this development posed a particular challenge for German and international law enforcement agencies. He said that, more and more, the cliched image of organized crime — discretion, isolation and closed structures — was a thing of the past. The fact that people can purchase criminal services on the dark web represents a paradigm shift, according to Münch: "It's not just a question of who commits a crime, but of who ordered it, who financed it, who is profiting from it?"
Moreover, there is a suspicion on the part of investigators that state actors are increasingly involved in opaque crime activities, launching attacks as "hybrid threats."
Münch said that "money laundering, corruption and violence can contribute to social destabilization."
In 2025, there were about 600 investigations into cases of organized crime in Germany, which has been the average for the past five years. The German police considers one of its major successes to be the shutdown of the Archetyp Market, an online drug marketplace on the darknet. Its administrator was arrested in June 2025. He had overseen the sale of cocaine, heroin, cannabis and other drugs, amounting to 250 million. When the platform was shut down there were 3,200 registered sellers and 612,000 customer accounts according to the police.
This article was translated from German.
description: Presenting its annual report for organized crime, the German police said that cocaine was a danger for the state and society, and that the cases of money laundering had increased.

title: EU-Finanzminister beraten in Dublin über mögliche Übergewinnsteuer
content_c:
Treffen der EU-Finanzminister Übergewinnsteuer als europäische Antwort auf hohe Spritpreise?
Die EU-Finanzminister beraten heute in Dublin über mögliche Entlastungen für Autofahrer. Bundesfinanzminister Klingbeil wirbt für eine Übergewinnsteuer, doch sein Vorschlag ist umstritten - auch unter Ökonomen.
Bei vielen Autofahrern ist die Stimmung gerade schlecht. "Ich denke mal, da geht es jedem schlechter mit den erhöhten Preisen", sagt ein Autofahrer an einer Tankstelle in Leverkusen. "Es wird immer schwieriger zu tanken, täglich oder wöchentlich einmal die Woche", sagt eine Pendlerin. Ein anderer Autofahrer fragt sich: "Wie wird das noch tragbar sein?" Das wisse er nicht, es müsse nun eine Lösung her.
Die hat Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz zuletzt angekündigt. "Für viele Menschen, die täglich das Auto brauchen, ist eine Belastungsgrenze erreicht", sagte er. "Wir stehen dazu deshalb in engem Austausch in der Bundesregierung und mit den Ländern. Und ich bin der Meinung, dass wir handeln müssen."
Die große Frage ist aber das Wie. Auf dem Treffen der Finanzminister der EU-Mitgliedstaaten wird heute ein Vorschlag diskutiert, für den sich auch der deutsche Finanzminister ausgesprochen hat: eine Übergewinnsteuer. Damit könnten ungewöhnlich hohe Profite der Mineralölkonzerne abgeschöpft und mit dem Geld Entlastungen für die Bürger finanziert werden.
Sympathien für Übergewinnsteuer in mehreren Ländern
Gemeinsam mit seinen Kollegen aus Österreich, Italien, Portugal, Polen und Spanien hatte Lars Klingbeil bereits im August einen Brief an den irischen Finanzminister geschrieben, damit das Thema in Dublin auf der Agenda landet. In dem Brief heißt es konkret, man brauche einen gemeinsamen Ansatz, der sicherstellt, dass diejenigen, die von der Krise profitieren, ihren Teil dazu beitragen, die Belastung von der breiten Bevölkerung zu verringern.
Zwar können die Mitgliedstaaten auch individuell eine Übergewinnsteuer einführen und brauchen dafür nicht unbedingt eine gemeinsame Lösung. Aber in einem europäischen Ansatz sehen viele aufgrund des gemeinsamen Binnenmarkts Vorteile. Und 2022 hatte es schon mal eine Übergewinnsteuer gegeben, quasi als Notfallreaktion auf die hohen Energiepreise als Folge des Ukraine-Kriegs.
Energieexperte bei Übergewinnsteuer skeptisch
Bei einem gemeinsamen Mittagessen wollen die Finanzminister schauen, ob so eine Übergewinnsteuer wieder eine gemeinsame europäische Lösung sein könnte. Aber selbst in der Bundesregierung ist man sich nicht darüber einig. Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche etwa bevorzugt eine vorübergehende Senkung der Mehrwertsteuer und Direktzahlungen an Menschen mit vergleichsweise wenig Gehalt.
Und auch Fachleute äußern Bedenken bei der Übergewinnsteuer. Georg Zachmann, Ökonom und Energieexperte bei der Brüsseler Denkfabrik Bruegel, etwa, betont, dass eine Übergewinnsteuer komplex sei. "Die praktische Schwierigkeit wird sein, dass ein Großteil der Gewinne außerhalb Deutschlands entsteht und dass der deutsche Finanzminister es sehr, sehr schwer finden wird, auf diesen großen Teil der Gewinne irgendwie zuzugreifen", sagt Zachmann. "Und selbst wenn Übergewinne in Deutschland entstehen, sollte es den Firmen wahrscheinlich auch teilweise noch möglich sein, diese zu verschleiern. Da einen rechtssicheren Weg zu finden, wird sehr schwer."
Für die Finanzminister gibt es also viel zu besprechen bei ihrem Treffen in Dublin. Und neben der Übergewinnsteuer stehen noch viele weitere Themen auf der Agenda: die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit des europäischen Bankensektors, der digitale Euro, die Chancen und Risiken von Künstlicher Intelligenz. Dass man heute also bei einer europäischen Lösung gegen die hohen Spritpreise weit kommt, ist fraglich.
author: Sarah López, zzt. Dublin
description: Die EU-Finanzminister beraten heute in Dublin über mögliche Entlastungen für Autofahrer. Bundesfinanzminister Klingbeil wirbt für eine Übergewinnsteuer, doch sein Vorschlag ist umstritten - auch unter Ökonomen. Von Sarah López.

title: DFB-Team: Bundestrainer Jürgen Klopp startet mit XXL-Kader
content_c:
DFB-Team: Bundestrainer Jürgen Klopp startet mit XXL-Kader
17. September 2026
Alles anders, alles neu - das ist die Maßgabe des neuen Bundestrainers Jürgen Klopp. Doch wird unter ihm auch wirklich alles besser beim DFB-Team? Nach dem Ende von Julian Nagelsmann, der nach der verpatzten Weltmeisterschaft seinen Hut nehmen musste, möchte Klopp nun eine neue - und wieder erfolgreiche - Ära beim Deutschen Fußball-Bund einleiten.
Der Bundestrainer berichtete von "super" Gesprächen mit seinen möglichen Kandidaten für das DFB-Team. "Es bedeutet ihnen allen unglaublich viel, für die Nationalmannschaft zu spielen. Wir haben gemeinsam beschlossen, das wieder sichtbar zu machen."
Mit Basecap und Trainingsjacke betrat Klopp den gut gefüllten Presseraum auf dem DFB-Campus in Frankfurt. Ein knappes "Guten Morgen" in Richtung der wartenden Medienvertreterinnen und Vertreter und dann startete der Bundestrainer mit seiner ersten Kader-Nominierung - und sorgte gleich für ein Novum.
Alte Bekannte nicht mehr dabei
Der 59-Jährige geht mit zwei Kadern in Rekordgröße in seine ersten Spiele mit der DFB-Elf. Das Aufgebot der Fußball-Nationalmannschaft für den Auftakt in der Nations League umfasst insgesamt 44 Spieler, darunter noch 16 WM-Fahrer und gleich 16 Akteure ohne Länderspieleinsatz.
"Die Kaderzusammenstellung hat Spaß gemacht, ich bin ganz happy damit", freute sich Klopp und betonte: "Wir haben ganz viele Fußballtalente gefunden. Ich möchte so viele Spieler wie möglich kennenlernen."
Ganz neu in den beiden Kadern für je zwei Spiele sind Hennes Behrens vom FC Augsburg, die Freiburger Max Rosenfelder, Philipp Treu, Yannik Engelhardt und Derry Scherhant, Bambasé Conté von Hoffenheim, Younes Ebnoutalib von Eintracht Frankfurt, der Stuttgarter Finn Jeltsch, der Elversberger Felix Keidel sowie die Legionäre Vitaly Janelt vom FC Brentford und Mika Baur von Celtic Glasgow.
"Wir sehen was in den Jungs, wir sehen ganz viel Potenzial. Es ist uns ganz viel Talent ins Auge gesprungen", sagte Klopp. "Wir haben nicht geguckt, was haben wir nicht, sondern was haben wir. Ich bin happy mit der Auswahl."
Dafür verzichtet Klopp neben Deniz Undav und Leroy Sané auch auf Oliver Baumann, den verletzten Leon Goretzka, Pascal Groß, den angeschlagenen Angelo Stiller oder Jamie Leweling. Manuel Neuer und Antonio Rüdiger waren nach dem neuerlichen WM-Desaster zurückgetreten.
Noch 15 Turnierverlierer um Kapitän Joshua Kimmich sind dabei. Und gleich fünf Torhüter, darunter erstmals seit 15 Monaten auch wieder die alte und neue Nummer eins Marc-André ter Stegen, der aktuell bei Ajax Amsterdam unter Vertrag steht. "Er ist fit und bringt die notwendige Erfahrung mit", erklärte Klopp. "Es wird aber immer von der Leistung abhängig sein. Wir haben keinerlei Torhüterproblem."
Klopp: "Wollen uns gerne die Fahne zurückholen"
Neben den sportlichen Themen wurde der neue Bundestrainer auch politisch und nutzte die Pressekonferenz auch für eine Grundsatzrede gegen rechts und für "positiven Patriotismus."
"Ich würde mir oder uns gerne die Fahne zurückholen", sagte Klopp. "Ich möchte, dass wir sie immer so schwingen, dass niemand denkt, was mit dir nicht in Ordnung ist. Sondern dass man einfach nur das Gefühl hat, du bist happy und verstehst, dass du Glück hattest, dass du in diesem wundervollen Land geboren, aufgewachsen und zugezogen bist."
Er sei "kein Fachmann" für Politik, aber er wolle "Nationalstolz nicht den falschen Leuten überlassen. Aber ich weiß nicht mehr, ob man das Wort überhaupt so benutzen kann, darf. Ohne dass das falsch verstanden wird."
Der Fußball sei dann dazu da, die Stimmung aufzuhellen. "Es ist wichtiger, dass wir Ärzte haben. Es ist wichtiger, dass wir Pflegepersonen haben. Es ist wichtiger, dass wir ganz, ganz viele Menschen in ganz vielen Berufen haben." Der Fußball könne hier aber "ein Gemeinschaftsgefühl entwickeln, dass wir wirklich die Kraft des Sports spüren."
description: Mit einer radikalen Erneuerung mit gleich zwei Kadern und 16 möglichen Debütanten startet Klopp in die Fußball-Nations-League. Zudem sendet er ein klares Zeichen gegen rechte Politik in Deutschland.

title: Садовий заявив про виявлення пристрою, схожого на прослуховуючий, у службовому автомобілі
content_c:
Міський голова Львова Андрій Садовий заявив про виявлення у службовому автомобілі пристрою, схожого на прослуховуючий, та повідомив про знахідку правоохоронним органам.
"Знову знайшли пристрій, схожий на прослуховуючий. Цього разу у службовому автомобілі", – написав Садовий у дописі, поширеному в його Телеграм-каналі у п'ятницю.
За його словами, пристрій виявили після того, як протягом останнього місяця двічі повністю розряджався акумулятор автомобіля, а також після того, як почала стукати стійка. Після її розбирання, за словами Садового, і було виявлено пристрій.
"Що з тим робить? Я навіть не маю гадки, хто це міг сюди поставити. Але якщо це зроблено офіційно, за рішенням суду, нашими органами, окей, будь ласка, прийдіть, заберіть", – сказав Садовий у відео, поширеному на його сторінці.
Садовий повідомив, що має намір поінформувати про знахідку керівників відповідних служб.
"До речі, це ж якраз рік тому назад в кабінеті ми виявили прослуховуючий пристрій, звернулися тоді в правоохоронні органи, там отримали листи, але конкретно відповіді що і як – не було", – зазначив міський голова.
Він також наголосив, що не заперечує проти встановлення таких пристроїв, якщо це здійснюється законно: "Це моя робота. Якщо це все законно, будь ласка, поставте".
Як повідомлялося, у вересні 2025 року Садовий повідомив, що виявив прослуховуючий пристрій у своєму робочому кабінеті. За його словами, у звичайний зарядний блок радіотелефону "криво припаяли" сім-карту, карту пам'яті та мікрофон. Після цього слідчі Служби безпеки України розпочали кримінальне провадження за цим фактом.

title: What weapon could the US have put into space?
content_c:
What weapon could the US have put into space?
- Published
The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena.
Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.
So what could this weapon be, and what is the wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry?
Space has been a militarised domain since the start of the space age - in the late 1960s, the Soviet Union deployed weapons up there. The Istrebitel Sputnikov (IS; Satellite Destroyer) programme was made up of satellites that were designed to release projectiles that detonated, releasing shrapnel into the path of another (usually American) satellite.
Nowadays, advanced militaries deploy satellites in space for a range of purposes, including reconnaissance, secure communications, detecting missile launches and providing precise location information for targeted strikes.
As warfare becomes more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase.
Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US.
"I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless."
Bowen also would not rule out a riskier and more disruptive type of weaponry, which could create debris and destruction.
"Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said.
A type of "close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well."
As to whether rivals such as Russia and China have similar weaponry already in orbit, is difficult to tell.
"If we're looking towards China and Russia, they have both displayed activity," Juliana Suess, a former research fellow at RUSI and researcher at the Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (German Institute for International and Security Affairs), told the BBC.
"For example, with Russia, we've seen some activity that hints at being a co-orbital weapons test. So we saw something that might indicate that they shot a projectile as a test in orbit.
"There are others out there, but without knowing the details, what the American [weapon] is, it's difficult to draw comparisons."
But while the weapon placed in orbit may be unusual, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time.
In a later BBC interview, Bowen was dismissive of China's reaction to the US announcement which warned against an arms race in space, describing it as "the pot calling the kettle black".
"If you're already an expert... you know how hollow those words are coming from the Russian and Chinese governments," he said.
"The United States, Russia and China and also India have all developed different kinds of anti-satellite or counter-space weapons, and Russia and China have put a lot of technologies in space which have a lot of weapons potential," he added.
In fact in the past 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites.
"Theoretically, these RPO [satellites]can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC.
Bowen added that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit."
This, he said, could be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites.
However, some types of space weaponry also have the potential to create huge amounts of space junk.
Dr Mark Hilborne, a specialist in space security and weaponisation at King's College, said direct ascent anti-satellite missile tests, such as one carried out by China in 2007, leave a great deal of debris in orbit for a very long time.
Suess said debris from that test was still in orbit and still dangerous.
"It doesn't have to be a sort of huge piece of metal to do any damage, it can be a tiny piece of plastic, given the velocity that we're talking about in orbit," she said.
The nuclear threat
Thornton said that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability.
"The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike [satellites] in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT [air-launched antisatellite] missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he said.
"From the Russian point of view, they see Nato as having much better and more satellites than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat."
Thornton added a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EMP [nuclear electromagnetic pulse] blast would 'fry' any unhardened satellite over a wide expanse."
So what is the likelihood of a nuclear conflict in space? Only if it was happening on the ground as well.
"What could happen in space is not something that would happen in isolation, really," Bowen said. "Nothing could happen, or something could."
Given that weapons for use in space have been around for so long, why did the US announcement come when it did? Experts agree that it's not a major development as such, more a political signal.
Bowen suggested that it could be a response to Chinese developments.
"China has modernised its military forces over the past 30 years," he said. "It has put a lot more military satellites in space and has presented a lot more targets that are worth the American military going after and hitting."
"There's much more incentive for American space weapons now because China has a lot of vulnerability to space in the same way that the Americans have."
This situation seems to have created a curious imbalance.
Thornton said that, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, because it has so few satellites, unlike China and the US. It would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring satellites designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers," he said.
description: The announcement by the US points to a developing field of modern warfare in the Earth's orbit.

title: Call for £375k elected mayor referendum rejected
content_c:
Call for £375k elected mayor referendum rejected
- Published
An attempt to force a referendum on whether an elected mayor should be abolished has failed.
Councillors in Bedford rejected a Labour motion to let residents decide the future of the role.
They were told a referendum would cost £375,000 to organise.
Opponents of the elected mayor system said the poll could still happen if enough residents signed a petition.
Bedford has had an elected mayor since 2002, when residents voted in favour of the move in a referendum.
The leader of the Labour group, Abu Sultan, told a meeting of the full council on Wednesday that, after more than 20 years, it was time to give the people a chance to vote again.
Sultan added that the motion was "not about settling a political score with any particular person".
No confidence vote
Carl Meader (Labour, Kempston South) said abolishing the role would save money and the referendum would give people under 40 their first chance to vote on the issue.
Others said it was difficult to remove a serving mayor and noted the current incumbent had remained in post, despite a vote of no confidence in his leadership.
Opponents questioned whether spending £375,000 on a referendum was a valid use of the council's money.
The current mayor, Tom Wootton (Conservative, Wyboston), told the meeting he had not seen "Bedford residents marching through the streets demanding a referendum".
Christine McHugh (Liberal Democrat, Goldington) said she had originally campaigned against having an elected mayor but "found, to my surprise, that the public seemed to like the system as there was a clearly identifiable, responsible individual, and the buck stopped there".
Labour has 12 seats on the council, while the Conservatives have 14 and the Liberal Democrats have 13.
The Green Party has four.
When it came to the vote, 16 councillors voted for a referendum while 24 opposed it.
The Liberal Democrat leader, Henry Vann, said: "The vote in the end wasn't even close at 24 to 16.
"So, frankly, we now need to all, as councillors of all parties, actually get down to the job of protecting services and sorting out the financial crisis at Borough Hall."
Zara Layne (Labour, Harpur) said: "I think it was a shame that residents aren't going to get a chance to have their voice heard on a matter that we believe as a Labour group is really important."
If a referendum had been successful and the post of mayor had been abolished, it is likely that the council would have adopted a strong leader model.
The full council would have elected a leader who would then select a cabinet.
One advantage of that system would be the ability of the full council to remove a leader, something that councils cannot do with an elected mayor.
But opponents argue that a strong leader system puts too much power in the hands of one person who residents had no say in appointing.

title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows
content_c:
The extreme engineering of aircraft windows
- Published
An industrial nightmare was brewing south of Los Angeles.
In late May, a chemical storage tank with more than 7,000 gallons of toxic material began heating up – fast. The tank belonged to GKN Aerospace, a company that supplies parts to the aviation industry, including aircraft windows.
As the temperature inside the shiny metal storage vessel rose, workers realised they had a problem. The tank was at risk of exploding, potentially showering nearby neighbourhoods with methyl methacrylate (MMA), a skin and lung-irritating, external compound used in plastics production.
The tank's temperature reached 100F (38C) – though possibly went higher - 100F was simply the maximum reading, external on the temperature gauge inside.
More than 50,000 residents of Garden Grove city were evacuated and fire crews began hosing down the tank in a bid to cool it. At one point, the vessel "actually bulged" according to the local fire chief.
Thankfully, no explosion occurred. Months later, in August, GKN and local authorities announced a $100m (£74m) programme, external to compensate residents evacuated during the incident. But production of aircraft windows at the site, which had been halted, is still not fully restored.
This has sent a minor shockwave through the aircraft manufacturing industry because GKN is one of surprisingly few companies, anywhere in the world, that make aircraft windows – highly engineered, safety-critical parts for planes.
Production at GKN's Garden Grove facility currently remains hobbled, at roughly 50% of normal, according to public statements, external by its UK parent company Melrose Industries. The aim is to have full production restored by 28 September. GKN declined an interview with the BBC.
"They're one of only a handful of suppliers – less than a handful, really – of critical windows," says Marisa Garcia, an aviation industry analyst. "One of the breaking points of supply chain in aviation is you have very few companies qualified to do something and, when something goes wrong, it really upsets the entire system."
Boeing tells the BBC it is "taking steps to mitigate any potential impacts", describing the shortfall in production as an "industry-wide" situation.
"We are supporting our supplier," a spokesman adds. An Airbus spokeswoman says, "We are closely monitoring and are seeing positive progress toward a return to normal."
It comes at a time when airlines "can't get new aircraft fast enough," says Mike Stengel of AeroDynamic Advisory, a consultancy. "They're holding on to aircraft for longer."
Even though there are just a few aircraft window-manufacturing firms in existence, it's hard for new competitors to emerge because of how regulated the industry is, adds Stengel. "It can take time to pivot to a new supplier."
This leads to a "balancing act" between plane-makers and the firms they rely on for various parts, Stengel says.
To find out what goes into the making of an aircraft window, I spoke to Jean-Eric Vermont, general manager of French company Saint-Gobain Aerospace.
"We focus mostly on commercial aircraft, regional aircraft and helicopters," he says. Vermont declines, though, to say how much market share his company has in aircraft windows – or transparencies, as they are known in the trade.
The oval-shaped windows in the cabin, next to passengers' seats, are typically made of plastic-based materials, says Vermont. "You start from a sheet of acrylic," he explains. "Then you cut to size, [to] give the shape."
A Saint-Gobain spokesman confirmed to the BBC that the company does not store or process MMA like GKN, but rather purchases sheets of polymerised MMA, or acrylic.
Aircraft manufacturers are increasingly ordering larger cabin windows, says Vermont, in order to offer passengers a wider view of the world outside. It's a selling point but it requires additional testing to ascertain whether the bigger windows hold up as well as the smaller ones.
Saint-Gobain tests its windows by exposing them to pressures many times what would be normal on an aircraft flying at altitude.
These acrylic-based cabin windows are usually made out of two layers or plies, and Saint-Gobain also performs tests to confirm whether the window will survive even if one of those plies gets damaged.
Cockpit windows, Vermont says, are "totally different".
They are generally made of glass, which is chemically reinforced by adding potassium to it. This involves swapping smaller sodium ions for larger potassium ions, which helps to fill out the molecular structure of the glass, meaning that when it cools during production, it compresses into an extra strong, tight formation as it cools.
Some of the latest aircraft feature cockpit windows that are also curved, to make the plane more streamlined, which improves fuel efficiency. But curved cockpit windows are challenging to make – the slightest distortion or defect is clearly visible to the pilot.
Quality control checks are used to ensure no such impediments exist in the final product.
All aircraft windows must be resistant to impacts but cockpit windows, at the front of the plane, are especially vulnerable to bird strikes, says Vermont: "The issue is not the speed of the bird, the issue is the speed of the aircraft."
Saint-Gobain uses numerical simulations and "physical tests representative of a sizeable bird impact" to test its windows against this threat.
"Typically, if you go through a hailstorm or if you hit a large enough bird, the external ply will crack," says Vermont. "The cockpit window is designed for that."
A London to Londonderry flight was recently affected by a cracked cockpit window. While a mid-air emergency was declared, the plane landed safely. "There can be [such] cases," says Vermont, though he adds that Saint-Gobain's windows have not been involved in any recently.
"You're obviously dealing with a surface that is interfacing with two very different environments," says Stengel. "That's why these are more highly-engineered products."

title: Poorest countries hit hardest by UK aid cuts under Keir Starmer government, new figures reveal
content_c:
The world’s poorest countries were worst hit by British aid cuts under Keir Starmer’s government, while higher-income countries saw their share of aid increase, new figures reveal.
The latest figures released by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office show a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed countries and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.
The UK’s overall Official Development Assistance budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income (GNI), compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m. Further cuts are expected as part of the plans announced last year by Keir Starmer, who said money would be redirected towards defence spending.
Gideon Rabinowitz, the director of policy and advocacy at the charity network Bond, said it was “shocking” that the least-developed countries had borne the brunt of the cuts.
“The human cost of these cuts is already being felt, with critical humanitarian programmes – from maternal health provision in Sierra Leone to education for children with disabilities across Africa – already being forced to close,” said Rabinowitz.
“Marginalised communities around the world, including in climate-vulnerable and conflict-affected areas, are being left to pay the highest price for the Starmer government’s political choices.”
The highest share of aid, 18.4%, was spent within the UK on in-country costs for asylum seekers. This was a reduction from 20% in 2024.
The top three recipients of aid were Ukraine, Yemen and Afghanistan, but while aid to Ukraine is ringfenced, further upcoming cuts will see Yemen receive 28% less and Afghanistan 39% less by 2028/29.
While low-income countries saw their aid decline, it increased to lower-middle-income countries by 13% and by 2% to upper-middle-income countries.
Aid experts have warned that aid cuts by the UK, United States and Europe are forcing aid workers to cut anything but immediate life-saving support, even when this could lead to millions of avoidable deaths.
Earlier this month, a report by Active Learning Network for Accountability and Performance (Alnap) revealed that 64 million fewer people received aid last year as a result of the cuts.
“Across the humanitarian system, these cumulative reductions have contributed to the largest funding gap on record and forced increasingly difficult prioritisation,” said Jennifer Doherty, the report’s co-author.
“The longer-term consequences will depend not only on future decisions by donor governments, but also on how crisis-affected governments and other local and regional support systems adjust their own policies and approaches in response to reduced external assistance. Where those systems are unable to absorb the shock, there is a risk that more people will be left without support.”
Bond, the charity network, is calling for the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, to reconsider the aid cuts introduced by his predecessor.
“What little remains of the UK aid budget must go where it is most needed: and contribute to the reduction of poverty and inequality – particularly in fragile and conflict-affected countries, where humanitarian needs are most acute,” said Rabinowitz.
author: Kaamil Ahmed

title: Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases
content_c:
Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases
September 17, 2026
Yulia and Dmitri (whose names have been changed for reasons of safety) flew from Russia to Brazil this summer so that their child could be born there. Yulia was 32 weeks pregnant at the time of travel.
"Of course, we didn't say that I was pregnant at border control," Yulia told DW.
Her daughter was born at a private clinic in Santos, a city in southern Brazil. Anybody born in the country has an automatic right to Brazilian nationality. The family is currently preparing all the paperwork.
"We've achieved our minimum goal," said Dmitri. "With a Brazilian passport, our daughter will be able to travel without a visa to almost any country in the world. She won't have to apply for an expensive and time-consuming Schengen visa. We want her to be able to decide for herself where she studies, works or lives."
He said that a colleague of his had traveled to Brazil in early August with his pregnant wife for the same reasons.
Yulia and Dmitri said that they had spent the equivalent of about €10,000 (about $11,500) during the first six weeks of their stay in Brazil, which included the costs for several days of treatment for their daughter in intensive care. Dmitri quit his job at a bank for the trip and hopes to find work again after the family returns to their home in the Russian capital Moscow.
However, they are only planning to return once all the documents for their daughter are ready and that could take months. Other Russian families have decided to stay in Brazil permanently.
According to organizations and lawyers that provide support to Russians in Brazil, there has been an increase in immigration from Russia, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, after which visa requirements for Russian nationals entering certain countries were tightened.
Argentina tightens visa regulations
Birth tourism to Brazil has also increased since Argentina, which used to be one of the main destinations for people wanting their children to be born in a country that automatically grants citizenship to newborns, tightened its regulations. People who want their children to obtain Argentinian citizenship now have to have resided in Argentina for at least two years. Since 2025, the access of people who do not have a permanent residence permit to free healthcare has also been restricted.
According to the Russian news outlet RBC, more than 7,000 Russians applied for a residence permit in Argentina in 2023. By mid-2025, the number had decreased to about 1,800.
Meanwhile, almost 500 Brazilian passports were issued to Russians in 2024 and more than 600 the following year. More than half of the new citizens were women.
The parents of a child born in Brazil can apply for a residence permit, which they can obtain within a year, under certain circumstances.
Yana (name changed) and her husband chose to do this in 2023.
"The events of 2022 certainly played a role, but we had already toyed with the idea of giving birth abroad," Yana told DW. "A lot can happen in Russia. I always wanted a second passport and to give birth to my child in another country. When I became pregnant unexpectedly, all we had to do was decide which country made sense."
Yana gave birth to a boy at a public hospital in Florianopolis, the capital of the southern state of Santa Catarina, and the family stayed in Brazil for about three years.
"It was important to get passports for us and our child. I really enjoyed living there, and I learned Portuguese," Yana said, adding that she and her husband have lived as "digital nomads" in various countries over the years.
Even though they no longer live in Brazil, they want their son to have a connection to his birth country: "We read Portuguese books and talk a lot about Brazil. I want him to be able to travel without a visa and remain open to the world."
Big Russian community in Florianopolis
One of the largest Russian communities in Brazil lives in Florianopolis, and it's growing. According to the local health authorities, 119 Russian women took advantage of prenatal consultations in the first six months of this year. In all of 2025, it was 136 Russian women.
A lawyer who preferred to remain anonymous told DW that Brazil neither expressly prohibited nor permitted foreign nationals to enter the country for the purpose of giving birth. Often pregnant women do not disclose their reason for traveling to Brazil at border control. And once they are in the country they have access to free public hospitals and medical facilities regardless of their immigration status.
As Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases, a whole industry has emerged. Often, recent Russian immigrants to Brazil act as intermediaries and help others find housing or medical care. They provide assistance with complicated administrative procedures or the language. Depending on the level of care, the cost can reach into the thousands of dollars.
However, providers of such services, lawyers, and volunteers report stricter controls by Brazilian authorities, particularly in cities with larger Russian communities, such as Florianopolis. They say authorities are requesting more documents than in the past.
"The police are conducting more thorough checks to verify whether people actually live at the addresses they provide," one lawyer said, explaining that in the past, false addresses had been given by people hoping to obtain residence permits more quickly.
No evidence of Brazil systematically denying entry to Russians
But DW did not find any evidence to suggest that Russians were being denied entry to Brazil en masse.
In late July, the Russian Telegram channel Baza reported that 10 pregnant women had been "deported" from Russia. The information was later picked up by various media outlets. However, the Brazilian police denied the veracity of the report to DW, explaining that decisions to deny somebody entry to the country were always made on a case-by-case basis, and that pregnancy played no role in the process.
DW was only able to find one documented case of a pregnant Russian woman being initially refused entry into Brazil. She was allowed to enter the country after a lawyer intervened. According to the court records, the Brazilian border authorities had doubts as to how the Russian national would be financing her stay in Brazil.
The woman did not respond to the DW's inquiries.
This article was originally written in Russian.
description: Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and stricter regulations in Argentina, more and more Russians are choosing to travel to Brazil to give birth to children, who will obtain Brazilian nationality.

title: Berkshire Hathaway: Warren Buffett legt nun auch Verwaltungsratsvorsitz nieder
content_c:
Berkshire Hathaway Warren Buffett legt nun auch Verwaltungsratsvorsitz seiner Investmentfirma nieder
Kurz nach seinem 96. Geburtstag rückt der Ruhestand für Warren Buffett näher: Der US-Starinvestor legt den Verwaltungsratsvorsitz seiner Holding Berkshire Hathaway nieder. Allerdings bleibe Buffett Mitglied des Verwaltungsrats und sei zudem zum »Ehrenpräsidenten« ernannt worden, teilte die Holding nun mit.
Buffett war zum 1. Januar bereits als Geschäftsführer ausgeschieden. Seinen Rückzug hatte er im Mai 2025 überraschend bei einer Aktionärsversammlung angekündigt. Sein Nachfolger in dieser Funktion ist Greg Abel. Den Vorsitz des Verwaltungsrats übernimmt Buffetts Sohn Howard, wie die Holding weiter mitteilte.
Das »Orakel von Omaha«
Buffett gilt als Legende unter den Investoren und wird wegen seiner Erfolge das »Orakel von Omaha« genannt. Berkshire Hathaway hat seinen Sitz in Omaha, der größten Stadt des US-Bundesstaats Nebraska. Die Firma war ein marodes Textilunternehmen, als Buffett es in den Sechzigerjahren übernahm und über die Jahre zu einer riesigen Holdinggesellschaft ausbaute. Mit einer konservativen, auf Substanzwerten aufgebauten Anlagestrategie entwickelte er sie zu einem der zehn wertvollsten Unternehmen weltweit. Heute ist Berkshire Hathaway an der New Yorker Börse 1,1 Billionen Dollar wert.
Auf seinen Nachfolger hält Buffett offenbar große Stücke: »Meine Erwartungen an ihn waren von Anfang an unermesslich, und er hat sie übertroffen«, bilanzierte Buffett zum Jahreswechsel in einem Brief an die Aktionäre mit Blick auf Abel. »Deshalb ist die Zeit reif, um den Übergang abzuschließen.« Er habe seit 1965 für Berkshire gearbeitet, »und ich habe immer noch den besten Job der Welt«, schrieb er. Aber »Gevatter Zeit gewinnt immer. Er war gleichwohl großzügig mit mir.«
Buffetts Sohn Howard ist seit 1993 für Berkshire Hathaway tätig und hatte das Unternehmen in zahlreichen Aufsichts- und Verwaltungsräten vertreten. »Das ist eine längere Lehrzeit als ich sie hatte, bevor ich mit 34 die Zügel in die Hand nahm«, schrieb Warren Buffett. »Greg leitet das Unternehmen, Howard wird auf seine Kultur und seine Werte achten.«
Howard Buffett leitet seit 1999 auch eine nach ihm benannte Stiftung, die sich um die weltweite Ernährungssicherheit und die Beilegung von Konflikten bemüht.
Warren Buffetts Wort bewegte die Finanzindustrie, er gilt als einer der erfolgreichsten Investoren der Welt und der Geschichte. Welches Geheimnis steckt hinter seinem Erfolg? Und was kann man sich womöglich von ihm abschauen? Das lesen Sie hier.
author: DER SPIEGEL
description: Er galt als »Orakel von Omaha«: US-Starinvestor Warren Buffett machte aus einer maroden Textilfirma eines der wertvollsten Unternehmen der Welt. Nun tritt er als Verwaltungsratschef von Berkshire Hathaway ab.

title: Nach Schließung des Konsulats: Deutschlands schwieriger Kurs gegenüber Russland
content_c:
Nach Schließung des Konsulats Deutschlands schwieriger Kurs gegenüber Russland
Flagge eingeholt, Personal ausgeflogen: Das russische Generalkonsulat in Bonn ist seit heute als Reaktion auf den Leipziger Drohnen-Vorfall geschlossen. Außenminister Wadephul nennt das eine harte Reaktion, er setzt aber weiter auf Dialog.
Vor zweieinhalb Wochen hat die Bundesregierung ihre Sanktionen gegen Russland verkündet. Eine der Maßnahmen tritt heute in Kraft: die Schließung des russischen Generalkonsulats in Bonn. Die hatte Außenminister Johann Wadephul damals angeordnet. "Das ist eine harte Reaktion", sagte er. "Das Generalkonsulat in Bonn zu schließen. Das ist eine erhebliche Einschränkung der russischen Möglichkeiten in Deutschland."
Schon am Dienstag wurde am Bonner Konsulatsgebäude die russische Flagge eingeholt. Am Mittwoch wurden die Beschäftigten mit einer russischen Staatsmaschine nach Moskau ausgeflogen. Die Bundesregierung erteilte für diese Abholaktion eine Ausnahmegenehmigung. Schnell raus aus Deutschland sollten die, die in Bonn als Diplomaten und Konsularbeamte angemeldet waren. Viele von ihnen - so der Vorwurf - sollen nicht nur russische Pässe und Visa bearbeitet haben, sondern womöglich ganz andere Aufträge gehabt haben.
Die Politikwissenschaftlerin Stefanie Babst beschreibt das Bonner Konsulat genauso wie das Russische Haus in Berlin, das ebenfalls schließen muss, als Ort, "wo sich normalerweise russische Agenten und Spione tummeln, die Desinformationskampagnen und andere Spionagetätigkeiten ausüben".
Botschaft soll lauten: Hybride Angriffe haben Folgen
Der deutsche Außenminister will die Arbeit der russischen Geheimdienste in Deutschland schwächen. Es geht ihm aber auch um ein Signal, dass hybride Angriffe wie der Leipziger Drohnenvorfall nicht folgenlos bleiben. "Man darf Russland nicht in dem Irrglauben lassen, dass es derartige Dinge tun kann, ohne dass Deutschland reagierte", sagte Wadephul.
Die russische Regierung bezeichnete das Vorgehen der Bundesregierung als "grundlose Provokation". Sie ordnete im Gegenzug an, dass deutsche Einrichtungen in Russland schließen müssen. Das war in Berlin erwartet und einkalkuliert worden. Und auch, dass im deutsch-russischen Verhältnis jetzt noch mehr zerbrochen ist.
Ankündigung, stärker gegen Schattenflotte vorzugehen
Doch wie soll es weitergehen? Die Bundesregierung bleibt bei ihrer Linie. "Wir wollen zu Russland ein anderes Verhältnis, wir wollen ein konstruktives Verhältnis", sagte Wadephul. "Wir bleiben offen für das Gespräch."
Und gleichzeitig demonstriert die Bundesregierung weiterhin Härte. Sie hat angekündigt, nach dem Drohnenvorfall stärker gegen die Öltanker der sogenannten russischen Schattenflotte vorzugehen. Mit maroden Tankschiffen unter der Flagge anderer Länder exportiert Russland weiterhin Erdöl durch die Ostsee, beispielsweise an den EU-Sanktionen vorbei.
Womöglich nicht letzte Stufe im Konflikt
Die Politikwissenschaftlerin Stefanie Babst hält die deutsche Handhabe dagegen aber für begrenzt. "Wir können natürlich auch unsere eigenen militärischen Möglichkeiten nutzen und stärker auch die Schattenflotte verfolgen", sagte sie. "Aber richtig stoppen können wir sie aus einer Vielzahl von Gründen, vornehmlich internationalen rechtlichen Gründen, nicht."
Die Spannungen zwischen Deutschland und Russland dürften also weitergehen, und die Schließung des russischen Generalkonsulats in Bonn war womöglich nicht die letzte Stufe in diesem Konflikt.
author: Markus Sambale

title: US-Kongress beschließt schärfere Russland-Sanktionen
content_c:
US-Kongress beschließt schärfere Russland-Sanktionen
17. September 2026
Das US-Repräsentantenhaus hat mit breiter Mehrheit einem neuen Sanktionspaket gegen Russland zugestimmt. 262 Abgeordnete votierten dafür, 159 dagegen. Damit hat das Gesetz nach dem Senat auch die zweite Kammer des Kongresses passiert. Nun muss US-Präsident Donald Trump es noch unterzeichnen.
Das Paket ist das erste neue Sanktionsgesetz gegen Russland in Trumps zweiter Amtszeit. Es soll vor allem Einnahmen aus russischen Energieexporten verringern, mit denen Moskau seinen Krieg gegen die Ukraine finanziert. Zugleich erhält Trump weitreichende neue Befugnisse für Strafzölle.
Sanktionen gegen Putin und russische Banken
Das Gesetz sieht unter anderem Einreiseverbote gegen den russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin und mehrere Militärvertreter vor, die für den Angriffskrieg gegen die Ukraine verantwortlich gemacht werden. Ihr Vermögen in den USA soll eingefroren werden. Das gilt auch für russische Banken.
Zudem nimmt das Paket die sogenannte Schattenflotte ins Visier. Mit diesen Schiffen versucht Russland, bestehende internationale Sanktionen gegen seine Ölexporte zu umgehen.
Trump kann außerdem Importe aus Russland mit Strafzöllen von bis zu 500 Prozent belegen. Noch größere wirtschaftliche Auswirkungen könnten jedoch Maßnahmen gegen Staaten haben, die weiterhin große Mengen russischer Energie kaufen.
China und Indien könnten betroffen sein
Das Gesetz erlaubt Sanktionen gegen die fünf größten Abnehmer russischer Energieträger sowie gegen die fünf Länder, die Russland am stärksten beim Umgehen von Energiesanktionen helfen.
Auf Waren aus diesen Staaten könnten Zölle von bis zu 100 Prozent erhoben werden. Zu den größten Käufern russischen Öls gehören China und Indien. Damit könnte das Gesetz die ohnehin angespannten Handelsbeziehungen Washingtons zu beiden Ländern weiter belasten.
Zunächst sollen die größten Abnehmer im Zwölfmonatszeitraum vor Inkrafttreten des Gesetzes ermittelt werden. Die Liste soll anschließend alle 180 Tage überprüft werden. Die Höhe der Zölle kann angepasst werden, wenn ein Land seine Käufe russischer Energieträger reduziert.
Ausnahmen sind unter anderem für Staaten vorgesehen, deren Importe weniger als 15 Prozent der russischen Erdgasexporte ausmachen. Auch Länder, die konkrete Schritte zur Verringerung ihrer Käufe unternehmen, können verschont bleiben. "Unsere europäischen Verbündeten sind hier also nicht betroffen", hatte der demokratische Senator Richard Blumenthal im Juli betont.
Für besonderes Interesse sorgt die mögliche Wirkung auf China. In der kommenden Woche wird Chinas Staats- und Parteichef Xi Jinping in Washington erwartet. Trump hatte ihn während seiner Chinareise eingeladen. Zwischen den USA und China schwelt bereits seit Langem ein weitreichender Handelskonflikt.
Demokraten kritisieren neue Befugnisse für Trump
Die Zustimmung im Repräsentantenhaus war trotz der deutlichen Mehrheit nicht selbstverständlich. Sieben republikanische Abgeordnete stimmten gegen das Gesetz, sodass auch Stimmen der Demokraten notwendig waren.
Mehrere führende Demokraten äußerten vor der Abstimmung Bedenken. Sie unterstützen zwar grundsätzlich stärkeren Druck auf Russland, kritisierten aber die zusätzlichen Zollbefugnisse für den Präsidenten.
Gregory Meeks, der ranghöchste Demokrat im Auswärtigen Ausschuss des Repräsentantenhauses, bezeichnete den Entwurf als "zutiefst mangelhaft". Die Juristen des Weißen Hauses hätten den Text so gestaltet, dass Trumps Möglichkeiten für neue Zölle "maximiert" würden. Gleichzeitig werde "jegliche Verpflichtung zur tatsächlichen Verhängung neuer Sanktionen gegen Russland oder dessen Unterstützer minimiert".
Ob Trump die neuen Möglichkeiten tatsächlich umfassend nutzen wird, bleibt damit offen. Bislang hatte er insbesondere davor zurückgeschreckt, China wegen seiner Energieimporte aus Russland mit Sanktionen zu belegen. Auf Waren aus Indien hatte seine Regierung zeitweise einen zusätzlichen Zoll von 25 Prozent wegen des Kaufs russischen Öls verhängt.
Ukraine begrüßt Entscheidung
Die ukrainische Regierung begrüßte die Zustimmung des Repräsentantenhauses. "Das ist die richtige Reaktion auf Russlands Weigerung, seinen Terror zu beenden: kompromissloser Druck auf den Aggressor, um seiner Kriegsmaschinerie die Finanzierung zu entziehen", schrieb Außenminister Andrij Sybiha auf der Plattform X.
Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj hatte bereits im August die Zustimmung des Senats zu dem Sanktionspaket begrüßt. Bei einem Besuch in Washington im Juli hatte er auf weiteren wirtschaftlichen Druck der USA auf Russland gedrängt.
Gesetz trägt Namen von Lindsey Graham
Das Sanktionspaket ist nach dem im Juli gestorbenen republikanischen Senator Lindsey Graham benannt. Der langjährige Trump-Vertraute hatte sich mehr als ein Jahr für die Maßnahmen eingesetzt und kurz vor seinem Tod erklärt, mit dem Weißen Haus eine Einigung über das Paket erzielt zu haben.
Ein erster Entwurf war bereits 2025 eingebracht worden, steckte anschließend jedoch lange im Senat fest. Nach Grahams Tod nahm das Verfahren wieder Fahrt auf. Der Senat verabschiedete das Gesetz Anfang August mit deutlicher Mehrheit.
Trump hatte seine Zustimmung bereits zuvor angedeutet, sich aber zunächst nicht eindeutig festgelegt. "Nun, ich weiß, dass Lindsey das unbedingt wollte", sagte er im Juli im Weißen Haus. "Das war sein Anliegen." Die Chancen stünden gut, dass die Sanktionen umgesetzt würden.
Neben den Russland-Maßnahmen schafft das Gesetz auch den Rahmen dafür, US-Sanktionen gegen den Iran bis 2031 zu verlängern.
pgr/wa (dpa, afp)
Redaktionsschluss: 17.00 Uhr (MESZ) - dieser Artikel wird nicht weiter aktualisiert.
description: Mit neuen Sanktionen wollen die USA Russlands Einnahmen aus Öl und Gas treffen. Das Gesetz richtet sich auch gegen Präsident Putin und die Schattenflotte - und könnte China und Indien unter Druck setzen.

title: Міноборони започаткувало формат регулярних зустрічей з родинами зниклих безвісти військових
content_c:
Міністерство оборони України започаткувало регулярний формат зустрічей із координаторами родин загиблих, зниклих безвісти та військовополонених військовослужбовців.
"Мета такого формату – підтримувати прямий діалог з родинами для збору проблематики та напрацювання рішень", – повідомляє пресслужба міністерства.
Перша зустріч заступниці Міністра оборони України Любові Галан відбулась з координаторами родин Сухопутних військ ЗСУ. На наступних етапах послідовно залучатимуться родини військовослужбовців інших родів та видів військ.
На зустрічі з координаторами родин загиблих, зниклих безвісти та військовополонених військовослужбовців Сухопутних військ ЗСУ обговорили встановлення обставин зникнення безвісти, відбір і зберігання біологічних зразків, пошук зниклих безвісти військовослужбовців, зміну статусу військовослужбовця у полоні, особисте розпорядження військовослужбовця, роботу військово-лікарських комісій, повернення особистих речей, соціальний супровід родин, грошове забезпечення, ОГД та інші соціальні виплати, а також нагородження родин загиблих військовослужбовців.
Координатори також порушили питання тривалого опрацювання документів, відсутності зрозумілих алгоритмів дій та необхідності повторно звертатися до різних органів для отримання інформації.
Питання, які потребують рішень інших державних органів, Міноборони розглядатиме у співпраці з ними в межах своїх повноважень.
