title: Saint, sinner or feminist icon: How Mary Magdalene's image evolved through time
content_c:
Saint, sinner or feminist icon: Mary Magdalene through time
September 17, 2026
Apostle, prostitute, penitent and confidante of Jesus — just a few of the roles assigned to Mary Magdalene since the early days of Christianity.
Artists from the Renaissance to the Baroque period, including Titian, El Greco and Georges de la Tour, depicted her in the 16th and 17th centuries as a repentant penitent; Rembrandt portrayed her as a witness to Christ's resurrection; and Max Beckmann, a representative of the New Objectivity movement, depicted her as a sinner in 1917.
Nearly a century later, she was portrayed by Lady Gaga in a music video.
"Mary Magdalene is probably the most multifaceted and enigmatic figure in the Bible, and also one of the most enigmatic in European cultural history," said Bastian Eclercy, curator of the exhibition "Mary Magdalene: Sin. Pray. Love" at the Städel Museum in Frankfurt. "She appears countless times in art history."
What do we know about Mary Magdalene?
Very little is known about Mary Magdalene from the Bible, yet she plays an important role in the New Testament.
The Gospels recount that Jesus delivered her from seven demons, and that she accompanied Jesus and witnessed his crucifixion and burial. On Easter morning, she discovered the empty tomb and became the first witness to the Resurrection. She then proclaimed the message of the risen Christ to Jesus' disciples.
"She is then referred to as the Apostula Apostulorum, that is, the Apostle of the Apostles," explained Eclercy. "This gives her a very central role in the history of salvation."
But it didn't stop there.
Around 600 AD, Pope Gregory the Great permanently distorted the image of Mary Magdalene by merging her with two other women mentioned in the Bible: an unnamed woman, the "sinner" mentioned in the Gospel of Luke who washed Christ's feet, and Mary of Bethany (who also washed his feet). The Pope claimed that the seven demons cast out of Mary Magdalene by Jesus represented the seven deadly sins. His sermon played a decisive role in shaping Mary Magdalene's reputation as a repentant prostitute — something for which there is absolutely no evidence in the Bible.
Mary Magdalene's remains are in France — allegedly
In the High Middle Ages, a legend emerged to the effect that Mary Magdalene, together with Lazarus and a group of companions, had been cast adrift in a boat on the Mediterranean; with divine help, she is said to have reached the coast of Provence in France, where she first preached the Gospel and then lived in a cave for some 30 years, doing penance.
Even today, two French towns claim to hold her remains: Vezelay in Burgundy and Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume in Provence.
In the 16th century, finally, the Reformation and Renaissance humanism brought about a change in thinking and opposition to the conflation of the three women into one.
However, it was not until the Second Vatican Council (1962 to 1965), which adopted far-reaching reforms to the Roman Catholic liturgy, that the identification of Mary Magdalene with the anonymous sinner was officially revoked.
"This very broad range of roles, which have been attributed to her throughout history and which are in a certain state of tension with one another, has evidently held a particular fascination for artists of all eras and genres time and again, whilst also presenting them with a challenge," said Eclercy.
A new image through the Gospel of Mary
With the rediscovery of the Gospel of Mary in modern times, the image of Mary Magdalene got something of a makeover.
This text, not included in the biblical canon, portrays her as a particularly close confidante of Jesus and has given fresh impetus to discussions about her role.
Today, she is regarded as one of the most influential women of early Christianity and a key figure in feminist theology.
"In recent decades in particular, she has thus become a role model for women — that is, for female observers — but also, and especially, for contemporary female artists, who see in her the qualities of a woman who lives on her own terms," said Eclercy.
Lady Gaga portrayed Mary Magdalene in her 2011 video for "Judas" — "the most exciting artistic moment of my career," as she wrote on Twitter (now X) at the time.
The most recent portrait in the Frankfurt exhibition — which features more than 100 depictions of Mary Magdalene — is by the Spanish artist Nieves Gonzalez and was completed in 2025: "La Sfida" (The Challenge) deconstructs virtually all the traditional attributes ascribed to Mary Magdalene by artists of earlier centuries.
Where she once gazed penitently towards the heavens, the painting depicts the female apostle looking down at the viewer with a self-assured gaze. Where her hair would otherwise have hung loose — alluding to the figure's sinful past — here it lies carefully brushed around her neck like a scarf. And where much bare skin would normally be visible, her body is now wrapped in a thick red down coat. In her hands, the disciple holds an equally (blood-) red skull — for centuries a symbol of transience — a gesture that clearly expresses her power.
Mary Magdalene has now also been officially recognized as an equal within the Catholic Church: In 2016, Pope Francis elevated her liturgical celebration on July 22 from a Memorial to a Feast, thereby aligning her legal and ritual status with that of male apostles within the faith. It's yet another chapter in the illustrious life story of Mary Magdalene, and unlikely to be the last.
The exhibition "Mary Magdalene: Sin. Pray. Love." runs at the Städel Museum in Frankfurt from September 17 through January 17, 2027.
This article was originally written in German.
description: From "Apostle of the Apostles" to prostitute, Mary Magdalene has been assigned a wide variety of roles, as a new exhibition shows.

title: Urteil des Bundesgerichtshofs: Orange gehört Obi nicht allein
content_c:
Urteil des Bundesgerichtshofs Orange gehört Obi nicht allein
Die Baumarktkette Obi kann laut einem BGH-Urteil keinen Markenschutz für die Farbe Orange beanspruchen. Verbraucher sehen die Farbe nicht als Hinweis auf ein bestimmtes Unternehmen, so die Begründung.
Im Streit um Markenschutz für ihr "Obi-Orange" hat die Baumarktkette Obi eine Niederlage kassiert. Der Farbton, eine Art Hellrot-Orange, sei nicht schützenswert, entschied der Bundesgerichtshof (BGH) und wies die Revision des Unternehmens gegen eine Entscheidung des Bundespatentgerichts zurück.
Konkurrenten klagten gegen Farbmarke
Dieses hatte zuvor die von zwei Konkurrenten, den Ketten Hornbach und Globus, beantragte Löschung dieser sogenannten abstrakten Farbmarke beim Deutschen Patent- und Markenamt für rechtens erklärt. Daraufhin war Obi vor den BGH gezogen - und unterlag.
Die Farbe Orange sei höchstens ein Hinweis auf Baumarktketten im Allgemeinen, aber nicht auf einem speziellen Baumarkt wie Obi, so der Vorsitzende Richter des Ersten Zivilsenates, Thomas Koch. Abstrakten Farbmarken - das sind Marken, die einen Farbton als solchen schützen - fehle es in der Regel an Unterscheidungskraft. Verbraucher könnten, wie im vorliegenden Fall, nicht aufgrund der Farbe eines Produktes auf dessen Herkunft schließen.
Obi will bei Orange bleiben
"Unsere Hausfarbe bleibt Orange", teilte Obi in einer ersten Reaktion mit. "Unabhängig von der formellen Registereintragung bleibt die Farbe Orange natürlich weiterhin eines der zentralen visuellen Erkennungsmerkmale von Obi." Die BGH-Entscheidung ändere in der Praxis nichts an der Markenidentität in den Märkten und der täglichen Kommunikation des Unternehmens.
"Wir begrüßen das Urteil des Bundesgerichtshofs zur Farbmarke Orange sehr", hieß es von einem Hornbach-Sprecher.
Widersprüchliche Gutachten
Für den BGH hatten auch mehrere Gutachten, die die Parteien im Zuge des Rechtsstreites vorlegten, eine maßgebliche Rolle gespielt. Obi hatte dabei im Abstand von mehreren Jahren gleich zwei demoskopische Expertisen erstellen lassen, denen zufolge 45,6 und später 49,6 Prozent der Gesamtbevölkerung die Farbe Orange mit Obi verbanden.
Das sei zu wenig, so sah es nach dem Bundespatentgericht auch der BGH. Ein Gutachten von der Gegenseite war auf einen "Zuordnungsgrad" von sogar nur 30 Prozent gekommen.
Andere Unternehmen vor Gericht erfolgreicher
Für das "Obi-Orange" gilt damit nicht, was andere Unternehmen in ähnlichen Fällen erreicht hatten: So hatten die Sparkassen vor rund zehn Jahren einen Rechtsstreit um "ihr" Rot für sich entschieden.
Ebenfalls erfolgreich war der Schweizer Süßwarenhersteller Lindt, der den charakteristischen Goldton der Folie seines Schoko-Osterhasen schützen ließ. Auch die Farbe Lila gilt seit einer BGH-Entscheidung als Inbegriff für "Milka"-Produkte. Gleiches gilt für die Farbe Magenta als Markenzeichen der Telekom.
(Aktenzeichen: I ZB 58/25)
description: Die Baumarktkette Obi kann laut einem BGH-Urteil keinen Markenschutz für die Farbe Orange beanspruchen. Verbraucher sehen die Farbe nicht als Hinweis auf ein bestimmtes Unternehmen, so die Begründung.

title: Huthi-Offensive setzt auch Ägypten unter Druck
content_c:
Huthi-Offensive setzt auch Ägypten unter Druck
16. September 2026
Alle Schiffe dürften passieren - zumindest vorerst. So erklärte es ein Sprecher der jemenitischen Huthi-Miliz. Die Schifffahrt im Roten Meer sei sicher - mit einer Ausnahme: Schiffe saudischer Herkunft dürften die Meerenge nicht passieren, so der Sprecher. Gleichzeitig hat die vom Iran unterstützte Miliz durch militärische Kämpfe ihre Positionen am südlichen Zugang zum Meer ausgebaut. Sie kontrollieren nundie Insel Perim (Mayun) in der Meerenge sowie weitere Inseln und Abschnitte der jemenitischen Küste.
Damit wächst vor allem der Druck auf den erklärten Huthi-Gegner Saudi-Arabien - aber auch auf Ägypten. Denn jede ernsthafte Störung des Schiffsverkehrs im Roten Meer trifft den Suezkanal - und damit eine wichtige Devisenquelle des Landes am Nil.
Noch allerdings ist der Verkehr nicht eingebrochen, sogar das Gegenteil scheint zunächst der Fall: Der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters zufolge passierten am vergangenen Samstag 24 und am Sonntag 27 Frachtschiffe die Meerenge Bab al-Mandab, etwa so viele wie sonst im Zehn-Tage-Schnitt. Die Huthi wollen damit offenbar signalisieren, dass sie den Verkehr nicht grundsätzlich stoppen wollen.
Allerdings ist der Schiffsverkehr nach Angaben des Datenanbieters Kpler insgesamt rückläufig: Am Donnerstag passierten noch 37 Schiffe die Meerenge, am Montag waren es 21. Mitte Juli hatte der Tagesdurchschnitt noch bei knapp 47 Durchfahrten gelegen.
Wie wird es weitergehen? "Die Huthi könnten die Verbindung zwischen Asien und Europa tatsächlich unterbrechen oder zumindest erheblich stören", sagt der Nahost-Wissenschaftler Stephan Roll von der in Berlin ansässigen Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (SWP) im Gespräch mit der DW. "Man muss deshalb zunächst abwarten, wie groß die tatsächliche Störung für den Suezkanal sein wird." Eine vollständige Kontrolle des Bab al-Mandab bedeutet dabei nicht automatisch eine Kontrolle des Suezkanals. Sie gibt den Huthi aber die Möglichkeit, die wichtige Zufahrt zum Roten Meer zu bedrohen und damit den Verkehr indirekt zu behindern.
Für Ägypten kommt die neue Eskalation zu einem ungünstigen Zeitpunkt. Angriffe der Huthi hatten den Suezkanal bereits seit Ende 2023 wirtschaftlich schwer getroffen. Nach Angaben des Internationalen Währungsfonds (IWF)gingen die Einnahmen 2024 um rund sechs Milliarden Dollar (5.2 Milliarden Euro) zurück. Vor der Krise nahm Ägypten mit dem Kanal jährlich rund neun bis zehn Milliarden Dollar (8,67 Milliarden Euro) ein.
Prekäre Situation
In letzter Zeit hatte sich die Lage allerdings etwas gebessert. "Die Situation ist im Vergleich zu 2023 sicherlich problematisch, im Vergleich zur Lage vor ein, zwei oder drei Monaten aber nicht unbedingt eindeutig negativ", sagt Roll. Wegen der gestiegenen Ölpreise und der dadurch teureren Umfahrung Afrikas hatten Reedereien zuletzt wieder erwogen, auf der Route zwischen Asien und Europa stärker durch das Rote Meer zu fahren. Die neue Huthi-Offensive könnte diese Pläne nun bremsen.
Hinzu kommt ein zweiter kritischer Faktor: Saudi-Arabiens Ost-West-Pipeline in die Stadt Yanbu ist nach den jüngsten Angriffen weiterhin außer Betrieb. Über die Leitung wurden zuletzt rund vier bis fünf Millionen Barrel Öl pro Tag transportiert. Reuters zufolge könnten dadurch bis zu vier Millionen Barrel täglich gefährdet sein - etwa vier Prozent des weltweiten Angebots. Auch Ägypten muss befürchten, dass das Öl an dieser Stelle vorerst versiegt.
Dabei hatte sich die finanzielle Lage des Suezkanals zuletzt verbessert. Im Haushaltsjahr 2025/26 stiegen die Einnahmen nach Angaben der Suezkanalbehörde um 23 Prozent auf 4,67 Milliarden Dollar (4,5 Milliarden Euro). Auch die Zahl der Schiffspassagen und die transportierte Ladungsmenge nahm zu. Das war, trotz Iran-Krieg und Huthi-Konflikt, immerhin eine Teil-Erholung. Eine erneute längere Unterbrechung könnte sie schnell wieder zunichtemachen.
Eine Analyse des in Katar residierenden Think Tanks 'Middle East Council for Global Affairs' warnt deshalb vor einem Szenario, in dem sowohl der Persische Golf als auch das Rote Meer unsicher werden. Ähnlich sieht es der in Seoul ansässige Think Tank 'East Asia Institute', der von einem "doppelten Nadelöhr" spricht: Beide Seewege seien keine unabhängigen Alternativen, weil Öl- und Warenströme an mehreren Punkten auf sichere Verbindungen angewiesen seien. Für Ägypten würde eine solche Entwicklung den wirtschaftlichen Druck weiter erhöhen.
"Gute Miene zum bösen Spiel"
Was kann Kairo tun? Machtpolitisch vermutlich eher wenig - zumal die Huthi bisher ägyptische Interessen eher indirekt verletzt haben. "Die militärischen Möglichkeiten Ägyptens sind sehr eingeschränkt", sagt Steffen Krüger, Leiter der Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung (KAS) in Kairo, gegenüber der DW. Die Erfahrungen der ägyptischen Intervention im Jemen in den 1960er-Jahren wirkten bis heute nach. Das Land sei daher eher um Zurückhaltung bemüht. "Zwar gehört Ägypten formal weiter der von Saudi-Arabien geführten Koalition gegen die Huthi an. Die ägyptische Beteiligung ist aber weitgehend symbolischer Natur."
In Kairo dürfte man zudem registriert haben, dass auch Länder wie die USA und Saudi-Arabien bisher kaum größere militärische Erfolge gegen die Huthi erzielen konnten. "Die Ägypter haben schlicht keine wirkliche Alternative", sagt Roll. Wahrscheinlich sei deshalb, dass Kairo zunächst auf Diplomatie setze. "Man muss im Grunde versuchen, gute Miene zum bösen Spiel zu machen und mit den Huthi entsprechende Arrangements zu treffen."
"Zunächst abwarten"
Einen Bericht des katarisch finanzierten Onlinemediums 'The New Arab', demzufolge die Huthi Ägypten über die International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) Gespräche über die Sicherheit der Schifffahrt angeboten haben sollen, hat die ICS inzwischen dementiert.
Am Dienstag reiste Saudi-Arabiens Kronprinz Mohammed bin Salman nach Kairo, dessen Land wirtschaftlich ungleich stärker und militärisch unmittelbar von Huthi-Attacken betroffen ist. Für Ägypten dürfte dabei nicht zuletzt die Frage eine Rolle spielen, wie sich die Sicherheitslage im Roten Meer und die Folgen für Energieversorgung, Handel und Suezkanal entwickeln.
"Die Ägypter dürften zunächst abwarten", sagt Roll. Tatsächlich vollzieht Kairo einen schwierigen Balanceakt: Ägypten ist eng mit Saudi-Arabien verbunden, würde aber unter weiterer Eskalation wirtschaftlich zu leiden haben. Entscheidend dürfte daher sein, ob die Huthi den Schiffsverkehr tatsächlich einschränken, möglicherweise auch über Schiffe mit saudischem Hintergrund hinaus - oder ihre verbesserte militärische Stellung am Bab al-Mandab eher als Drohmittel dient.
Eine frühere Version dieses Beitrags hatte unter Berufung auf einen Bericht des Onlinemediums "The New Arab" ein angebliches Gesprächsangebot der Huthi an Ägypten erwähnt. Dieser Bericht wurde inzwischen von der ICS dementiert.
description: Die Huthi haben ihre militärische Kontrolle über die Meerenge Bab al-Mandab ausgeweitet - das trifft vor allem Öl-Exporteur Saudi-Arabien und damit die Weltwirtschaft. Doch auch für Ägypten steht viel auf dem Spiel.

title: Henry Zeffman: How Burnham got ready to govern with four key moments mapped out
content_c:
Henry Zeffman: How Burnham got ready to govern with four key moments mapped out
- Published
At the start of summer, in the pillared room in 10 Downing Street, Andy Burnham looked out at his new special advisers, the few dozen political officials tasked with driving hundreds of thousands of civil servants to deliver his government's agenda.
Some had been with him in Manchester or Makerfield. Others had spent the past few months trying everything to prevent his hostile takeover of Sir Keir Starmer's government - and the new prime minister showed he was aware of it, going out of his way to praise those who had stayed on, for their efforts in the preceding years.
At that meeting, Burnham's team mapped out four key moments in the coming months.
First, the return to Parliament in September, when Burnham and other leading ministers would make their first statements to MPs.
Second, Labour's annual conference at the end of September - Burnham's first as leader.
Third, the Budget, taking place on 28 October.
And fourth, the 10-year plan for Britain which Burnham intends to unveil in November.
As MPs prepare to leave Parliament on Tuesday for almost a month and party conference season gets underway, the first phase of that route map is almost complete - enough for figures at all levels of the Labour Party to begin answering some questions about the shape of this new government.
Most importantly, perhaps, how new actually is it? Does Burnham represent continuity or change?
That question is especially relevant because those Labour MPs who pushed for Sir Keir to be replaced always fell into two broad camps: those who wanted a change of style and emphasis but continuity in policy, and those who wanted a major shift in policy. Both groups saw what they wanted in Burnham.
Going by the words of the new prime minister himself, he represents a profound break with the past, and not only the immediate past.
In his first speech as Labour leader in July, Burnham described his ascendancy as "the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years".
That is the timeframe he has returned to again and again, signalling not just a desire to reverse issues he believes stem from the Thatcher era but also to break with aspects of the Labour governments since then, including his immediate predecessor's.
Some in government are already quietly questioning, though, whether the ambition of that rhetoric can be squared with the early signals emerging from the Treasury under the new Chancellor John Healey.
- Who's in Andy Burnham's cabinet? 
  - Published28 July
In interviews over recent weeks, and especially in his first major speech on Monday, Healey has said he will stick to Rachel Reeves's commitments not to increase the main rates of income tax, national insurance and VAT, as well as her rules on government borrowing.
In the speech, he promised to "control public spending", and hailed Reeves for beginning to "recover Britain's fiscal discipline".
It led to opposition parties labelling Healey a continuity chancellor. A similar critique is being voiced among some of his government colleagues.
Most are more generous for now, arguing that Healey's first imperative - especially at a time of turmoil in the global bond markets - is reassurance, and that the Budget is the moment for him to show how he plans to substantiate Burnham's rhetoric.
Even one official sympathetic on that point, though, asks: "Why did he do a big speech before he has something to say?"
Those close to Healey argue that his emphasis this week on securing the economic growth which has eluded successive governments by spreading wealth around the country is a clear difference from Reeves.
And finding ways to boost regional growth has been one of Healey's major causes since he was a junior minister at the Treasury more than 20 years ago - long before it was at the heart of Burnham's political personality.
There is no question, though, that this week the minister who most starkly signalled change from the previous government was a man who coveted Healey's job - Ed Miliband, who was instead appointed foreign secretary.
In announcing new sanctions on Israel over illegal settlements in the West Bank, Miliband explicitly cast the policy as a break from Sir Keir's approach, telling MPs: "We should have acted earlier, and it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation."
On the other hand, acting alongside Canada and France in announcing the sanctions represented - in form if not substance - continuity with the previous government, the three countries having moved together to recognise the state of Palestine a year ago.
The sanctions announcement was received with near-universal warmth from Labour MPs, itself a marker of change from the Starmer government.
It was also seen as a sign of the ability of Miliband in particular, but this government in general, to drive its agenda through the civil service machine.
"There is a much clearer sense now from No 10 of what they want," one official who worked under Sir Keir as well as Burnham says. "Before there was a bit too much of 'let us know your ideas for what we should do', now it's 'this is what the PM wants, give us options to deliver it'."
That is a culture shift which Burnham sought to drill into his cabinet at their weekly meeting on Tuesday, still only their third such meeting.
According to one present, the prime minister said: "We need to be on the front foot. We need to be bolder. Let's get on and do things. It's about deeds not words."
Perhaps the most significant way in which Burnham is trying to make boldness easier for his ministers is by encouraging them to press ahead with policies when there is a risk they will face a serious legal challenge.
The new attorney general, Ellie Reeves, has pared back rules introduced under Sir Keir which some ministers believed forced them to be over-cautious about legal risk, thereby slowing down or blocking new policies altogether.
Louise Haigh, Burnham's deputy, has vowed to "strip out needless bureaucracy" from government more generally, citing an example of there being three public consultations between 2019 and 2023 on whether to microchip cats.
"If we can't microchip cats without getting tied up in red tape, it should come as no surprise the public is losing faith that governments can get things done," she said.
As Burnham moves into the next phase of his autumn, there is a recognition from some around him that he will need to produce some more significant policies to underpin his rhetoric.
Those in government familiar with early work on fleshing out his commitment to "public control" of essential services insist the direction of travel is truly radical.
Haigh is responsible for this, chairing a taskforce on how to reverse "over-privatisation" specifically of housing, water, energy and transport.
Burnham may offer more details on these policies at Labour's conference, while he is likely to wait until after then to show his hand on whether he wants continuity or change when it comes to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's reforms to the legal immigration system - a much more divisive issue among Labour MPs.
And whatever their differences on policy, Labour MPs are united on one thing. The fundamental reason they installed a new prime minister was because many of them believed that continuing on the same path meant losing the next general election.
For them, a long-term improvement in Labour's poll ratings would be the most important change of them all.

description: As the prime minister looks ahead to autumn, Labour figures are asking whether his government represents continuity or change.

title: Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned father
content_c:
The sons of Imran Khan have accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief of a “personal vendetta” against the incarcerated former prime minister and expressed fears their father is being “slowly killed” in jail, as international pressure mounts over his prison conditions.
Kasim Khan, 27, and Sulaiman Khan, 29, have become strong advocates for the release of their father, who has been held in Adiala prison in Rawalpindi since his arrest in 2023, and is serving a 14-year sentence on corruption charges.
They have not been allowed to speak to Khan for more than six months and have been prevented from travelling from the UK to Pakistan to lobby for his release.
On Wednesday, the supreme court will rule on a case alleging the Pakistan government has been in contempt of court by denying Khan private hospital treatment for a worsening eye condition and preventing family from visiting him or speaking with him in jail for more than six months, in violation of a court order. Khan is being held in solitary confinement, in a cell alleged to be 6ft by 8ft.
Later this month, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) – the political party Khan founded in 1996, four years after retiring from international cricket – is planning a nationwide march demanding his release.
Speaking to the Guardian from London, Khan’s sons – from his first marriage to Jemima Goldsmith – said they were “deeply, deeply concerned” about their father’s health, and that the conditions he was being kept in amounted to “a form of mental and physical torture”.
“The reality is that he is locked in a tiny 6x8ft cell without human contact,” said Sulaiman. “He hasn’t been allowed new books for months and he’s not been allowed to see or speak to his family or a neutral doctor. He has an eye condition which was neglected for months and has meant he’s probably almost lost sight in one eye.”
Late last month, Sky Sports aired an interview with Khasim and Sulaiman during its coverage of a test match between England and Pakistan. The Pakistan Cricket Board, which has close links to the government and whose chair is also the interior minister, made a formal complaint to Sky Sports after the broadcast and the Pakistani team threatened to refuse to return to the field after the lunch break.
“It shows how out of touch they are with the rest of the world, that they thought they could silence media like they do at home,” Sulaiman said of the complaint. “It just exposed them for the authoritarian regime that they are.”
The UN has said Khan’s prolonged detention violates international law and the UN’s special rapporteur on torture said his solitary confinement and detention conditions could amount to psychological torture.
Sulaiman said the family had been told their father, 73, had also been diagnosed with high blood pressure. “More than anything, we just want to speak to him and make sure he’s OK,” he said.
Khan’s sons said they were particularly concerned that the “cruel” treatment was being driven by a “personal grudge” by Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of defence forces and army chief.
When Khan was the prime minister, he unceremoniously demoted Munir, and the bad blood between them was well known. When Munir was made army chief in 2022, the persecution of Khan increased notably.
“It’s very clear this is being driven by personal grudge and that’s one of the reasons he’s being treated so harshly, on the orders of Asim Munir,” said Sulaiman. Munir’s powers expanded over the past year as he established himself as a close ally of Donald Trump, who referred to him as “my favourite field marshal”.
Last month, the supreme court ruled that Khan should be taken to a private hospital for treatment for a blood clot in his retinal vein, believed to have destroyed 85% of the sight in his right eye because of a prolonged lack of medical attention.
Khan was instead taken briefly to a government hospital, where he was given several injections and ruled fit to return to prison, prompting outrage from his family and political party.
“There’s still been no light shed on our father’s real condition from an unbiased, neutral physician,” said Kasim. “We believe they’re trying to slowly kill him in there. Just as soon as there’s less pressure, we are sure they will put even harsher restrictions on him and try to finish him off.
“The one with the real vendetta here is the army chief Asim Munir.”
In a statement, the Pakistan government called the allegations around Khan “fake propaganda” and said he was being kept in adequate conditions, with access to home-cooked food, nuts, bottled water, exercise equipment, family visits and regular medical examinations.
“The government of Pakistan categorically rejects allegations that the convicted prisoner is being subjected to punitive solitary confinement, cruelty or deprivation,” the statement said.
It was widely acknowledged that Khan came to power in 2018 with the backing of Pakistan’s military, widely referred to as the “establishment”, which has long held an oversized role in the country’s governance. Khan had promised to build a “naya Pakistan” (new Pakistan), which would end corruption and follow the rule of law. However, his time in power was plagued by allegations of corruption, press censorship and persecution of his opponents.
He was toppled in 2022 after falling out with his military benefactors. He then began a campaign calling for the generals to be kept out of government.
By 2023, as his accusations against the military grew, Khan turned from alleged persecutor to the persecuted. He was arrested and charged with more than 100 crimes, including alleged corruption and sedition, which he claims are trumped up to keep him out of power.
Despite his toppling and imprisonment, Khan still remains popular. “They want to do everything they can to sideline him and disappear him from public life,” Kasim said.
Sulaiman said that while it was “clear the establishment think they can get away with it without any kind of repercussions”, it was also evident the government had been rattled by international coverage of Khan’s case.
Khan’s sons said that while they were keen to travel to Pakistan, their visas had still not been granted more than nine months after applying.
They emphasised they had no interest in entering politics in Pakistan or leading Khan’s PTI party in his absence.
“We definitely don’t want to get involved in politics in Pakistan in the long term,” said Sulaiman. “Our father always said that one of the biggest problems with Pakistani politics is this dynastic nepotism; that power’s been held by just two families for the last 40 years. It’s a sign of what’s wrong with the political system in Pakistan.”
Speculation has abounded on whether Khan would strike a deal with the military to secure his release. Khan’s closest aide, Zulfi Bukhari, said: “There is only one deal Khan would ever accept: the restoration of democracy, the rule of law and the people’s mandate in Pakistan. If they’re genuinely willing to do that, then fine – let’s talk.”
Kasim and Sulaiman said they did not believe Khan would give up his politics to secure his release. “He’s a very single-minded person,” said Kasim. “I don’t think there’s a chance that he’d ever give it up.”
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi and Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad

title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
content_c:
How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
September 17, 2026
Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing.
The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26.
"This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone."
How the disaster unfolded
The floods began upstream with a large rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung. That caused a section of the glacier to collapse at the same time, sending roughly 110 million cubic meters of rock and glacier ice, the size of 44,000 Olympic swimming pools, hurtling downward. That type of rock avalanche is rare, occurring at this size only once every 1,000-10,000 years.
The material fell about 1,400 meters (4,593 feet) from the mountain to the valley floor, picking up debris, water, ice, rock and sediment as it descended. The impact released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. As it crashed into the valley, it also tore up buried glacier ice, adding up to 30 million more cubic meters of debris and water to the flow.
Within about seven minutes, the flood reached Nepal and China's Rasuwagadhi border, 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) downstream, moving at an average speed of 170 kilometers per hour (about 106 miles per hour). The flood continued downstream, traveling 200 kilometers in under seven hours.
How did this happen?
It was a complex combination of conditions, exacerbated by climate change, that allowed the slope to collapse in the first place. That's according to researchers with World Weather Attribution, an international collaboration of scientists that looks at the role of climate change in extreme weather and disaster events.
Rising temperatures, due to the burning of fossil fuels, have reshaped this stretch of the Himalayas for decades.
Near the failure site, the glacier's edge had retreated just 75 meters between 1964 and 2000. But between 2010 and 2026, it dramatically accelerated, retreating another 373 meters. That stripped away the ice supporting the rock wall above it.
Permafrost — or permanently frozen ground within the rock — had also started to thaw. That took place between 4,500 and 5,500 meters of elevation, a critical band that's most sensitive to warming. As it thawed, the mountain walls became more and more unstable.
In the immediate run-up to the collapse, conditions were extreme. July and August overall were the warmest on record in the area, with climate change adding about 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to the region. On August 24 and 25, temperatures ran roughly 2.5 to 2.7 degrees Celsius above the 10-year average. A day before the catastrophe unfolded, the maximum temperature was approximately 7 degrees Celsius above the reference mean.
An unusually snowy October in 2025 likely also played a role, generating more meltwater.
Researchers also believe a 2015 earthquake played a role. That magnitude-7.8 quake triggered an earlier avalanche at Langtang Lirung, which may have weakened the rock mass in the years since, priming the slope for failure.
A disaster beyond adaptation
Researchers also tried to find out whether this was a disaster the region could have prepared for and adapted to. They determined it was uniquely hard to detect, as Nepal's early warning systems are designed for forecastable rainfall-driven floods, not quickly developing, cascading events like this one.
Essentially, this kind of complex threat exceeds the limits of adaptation.
The flood outran Nepal's early warning systems and destroyed several monitoring gauges in its wake. The first mass SMS warning was sent about 38 minutes after the initial collapse, but the flood had already reached the border 7 minutes in.
"When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction," Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said.
"Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come."
Edited by: Sarah Steffen
description: A glacier and rock collapse in Nepal killed nearly 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Scientists say decades of warming helped set the disaster in motion.

title: Warum die SPD jetzt auf Manuela Schwesig hofft
content_c:
SPD vor den Wahlen Hoffen auf Schwesig
Die SPD hofft bei der Wahl in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern auf die Zugkraft von Ministerpräsidentin Schwesig. Ein Erfolg könnte die Partei etwas stabilisieren, doch die Stimmung bleibt angespannt.
Für die Bundes-SPD ist klar: Die Partei braucht dringend ein echtes Erfolgserlebnis. Da es dem SPD-Politiker Steffen Krach in Berlin kaum gelingen wird, den Posten des Regierenden Bürgermeisters zu gewinnen, hängt für die SPD viel von der amtierenden Ministerpräsidentin Manuela Schwesig in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern ab.
Die holt gerade gegen die AfD auf, es könnte am Sonntag also seit Langem mal wieder was zu feiern geben bei den Sozialdemokraten. Die Stimmung ist trotzdem mies und das hat viele Gründe.
Rennen in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern scheint offen
Die Ministerpräsidentin von Mecklenburg-Vorpommern führt einen Wahlkampf, wie ihn die SPD lange nicht gesehen hat. Sie positioniert sich als die "Frau gegen Blau" - so ihr Slogan - will die AfD überholen. Die liegt in Umfragen zwar bisher noch knapp vor der SPD, doch das Rennen scheint offen. "Wer möchte, dass ich bleibe, muss zur Wahl gehen und SPD wählen", sagt Schwesig selbstbewusst. Sie ist das Zugpferd der SPD.
Vieles macht sie besser als andere SPD-Spitzenleute. Zum Beispiel ihre Social-Media-Präsenz: Dort zeigt sie sich im Hoodie am Grill oder mit älteren Damen auf der Parkbank. Und das ist keine reine Show. Schwesig tourt im Wahlkampf durch die Dörfer. "Ich glaube, die SPD ist gut beraten, wenn sie vor Ort ist, wenn sie die Alltagsthemen kennt und die Menschen müssen spüren, dass sich ihr Alltag verbessert."
Im Wahlkampf grenzt sich Schwesig ab von Reformvorschlägen aus Berlin. Zum Beispiel davon, die abschlagsfreie Rente nach 45 Beitragsjahren abzuschaffen: "Ich kenne die Lage der Menschen hier und weiß, dass viele 45 Jahre lang und noch viel länger gearbeitet und eingezahlt haben und trotzdem nur kleine Renten erhalten. Deshalb finde ich es nicht richtig, wenn dann solche Vorschläge zur Rentenkürzung kommen."
In Berlin ist Krach in Umfragen abgeschlagen
Ganz ähnlich kritisch sieht ihr Kollege Steffen Krach, SPD-Spitzenkandidat in Berlin, das Thema Rentenreform. Krach steht ebenfalls am Sonntag zur Wahl, will Regierender Bürgermeister werden: "Ich sage ganz konkret, wenn ich der Meinung bin, dass Dinge falsch laufen. Zum Beispiel wenn die Bundesebene sagt, wir wollen 1 ,5 Milliarden beim Wohngeld kürzen, dann halte ich das für falsch."
Aber Krach kann mit Parteikollegin Schwesig nicht mithalten, ist in Umfragen weit abgeschlagen. Zudem belasten ihn Ermittlungen wegen Korruptionsvorwürfen. Damit bleibt die klare Abgrenzung von der Reformpolitik der Bundesregierung seine einzige Gemeinsamkeit mit Schwesig.
Unzufriedenheit mit der Bundespolitik ist groß
Eine naheliegende Strategie, sagt Politikwissenschaftler Uwe Jun - gerade für Schwesig - denn in den ostdeutschen Ländern sei die Unzufriedenheit mit der Bundespolitik groß: "Das haben wir auch in Sachsen-Anhalt gesehen. Aber da war dann eben keine so populäre Spitzenpersönlichkeit, die das kompensieren konnte. Einzelne Ministerpräsidentinnen und Ministerpräsidenten schaffen es, diese Unzufriedenheit zu kompensieren und eine Wahl stark zu personalisieren. Wenn ihnen das gelingt, dann können sie sich von der Bundespartei abkoppeln."
Krach und Schwesig sprechen aus, was sie im Wahlkampf immer wieder von Wählerinnen und Wählern zu hören bekommen. Die Menschen spiegeln ihre Unzufriedenheit.
Das Dilemma der SPD
Für die SPD auf Bundesebene ist das ein Problem, denn in der Koalition mit CDU und CSU muss die Partei für sie und die Wählerinnen und Wähler schmerzhafte Kompromisse eingehen. Bis jetzt hat die Parteiführung keine Lösung für dieses Dilemma gefunden. Im Gegenteil: Die Partei ist nach der Landtagswahl in Sachsen-Anhalt sogar noch deutlicher unter Druck geraten. So wirkte es wie die Flucht nach vorn, als die SPD-Spitze sofort ankündigte, noch einmal über den mit der Union eingeschlagenen Reformkurs reden zu wollen: "Keine Sozialreformen gegen die Menschen", so Arbeitsministerin Bärbel Bas.
Zudem muss die SPD mit dem durch das Sachsen-Anhalt-Ergebnis geschwächten Koalitionspartner CDU/CSU fertig werden und seine Angriffe aushalten. So forderte der Chef des Parlamentskreises Mittelstand Christian von Stetten den Rücktritt von Bärbel Bas. Innerhalb der SPD hat das aber eher zu mehr Rückhalt für die Arbeitsministerin geführt.
Zudem treten in der Spritpreis-Debatte wieder deutlich die wirtschafts- und finanzpolitischen Differenzen zwischen SPD und CDU/CSU zutage. Beide Seiten tauschen die immergleichen Argumente aus aber finden keinen gemeinsamen Nenner. Es bleibt der Wille, noch vor den Landtagswahlen am Sonntag Handlungsfähigkeit zu beweisen.
"Niemand will wohl auf ein untergehendes Schiff"
Auch intern gibt es Personaldiskussionen in der SPD, die nach den Wahlen in Berlin und Mecklenburg-Vorpommern Fahrt aufnehmen könnten. Politikwissenschaftler Wolfgang Schroeder sagt, es rumore schon lange in der SPD wegen der Doppelämter der beiden Parteivorsitzenden Bärbel Bas und Lars Klingbeil, die beide zugleich Ministerien leiten. Schroeder sieht jedoch keine Alternativen "die nach vorne drängen". Mit Blick auf den angeschlagenen Koalitionspartner CDU/CSU werde die SPD erst einmal auf Zeit spielen und die Füße stillhalten.
Personalprobleme an der Spitze attestiert der Politologe beiden Lagern: "Die sind so groß wie nie zuvor in der Geschichte der Bundesrepublik. Wir haben ein richtiges Elitenproblem auf der Ebene der Führung von Parteien. Und das in der schwierigsten Lage der bundesdeutschen Entwicklung. Parteivorsitzende, mit denen nicht nur die Öffentlichkeit unzufrieden ist, sondern auch die eigenen Leute. Und gleichzeitig niemand, der dieses Amt wirklich anstrebt und dem zugetraut wird, dass er das Amt besser ausfüllt als die, die das gegenwärtig innehaben. Will wohl niemand auf ein untergehendes Schiff aufsteigen. Aber die Union muss handeln, weil für sie das Problem am größten ist."
Gewinnt die SPD die Wahl in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, dürfte das die beiden Vorsitzenden Klingbeil und Bas zunächst stabilisieren. Mit größeren Umwälzungen ist am Montag nicht zu rechnen.
In einer früheren Version dieses Artikels wurde Wolfgang Schroeder als SPD-Mitglied bezeichnet. Auf seinen Hinweis haben wir diese Textstelle geändert.
Mehr zum Hintergrund dieser und anderer Korrekturen finden Sie hier: tagesschau.de/korrekturen
author: Anne-Katrin Mellmann, Moritz Rödle
description: Die SPD hofft bei der Wahl in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern auf die Zugkraft von Ministerpräsidentin Schwesig. Ein Erfolg könnte die Partei etwas stabilisieren, doch die Stimmung bleibt angespannt. Von Anne-Katrin Mellmann und Moritz Rödle.

title: Sommer 2026 - historischer Höchststand an Hitzetoten
content_c:
Sommer 2026 - historischer Höchststand an Hitzetoten
16. September 2026
Der Sommer 2026 war der wärmste in Europa sei Beginn der Aufzeichnungen und hat damit das bisherige Rekordhitzejahr 2003 vom Spitzenplatz vertrieben. Das hat das Erdbeobachtungsprogramm Copernicus ermittelt.
Und auch Deutschland verzeichnet Rekorde: "Beispiellos" nennt der Deutsche Wetterdienst (DWD) die Anzahl der heißen Tage im Sommer 2026. "Im Deutschlandmittel wurden rund 22 heiße Tage mit mindestens 30 Grad Celsius und etwa fünf sehr heiße Tage mit mindestens 35 Grad Celsius ermittelt", schreibt der DWD in einer Pressemitteilung Ende August.
Und noch ein deutscher Rekord: Die geschätzte Zahl der Hitzetoten war diesen Sommer so hoch wie noch nie - mindestens 16.300 Menschen starben bis Ende August.
Wie wird die Zahl der Hitzetoten ermittelt?
Die wenigsten Menschen sterben direkt an der Hitze, durch einen Hitzschlag beispielsweise. Die Todeszahlen ergeben sich vielmehr durch einen statistischen Zusammenhang zwischen den Sterbefallzahlen, die das Statistische Bundesamt in Deutschland erhebt, und den Temperaturen innerhalb eines bestimmten Zeitraums, die der Deutsche Wetterdienst misst.
In Deutschland wird ab einer Wochenmitteltemperatur von 20 Grad Celsius mit hitzebedingten Sterbefällen gerechnet. Die Wochenmitteltemperatur ist der Durchschnitt aller stündlich gemessenen Temperaturen in einer Woche, inklusive der Nachtstunden.
Während mehrerer Wochen stiegen die Wochenmittelwerte in Deutschland über die 20 Grad Celsius-Marke. Ende Juni war es besonders heiß: Vom 22.-28.06. betrug die Temperatur im Wochenmittel mehr als 26 Grad Celsius.
Obwohl sich mit einer statistischen Methode nicht klären lässt, woran die Menschen gestorben sind, wissen Forschende und Mediziner ziemlich gut, wie Hitze auf den menschlichen Körper wirkt. Eine Übersterblichkeit in Hitzeperioden ist deshalb plausibel. 
Was sind Gründe für einen Hitzetod?
"Nicht allein die Spitzenwerte auf dem Thermometer waren entscheidend, sondern vor allem, wie lange die Hitze anhielt und dass es nachts kaum abkühlte", sagt Andreas Matzarakis, Professor für Umweltmeteorologie an der Albert-Ludwigs-Universität in Freiburg.
In heißen Nächten schlafen viele Menschen schlechter. Genügend Schlaf ist allerdings wichtig, damit der Körper den Hitzestress des Tages kompensieren kann.
Wie stark die Belastung durch Hitze ist, hänge zudem nicht allein von der Lufttemperatur ab, sagt Matzarakis. Auch Luftfeuchte, Sonneneinstrahlung und Wind spielten eine Rolle – die sogenannte gefühlte Temperatur. Schwüle und Windstille bei gleichzeitig moderaten Temperaturen könnten ebenfalls eine hohe Belastung für den Körper sein.
Besonders von Hitzestress betroffen sind ältere Menschen und solche mit Vorerkrankungen, aber auch Schwangere und Säuglinge. Hitze kann zudem negativ mit Medikamenten wie Blutdrucksenkern oder Antidepressiva interagieren.
Weniger privilegierte Menschen gehören ebenfalls zu den stärker gefährdeten Gruppen. "Sie leben häufiger in weniger gut isolierten Wohnungen oder gehen einer Arbeit draußen nach", sagt Martin Röösli, Umweltwissenschaftler am Schweizerischen Tropen- und Public-Health-Institut Basel.
"Harvesting-Effekt" erklärt die Zahl der Hitzetoten nicht ausreichend
Ein großer Teil der Hitzetoten habe wahrscheinlich - aufgrund ihres Alters und Erkrankungen - nur noch eine kurze Lebenserwartung gehabt. Dennoch gebe es wissenschaftlichen Konsens, "dass ein Teil der Verstorbenen noch lange hätte leben können und einfach zum Zeitpunkt der Hitzewelle in einem fragilen Zustand war", sagt Röösli.
Auch Alexandra Schneider, Meteorologin und Epidemiologin am Helmholtz Zentrum München, sagt, dass es sich bei den während der Hitze verstorbenen Menschen sehr wahrscheinlich nicht um einen reinen "Harvesting-Effekt" handelt. Dieser Effekt beschreibt, "dass eine Hitzewelle vor allem sehr vulnerable Personen einige Tage oder Wochen früher sterben lässt", so Schneider.
Dann allerdings müsste es in den Wochen darauf eine deutliche Untersterblichkeit geben, was bisher aber nicht zu sehen sei. Deshalb gehe sie davon aus, dass ein relevanter Teil der Menschen noch Monate bis Jahre hätte leben können.
description: Der Sommer 2026 war einer der wärmsten seit Beginn der Aufzeichnung. Nach Schätzungen des RKI sind mehr als 16.000 Menschen in Deutschland hitzebedingt gestorben.

title: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises
content_c:
Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises
- Published
The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning.
It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose to make it in the Coventry Manufacturing and Technology Centre (MTC), just a few minutes' drive from the city's totemic HQ of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR).
In the event, no one was pulling punches. The 4,000 office-based job losses at JLR were confirmed as John Healey answered questions a few miles away.
Healey chose to lean into it as an example of the global turbulence against which the UK needs more resilience.
The difference between this chancellor and his predecessor was he also feels that stressing fiscal discipline should instil confidence in consumers, businesses and investors, and not sap it away amid rolling fears of tax hikes.
So the prime minister and his chancellor have been engaged in a conscious attempt to boost the economic vibes - "a new story", as he called it.
In his speech, and in a BBC interview afterwards, this was clear. There are some positive underlying signs from consumer, business and recruiter confidence measures that indicate this message has been heard, although the hot weather and World Cup have also been factors.
The Downing Street duo are trying to maintain this precious commodity of confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits that have been suppressed by years of political and economic chaos.
"Borrowing costs are too high," Healey acknowledged at the start of his speech. The global rise in bond yields is like a boa constrictor squeezing the Budget maths, slowly and relentlessly, occasionally loosening its grip, but never actually slithering away entirely.
It raises some reasonable questions therefore about how to balance reining in borrowing with protecting mildly better confidence?
The speech did not seem to me to prepare the ground - a "pitch roll" - for significant tax rises, as I heard at the equivalent Budget "scene setters" for the past two years.
"Am I right?" I asked the chancellor on this point. A pause as he sought precisely the right word formulation. "I won't comment. I can't comment. No chancellor can ahead of a Budget I will take and announce on October 28th".
OK, what about the advice from one of the PM's favourite economists Lord O'Neill that the rise in borrowing rates is a golden opportunity to scrap the triple lock?
This lock guarantees the state pension rising each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but some have argued it is unaffordable.
"The prime minister has said, like I have, that we must bring down welfare costs, but we are also responding to the extreme pressure that is there in wider markets," Healey said.
Neither answer was a denial, but nor were they any type of confirmation. Like a stubborn batsman, the chancellor is going to stay at the crease, giving little away, in his case, about next month's Budget.
- Chancellor refuses to rule out tax hikes in October Budget 
  - Published7 September
- UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget 
  - Published2 September
There was a focus on growth. As he toured the MTC, a centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing, he said the UK's "great talent and latent potential" made it the third most innovative country in the world, and he wanted to translate that into economic growth and success in more areas.
Two decades ago, Healey was responsible for the Regional Development Agencies, scrapped by the Coalition Government, that helped fund this very facility.
In his speech there was a big clue about how to square the circle of investing in industrial policy at a time of tricky public finances.
The "Pufins" - public finance institutions - such as the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund can invest strategically, less constrained by the government's borrowing rules. Part of the plan is Pufins to breed more unicorns ($1bn tech startups) in the UK.
This is the other part of the global backdrop. Amid the tumult of trade and military wars, there is arguably one of the biggest financial events in world history.
In the coming weeks, hundreds of billions of dollars will be invested and trillions in value confirmed from flotations of big American AI firms. The UK has some standout technology in this sector. The government wants to promote it.
The chancellor was also, however, cautious about the impact of AI on security and on jobs. Some degree of "public control" could be required to make these changes work for everyone. It appeared a little less cheerleading than the stance of the Starmer administration.
The chancellor was perhaps mindful of the army of manufacturing robots, laser welders, 3D metal printers, whirring into action around him.
Long term, it will be growth that will determine whether his borrowing rules are met, he said.
Ultimately he will be judged by his actual policy choices, but where there are trade-offs between balancing the books and economic growth across the country, this sounds like a chancellor who might prioritise the latter.
description: The new leadership is trying to maintain both confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits.

title: Councils to share £5m in 'emergency food aid' as living costs rise
content_c:
Councils to share £5m in 'emergency food aid' as living costs rise
- Published
Welsh councils will receive £4.8 million to provide "emergency food aid" and other support for people struggling due to cost of living pressures.
The cash from the Welsh government will be split between the 22 local authorities, with those in rural areas getting a premium due to "the added challenges" of delivering support to more sparsely populated regions.
Deputy First Minister Sioned Williams said rising fuel and energy costs meant many families faced another "tough winter" and she was "targeting support where it's needed most".
Reform UK Wales said the Welsh government would have more money to spend on supporting people in need if they did not "waste money" on international spending.
The ongoing US-Iran war and pressures on oil supply in Saudi Arabia have caused fuel prices to spike in recent days.
With inflation increasing and energy bills going up next month, many people could feel more of a squeeze on their household budgets.
Local authorities will be able to give the emergency money to community organisations like food banks, lunch clubs and advice providers.
Down To Zero, a project which has received funding previously, grows vegetables on allotments near Llantrisant in Rhondda Cynon Taf, and provides free vegetable boxes to low income families as well as lower cost subscriptions to other households within the county.
Gareth Banks has volunteered with the organisation for two years and "absolutely loves it".
"We can offer really good value, organically grown, fruit and vegetables to local people who might not always be able to afford that kind of thing," he said.
The project is run by Cynon Taf, a social housing provider.
Angharad Rogers, Cynon Taf's director of housing and communities, said food poverty was a growing problem for tenants.
"We've seen quite a shift lately in the people... who are most in need and accessing food banks," she said.
"Families with incomes coming into the household are still not able pay for food and things like that, so we're seeing a lot families coming to us and asking for help."
Where to get help if you are struggling with bills
- Contact advicelink Cymru, external for free, impartial advice on debt and benefits
- Contact your local council to see if you are eligible for emergency help from the Discretionary Assistance Fund, external
- If you are on a prepayment meter and cannot afford fuel you can contact the Fuel Bank Foundation, external for help
- If you are on a low income, you may be able to get your council tax reduced via the council tax reduction scheme, external
UK inflation hit its highest level in five months in the year to August, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Overall, motor fuel prices rose by 23% compared to August last year.
In Ystradowen, Vale of Glamorgan, drivers filling up their cars said they feared prices would increase further.
Ron Jones, from Cowbridge, said he was driving less but higher prices were "to be expected, given the world as it is".
Joy Thomas said prices were "extraordinarily high" and she had searched for the cheapest petrol station she could find.
Lewis Wall, 28, from Ystradowen, said prices were "ridiculous".
"But what can we do about it? You can't control the price and everyone needs fuel."
Williams said the government would "do all we can to support families who are going to be finding it tough this winter".
"But we need to see wider measures and many of those leavers reside in Westminster," she added.
She called on the UK government to bring in a system of cheaper energy prices for low income households, known as social tariffs.
"Social tariffs on energy is one of the main things I think that could really make a difference to people," she said.
The UK government said: "We have cut VAT on electricity bills from October, on top of the £150 we removed from bills earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills."
Reform said support to help ease the pressures of the cost of living "should be welcomed if delivered in the right way".
But it also said the Plaid Cymru government "could be doing more" if it did not "waste money" on projects like "spending taxpayer cash on planting trees in Uganda", referencing the long-running climate resilience program funded by it.

title: What would it take to make India’s cities better – and safer?
content_c:
Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.
On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.
Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.
I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.
As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.
The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.
Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.
So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.
For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.
Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.
In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.
“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”
The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.
India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.
For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.
In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.
A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)
“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.
Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.
What else we’re reading about
New Delhi declaration | The Brics summit held in New Delhi over the weekend adopted a declaration with Iran and the United Arab Emirates agreeing to a late-stage compromise on the language about the war in the Middle East. Chinese president, Xi Jinping, who visited India for the first time in almost seven years, announced that China would helm the group’s presidency for the next year.
Political donations | An investigation by the BBC’s Shubhangi Misra claimed that six unrecognised political parties registered in Gujarat received donations of £132m (Rs 1,700 crore) in 2023-24, higher than the income of national parties excluding the BJP. Despite fielding few candidates and evidence of little political activity, the high amounts expose glaring gaps in oversight of political finances.
Women’s health support | Two south Indian states, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, have recently announced policies aimed at supporting women through perimenopause and menopause. Karnataka plans to introduce a women’s health programme that will integrate menopause into the public health system. Tamil Nadu will assess the physical and mental health needs of perimenopausal women.
Calling all emerging writers | Applications are open for South Asia Speaks, a wonderful platform for emerging writers from the region offering free, year-long mentorship and resources to develop a book-length project. The deadline is 30 September – find out more and apply here.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
This week, writer and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:
“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.
A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing
2,192
That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check
As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.
Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.
“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”
Get in touch
Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

title: UK: Village votes to 'secede' in asylum center plan protest
content_c:
UK: Village votes to 'secede' in asylum center plan protest
September 16, 2026
An English village of about 350 people has voted to "secede" from the United Kingdom, in a symbolic protest against government plans to set up an asylum reception center nearby.
Residents of Piddington, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Oxford, celebrated with a placard reading "Principality of Piddington" near the village road sign on Wednesday.
They oppose plans, still under review, to house asylum seekers in a disused military base, MoD Bicester (Site A).
What happened in the tongue-in-cheek breakaway vote?
The village's parish council said that 312 people cast ballots in the vote, a turnout of almost 92%.
Participants in the vote, which had no legal basis, were asked to agree or disagree with the statement: "I support Piddington seeking to secede from the United Kingdom and pursuing self-determination."
Of them, 285 voted to secede, 26 voted against, and one spoiled their ballot.
Parish council chair Tim McNally said that, going forward, the village would identify as the "Principality of Piddington."
"For us, it's about proportiality," McNally told Sky News. "How does a small village of 350 odd people assimilate with 1,250 males?"
He accused the government of "trying to rush this whole plan through."
An Oxfordshire County Council official told the BBC the plan risked making the village and the facility a "lightning rod" for potentially violent far-right protests.
The vote attracted the attention of self-styled anti-migration "influencers" online.
How did the government react?
The Labour government has been trying to move asylum seekers housed in hotels, an unpopular legacy they inherited from previous British governments, into disused military facilities by 2029.
This follows repeated protests at or near hotels and rented accommodation used for the purpose.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who only recently took over the rapidly rotating top job in British politics, promised to "look at the issues raised by the community and in the referendum."
But he also said that the "vast majority" of British people backed a government plan to stop housing asylum seekers in hotels and argued that it was "fair" to locate holding centers around the country.
Speaking to the BBC, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said a former military base was "a better option for housing asylum seekers" than hotels or rented accommodation.
One drawback with disused military bases, however, is that they are often intentionally placed in remote and rural areas. This can be ideal for military training and activity, but is less obviously suited to housing migrants with limited mobility and resources.
Migration and asylum have been contentious political issues in the UK for decades. But successive governments have faced particular pressure in recent years, with the populist right-wing Reform UK and Restore Britain parties gaining ground against the established political giants the Conservatives and Labour.
The most recent manifestation of this was anti-migrant protests in the coastal city of Portsmouth earlier this month.
What does the government say about its plans for MoD Bicester?
In a Q+A published in July about its plans for Ministry of Defense (MoD) Bicester (Site A), the British government said the site "would provide basic, safe accommodation and would be designed to be largely self‑sufficient to minimize any impact on the local community."
It stressed the plan was still subject to feasibility studies, planning permission requirements and other red tape.
It didn't state how many people would be housed there, except to say: "The Home Office would take a phased approach to full occupancy, starting with smaller numbers at first."
It did specify that the facility would hold males aged 18-65.
The government said that if used, the site would be in operation for a minimum of 10 years. Relocating to military bases was "just the first step in the government’s work to exit hotels and source more appropriate accommodation to meet our statutory obligations," it said.
Safety for the local community, staff, and those accommodated on site would be "of the utmost importance," it said. The facility would be monitored round the clock by a security provider and via surveillance footage.
It would also be "designed to be as self-sufficient as possible including laundry facilities and communal spaces," the British government said.
