title: Reform donor Ben Delo loaned £350k to academic found to have engaged in online bullying
content_c:
Reform UK’s new mega-donor Ben Delo gave a £350,000 loan to a conservative writer fighting a legal case in which a judge later found she had engaged in online bullying and regrettable conduct with a “whiff of threat and antisemitism”.
Nina Power and her friend, the writer Daniel DC Miller, brought the legal action for defamation against the performance artist Luke Turner, who they had accused of falsely calling them antisemitic. At the same time, Turner brought a counter-claim against the pair accusing them of harassment.
Their libel action failed on the grounds that Turner’s online reach was not big enough to have caused harm to their reputations, while the harassment case also failed on the basis that their conduct was not unlawful.
The loan from Delo to help fund Power’s case before the 2023 trial shines a light on the Reform supporter’s involvement in backing a landmark legal tussle over the boundaries of free speech.
It is understood Delo did not and does not believe Power and Miller held antisemitic views as alleged by Turner, and would never knowingly provide financial or any other support to those who did.
In the case, Miller, who is Jewish, and Power denied promoting fascist or antisemitic views, and said they did not know Turner was Jewish. The judge found there was “no overt antisemitism” displayed by the pair.
But in the counter-claim of harassment, the judge described social media posts by Miller and Power as having “the whiff of threat and antisemitism which they themselves can fairly be held to have created”, although she ruled it was “too occasional, intangible, diffuse and unconsolidated” to have been unlawful.
She said the “radio frequencies of macabre imagery and casualness around antisemitic tropes into which Mr Turner tuned do yield a discernible signal but not one strong enough to be recognised objectively as antisemitic hate speech or a resolved engagement with physical violence sufficient to render this conduct quasi-criminal”.
The judge also said: “Mr Turner evidently had been harassed to a quasi-criminal (or indeed criminal) degree by other people. But what Mr Miller and Ms Power did was not of that order.”
After the failure of the cases, Turner was awarded costs of £1m amounting to 80% of the total, and Power was declared bankrupt. In the course of the bankruptcy proceedings it emerged that Delo had loaned her a sum in the region of £350,000 to help pay her lawyers.
It is understood the loan was made by Delo weeks before the trial started when Power’s conditional fee arrangement with her lawyers collapsed. The loan was made on a commercial basis and secured against the value of a London property she owns, with a repayment schedule.
Delo has been known to be a supporter of the Free Speech Union, run by the Conservative peer Toby Young, and has funded a base known for anti-woke causes.
Power is a former leftwing academic who has written in publications including the Guardian about feminism. She has since described her journey towards being “conservative in the true sense of that word” and wrote a book, What Do Men Want? Masculinity and Its Discontents, in which she argues men have been demonised.
The 2023 high court ruling describes how Miller and Turner were involved in an online incident which emerged from Turner’s involvement in the London arts scene. The artist had risen to prominence thanks to his creative collaborations with the Hollywood actor Shia LaBeouf.
The pair took opposing sides in relation to the London art gallery LD50, which had staged a symposium featuring neo-reactionary speakers and a show advertised online with a quotation from Adolf Hitler, in German gothic font. While Turner described the venue as an alt-Nazi gallery, Miller joined the counter-protest, standing outside LD50 with a placard calling for “the right to openly discuss ideas”.
Miller, who told the court he was of Jewish heritage, is closely associated with the magazine IM-1776, which platforms hard-right views, having previously contributed to the title as an editor and an author. Among the articles published by IM-1776 are pieces celebrating the “Unabomber” Ted Kaczynski and the proto-fascist Italian nationalist Gabriele D’Annunzio.
In the trial, Turner acknowledged he had been wrong to claim Miller was the author of a blog advocating a Hitler-style disability policy.
WhatsApp chats between Miller and Power, disclosed as part of the 2023 trial, did show them dismissing anti-racism as a “psyop”. The term refers to psychological operations used by the military or governments to influence public behaviour.
Power wrote: “The social disapproval for ‘racism’ is a psyop to stop people realising that there *are* alien and fairy races,” and that “black and white were alien races and very different”.
In a later exchange Power brought up Hitler’s autobiographical political manifesto, Mein Kampf, writing “I think … at some point … we need to read Mein Kampf properly …”, adding that she wanted to “understand it”.
In an episode referenced in the judgment, Miller performed at a public event in Athens, delivering a lecture in the persona of the Italian far-right philosopher and antisemite Julius Evola. During the rise of fascism, Evola called for measures to counter “the Jewish menace”. He opposed democracy in favour of a caste-based aristocratic order and was convicted on appeal during the 1950s of trying to revive fascism.
The judge found the pair had between them labelled Turner “low IQ’, ‘sociopathic’, ‘paranoid’, ‘deranged’, ‘obsessive’, ‘paranoid schizophrenic’, ‘dangerously mentally ill’ and so on and on – sometimes accompanied by messages to ‘get help’.” She said in her ruling that Power told her from the witness box that the latter proceeded from genuine and empathetic concern. The judge was unconvinced.
During the trial, Miller and Power denied promoting antisemitic philosophies, describing their interest in the subject as a quest to “critically understand” the issues.
Power and Delo declined to comment. Miller said the story was “based on a systematic distortions of facts”, adding: “I am myself Jewish and proudly Jewish.”
author: Rowena Mason and Juliette Garside
description: Judge said Nina Power and her friend’s social media posts had ‘the whiff of threat and antisemitism’Reform UK’s new mega-donor Ben Delo gave a £350,000 loan to a conservative writer fighting a legal case in which a judge later found she had engaged in online bullying and regrettable conduct with a “whiff of threat and antisemitism”.Nina Power and her friend, the writer Daniel DC Miller, brought the legal action for defamation against the performance artist Luke Turner, who they had accused of falsely calling them antisemitic. At the same time, Turner brought a counter-claim against the pair accusing them of harassment. Continue reading...

title: British-American writer Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
content_c:
British-American writer Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
September 16, 2026
Playwright and author Bonnie Greer died aged 77, her husband David Hutchins said on Wednesday in a statement to British media.
A celebrated writer born in Chicago who at first plied her trade in New York, Greer spent most of her adult life in the UK.
She took up dual citizenship and became a regular and prominent political commentator in Britain.
What did Greer's husband say about her death?
Greer's widower Hutchins hailed her as "an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life."
Hutchins said his late wife had suffered succumbed to a brief illness.
He said those closest to Greer would remember her warmth, humor, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together.
"To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her," Hutchins said. The pair married in 1993, seven years after Greer emigrated.
Who was Bonnie Greer?
Greer was born in Chicago in 1948, the eldest of seven children from a family of Mississippi sharecroppers.
Her familial exposure to the UK predated even her birth — her father Ben was stationed in Britain during World War II and had taken part in the D-Day landings.
She gravitated towards creative writing amid the civil rights movement in the US after a college professor told her he did not believe women should pursue a legal career.
Having studied theater in Chicago she moved to New York as a young aspiring writer.
Greer settled in the UK in 1986 and worked mainly in theater with women and ethnic minorities.
She acquired British citizenship in 1997 and wrote a series of successful radio plays aired on the BBC and musicals. Her 1993 play "Munda Negra" exploring mental health problems among black women won the Verity Bargate Award for best play.
Greer also became a frequent contributor to political and social debate in Britain, frequently appearing on topical shows like "Newsnight" and "Question Time".
Greer was a prominent supporter of Barack Obama and wrote a memoir and personal musical history in 2009 called "Obama Music." She also campaigned against the UK's exit from the EU, Brexit, and Donald Trump's first term as US president at around the same time.
She held a series of cultural roles, including being president of the Bronte Society, chancellor of Kingston upon Thames University in London, a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature, and a board member of the Royal Opera House and the London Film School.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko
description: Chicago-born playwright Bonnie Greer, who became a familiar face in British political discourse later in life, has died. Her husband David Hutchins announced news of Greer's death.

title: Premier Carney: Kanada ist offen für EU-Sondermitgliedschaft
content_c:
Premier Carney im EU-Parlament Kanada ist offen für EU-Sondermitgliedschaft
Kein volles EU-Mitglied, aber eine Art Sondermitgliedschaft - das könnte Kanada bekommen. Die EU hat einen solchen Vorschlag gemacht, Premier Carney begrüßt den Vorstoß. Ob es wirklich dazu kommt, ist aber ungewiss.
Die aggressive Handels- und Außenpolitik von US-Präsident Donald Trump hat das eigentlich enge Verhältnis der USA zu Kanada schwer belastet. Das nordamerikanische Land ist deshalb auf der Suche nach neuen, verlässlichen Partnern - und könnte in Europa fündig werden. Zwischen der Europäischen Union und Kanada bahnt sich eine deutlich engere Zusammenarbeit an.
Das wurde heute beim Auftritt des kanadischen Premierministers Mark Carney im EU-Parlament deutlich. In einer Rede vor den Parlamentariern machte Carney deutlich, dass sein Land offen ist für die Idee einer Art EU-Sondermitgliedschaft. "Wir begrüßen diesen Vorstoß", sagte er. Umfragen zeigten, dass eine überwältigende Mehrheit der Kanadierinnen und Kanadier deutlich engere Beziehungen unterstützen würde, so Carney.
"Gemeinsam sind wir stärker"
"Wir sind keine Schönwetterverbündeten", sagte der Kanadier den Abgeordneten. "Wir stehen für gemeinsame Werte, für die wir immer gekämpft haben." Kanada und die EU seien jeweils stark, fuhr Carney fort, "gemeinsam sind wir stärker".
EU-Kommissionspräsidentin Ursula von der Leyen hatte am Mittwoch dafür geworben, Kanada zum ersten "assoziierten Mitglied" der Europäischen Union zu machen. Als konkrete Bereiche für eine noch engere Zusammenarbeit nannte von der Leyen Technologiefragen, die Produktion von Rüstungsgütern sowie die Künstliche Intelligenz und die Arktis-Politik. Wie eine assoziierte EU-Mitgliedschaft konkret gestaltet werden soll, erklärte sie allerdings zunächst nicht.
Keine Rivalität zu Großmächten
Carney sagte nun, Kanada und Europa sollten ihre strategische Autonomie durch eine enge Zusammenarbeit über das gesamte Spektrum strategischer Fähigkeiten hinweg sichern. "Wir wollen widerstandsfähiger werden, damit niemand unsere offenen Märkte kontrollieren, unsere Souveränität beeinträchtigen, unsere territoriale Unversehrtheit bedrohen oder unsere Freiheiten, unsere Demokratien und unsere Rechtsstaatlichkeit untergraben kann", erklärte er.
Carney betonte, es gehe nicht darum, einen dritten Block zu schaffen, der zu einem Rivalen der Großmächte werden solle. Man strebe nicht nach Macht, um andere zu beherrschen.
Trump warnt, Brüssel beschwichtigt
US-Präsident Trump hatte zuvor auf den Vorschlag von der Leyens mit einer Drohung reagiert. "Ich halte das für lächerlich", sagte er auf den Vorschlag angesprochen. Falls er es als "feindseligen Akt" empfinden sollte, würde er hohe Zölle verhängen oder den Handel mit Europa in vielen Bereichen einstellen, warnte Trump.
Ein Sprecher der EU-Kommission erklärte darauf nun: "Wie unsere Präsidentin gestern klargemacht hat, richtet sich die vorgeschlagene Stärkung unserer Partnerschaft mit Kanada gegen niemanden. Sie soll vielmehr unsere gemeinsame Stärke fördern."
Freihandelsabkommen noch nicht in Kraft
Eine reguläre EU-Mitgliedschaft Kanadas ist nach den geltenden Verträgen nicht möglich. Nach Artikel 49 des EU-Vertrags können nur europäische Staaten der Union beitreten.
Mit der EU ist Kanada derzeit vor allem über das Freihandelsabkommen CETA eng verbunden. Dieses wird seit 2017 vorläufig angewendet, ist aber noch immer nicht endgültig in Kraft. Zehn Mitgliedstaaten wie Belgien, Frankreich und Irland haben es bis heute nicht ratifiziert. Auch deswegen gilt es als äußerst ungewiss, ob die Idee für eine assoziierte EU-Mitgliedschaft Kanadas umgesetzt werden kann.

title: Geniale Züge in Samarkand: Usbekistans Aufstieg zur Schach-Großmacht
content_c:
Usbekistans Aufstieg zur Schach-Großmacht
15. September 2026
Es ist gar nicht so einfach, in diesen Tagen mit Rustam Kasimjanov ins Gespräch zu kommen. Der Usbeke ist Großmeister und einer der weltweit bekanntesten Trainer im Schachsport. Im Augenblick ist Kasimjanov viel in seiner Heimat unterwegs.
Dort findet die "Schach-Olympiade" statt, die Mannschafts-WM der Männer und der Frauen. Rund 2000 Spieler treten bis zum 27. September in der historischen Seidenstraßen-Metropole Samarkand gegeneinander an.
"Die Vorfreude ist definitiv da", berichtet der 46-jährige Kasimjanov der Deutschen Welle über die Stimmung vor Ort. "Schach ist inzwischen in Usbekistan sehr populär und das wird nach der Olympiade wahrscheinlich zu einem richtigen Boom werden", so Kasimjanov. "Vorausgesetzt unsere Mannschaft spielt vernünftig", fügt er mit einem Augenzwinkern hinzu.
Schach-Dekret des Präsidenten
Dass Schach in dem zentralasiatischen Land inzwischen eine große Bedeutung hat, ist auch ein Verdienst Kasimjanovs. Der Usbeke war 2004 für kurze Zeit der offizielle Weltmeister des Weltschachbunds FIDE - allerdings kam es nie zu dem Duell gegen den damals mit der FIDE zerstrittenen russischen Superstar Garri Kasparow.
Aufgrund seiner Erfolge vor 20 Jahren ist Kasimjanov in seinem auch heute noch Land ein bekannter Sportler und hat viele Usbeken für das Schachspiel begeistert.
"In Usbekistan unterstützt der Staat seit einigen Jahren den Schachsport mit substanziellen Mitteln", berichtet Kasimjanov. Shavkat Mirziyoyev, der Präsident des Landes, erließ sogar ein Dekret zum Thema Schach: "Maßnahmen zur weiteren Entwicklung und Popularisierung des Schachs sowie zur Verbesserung des Systems der Ausbildung von Schachspielern".
Mit Erfolg: Schon 2022 holten die usbekischen Männer die Goldmedaille bei der "Schach-Olympiade" und Ende 2026 bestreitet Usbekistans Nachwuchs-Star Javohir Sindarov den WM-Finalkampf gegen den indischen Titelverteidiger Dommaraju Gukesh.
Favoriten aus Asien - und Deutschland
Usbekistans rasanter Aufstieg steht für eine langfristige Entwicklung im internationalen Schach: Asien dominiert zunehmend das Geschehen an den Brettern - sowohl im Männer- als auch im Frauenschach.
Für Kasimjanov gibt es bei dieser "Schach-Olympiade" bei den Männern vier klare Favoriten: "Indien, China, USA und Usbekistan - in beliebiger Reihenfolge." Aber der 46-Jährige, der mit seiner Familie in der Nähe von Bonn wohnt, hat auch die Deutschen im Blick: "Ich erwarte schon lange, dass Deutschland ernsthaft um die Medaillen kämpft", so der Usbeke, der die Entwicklung im deutschen Schachsport genau beobachtet.
Dass Deutschland inzwischen zum Kreis der Favoriten gehört, hat vor allem mit Vincent Keymer zu tun. Der 21-jährige hat sich in der absoluten Weltspitze etabliert und gehört zu den Stars in der Schach-Szene. Das liegt auch an seiner Art, Schach zu spielen: "Ich habe sehr wenige Top-Turniere, in denen ich keine einzige Partie verliere, aber dafür gewinne ich auch mehr Partien als die meisten anderen Spieler", beschreibt Keymer seinen Stil im Gespräch mit der Deutschen Welle.
Schach ist eine Einzelsportart, aber bei den Olympiaden geht es um die Mannschaft. Vier Spieler sitzen bei einem Match für ihr Land an den Brettern. In dem immer noch jungen, aber schon sehr erfahrenen deutschen Team hat sich neben Keymer inzwischen auch Mathias Blübaum international ins Rampenlicht gespielt.
Der studierte Mathematiker qualifizierte sich Ende 2025 überraschend für das Kandidaten-Finale zur WM. Auch wenn es bei Blübaum in den letzten Monaten nicht mehr ganz so gut lief, tritt der 29-jährige mit breiter Brust in Samarkand an. "Nach diesem Jahr habe ich auf jeden Fall keine Angst, gegen die Weltspitze zu spielen, da habe ich inzwischen genug Erfahrung."
Magnus Carlsen tritt nicht an
"Bei der Olympiade gehört immer ein bisschen Glück dazu," sagt Mannschaftskollege Keymer. Glück, das bei den letzten Auftritten fehlte: Trotz vieler Vorschusslorbeeren reichte es für die deutschen Männer nie zu einer Medaille.
Beispiel Europameisterschaft 2025: Die deutschen Frauen erreichten einen starken dritten Platz - Keymer & Co. hingegen gingen einmal mehr leer aus. "Wir müssen diesmal vor allem die unnötigen Verluste gegen schwächere Teams vermeiden", lautet die Analyse des deutschen Spitzenmanns.
Ein Spieler, dem Keymer in Samarkand definitiv nicht am Brett begegnen wird, ist Ex-Weltmeister Magnus Carlsen. "Er beschäftigt sich natürlich nicht mehr so viel mit Schach," hat Vincent Keymer beobachtet. Carlsen - vor einigen Monaten Vater geworden - tritt diesmal nicht für seine Heimat Norwegen an.
Doch trotz einiger durchwachsener Turnierergebnisse in der letzten Zeit führt Carlsen immer noch die Weltrangliste an. Für Keymer ist es daher noch zu früh, den Norweger abzuschreiben: "Nur weil man von ihm gewöhnt ist, dass er alles zerlegt, kann man nicht sofort sagen, er ist nicht mehr Nummer Eins."
description: Usbekistan ist zwei Wochen lang das Zentrum der Schach-Szene: Bei der Team-WM ist der Gastgeber einer der Favoriten. Aber auch Deutschland hat Chancen.

title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
content_c:
Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
- Published
The tone over the Falkland Islands dispute has been sharpening in Argentina from well before President Javier Milei's late-night national address on sanctions earlier this week.
It's tempting to see a visual representation of the tension in the jubilant Argentine players celebrating their hard-fought win over England at the Fifa World Cup this summer holding a banner which read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" - the Falklands are Argentine - in front of their deliriously happy fans. However, the ill-feeling has been fomenting for much longer.
President Milei began his Thursday address with a brief history of the Falklands, very much from the Argentine perspective. He repeated the refrain at the heart of their position: the islands "rightfully belong" to Argentina. The British had invaded and colonially occupied the islands in 1833, he said, violently wrestling the territory from Argentina's hands.
The UK Government would say he conveniently overlooked a few details. The European powers interchanged control over the islands throughout the 17th and 18th centuries. In December 1831, an Argentine settlement was largely dismantled not by the British but by an American warship, the USS Lexington, amid a dispute over local fishing and sealing rights, after which many inhabitants left. An Argentine garrison which arrived in 1832 was expelled by the British when they reoccupied the land in 1833.
Still, if the Americans had a hand in forcing the Argentines out two centuries ago, they may now play a central role in strengthening the Argentine claim. President Milei certainly thinks so.
"Winds of change" were blowing, he assured the Argentine people, after President Trump said he was "re-evaluating" the US position on the Falklands.
That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course, given that President Reagan provided material support to Margaret Thatcher during the Falklands War in 1982 – an act which reinforced the long-standing alliance between London and Washington in times of conflict.
For Trump, however, that mutual support – the "Special Relationship" – was eroded by Sir Keir Starmer when the UK Government chose not to join the US war on Iran.
"You weren't there to help me", the president retorted in an interview with GB News this week. The Falklands were "a long way away", he said. The Falkland Islanders – who voted almost unanimously to remain a British overseas territory in 2013 – would point out that distance from London to the Falklands is fractionally shorter than the distance between Washington DC and the US territory of Guam, in the western Pacific.
Still, Trump's words have undoubtedly galvanised Milei. As have the opinion polls. He urgently needs a boost ahead of a presidential election next year in which one of his challengers, his estranged vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, has presented herself as a tougher defender of national sovereignty and attacked Milei's diplomatic approach on the Falklands as failing.
Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.
With two energy companies – the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK – due to undertake work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.
On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have.
In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally.
The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.
Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.
Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".
Correction 11 September: An earlier version of this report said that a US warship had forced out an Argentine settlement from the Falklands in 1831, leaving the islands uninhabited. In fact, while many inhabitants left, some remained. An Argentine garrison was also expelled when the British reoccupied the land in 1833. The article was amended to reflect this.
description: With Argentina's President Milei promising "winds of change" over the Falklands, will Donald Trump shift his stance on British rule?

title: The furious dispute over what caused Air India flight 171 to crash
content_c:
It was a hot and dry afternoon on 12 June last year, when Air India Flight 171 left the terminal at Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Airport in Ahmedabad in the western Indian state of Gujarat. Settling into their seats for the nine-and-a-half-hour journey to London were 230 passengers - including 169 Indian nationals and 53 Britons. Looking after them were 10 cabin crew.
On the flight deck were Captain Sumeet Sabharwal, a pilot with decades of experience, and his younger colleague, first officer Clive Kunder. Just 32 seconds after take-off the plane crashed, killing all but one of those on board. Another 19 people on the ground were also killed.
CCTV footage from the airport and a social media video show the aircraft taking-off in what looks like a normal fashion, but rather than gain height it appears to hang in the air, before gliding gently downwards.
It disappears from view behind buildings and trees. Seconds later a huge cloud of flame and black smoke appears, and the magnitude of the disaster becomes apparent. What is not at all clear from the footage, however, is what actually caused the crash.
Finding out why so many people died is the job of India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB), part of the country's Ministry of Civil Aviation. Under international law, as set out in Annex 13 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation, the country in which an accident occurs is directly responsible for the official investigation.
Other parties, including the country where the aircraft or its engines were built, can also take an active part as "accredited representatives". In the case of AI171, that means the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB). The NTSB sent a delegation which included technical experts from Boeing, which made the plane itself and GE Aerospace, which built the engines, as well as the US aviation regulator, the Federal Aviation Administration.
According to Annex 13, "the sole objective of the investigation of an accident or incident shall be the prevention of accidents or incidents. It is not the purpose of this activity to apportion blame or liability".
Nevertheless, there is a great deal at stake.
For Boeing, a company already reeling from years of safety scandals, it is about the integrity of one of its premium products: the 787 Dreamliner, an aircraft with a hitherto impeccable safety record. Air India, a loss-making airline belonging to the Tata Group, can ill-afford to see its brand tarnished. Families of those who died, meanwhile, want to know what really happened to their loved ones.
The final conclusions of the investigation have yet to be published, although more could become apparent in the coming days. But it has already generated intense controversy, which has exposed deeper questions about the way inquiries into major air incidents are carried out. So can national authorities be trusted to conduct investigations that critics say are vulnerable to perceptions of political pressure and corporate influence?
The inquiry backlash
In theory, the inquiry should be impartial and informative – a learning process focused solely on improving passenger safety. But in the case of AI171, the information revealed by the investigation so far has triggered a major backlash from safety campaigners, pilots' groups and lawyers acting for the bereaved relatives.
A key factor in this has been the preliminary report issued by the AAIB a month after the accident. The 15-page document did not draw any conclusions about the causes of the crash, or make any recommendations.
Nonetheless, just two short paragraphs generated a great deal of controversy.
First, it was noted that according to the aircraft's flight data recorder, the two fuel cutoff switches - normally used when starting the engines before a flight and shutting them down afterwards – transitioned from the run to the cutoff position seconds after take-off. This would have deprived the engines of fuel, causing them to lose thrust rapidly.
The report then says: "In the cockpit voice recording, one of the pilots is heard asking the other why did he cutoff. The other pilot responded that he did not do so."
This brief statement, provided without a transcript or any indication of who was speaking, sparked intense speculation about the actions of the pilots. Newsweek, for example, focused on the "troubling possibility: that a seasoned captain may have deliberately doomed his jet – and nearly 250 lives". Former NTSB chairman Robert Sumwalt told CBS News the report showed "this was not a problem with the airplane or the engines. Instead…somebody in the cockpit shut the fuel off to those engines."
A few days later, The Wall Street Journal weighed in. Citing people familiar with the matter, it claimed that recordings of dialogue between the pilots suggested it was the Captain, Sumeet Sabharwal, who had flipped the fuel switches.
It is important to note that this was merely a preliminary report, and within days, the AAIB issued a statement condemning "selective and unverified reporting" in the international press as "irresponsible". It urged the public and the media to "refrain from spreading premature narratives that risk undermining the integrity of the investigative process."
By then, arguably, the damage had already been done.
"When a pilot is alive he can defend himself" says Capt. CS Randhawa, president of the Federation of Indian Pilots (FIP). "When the pilot is dead, all the agencies can collude – and they put the blame on the pilot, to save the manufacturer. And this is seen the world over. It's not the first time".
His organisation, which represents around 6,000 pilots, condemned the preliminary report as "irrevocably compromised". Together with Sumeet Sabharwal's 91-year-old father, Pushkar Raj Sabharwal, they took their concerns to India's Supreme Court, demanding a judicial investigation into the crash.
Former UK air accident investigator Tim Atkinson agrees that there is always a temptation to blame a dead pilot for a serious accident.
"It's incredibly, incredibly convenient for all concerned," he says. "You know, the regulator's off the hook, the operator's off the hook, the manufacturer's off the hook. And that's why you have to push back against it so hard."
However, he personally believes that in this case, there is no other credible explanation – a view that is common among aviation professionals.
"I am in absolutely no doubt this is a homicide-suicide. And if you set out to investigate one of those, and try to show it is an aviation accident, you'll fail – because it isn't", he explains.
Nevertheless, safety campaigners in India and the US, along with the FIP, have pushed back vigorously against the pilot suicide theory. They point to reports alleging prior faults with the aircraft, as well as apparent anomalies in the timelines set out in the preliminary report, as evidence that the crash could realistically have been caused by a serious electrical failure.
The plane – registered as VT-ANB – was delivered to Air India in 2014. According to the Foundation for Aviation Safety, a US body led by the former senior Boeing manager turned whistleblower, Ed Pierson, it suffered from a series of serious electrical problems throughout its lifetime. Air India denies this.
Documents seen by the BBC show an incident of "burning" in one of the plane's main power panels in 2022. Air India says repairs were "carried out in accordance with Boeing-approved maintenance procedures" and that "the aircraft was returned to service only after applicable airworthiness requirements had been satisfied".
The preliminary report, meanwhile, notes that the aircraft had been permitted to fly with a known fault in its "core network", a framework that links the aircraft's computers and associated electronics and is often described as the "central nervous system" of the plane.
Boeing has referred all questions about what happened to the Indian AAIB.
Competing theories
A key theory put forward by campaigners is that the crash may have occurred because a major electrical failure caused the aircraft's main flight computers to reboot seconds after takeoff. They say this created a situation where the aircraft's systems briefly believed the plane was actually on the ground, even though it was in the air. A safety system detected dangerous levels of engine thrust, assumed a malfunction, and ordered the fuel supply to be cut off, the theory goes.
Under this scenario, fuel switches in the cockpit were not actually touched – the flight data recorder may instead have registered the electronic command to cut the fuel supply, rather than the physical movement of switches.
Rachel Chitra, an investigative journalist who has published a series of technically detailed articles in India, has promoted this theory. In her work, she points out a series of inconsistencies in the preliminary report. Among these is an account of how the engines attempted to relight after their fuel supply was restored.
The report indicates that "Engine 1's core deceleration stopped, reversed and started to progress to recovery. Engine 2 was able to relight but could not arrest core speed deceleration…". But Chitra claims her research, which she says is backed up by engineering documents, suggests that any such relight would have been physically impossible at the speed the aircraft had reached and with the power sources available.
Meanwhile, lawyers acting on behalf of victims' families have focused on the moment at which an emergency power system began to operate. The Ram Air Turbine (RAT) is a small propeller which can rotate in the airstream to provide electricity and hydraulic pressure when other systems in the plane fail. On AI171, CCTV footage shows that the RAT had deployed immediately after take-off.
According to the preliminary report, the RAT was providing hydraulic power within five seconds of the fuel switches being cut off. However, simulator tests, the results of which have been shared with the BBC, appear to demonstrate that it would actually need 14-18 seconds. This would imply that it had actually deployed far earlier, potentially while the aircraft was on the ground, and well before the fuel was cut off.
Mike Andrews is an attorney with the Beasley Allen law firm which represents the families of 135 victims of the crash. He says the findings raise important questions, which cast doubt over the pilot suicide narrative.
"The RAT deployment is a symptom of something else going on," he explains. "In order for it to be out, something has happened…if it is out prior to the fuel switch allegation, our question still is: why?
"It is a symptom of something that has gone wrong".
Safety consultant and author Eckhard Jann thinks such controversy in a case like this is inevitable.
"We have gotten used to safe airline travels," he says, and as the reason for the B787 crash in Ahmedabad is unknown, it "rattles the world".
Former investigator Tim Atkinson thinks the "incredibly complex multiple electrical failure scenario" is unrealistic. He believes the physical architecture of the plane's systems would not allow it to happen.
For him, the controversy over AI171 comes down to "just the difficulty we all have talking about homicide and suicide".
Under Annex 13, those investigating a serious air accident are meant to publish a final report within 12 months if they can. However, this is not always possible. If a final report cannot be issued, an interim report must be published on the anniversary of the accident.
This means India's AAIB must publish an update of some kind by Friday, 12 June.
There is now widespread doubt that it will be conclusive. In May, India's civil aviation minister muddied the waters when he told reporters the investigation into the crash was into its "last stage", and that the final report would "mostly…come after a month".
Controversy and cynicism
Whatever report is published, it looks highly unlikely to reverse the wave of controversy and cynicism that has already engulfed the AI171 investigation.
A great deal of that stems from perceptions that the companies involved are being protected from blame.
Boeing, certainly, can ill-afford to see questions raised about the safety of the 787. Although it suffered severe teething problems in its early days, including a major battery fire on one aircraft at Boston airport in 2013, the 787 has since racked up a very impressive safety record. AI171 was the first time a 787 had been lost due to an accident. However, production of the plane has proved deeply problematic over the years with reports of defects and manufacturing problems, while whistleblowers have drawn attention to what they considered to be dangerous practices on the production line.
Boeing has consistently denied allowing potentially dangerous planes to enter service.
The manufacturer's corporate culture has, however, come under fire thanks to a series of issues involving the smaller 737 Max - including two fatal crashes. It has been forced by regulators to implement a comprehensive safety and quality improvement plan.
Air India, meanwhile, has struggled for years, racking up heavy losses. After being under government ownership until 2022, it was then taken over by the giant Tata Group. This was meant to herald a turnaround, but it has continued to struggle in what has been a difficult environment for the industry as a whole. It can not afford further damage to its brand.
This is not the first time the current system for investigating major air accidents has faced criticism. It has however highlighted ongoing concerns about the integrity of high-profile and often politically sensitive inquiries.
According to the non-profit Foundation for Aviation Safety, asking the country where the accident occurs to oversee an investigation "can trap the process within local bureaucracies or political pressures. Even more troubling, manufacturers' technical experts, while ostensibly assisting investigators, may face intense pressure to deflect corporate culpability."
"Diagnosing an extremely complex airplane with an outdated playbook is impossible," says the Foundation's executive director, Ed Pierson.
Eckhard Jann points out that the current system is still largely founded on principles set out in 1944. In today's more globalised world, he thinks "investigating authorities are having more and more difficulty fulfilling their duties: to investigate independently and make solid recommendations in order to improve aviation safety."
The International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), the UN agency which oversees international air travel, is well aware that investigations can be vulnerable to conflicts of interest. In March, it set out a series of changes to Annex 13. These set out guidance on what states can do to enhance credibility and improve transparency, including by delegating investigations to a third party if necessary. The new measures will take effect in late 2028.
More from InDepth
- 'Carspreading' is on the rise - and not everyone is happy about it 
  - Published18 December 2025
- The true cost of cyber attacks - and the business weak spots that allow them to happen 
  - Published6 October 2025
But according to Jann, this is just a sticking plaster. "Whatever ICAO is trying to change and improve is only trying to reduce the symptoms, but global aviation, global manufacturers and global airlines demand a global answer," he says.
Such an answer, he believes, would be "a global investigation authority with enough power to demand changes based on their recommendations."
But others question whether such investigations are even worthwhile in the modern era, given the tremendous cost and effort involved, among them, former investigator Tim Atkinson.
"This cycle of an accident happens, you investigate it impartially, make recommendations, prevent future occurrences… it doesn't really happen any more.
"The things that prevent people dying these days are nothing to do with that. They're to do with better technology."
However, if investigations are to continue, he says, much more transparency is needed, with information being provided much more freely at an early stage.
"I've always believed that", he says. "And I've never seen negative consequences of it".

When an Air India plane heading to London crashed in a residential area of the Indian city of Ahmedabad, just seconds after take off, it killed all but one onboard. We hear from eyewitnesses, aviation experts and the families of those who died.

title: Burnham urged by opposition parties to follow Macron and act with more urgency on Russian threat – as it happened
content_c:
Burnham urged by opposition parties to follow Macron and act with more urgency on Russian threat
The French president, Emmanuel Macron said today that the threat posed by Russia’s shadow operations was growing across Europe, and he had ordered measures to protect France’s critical infrastructure from increasing Russian “hybrid attacks”, AFP reports. AFP says:
“The Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified,” he said after a meeting with French political leaders, before he heads to the UN General Assembly next week.
France’s interior minister had met regional prefects to step up “vigilance in response to the Russian hybrid attacks”, Macron said after the meeting with presidential hopefuls and party leaders ahead of next year’s election.
He said he had ordered “the government to prepare a plan to protect our critical infrastructure” and the “most sensitive” defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyber-attacks.
The French president said that despite the Russian threats France would continue to support Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion of the pro-Western country in February 2022.
He also vowed that France would respond to Russia’s shadow attacks.
“This will not go unanswered,” Macron said, without elaborating.
“The intention behind it is to intimidate us and to derail the effort to support the Ukrainians. The consequence will be the opposite,” he added.
“We are not intimidated, because we know that what is at stake today in Ukraine is our security.”
Commenting this morning on the news that Macron had summoned of French political leaders to discuss the Russian threat, Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said:
Given how seriously the French government is taking Russian drone threats, it is fair to ask, are we doing enough?
It’s high time the government started taking this threat seriously and briefed opposition leaders on the threats and consequences for UK security.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, made a similar point in a post on social media late last night. Referencing a statement by Donald Tusk, the Polish PM, she said:
Macron and Tusk are speaking and acting with an urgency that makes the latest reports about Russia violating Lithuanian airspace even more concerning. It is not clear that the Government is taking the threat from Russia seriously enough. Its own intelligence assessment says an attack on NATO could come by 2030, while repeated smaller-scale incursions are already taking place. It comes only weeks after CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow, reportedly to warn Russia against attacking a NATO member. Our European allies are responding with growing urgency, yet the Government still will not say what it intends to do on defence. The NATO Secretary General was in Britain only yesterday calling for that path to be set out, and I agree with him.
The Conservatives and Reform UK have urged urged Andy Burnham to address the threat posed by Russia with the same urgency as Emmanuel Macron. (See 2.43pm.) At a news conference, Macron declared:
In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified. The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine.
Andy Burnham has used a meeting with Irish counterpart Micheál Martin to push for deeper ties between the UK and the European Union. As the Press Association reports, e said the relationship with Ireland “matters so much on every single level” as the taoiseach became the first international leader to visit No 10 North. Burnham said it was “very fitting” for Martin to be the first head of government to visit the Manchester site because of the close ties between the north-west and Ireland.
Social care review chief Louise Casey says she is opposed to 'profiteering' by privately-run homes
Louise Casey, the crossbench peer and former Whitehall official leading the government’s review of adult social care, has said she is opposed to what she calls “profiteering” in the case sector.
In an interview with ITV News, Casey said that she thought that allowing large parts of adult social care to be run by private companies for profit was a “mistake”.
She told ITV:
What I would just personally object to on behalf of the taxpayer is what I call profiteering.
You’ve got, in some cases, I would say profiteering on the back of taxpayers and specifically on the back of people with higher levels of need. Where I think people are making bag loads of money, I think that’s wrong.
If you look back to the history of what we now call social care, we saw a massive shift in the 1980s. Essentially, the sort of outsourcing of all of that [care] to the private sector, without it being organised and managed, I think was probably a mistake.
Casey suggested she was particularly opposed to foreign-based private equity companies making huge profits from the UK care sector. She said:
I’m a great believer in not letting other people take British taxpayers money, whoever they are. And I think if we could provide those services and those resources here, then we should do it …
If there’s a private provider that’s taking 12 or 15% profit out of running care services for people, is that a good use of how we would plan for the next decade, when actually lots of FTSE 100 companies are very happy to take 5% profit? So these are the things we need to look at.
But Casey also suggested she would be wary of sudden changes to the system.
I think at the moment though, I would say one ought to be a bit careful because a lot of those companies, if you pulled them, the lifeline for the people we’ve met the same afternoon would stop. So you’ve just got to be really measured.
Casey is due to present her final report to the government next year. Andy Burnham has said that, for him, reforming adult social care is a priority, and he is prepared to use a lot of poltical capital pushing through change.
Most of the public discussion about adult social care focuses on the needs of people with dementia. But it is also a lifeline for adults with learning disabilities and Casey focused on this in her interview with ITV News, which has run a series of investigations into how public services look after people in this category.
Casey said she thought the NHS was failing people with learning disabilities and hospitals and that was why people with a learning disability have a life expectancy more than 20 years shorter than the average.
She told ITV:
I think that the National Health Service, particularly hospitals, are unable to sufficiently treat and look after people with learning disabilities,.
[There was] a case very recently of a woman who was 70 and had a stroke.
She had profound learning disabilities, ended up at a general ward, and they wouldn’t let her carers come into the ward, and her carers were the only people that could probably fully understand what she was saying and thinking.
Now people watching this tonight on the news will think, well, that’s insane, isn’t it? It’s almost hard to explain how the system just does that.
It’s like it’s got a one-track mind: it’s a medical condition, if I can’t medically treat you, it’s game over, not our responsibility anymore.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson urges unionists to cooperate ahead of next year's Stormont elections
Gavin Robinson, the DUP leader, has said unionists will not tolerate “egos” scuppering the “huge opportunity” that is next year’s Stormont assembly election, the Press Association reports. Speaking ahead of his party conference, starting later today, Robinson said unionists want to see unionist parties co-operating, and revealed he has met with UUP leader Jon Burrows and has more meetings planned. PA says:
The last assembly election in 2022 saw Sinn Féin make history by being the first non-unionist party to top the poll, and Michelle O’Neill become the first nationalist first minister.
Then Sinn Féin (27 MLAs) finished two seats ahead of the DUP (25), which now has 26 Assembly seats following the co-option of Peter Martin after the election of independent Alex Easton to Westminster in 2024.
Asked whether he believes his party can top the poll and reclaim the post of first minister, Robinson described a “huge opportunity for the wider unionist community” and called for unionist parties to co-operate.
He said the UUP benefited from co-operation in the past, referring to the election of Tom Elliott to the Fermanagh South Tyrone Westminster seat in 2015.
“If 2022 taught us anything it’s that division costs – there are fewer unionists around the executive table because of division within unionism, and so I believe that in this election in May, unionism can win if it is prepared to cooperate,” he told Press Association.
“I am willing to cooperate with other unionists. That’s not a new thing. I benefited from cooperation in 2015.
“The Ulster Unionists benefited from co-operation in 2015, and actually throughout the history of our party there has been a willingness to co-operate within the wider strategic interests of unionism.”
Burnham urged by opposition parties to follow Macron and act with more urgency on Russian threat
The French president, Emmanuel Macron said today that the threat posed by Russia’s shadow operations was growing across Europe, and he had ordered measures to protect France’s critical infrastructure from increasing Russian “hybrid attacks”, AFP reports. AFP says:
“The Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified,” he said after a meeting with French political leaders, before he heads to the UN General Assembly next week.

He also vowed that France would respond to Russia’s shadow attacks.
“This will not go unanswered,” Macron said, without elaborating.

Commenting this morning on the news that Macron had summoned of French political leaders to discuss the Russian threat, Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said:
Given how seriously the French government is taking Russian drone threats, it is fair to ask, are we doing enough?
It’s high time the government started taking this threat seriously and briefed opposition leaders on the threats and consequences for UK security.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, made a similar point in a post on social media late last night. Referencing a statement by Donald Tusk, the Polish PM, she said:
Macron and Tusk are speaking and acting with an urgency that makes the latest reports about Russia violating Lithuanian airspace even more concerning. It is not clear that the Government is taking the threat from Russia seriously enough. Its own intelligence assessment says an attack on NATO could come by 2030, while repeated smaller-scale incursions are already taking place. It comes only weeks after CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow, reportedly to warn Russia against attacking a NATO member. Our European allies are responding with growing urgency, yet the Government still will not say what it intends to do on defence. The NATO Secretary General was in Britain only yesterday calling for that path to be set out, and I agree with him.
Crypto millionaires would gain £500m over 5 years from Reform UK's crypto tax cuts, Labour analysis says
The Labour party has released an analysis suggesting that cryptocurrency millionaires could benefit to the tune of around £500m from Reform UK policies over the course of a parliament.
It is based on proposals in a bill published by Reform UK last year, and new figures published by HM Revenue and Customs about the number of Britons making large profits from cryptocurrency.
Last weekend it was announced that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, have given £72m (£36m each) to Reform UK. These donations dwarf previous record donations to British political parties – although legislation going through parliament about residency requirements for donors may result in the donations being deemed impermissible.
Reform UK insists that Delo and Harborne have not asked for anything in return for their donations, and it says they are just contributing out of a sense of patriotic duty to a party they believe will rescue the UK.
But it has been noted that a sharp rise in crypto donations to the party in recent years has coincided with Nigel Farage and his colleagues showing increasing interest in policies that would help the sector grow.
One example came last year when the party published a cryptoassets and digital finance bill. At the time it was the only draft legislation published by the party, suggesting policy in this area was more advanced than in others.
The bill proposes cutting capital gains tax on crypto investments to 10%, and this has allowed Labour to calculate that crypto millionaires could gain a total of around £500m over the course of a parliament.
The calculation is based on figures released in August by HM Revenue and Customssaying that “240 people reported more than £1m in capital gains from cryptoassets in the 2024 to 2025 tax year … accounting for £717m of cryptoasset gains between them.”
Explaining its figures in a briefing, Labour said:
Reform’s policy on crypto includes cutting capital gains tax (CGT) on crypto assets from the current level of 24% (for higher-rate taxpayers) and 18% (for basic-rate taxpayers) to a flat 10%.
Analysis of this policy shows that most of Reform’s tax giveaways would go to a very small high-earning group, after official HMRC statistics published last month found that 240 people in 2024/25 reported more than £1m in capital gains from crypto assets.
The HMRC stats show that this tiny group of crypto millionaires made £717m of the total £1.38bn crypto asset gains – reported by 17,600 people – in 2024/25.
The high-earning group of crypto investors could save around £100m a year in total under Reform’s policy. That means a tax cut worth half a billion pounds going to just 240 millionaires over the course of the next parliament.
A Labour spokesperson said:
Farage and Reform are drowning in sleaze and scandal. They can’t buy their way out of the questions that the public need answers to. It’s clear Reform are on the side of a handful of crypto-billionaires, while Labour is delivering the change people across the country want to see.
In response, Reform UK said it was the only party with a plan for crypto. A Reform UK spokesperson said:
Reform UK are the only party calling for proper regulation of cryptocurrency and ensuring that consumers are protected. Labour and the Tories don’t even have a plan.
Downing Street has issued its readout of Andy Burnham’s meeting with his Irish counterpart, Micheál Martin, this morning. A No 10 spokesperson said:
The two leaders began by reaffirming the close partnership between the UK and Ireland, as well as their shared commitment to upholding the Good Friday agreement.
They next discussed the importance of their joint commitments to addressing the legacy of the Troubles and working towards lasting reconciliation in Northern Ireland.
The prime minister then underlined the UK’s desire to work closely with Ireland during its presidency of the European Union as the UK seeks a closer relationship with Europe.
On Ukraine, the two leaders were clear in their united support for Ukraine against Russia’s illegal full-scale invasion and their determination to continue working to help Ukraine defend itself against Russian aggression.
They also looked ahead to the UK’s hosting of the next UK-Ireland summit in the first half of next year and agreed its importance in working together across priorities including security and trade.
Reform UK says it would intensify immigration checks on coaches and trains travelling from Ireland into Northern Ireland
Tonight the DUP is starting its annual conference in Belfast. One speaker will be Danny Kruger, the Reform UK MP in charge of the party’s plans for government. He has announced that Reform UK would intensify immigration checks on coaches, buses and trains travelling from Ireland into Northern Ireland.
In his speech, Kruger is expected to say:
Illegal and unvetted dangerous criminals, who cross into Northern Ireland, are abusing the soft Irish border, using it as a backdoor route into the UK. The absence of checkpoints at the border does not remove the requirement to have a right to enter.
Almost all illegal movement from the Republic into Northern Ireland is by scheduled coach or train, arriving at a handful of terminals. We will impose a civil penalty of £10,000 per passenger on any bus or rail operator for each illegal immigrant transported into Northern Ireland.
Reform UK says the checks would be carried by immigration enforcement officers and they would happen at terminals, not at the border crossing. Under the common travel area rules, there are no checks on people at the point they cross the Ireland/Northern Ireland border and, when Brexit took the UK out of the EU, both sides went to enormous efforts to ensure that border posts would not start having to go up.
In his speech, Kruger will insist that what he is proposing is “not a border check”. Reform UK says the Irish government already carries out immigration checks on vehicles on north-south transit routes but it claims these are “grossly insufficient”.
Disabled people in UK need right to travel abroad, say MPs, after ‘ridiculous’ restrictions
Disabled people must have a guaranteed right to travel abroad, MPs and peers have said, as further cases emerged of individuals barred from taking holidays as a result of “ridiculous” rules imposed by local NHS care boards and local councils, Frances Ryan and Patrick Butler report.
Kemi Badenoch says the Tories might take the government to court to stop council tax in Wandsworth having to almost double. (See 10.16am.)
But why is it going up so much?
In part, it is because it has always been so low for a long time. Wandsworth currently has the lowest council tax in England, at £509.84 for a band D home, plus a £510.51 precept set by the Greater London Authority.
In a blog about its funding situation this week, Wandsworth Conservatives say “a major factor behind the financial pressure is the Labour government’s decision to cut Wandsworth’s government funding by 40%”. Other factors are relevant too. They illustrated them with this chart.
The review updated and replaced the formulas that are used to assess each local authority’s level of relative need for funding, and which had last been updated in 2012/13. The new formulas take into account various socio-economic indicators such as deprivation, numbers of benefits claimants, and population (both resident and daytime).
The level of need, as assessed by these formulas, was then adjusted to take account of two things:
-the cost of delivering services in each area (using things like the costs of labour and of property, and travel times) – this was called the area costs adjustment;
-the resources that local authorities had available in the form of council tax; councils which charged less than the average level of council tax had their assessed level of need adjusted downwards, on the theory that they could raise their council tax to compensate for reduced central government funding. This was called the resource adjustment.
Tories argue that this means Wandsworth is now being penalised for the fact that it has been fiscally prudent in the past. Labour argues that this is just a matter of the system becoming fairer.
One government figure pointed to Wandsworth’s £194m of reserves. “For too long, an outdated council funding system, based on decades-old data, has entrenched inequality, leaving councils on a cliff edge and communities in deprived areas facing service cuts and rising bills, while some councils in less deprived areas have benefited disproportionately, building up their reserves.”
Labour has long argued that Wandsworth’s low rates were enabled by the decision of John Major’s Conservative government to bake in higher central government grants when it created council tax in 1993 to allow them to continue to hold it up as an exemplar.
They also quote Kate Ogden of the Institute for Fiscal Studies as saying the previous council funding formula was “arbitrary and quite hard to defend”. Residents in areas like Wandsworth would now have to accept that lower council tax “comes with consequences for public services”, she said.
Although Badenoch has described the cuts to funding in Wandsworth as “outrageous”, she seems to have glossed over the fact that, even with council tax going up 94%, residents will still be paying less then their counterparts in other London boroughs.
The Wandsworth Conservatives admit this. In their blog post, they say:
Under the proposals, the average band D council tax charge would increase by £958, taking the average total bill, including the amount paid to the Mayor of London, to £1,978. This represents an increase of 94% on today’s total bill …
Wandsworth currently has the lowest council tax in the country, with a band D property paying £1,020. Even with the proposed increase, Wandsworth would remain significantly cheaper than neighbouring boroughs including Lambeth and Merton, where current Band D charges are £2,047.11 and £2,146.76 respectively.
Irish PM praises Burnham for 'standing up for justice' with sanctions against illegal Israel settlements in West Bank
Micheál Martin, the taoiseach (Irish PM), thanked Andy Burnham for his stance on Israel as the two men met at No 10 North today.
Support for the Palestinian cause is particularly strong in Ireland because of its historical experience of colonialism, and, in a reference to the sanctions on West Bank settlements imposed by Burnham’s government, Martin said:
I think for the United Kingdom under your leadership to take the stance that it’s taken, I think, is important for … standing up for humanitarian values and justice and fulfilling the rights of all in the Middle East to security, to peace and to some decent future for their children and generations to come.
Before their talks, Martin also said he was looking forward to discussing with Burnham “even stronger and closer relationships between the European Union and the United Kingdom, which will be of benefit to the European Union and indeed to Ireland, quite frankly”.
Ireland currently holds the presidency of the EU and Burnham said he wanted “further steps to deepen the relationship with Europe”. He also said he was looking forward to a UK-EU summit later this year – even though no date for the summit has yet been agreed, and it keeps getting put back.
Burnham also told Martin he was particularly welcome in the north-west of England “where so many people have Irish connections”.
And Martin acknowledged that it had been a “very challenging and difficult week” for the PM because of the death of his father. He told the PM: “I think your sense of duty shines through.”
The UK Youth Parliament is at risk of being scrapped as its funding has not been confirmed beyond March 2027, the Press Assocation reports. PA says:
Formed in 1999, the UK Youth Parliament (UKYP) sees more than 300 children aged 11 to 18 democratically elected by their peers to represent young people in their area, who then debate and campaign on a variety of issues.
Once a year, they hold a debate in the House of Commons chamber.
While UKYP has been funded up to March, it is understood that the government has not committed to continuing the programme in its current form.
A government review into the UKYP, published in October last year, which found that while the parliament was delivering on its intended goals, only a quarter of young people knew about it, and some schools felt “excluded from the process”.
Today peers are urging the government to drop this idea.
In a letter to Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, the Lords communications and digital committee says:
We believe there is a case for articulating the BBC’s vital support for the creative economy more explicitly in its public purposes. However, giving the broadcaster a broad new objective to drive economic growth across the UK has few obvious benefits and clear associated risks.
And Barbara Keeley, the Labour peer who chairs the committee, said:
The government should use the BBC charter review white paper to set out a coherent and ambitious strategy for public service media over the next decade. It must also be realistic about what can be asked of the BBC as it grapples with significant financial pressures.
We can see no obvious benefit in a specific requirement for the BBC to drive economic growth across the UK. It already makes a massive contribution to the UK’s creative economy. Including an explicit economic growth public purpose in the new charter risks both mission drift and skewing commissioning towards more generic, more exportable content.
The proposal for the BBC to have an “economic growth” obligation in its charter came when Keir Starmer’s administration was trying to ensure every aspect of government policy contributed to the drive to accelerate growth.
Retail sales bounce back in Great Britain amid brighter signs for economy
Retail sales across Great Britain unexpectedly rose last month, the latest economic indicator to defy gloomy forecasts as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to present next month’s budget. Mark Sweney has the story.
Polanski accuses Burnham of being 'copy and paste Starmer' after Sky News leak reveals policy overlap
Last night Sam Coates at Sky News released details of a 50-page policy memo produced by Keir Starmer’s aides earlier this year as they were struggling to find policies that would help him stay in office. The document, dated 23 April, says it contains “bold ideas that meet the moment”. Coates says it shows how much overlap there is between what Andy Burnham is doing now and what Starmer was doing anyway.
This is awkward for Burnham because he is keen to show that he represents “change” – the word at the heart of his byelection campaign in Makerfield.
Sky News has analysed this document and concluded that of the 50 ideas we studied, 20 were announced by Starmer before his departure in July; six have already been announced by Burnham, a further eight are expected to be announced in weeks.
Then there are 16 more ideas worked up by Whitehall but not announced by either PM …
One slide says: “We will make changes. Need to move from the politics of faction to the politics of project. Need to move from a politics of avoiding risk to a politics of ambitious optimism. Politics fit for the scale of the challenges.”
Much of this tone is similar to that used by Burnham.
Commenting on the report, Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, said:
This is one of the reasons why I am standing in Holborn and St Pancras.
Only a Green win will put the pressure on the prime minister for real change, and not copy and paste from Keir Starmer.
Badenoch says Tories could mount legal challenge against cuts being imposed on Wandsworth council
Kemi Badenoch says the Conservative party has “instructed lawyers” to challenge government cuts to a Tory-run London council, which they say amounts to 40%.
These cuts are forcing Wandsworth to increase its council tax by 94%, the Tory leader says.
In an interview with Matt Chorley for the BBC’s Newsnight, which is being shown tonight, Badenoch accuses the government of deliberately taking money away from areas that do not vote Labour and giving them to places that do.
Badenoch says:
I think it is outrageous that Wandsworth council is having to put up council tax. But they’re not doing it because they want to.
It is because the government has taken away 40% of their funding. So we have actually instructed lawyers, as the Conservative party, to see if we can challenge the government on this decision.
Because what it looks like Labour is doing is taking money from areas that don’t vote Labour and giving it to places that do vote Labour.
And I think that’s completely wrong. I think it is outrageous. So we’re talking to lawyers.
Andy Burnham has not found 40% of anything to cut, but he’s asking Wandsworth to do that. I don’t think that’s fair. I don’t think that’s right.”
Wandsworth is one of a handful of councils that have been granted two-year “funding realignment powers”, which enables them to increase council tax beyond the 5% threshold. This is because the government recognises that changes to the way local government is funded mean the council needs a big rise in council tax.
The council was Tory-controlled for more than 40 years and became famous for having very low council tax. In 2022 Labour took power. At the elections in May the Conservatives regained control as the largest party, but without a clear majority.
Watson says Palantir 'can transform public services' as he explains joining firm
Here is the statement Tom Watson issued about his decision to take a job with Palantir.
I’m terrifically excited to be joining the young Palantir team who make the tools that public service workers need to transform how they serve the British people.
Whether that means reducing the time it takes to be diagnosed, treated and discharged from hospital, helping our military personnel keep us safe and secure, or enabling our police to crack crimes and root out corruption, Palantir software can transform the country’s public services.
Through our partnerships across the UK, we will demonstrate Palantir’s enduring commitment to Britain, not only through the services we help deliver, but through the skills, jobs and opportunities we help create.
Watson has been on leave of absence from the House of Lords since March and he says that will continue while he is working for Palantir. According to Palantir, he has given up his parliamentary pass and the access privileges normally retained by members on leave.
Greens condemn Tom Watson taking job with Palantir, saying it shows 'corrosive revolving door' between politics and business
As Robert Booth reports, the former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson has taken a job with the controversial US AI company Palantir.
The Green party says this is an example of the “corrosive revolving door” between politics and business.
In a statement, Siân Berry, the Green MP, said:
Palantir, with its work for ICE in the US and the IDF, has no business at all in our NHS and public services. Tom Watson has been employed to lobby his friends in the Labour government.
This is yet another example of the corrosive revolving door between politics and big business lobbying that has no place in public life.
Burnham to meet Irish PM at No 10 North as UK bids to get exemptions from EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plan
Good morning. On Monday, at her summit in Cardiff with the leaders of the SNP and Plaid Cymru, Mary Lou McDonald, the Sinn Féin president, joked about Liverpool being the 33rd county of Ireland. Andy Burnham is basically a Scouser; he was born in Liverpool and supports a Liverpool football team, despite being brought up in Culcheth, a village mid-way between Liverpool and Manchester, which made him enough of a Manc to be the city’s mayor. He also has Irish ancestry, and so the mood should be very cordial today when he hosts Micheál Martin, the taoiseach (Irish PM) at No 10 North in Manchester this morning.
It is the first time that Burnham has used No 10 North to host an overseas visit, which should help a bit his efforts to establish that No 10 North is a proper government power base, and not just a branch office.
And, in its overnight release about the visit, No 10 says it is part of a deliberate attempt by Burnham to use meetings with overseas leaders to highlight parts of the UK outside London. No 10 says:
The historic visit to No 10 North comes as the prime minister shines a spotlight on towns up and down the country, days after he hosted Canadian prime minister Mark Carney in Liverpool and Nato secretary general Mark Rutte in Oxford.
No 10 also points out that, when Burnham met Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, they were at Portsmouth.
It should be a friendly meeting. When Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester, he had several meetings with Martin, including in Ireland, and when Burnham became PM Martin issued a statement praising him as someone who was “a great champion of deeper links between Ireland and Britain”. No 10 says the talks will focus on “shared objectives including boosting trade, supporting Ukraine, and working with the European Union as Ireland continues its presidency of the EU”. After the formal meetings, the two leaders will visit an Irish community centre.
While Burnham and Martin are meeting in Manchester, John Healey, the chancellor, will be in Dublin where he has been invited to an informal meeting of Ecofin, the meeting of EU finance ministers. And it is not just a social meeting. The UK is desperate to get some sort of exemption from the EU’s “Made in Europe” procurement laws and Healey will be making the case for this to his European counterparts.
According to Treasury sources briefing overnight, Healey will be urging the EU to implement the “Made in Europe” rules in a way that “lands a good deal for all” instead of “erecting new barriers”.
author: Andrew Sparrow
