title: After Neuer: Who will be Germany's new No. 1 goalkeeper?
content_c:
After Neuer: Who will be Germany's new No. 1 goalkeeper?
September 16, 2026
Manuel Neuer retired from international duty after Germany's early exit from the 2026 World Cup, opening the door for a new No. 1.
Jonas Urbig appears the obvious choice, but Neuer is still the starter at Bayern Munich, which severely limits Urbig's playing time. If the 23-year-old was Bayern's first choice, he would likely be Germany's number one too. As it stands, though, it appears doubtful that Germany's new coach Jürgen Klopp will even call him up to his first squad. On September 17, he will announce his squad for four UEFA Nations League games against the Netherlands, Greece, and Serbia. And no position in the current Germany team is more up for grabs than goalkeeper.
Oliver Baumann: The automatic Neuer replacement?
Oliver Baumann represents exactly the kind of selfless No. 2 who could be the next No. 1. The Hoffenheim goalkeeper even commendably dealt with the humiliation of being replaced by Neuer just before the World Cup.
Klopp isn’t just tasked with celebrating short-term success with Germany, however. His remit is to bring about lasting change making Germany favorites for a World Cup and a Euros once again. Oliver Baumann turned 36 this summer. The Bundesliga veteran will be 38 at the next Euros, 40 by the 2030 World Cup. His age might count against a sustainable rebirth of the Germany team.
The Hoffenheim goalkeeper, who has 13 caps, spoke to Bild in the days leading up to the squad announcement about his exchange with Klopp: "Yes, I was in contact with him. He'll say everything else on Thursday. We'll see about the rest—that’s for him to handle."
Ter Stegen: Back in Germany colors via Ajax?
Since Klopp prefers a highly attacking style of play in which all players press high up the field, he might opt for a goalkeeper who can also take on the duties of a field player. Marc-André ter Stegen would fit this profile better than Baumann. Ter Stegen is also two years younger than his competitor, though his career has been hampered by injuries.
After several serious injuries and a legal dispute with Barcelona, ter Stegen has gone on loan to Ajax, improving his chances of returning between the posts for Germany.
"As far as ter Stegen is concerned, I assume he’ll definitely be in the mix," Lothar Matthäus recently wrote for Sky. "If he continues to perform well in Amsterdam, he's a candidate for the number one spot."
Alexander Nübel: Out of the spotlight in Turkey
Alexander Nübel was Germany's third-string goalkeeper at the World Cup. He had been consistent at Stuttgart but moved to Besiktas this summer, where he has made a strong start. However, former national team goalkeeper Toni Schumacher sees the move as a disadvantage for the 29-year-old.
"His move to Turkey has taken him out of the spotlight," Schumacher, who also played for Fenerbahce for three years during his playing days, told Bild. "It simply has a positive effect when you play in your own country week after week and thrill the fans with your saves."
Loris Karius: History with Klopp at Liverpool
A goalkeeper who has never been called up to the Germany team but shares a history with Klopp is Loris Karius.
Karius, who has been at Schalke since January 2025, was at times Klopp’s No. 1 at Liverpool. However, he made two critical mistakes in the 2018 Champions League final against Real Madrid and was subsequently dropped.
Back in the Bundesliga aged 33, Karius is delivering consistent performances and may have played his way back into the spotlight.
"When people associate me with that, it's a testament to the performance I’m putting in. That's great," Karius said recently in an interview with Sky.
Keepers who could play for Germany or elsewhere
If none of the obvious candidates gets selected, there are a number of other good goalkeepers who might be considered. First among them is Noah Atubolu. The 24-year-old Eintracht Frankfurt keeper, who has Nigerian heritage, was the number one for Germany's U21s from 2022 to 2025, and was called up to the senior squad once last October.
Freiburg's Mio Backhaus is another promising talent. The 22-year-old’s mother is from Japan, meaning Backhaus is also eligible to play for Japan. He even played for the Japanese U15 team, but has since progressed through Germany's youth teams up to the U21 level.
In addition to Atubolu and Backhaus, there are also Augsburg's Finn Dahmen (28), Stuttgart's Dennis Seimen (20) and Diant Ramaj (24), who left recently relegated Heidenheim to join Copenhagen.
If Klopp wants to rely on one of the five, it might be worth playing them sooner rather than later in a competitive game. After all, just like Atubolu and Backhaus, the other three are also eligible to play for another country due to their heritage. Dahmen could also play for England, Seimen for Romania, and Ramaj for Kosovo.
Köpke: 'Develop a young goalkeeper as the No. 1'
"I think they need to develop a young goalkeeper as the No. 1 right now," Andreas Köpke, the goalkeeper on Germany's 1996 European championship team, told Bild.
Germany's former goalkeeping coach pointed to Bayern's backup goalkeeper, Urbig, alongside Backhaus and Atubolu — though only as and when Urbig plays regularly at club level.
And, given his standing at Bayern, that's bound to come down to how long Manuel Neuer chooses to continue to play.
This article was originally written in German.
description: Following Manuel Neuer's retirement, there are many candidates to succeed him, but which goalkeeper will Jürgen Klopp choose? What factors will play a role? And will Neuer's future have an indirect influence?

title: Was Wähler in Russlands Provinz beschäftigt
content_c:
Vor der Duma-Wahl in Russland "Es gibt eine große Unruhe"
Brennende Ölterminals, Drohnenangriffe, Benzinmangel an den Tankstellen: Wird sich die aktuelle Situation in Russland auf die Parlamentswahl ab Freitag auswirken? Eine Reportage aus der Stadt Twer.
Auf der Zugstrecke zwischen den Metropolen Moskau und St. Petersburg liegt die Stadt Twer. Eine der ältesten Städte in Russland. Im Zentrum gibt es noch zahlreiche antike, mit schönen Ornamenten verzierte Blockhäuser aus Holz. Sie drohen allerdings zu verfallen.
Deshalb kommt Jaroslaw nach dem Feierabend mit Freunden zusammen, um sie zu restaurieren und vor dem endgültigen Verfall bewahren.
"Tom Sawyer Fest" heißt das Projekt. Der Name bezieht sich auf den Roman von Mark Twain, wo der Held gezwungen wird, zur Strafe einen Zaun zu streichen und dann seinen Freunden vorgaukelt, dass das ein großes Vergnügen sei - woraufhin sie begierig sind, ihm die Arbeit abzunehmen, während er sich weiter herumtreiben kann.
"Tom Sawyer Fest" ist eine unabhängige Organisation der Zivilgesellschaft mit Ablegern in mehreren russischen Städten. Doch insgesamt gibt es nur noch wenige solche unabhängige Organisationen in Russland - die meisten wurden verboten oder unter Druck gesetzt. Weitermachen kann, wer sich lokal engagiert und vor allem unpolitisch ist.
Auch dieses Haus in Twer ist vom Verfall bedroht - Freiwillige wollen versuchen, es zu erhalten.
Was die Wähler insgeheim bewegt
Vor der Parlamentswahl, die am Freitag beginnt und über drei Tage abgehalten wird, beschäftigt ein Thema viele Bürger: "Man spürt die Stimmung in der Gesellschaft, es gibt eine große Unruhe wegen der Gerüchte um eine Mobilmachung nach den Wahlen", sagt Jaroslaw. "Es ist unklar, was mit dem Benzin ist. Die Inflation ist ziemlich hoch. Und das merkt man deutlich an den Preisen."
Auf einem lokalen Markt am Stadtrand von Twer verkaufen einige Anbieter auf dem Bürgersteig Tomaten, ein paar Zehen Knoblauch, getrockneten Fisch. Hier stehen vor allem Rentnerinnen und Renter, die sich etwas dazu verdienen müssen. Tatjana hat Preiselbeeren im Angebot, selbst gepflückt in ihrem Dorf.
Sie bezieht umgerechnet rund 190 Euro Rente im Monat und liegt damit knapp unter dem Durchschnitt: "Die Rente reicht nicht. Wovon soll man leben? Und wie sehen die Preise aus? Ein Wahnsinn - ob Medikamente oder Lebensmittel. Und ich muss auch Brennholz für den Winter kaufen."
Dennoch: Laut Umfragen führt weiterhin die Partei Einiges Russland. Es ist die Partei, der Kremlchef Wladimir Putin nahe steht, verlässlich in seinem Sinne handelt und in der bisherigen Duma mit 315 von 450 die mit Abstand größte Fraktion stellt.
Auf dem Bürgersteig verkaufen diese Bürger in Twer ihre Produkte - es ist ein Versuch, die schmale Rente etwas aufzubessern.
Keine kriegskritische Partei zugelassen
Die Wahlen seien wichtig, sagen die Leute hier. Das haben sie aus der Sowjetzeit gelernt - damals herrschte Wahlpflicht, ohne dass es eine wirkliche Wahl gegeben hätte.
Heute wählen sie freiwillig und aus sehr unterschiedlichen Gründen. Der Rentner Wadim will die aktuelle Regierung unterstützen: "Ich gehe hin, weil unsere Jungs im Krieg sind. Man muss sie unterstützen. Es ist schließlich unser Russland, unsere Großväter haben gekämpft. Wäre ich 40, würde ich selbst hingehen. Aber jetzt braucht mich niemand mehr."
Alle Parteien, die jetzt zur Parlamentswahl zugelassen sind, wollen den Krieg fortsetzen und kritisieren das System Putin nicht. Mit Jabloko wurde die einzige Partei, die gegen den Krieg ist, ausgeschlossen. Die meisten Menschen in Russland aber wissen ohnehin, dass ihre Stimme bei den Wahlen nichts am System ändern wird.
Besser die Augen verschließen
Auch das Vertrauen in die Staatsmedien und die Zeitungen sei ziemlich gering, erzählt die Kioskverkäuferin Inna. Mit einer Ausnahme:
                
                
                Hauptsächlich lesen Männer den Sport-Express, weil da zumindest ein Funken Wahrheit drin ist. Wir gucken ja selbst Sport und kennen daher die Ergebnisse. Bei allem anderen wissen wir, dass fast zwei Drittel - ja sogar mehr - Politik sind. Und was die Politik angeht, wissen die Leute auch alle, dass da, na ja, vielleicht zwei Prozent Wahrheit drin ist.
Kunden habe sie nicht mehr viele, sagt Inna. Zeitungen würden nur noch die alten Leute kaufen.
Im ganzen Land werben die zugelassenen Parteien vor der Wahl - doch auch in Twer ahnen viele Bürger, dass das Wahlergebnis längst feststeht.
Die Listen der Toten werden länger - und jünger
Auf der vorletzten Seite stehen in der Lokalpresse die aktuellen Todesanzeigen. Auffallend ist: Es sind immer mehr junge Männer aufgelistet. Inna stellt ernüchtert fest: "Du kannst nichts tun. Das einzige ist ausharren, am Leben bleiben. Wir können ja das Land nicht gegen ein anderes austauschen. Uns bleibt nichts anderes übrig, als tatenlos abzuwarten und zuzusehen, wobei wir vor vielem die Augen verschließen, damit es nicht zu sehr wehtut."
Die Regierung lockt mit hohem Sold. Daher ziehen gerade Männer aus der Provinz in den Krieg. Anders als in den großen Städten fällt es auf den Dörfern verstärkt auf. Vor allem, sagt Wadim, wenn die Männer nicht mehr zurückkommen. Und das seien "nicht nur viele, sondern furchtbar viele. Von uns sind Freunde begraben, alle da hinten. Keine Ahnung, wahrscheinlich sind schon fünf Hektar Feld mit unseren Leuten belegt. Und mit jedem Monat immer mehr."
Wie viele es genau sind, weiß niemand. Statistiken von Gefallenen veröffentlicht die russische Regierung nicht mehr. Auch niemand sonst darf Zahlen verbreiten - das könnte als bewusste Falschinformation über die Armee ausgelegt werden. Darauf stehen bis zu 15 Jahre Haft.
Also schweigen viele Menschen in Russland einfach, passen sich an oder versuchen, im kleinen Kreis noch ein wenig Freiraum zu finden.
Offizielle Zahlen der im Krieg Gefallenen veröffentlicht Russland nicht - doch auffällig ist, dass in den Zeitungen immer mehr junge Menschen auf den Listen der Toten auftauchen.
"Alle verstehen, dass es Risiken gibt"
In der restaurierten Fußgängerzone von Twer spielt ein älterer Herr auf einem Akkordeon die russische Nationalhymne. Die Menschen schlendern an ihm vorbei und genießen die letzten warmen Sonnenstrahlen des Jahres. Nur wenige verschlägt es in das Kulturzentrum. Seit Kriegsbeginn seien die Spenden für das Projekt um 70 Prozent weggebrochen, erzählt Jaroslaw, der das Zentrum leitet.
Besucherinnen und Besucher seien weniger geworden, auch, weil viele das Land verlassen hätten: "Für alle Fälle haben wir uns dazu entschlossen, uns einfach zu schützen. Einige Bücher mussten wir entfernen, aufgrund der politischen Situation, nach dem Jahr 2022. Wir sprechen nicht öffentlich darüber. Ich denke, alle verstehen, dass es Risiken gibt."
Kunst, Architektur und lokale Identität - das sind jetzt die Schwerpunkte im Kulturzentrum. Politikwissenschaftler lädt Jaroslaw nicht mehr ein. Früher gab es Vorlesungsreihen über Demokratie oder Geschichte. Das ist vorbei.
Immerhin kämen noch Menschen her, um Kultur zu erleben und hier eine Gemeinschaft zu erleben, berichtet Jaroslaw:
                
                
                Mittlerweile haben es viele einfach satt. Und die schweigende Mehrheit ist dafür, dass all das Schreckliche, was gerade geschieht, ein Ende findet. Aber sie haben einfach Angst um sich und ihre Familien.
Die Menschen in Russland wissen, dass sie mit ihrer Stimme wohl nichts an der aktuellen Situation ändern können. Sie können maximal das bestehende System unterstützen.
author: Silke Diettrich
description: Brennende Ölterminals, Drohnenangriffe, Benzinmangel an den Tankstellen: Wird sich die aktuelle Situation in Russland auf die Parlamentswahl ab Freitag auswirken? Eine Reportage aus der Stadt Twer. Von S. Diettrich.

title: Vier Jahre nach Jina Mahsa: Gesellschaft Irans im Wandel
content_c:
Vier Jahre nach Jina Mahsa: Gesellschaft Irans im Wandel
15. September 2026
Am 16. September 2022 starb die 22-jährige Jina Mahsa Amini in einem Krankenhaus in Teheran. Die junge Kurdin war zu Besuch in der iranischen Hauptstadt, als sie von der Sittenpolizei wegen eines angeblichen Verstoßes gegen die Hijab-Vorschriften festgenommen wurde. Drei Tage nach ihrer Festnahme wurde sie offiziell für tot erklärt.
Das gewaltsame Vorgehen der Behörden gegen Frauen, die das Kopftuch nicht richtig getragen haben sollen, war für viele Iranerinnen nichts Neues. Aminis Tod löste jedoch eine beispiellose Welle der Empörung aus. Unter dem Slogan "Frau, Leben, Freiheit" gingen über Monate hinweg Menschen im ganzen Land auf die Straße. Die Proteste wurden brutal niedergeschlagen.
"Aus meiner Sicht hat die Bewegung 'Frau, Leben, Freiheit' die größte soziale und kulturelle Veränderung im Iran der vergangenen Jahrzehnte angestoßen", sagt die iranische Bürgerrechtsaktivistin, Dichterin und Schriftstellerin Pouran Nazemi im Gespräch mit der DW. Nazemi wurde in den vergangenen Jahren wegen ihres friedlichen Engagements für Frauenrechte mehrfach verhaftet und muss jederzeit mit erneuter Strafverfolgung rechnen. Einschüchtern lassen will sie sich dennoch nicht.
Die Bewegung habe von Beginn an klare Forderungen formuliert: die Abschaffung des verpflichtenden Hijab und ein Ende staatlicher Gewalt gegen die Bevölkerung. Eine ihrer wichtigsten Folgen sei jedoch gewesen, dass viele Menschen ihre eigene gesellschaftliche Handlungsmacht erkannt hätten. "Die Behörden gehen immer noch mit physischer Gewalt und mit gelegentlichen Verhaftungen gegen uns vor", sagt Nazemi. "Aber etwas Grundlegendes hat sich verändert."
Diskussion um ein verschärftes Kopftuchgesetz
Trotz des Kriegs mit den USA beschäftigt heute viele iranische Politiker weiterhin die Frage des Kopftuchzwangs im öffentlichen Raum. In einer virtuellen Sitzung des iranischen Parlaments am 6. September forderten mehrere Abgeordnete Parlamentspräsident Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf auf, das umstrittene Hijab-Gesetz zur Unterzeichnung an den Präsidenten weiterzuleiten.
Das Gesetz, das seit Jahren zwischen verschiedenen staatlichen Institutionen umstritten ist, sieht deutlich strengere Strafen für Frauen vor, die gegen die Verschleierungsvorschriften verstoßen. Ein Abgeordneter erklärte, die fehlende Verschleierung sei zu einer "tiefen Wunde im Körper der Gesellschaft" geworden.
"Meine Mutter trägt auch kein Kopftuch mehr. Sie ist immer noch ein bisschen ängstlich und hat immer einen Schal dabei, für den Notfall. Ich denke aber nicht mehr daran", erzählt eine 17-jährige Schülerin im Gespräch mit der DW.
Wie viele andere junge Frauen postet sie Bilder und Videos von sich in bunten Röcken und Sommerkleidung in sozialen Netzwerken. Für sie ist das Teil einer neuen Normalität.
Diese neue Normalität war vor wenigen Jahren noch kaum vorstellbar gewesen. Erst nach den Protesten von 2022 begannen viele Frauen, sich offen über die staatlichen Vorschriften hinwegzusetzen und selbst zu entscheiden, ob sie ein Kopftuch tragen wollen.
Widerstand mit langer Geschichte
Der Widerstand iranischer Frauen begann allerdings nicht mit der Bewegung "Frau, Leben, Freiheit". Er hat eine Geschichte, die Jahrzehnte zurückreicht. Eine wichtige Phase dieser Entwicklung begann bereits vor rund 20 Jahren, erzählt die 68-jährige Frauenrechtlerin und Schriftstellerin Mansoureh Shojaee im Gespräch mit der Deutschen Welle. Shojaee verließ den Iran 2011 aufgrund politischer Repressionen und lebt heute in den Niederlanden.
Im September 2006 gründete sie im Iran gemeinsam mit anderen iranischen Aktivistinnen und Frauenrechtlerinnen die "Eine-Million-Unterschriften-Kampagne". Ziel war es, eine Million Unterschriften für die Änderung diskriminierender Gesetze gegen Frauen zu sammeln. Die Kampagne wurde zu einem wichtigen Beispiel für feministische Organisierung und gesellschaftliche Mobilisierung im Iran.
Die Unterstützerinnen gingen auf die Straße, in die Hörsäle an den Universitäten, in Wohnviertel und in Privathaushalte. Sie diskutierten mit Menschen über Scheidung, Sorgerecht, Erbrecht, Zeugenaussage und Polygamie. Gleichzeitig organisierten sie Bildungsworkshops, Diskussions- und Studiengruppen sowie kulturelle und mediale Aktivitäten.
Die Kampagne war von Beginn an massiver staatlicher Repression ausgesetzt. Aktivistinnen und Aktivisten wurden vorgeladen, verhaftet und strafrechtlich verfolgt. Viele zahlten für ihr Engagement einen hohen persönlichen Preis. Zu den Betroffenen gehörte auch Narges Mohammadi, die im Jahr 2023 mit dem Friedensnobelpreis ausgezeichnet wurde. Andere, darunter Mansoureh Shojaee, sahen sich gezwungen, den Iran zu verlassen. Auch die Menschenrechtsanwältin Nasrin Sotoudeh und die Friedensnobelpreisträgerin Shirin Ebadi gehörten zu den bekannten iranischen Aktivistinnen, die staatlicher Repression ausgesetzt waren.
Ihr ursprüngliches Ziel, eine Million Unterschriften zu sammeln, erreichte die Kampagne nicht. Dennoch veränderte sie den gesellschaftlichen Diskurs über die rechtliche und soziale Stellung von Frauen. Für Mansoureh Shojaee ist "Frau, Leben, Freiheit" deshalb kein vollständiger Bruch mit der Vergangenheit. Die Bewegung steht vielmehr in einer längeren Entwicklung.
description: 2022 starb Jina Amini nach der Festnahme, weil sie das Kopftuch nicht vorschriftsgemäß getragen haben soll. Die daraus entstandene Bewegung "Frau, Leben, Freiheit" hat die iranische Gesellschaft nachhaltig verändert.

title: Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics
content_c:
Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics
- Published
Throughout the summer Andy Burnham's been attempting to cultivate a new style of communicating with a steady stream of social media videos designed to speak directly to the public.
But alongside his digital push, the prime minister still has to master one of Westminster's weekly traditions; the political back and forth that is Prime Minister's Questions.
To some it might seem outdated in a modern media world, but the exchange across the despatch box is still deemed vital by many in Westminster as a moment of scrutiny; a chance for the public to peer into Parliament's workings and a crucial factor in setting the mood among backbench MPs as they watch – and judge – the performance of party leaders.
So the debut of a new prime minister matters.
Burnham took his place in the House of Commons chamber to raucous cheers from the packed Labour benches and struck a confident tone from the start, clearly keen to maintain the sense of optimism he's promised the country.
His initial exchanges with Kemi Badenoch were vaguely jocular. The Conservative leader started with a joke about the prime minister's stamina after a marathon Commons' session on Tuesday when he took questions for more than three hours; there was laughter from MPs and a cautious smile from Burnham.
But if there was an early twinkle in the eye of either party leader their exchanges soon slipped into more familiar territory, trading barbs over tax and borrowing with Badenoch making claims of profligate government spending.
Burnham, despite his promises to end what he's called political "point scoring" was soon pointing the finger at the Tories for their economic record, referencing the budget of former Prime Minister Liz Truss while promising he'd deliver fiscal discipline.
He's not the first prime minister to pledge a new style of politics only to find it hard to dodge the adversarial nature of PMQs.
David Cameron said he'd end "Punch and Judy politics" when he became Tory leader only to find himself in regular political knockabouts across the despatch box.
But while the political barbs continued it's clear that Burnham is a more comfortable communicator than his predecessor. His real challenge will be delivering more than a change in tone.
The backdrop to his first few days as prime minister with Westminster in full swing has been the increased cost of borrowing – a global trend but one to which the UK is exposed and which looks likely to limit the chancellor's room for manoeuvre at the budget come the end of October.
Burnham has promised a transformational government but he's facing many of the same challenges as Sir Keir Starmer, with difficult decisions on defence spending, welfare and social care - to name just a few - hurtling towards him.
These are the pressure points his political opponents will seek to exploit, as evidenced by Badenoch's approach at Prime Minister's Questions when she quizzed him over plans for taxes, spending and borrowing.
Burnham pointed to his early actions in office, cutting VAT on domestic electricity bills and business rates for pubs and music venues as a sign of his priorities, but he gave little more away – leaning back on another familiar refrain that prime ministers don't write budgets from the despatch box.
In reality, it would be unfair to expect much more in the way of detail about Burnham's plans for the economy during his very first session of PMQs, but these are questions his government will eventually have to answer.
And what is clear is that despite the promise of a more consensual style of politics, when it comes to the substance there are sharp ideological differences across the Commons.
Burnham's diagnosis for the country's problems centres on privatisation and deindustrialisation over recent decades, as well as Brexit.
Badenoch disagrees, pointing instead to high taxes and spending as constraints on economic growth.
While Burnham's early weeks in office have seen a shift in style with a summer tour around the country and heavy social media presence, the economic arguments between him and his political opponents remain, and now Westminster is back in session there will likely be a clamour for more detail about his planned direction.
Today's Prime Minister's Questions is a taste of what's to come.
As well as smart communications, the choices the prime minister makes against a tricky economic background will take careful navigation if he's to deliver the optimistic future he's promised.

title: How the High Street became a window on our political instability
content_c:
For a number of years, people around Britain have spoken of what they perceived to be "dodgy shops" on their High Street. To many, it seemed new businesses were popping up that had little obvious purpose or, in many cases, a huge number of direct competitors already in situ. Rumours spread between neighbours about money-laundering mini-marts and gang-owned vape stores.
There was a vague feeling of unease about all of this - but it was difficult for ordinary people living nearby to prove there was anything amiss.
And so when we started looking into the topic last February, I didn't truly appreciate the scale of what was really going on on our High Streets.
Our BBC team has travelled across the UK - including to Plymouth, Rochdale, Shrewsbury, Newport and Bradford - exposing what we have found to be brazen criminality on the High Street.
In Hull, we unearthed underground tunnels supplying sacks of illegal cigarettes to High Street mini-marts. In Swansea, we watched as officers smashed in windows of "stash cars" that were used to hide illegal cigarettes during the day, and deal drugs at night. And we exposed a network of high street shops selling illegal tobacco fronted by "ghost directors" masking the real owners.
Freedom of Information requests revealed for the first time that more than 3,600 shops across the UK had illegal goods - such as counterfeit cigarettes, tobaccos, and vapes - seized over 2024-25. The then-Home Secretary Yvette Cooper described some of our findings as a "disgrace". Throughout our reporting we were repeatedly attacked and threatened.
In lots of places, it seems, High Streets have become a front for organised crime. The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least £1bn of criminal cash is laundered through UK High Street stores each year.
"People want to feel safe… [going] down the local High Street," says John Herriman, chief executive of the Chartered Trading Standards Institute. "The concern is that they don't feel as safe as they used to."
Every episode of High Street criminality causes local angst. But when you look at the national picture - as we have done over the last year - another broader lesson emerges. High Streets seem to offer insight into Britain's troubles. Like a cracked mirror, they reflect other trends in British society, including lacklustre income growth, inequality and the boom in online shopping.
And some analysts tell us that obvious criminality on the High Street is shaping politics too, turning voters away from long-established parties and towards political newcomers.
So how did it get to this? And is there a solution for the decline of Britain's High Streets?
The psychological effect
Organised crime has always existed on the High Street, says Elijah Glantz, a research fellow into organised crime at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), a security think tank.
"Nail bars, pubs, certain restaurants - anything that's cash-intensive has always been vulnerable to organised crime exploiting it," he says. Criminals like cash because unlike card transactions or bank transfers, it is largely untraceable, which makes it useful for both transactions and money laundering.
But in the last decade, he says, both the police and Trading Standards - a body enforcing consumer protection laws - have been squeezed. In 2002, there were 4,260 staff employed by Trading Standards, but in 2025 there were 2,378. Since then, crime has seemingly become more visible.
"There does seem to be an increase in the visibility of it. We're looking at organised crime that has manifested because nobody has put it away, nobody has forced it underground," says Glantz.
And that brazenness has a sharp psychological effect, analysts say - particularly on politics.
Nick Plumb, a director at the Power to Change think tank, says that the sight of open criminality on the High Street fuels feelings of "powerlessness" - a force that's proving potent in UK politics.
"The sense of a lack of control… has been a key feature of our politics over the last decade," he says. "High Streets are incredibly important [to] how people feel about the country… and politics."
And it's not just criminality that people care about. There is the issue of empty shops too.
In particular, Plumb's analysis showed that in the 2024 general election, support for Reform UK was higher in the 100 places in England with the biggest increases in persistent High Street vacancy relative to the rest of the country. This is based on parliamentary seats they won, or came second in. It built on previous research - from academics at the universities of Warwick and Oxford, and Imperial College London - that linked visible High Street decline to support for the United Kingdom Independence Party, an earlier political outfit of Nigel Farage, between 2009 and 2019.
Plumb says that "High Street decline is only partially explained by deprivation," and points to the "rise of online shopping and out-of-town retail, distant and uninterested ownership [and] changing working habits" as a factors behind the decline.
This decline often starts with those vacant units.
Glantz from Rusi thinks that as legitimate businesses close, crime moves in. "Rents are down, there's a lot of empty spaces, so landlords are willing to pretty much take just about anybody," he says.
Plumb came up with a new name for these areas: the "shuttered front", a string of constituencies with struggling High Streets that Power to Change think could play a pivotal role in future elections.
Indeed, Reform's Nigel Farage and Richard Tice were among the first mainstream politicians to regularly talk about visible signs of High Street criminality.
In 2024, Farage said at an event: "You can see High Streets with five, six, seven barber shops in them." Tice added: "Seriously, how come lots of these new barber shops have got no customers in them? How come they all want cash only? These are fronts for money laundering and drug money, and someone has to talk about it."
And in a social media video he made last year - one that quickly set parts of the internet alight - Robert Jenrick, who was then the shadow justice minister, listed "weird Turkish barber shops" as a visible sign of decline, alongside bike theft, phone theft, and drugs in town centres. "It's all chipping away at society," he said. He later clarified that he was "obviously not talking about all Turkish-style barber shops". Jenrick defected to Reform earlier this year.
Some politicians argue the language around High Street decline is in danger of becoming racially coded. In January, Miatta Fahnbulleh, then the devolution, faith and communities minister, agreed when asked by the Guardian if she thought the focus on Turkish barbers had racist overtones. "Yes, I do. The fundamentals aren't to do with the colour of the skin of people running our High Streets. It's to do with long-term decline and neglect."
At the time a Reform spokesman was quoted as saying: "This is not a matter of ethnicity.
"The National Crime Agency itself has said many of these establishments are used as fronts for money laundering as well as a whole range of criminality which is why they carried out hundreds of raids on them last year."
Meanwhile, immigration - the issue that voters consistently highlight as among the most pressing, and that Reform campaigns heavily on - came up in our investigation too. We exposed a Kurdish gang that was enabling migrants to work illegally in mini-marts the length of Britain, by offering to put their own names to official paperwork. Trading Standards told us they find a constant supply of staff from asylum hotels, who are vulnerable to abuse by employers, working in those shops.
Josh Nicholson, a researcher at the Centre for Social Justice think tank, says, "Chaos and flux in Westminster are reflected in our High Streets.
"People feel powerlessness, they look at Westminster and see an inability of politicians to grapple with the basics and that feeds down to a local level."
This feeling of helplessness came up again and again in our travels.
"Nothing is going to change," Daniel, in Swansea, told us about the criminality on his High Street, which has become a hub for counterfeit rolling tobacco. He has seen violence on the High Street and an increase in raids on High Street shops. He's a dual British and Chinese national and was considering moving to Hong Kong.
"It doesn't make me feel safe. I've got kids."
Economic hardship
Oscar Selby, who researches troubled High Streets at the Centre for Cities think tank, sees them as a "bellwether" for the wider economy.
"High streets are ultimately… downstream of the broader economy's performance," he says. "The reason why people are so frustrated about High Streets is that people are also just annoyed that incomes have stagnated for the last 15 years. I think it all comes together in one package."
He thinks troubled High Streets are a "visual manifestation of the economic hardship that a lot of places feel".
High Street criminality sheds light on how bricks-and-mortar stores have been hammered by the boom in online shopping, with footfall 15-20% lower after the Covid lockdowns, according to a study from 2024. Amazon's net sales in the UK, however, have doubled since 2020. This has been exacerbated by the woes in the commercial property market, which was hit by the shift to working from home since lockdowns were introduced, and rising interest rates.
Of course, it's an uneven picture across the country. Some town centres appear to be thriving, and in those places you won't notice much visible sign of criminality - though the NCA did find organised High Street crime gangs in every part of the UK during an operation last year. Research from the Centre for Cities points to Cambridge, York, Edinburgh and Manchester as relative success stories. But this reflects another problem: inequality, because it tends to be places that are already wealthier that have less High Street crime. Towns that are already struggling, meanwhile, are the ones that attract money-laundering gangs.
Now, amid calls for Sir Keir Starmer's resignation, Westminster is paying more attention. Housing Secretary Steve Reed directly linked the state of High Streets to people's faith in politics.
"Each of the last four prime ministers have been the most unpopular ever and the reason for that is the public are very angry about the state of the economy, very angry about the state of our public services and very angry about what they see around them when they look at their High Streets and their hometown," Reed told the BBC.
So, what can be done about it?
The government has announced a new High Street organised crime unit, which will cost £30m over three years. About two-thirds of that will go towards the NCA, funding 75 officers. The rest will go to Trading Standards, with a small amount given to tax and immigration authorities.
The promise is that rogue barber shops, vape stores, mini-marts and sweet shops will face thousands of raids.
Glantz from Rusi thinks the extra cash will make some difference, and hopes the new officers hired at the NCA will spend time looking in detail through company documents and help to "peel back the layers of ownership structures, which is very difficult to do".
He adds: "If you get specialist investigators at the NCA to look, you will get a better threat picture and start to understand who is at the end of it."
But he doesn't think £30m over three years is enough to make up for long-term cuts to police and Trading Standards budgets - though he does say that a small number of flashy, highly visible raids on shops, if shared widely on social media, could have a deterrent effect.
"There hasn't been that visible community policing that might have in the past deterred these very obvious shops from springing up."
Strategic direction
To take truly tough action, Glantz says, authorities need extra powers.
Currently, if Trading Standards want to shut a business, they usually have to use anti-social behaviour powers. But it requires lots of paperwork, and it's a tough bar to meet: it must be proved that a business is a serious nuisance, or that disorderly, offensive or criminal behaviour is likely to occur.
On the few occasions when Trading Standards can shut a business permanently, it's generally by working with landlords, who evict tenants.
Instead, Trading Standards wants stronger, direct powers to close illegal shops quickly, and to shut down crime networks operating in multiple premises across High Streets (to end the whack-a-mole strategy where criminals simply shift their illegal goods to another shop they own next door).
Partly in response to the BBC's journalism, the government has now ordered a "rapid review" of local responders' powers; in particular, it will look at whether Trading Standards should be able to close a potentially criminal shop for longer than the initial three months.
Herriman, from the Chartered Trading Standards Institute, thinks that for too long High Street organised crime was seen as a local problem rather than a national one, in part because Trading Standards activities are devolved to councils.
"Actually what it needs is some strategic direction from [national] government… because then you can start to coordinate across the country," he says.
The newly announced cash, Herriman says "is not job done, it is just job started".
Perhaps the biggest lesson from our year-long investigation was this: people still fundamentally care about their High Streets.
In the 1990s, it was out-of-town shopping centres that were predicted to kill off High Streets; then it was online shopping, then working from home.
But travelling the country, we found that High Streets still occupy a special place in our psyche. That's why the sight of brazen criminality causes such distress.
One pensioner in Oldham urged us to keep going, because "nobody cared". Richard, in north-west London, asked us in desperation for tips to investigate gangs himself. And I'll never forget Errol, a Kurd from Turkey who had spent decades building his grocer's shop in Pill, south Wales. He said he could no longer compete with gangs, and was tempted to give up and leave. He stayed mostly for his children and grandchildren, who were born in Britain.
Now, it's the task of the government and police to fix it.

title: Duncan Sheik, singer and composer of Spring Awakening, dies at 56
content_c:
Duncan Sheik, the singer-songwriter behind the 90s alt-pop touchstone Barely Breathing and the composer of the Tony-winning musical Spring Awakening, died on Thursday at a Manhattan hospital. He was 56.
His death, from heart failure that led to cardiac arrest, was confirmed to the New York Times by his mother Suzanne Sheik.
“It is with profound sadness that we confirm the passing of Duncan Sheik,” a spokesperson for Sheik told People. “The world has a lost a singular talent, and deeply influential voice in music and theater … Duncan’s artistry touched many and leaves an indelible mark on the cultural landscape.
“Duncan was a father, husband, son, brother, and friend,” the statement continued. “He will be remembered for his sensitivity, wit, intelligence, and depth of spirit he brought to those who knew and loved him. We are deeply grateful for the outpouring of love from his fans, friends, collaborators, and the artistic community. His musical legacy will continue to inspire generations to come. Duncan passed away last night surrounded by love.”
According to Sheik’s social media, the musician was in and out of the hospital over the last month. On 20 August, he posted a photo captioned: “I would prefer to be home making music. But a bit of reflection is not too bad … boring hospital stays have their benefits (outside the obvious).” His team confirmed on Wednesday, a day before his death, that he was in “critical but stable condition”.
Cerebral and soft-spoken, with a semiotics degree from Brown, Sheik was perhaps an unlikely star when he moved to LA in 1992 to record a demo, after playing backup guitar for friend and fellow classmate Lisa Loeb. But he shot to fame with his self-titled debut album, an introspective alternative to the brash and distorted sound of grunge that permeated the decade.
The single Barely Breathing, a sweet-sounding but deceptively raw portrait of romantic suffering, became a radio staple, staying on the Billboard Hot 100 for 55 weeks – the fourth-longest-ever run, at the time.
But Sheik chafed against the expectations of an MTV heartthrob and status as a sensitive sex symbol, and by decade’s end felt adrift as pop music gravitated toward the more overtly artificial pop sounds of the Backstreet Boys and Britney Spears. “I thought, I’m not going to win in this game of trying to be Justin Timberlake,” he told the Houston Chronicle in 2022. “Maybe I should try and do something different.”
Along with the poet and playwright Steven Sater, with whom he collaborated on his 2001 album Phantom Moon, Sheik began developing a musical based on Spring Awakening, Frank Wedekind’s 1891 play on the tortuous sexual flowering of a group of German teenagers that was outlawed for obscenity in its time.
The resulting show, a heady rock musical that touched on such taboo topics as abortion, abuse and suicide, became an instant hit in 2006, winning eight Tony awards, including best musical. The show ran for over two years, turning then-unknown actors Lea Michele and Jonathan Groff into Broadway stars, and was revived in 2015; a new off-Broadway production opens this November.
Sheik went on to compose several more musicals, including Alice By Heart, a version of Alice in Wonderland set in second world war-era London that premiered on Broadway in 2019, and American Psycho, an adaptation of the Bret Easton Ellis novel. He also continued to release non-theater music, including a 2011 collection of covers by 80s British acts such as Depeche Mode and Tears for Fears. His final album, the ambient Claptrap, was released in 2022.
Sheik is survived by his wife, Nora Ariffin, whom he married in 2011, and their seven-year-old daughter, Ines.
author: Adrian Horton

title: Poland reaffirms support for Ukraine after drone strikes
content_c:
Poland reaffirms support for Ukraine after drone strikes
September 16, 2026
Russia's war against Ukraine is moving ever closer to the border with Poland.
After a drone attack by Russia destroyed a gas station and the locomotive of a passenger train near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine early Sunday, Warsaw has demonstrated its determination in the face of the immediate threat.
"Border crossings in Poland — as has previously been the case in Moldova and Romania — are being targeted in an attempt to discourage people and deter countries from supporting Ukraine," Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told the private broadcaster TVN on Monday.
"Support for Ukraine is part of Poland's reason of state," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. He added that Poland's own security situation would be worsened should Ukraine lose the war.
Poland prepares response
Early on Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk met with the ministers responsible for Poland's security. Senior military commanders also attended the meeting. "We discussed further measures to strengthen the security of our borders," Tusk subsequently wrote on the social media platform X.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski provided more details.
"Poland will provide a nonprovocative but serious response to Russia's escalation, such as the attack on the train in Ukraine near the Polish border, one that will strengthen security," Poland's top diplomat told TVN Monday evening.
On Sunday, Tusk spoke of an "escalation of activities" by Russia. The prime minister also announced that he would discuss the incident with Poland's allies in Europe.
"There is no doubt that we, if necessary, must be prepared, together with them, to deliver a coordinated response," Tusk said after a special session of the Government Centre for Security.
Drone attack on Kyiv-Warsaw train
Russian drones attacked a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw line just short of the Polish border on Sunday morning. The train's locomotive was destroyed in the attack. All passengers and crew were evacuated in time.
Two special trains carrying high-profile participants returning from a security conference in Kyiv were nearby at almost the same time as the attack.
Among those on board were former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin, former Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Polish political scientist Katarzyna Piskorska, who has organized the Warsaw Security Forum in the Polish capital for years, was also on the train.
"Our train was stopped beforehand, and the passengers were evacuated," she told TVN. "The situation was very tense, but everyone remained calm. We were given an evacuation plan and knew exactly what to do."
"The Russians wanted to intimidate us, but they achieved the opposite: The participants affected by this incident are determined to step up their support for the country that was attacked," she said.
Piskorska said the mood in Ukraine was "worse than at any time since the start of the war." She pointed to a new generation of drones equipped with jet engines that can reach their targets much faster.
Support for Ukraine slipping in Poland
Despite numerous acts of sabotage assumed to have be carried out by Russian agents and incidents involving Russian missiles and drones, Poland's government has remained firm in its commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Foreign Minister Sikorski has even called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that doing so is in Poland's own security interest.
But the government in Warsaw also has to consider the shift in Polish public opinion.
In a survey conducted in mid-July, 52% of respondents said they were in favor of continued military aid for Kyiv; 45% opposed it. These figures stood at 77.5% and 18.3%, respectively, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"Russia has won the propaganda war in Poland," Piskorska said. "It is absurd that we are taking the side of the aggressor and claiming that this is not our war," she said, appealing to fellow Poles to "finally wake up."
Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz has also expressed concern about what he described as a "radical shift in sentiment."
"In the past, there was consensus on this issue. Today, we are seeing great skepticism toward Ukraine," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "There are forces in Poland that are spreading Russian propaganda," he added.
Polish media sound alarm
The Polish media, too, are sounding the alarm.
"Putin is sending out a signal that he is prepared to kill our citizens," Bartosz Wielinski wrote in the Tuesday edition of the Polish daily Gazeta Wyborcza. The Kremlin, he wrote, had sent a message that Poland is "the next country in line."
"These are no longer arson attacks or cyberattacks. These are acts on the threshold of war," he wrote.
Polish daily Rzeczpospolita said that "Putin is knocking on NATO's door."
"The attack on the Warsaw–Kyiv railway line was not just another Russian provocation. It was an attempt to intimidate Poland and the West. The response from Poland's politicians will show whether they are capable of assuming responsibility for the country's security," wrote editor-in-chief Michal Szuldrzynski.
Incidents involving Russian drones are now almost a daily occurrence in Poland. On Monday, a drone washed up on a beach near Jaroslawiec on the Baltic coast. A preliminary investigation indicates that the aircraft was unarmed and appeared to be intended for reconnaissance rather than combat.
"We do not know where Russia believes the limits of the escalation spiral lie," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "But we do know that the Russians are prepared to go even further."
This article was originally published in German.
description: After Russia's recent drone attacks on targets close to the Ukraine-Poland border, Warsaw has doubled down on its support for Kyiv and pledged a "nonprovocative but serious response" to Moscow.

title: Nepal: Teurer Wiederaufbau nach Sturzflut
content_c:
Nepal: Teurer Wiederaufbau nach Sturzflut
15. September 2026
Fast drei Wochen nach den verheerenden Sturzfluten nahe der chinesischen Grenze verstärkt das Himalaya-Land Nepal seine Hilfs- und Wiederaufbaumaßnahmen. Nach Angaben der Behörden wurden in fünf betroffenen Distrikten mindestens 1386 Todesopfer geborgen, mehr als 5130 Menschen werden weiterhin vermisst.
Die Flutkatastrophe verwüstete ganze Ortschaften und riss mehr als ein Dutzend Wasserkraftanlagen mit sich. Während die Suchaktionen in den überfluteten Tunneln und entlang schlammiger Flussufer andauern, warten Familien verzweifelt auf ein Lebenszeichen ihrer vermissten Angehörigen.
Trauerfeier ohne Leichnam
Die Verluste an Menschenleben sind besonders im oberen Flusslauf gravierend, wo ganze Siedlungen innerhalb von Minuten verschwanden. An vielen Orten haben zerstörte Straßen und Brücken die Zugänge abgeschnitten, sodass Rettungs- und Hilfsteams auf Hubschrauber angewiesen sind, um lebenswichtige Hilfsgüter zu liefern.
Niranjan Paudyal, ein Bewohner des Dorfes Sole im nepalesischen Distrikt Nuwakot, verlor seine Eltern, seinen Onkel, seine Tante und seine Schwester. "Wir haben tagelang die Trümmer abgesucht, in der Hoffnung, Spuren meiner vermissten Eltern und meiner Familie zu finden", sagt er der DW. "Leider ließ uns die Katastrophe keine andere Wahl, als ihre Bestattungsriten ohne ihre Leichname durchzuführen."
In der Berggemeinde Uttargaya im Distrikt Rasuwa sind öffentliche Gebäude nicht mehr nutzbar oder wurden gleich ganz weggespült. "Nach der Flut gibt es noch nicht einmal Platz für einen Friedhof, um die Verstorbenen zu beerdigen", erklärt Chameli Gurung, Dorfvorsteherin der Gemeinde, gegenüber der DW. "Angehörige müssen nach Pashupati Aryaghat in Kathmandu reisen."
Gurung zählte in ihrer Gemeinde mindestens 618 weggespülte Häuser. 877 Mitglieder der Dorfgemeinschaft werden weiterhin vermisst. Bislang konnten nur zwölf Leichen geborgen werden. Die lokalen Behörden prüfen nach Angaben von Gurung die Möglichkeit, private Gebäude an anderer Stelle zu pachten, um noch vor dem kalten Winter zusätzliche Unterkünfte für Familien zu haben.
Nepals Kommunikationsminister Bikram Timilsina sagt im DW-Interview, die Betroffenen könnten in der Nähe ihrer ursprünglichen Wohnorte neu angesiedelt werden, sofern öffentliche oder private Grundstücke gesichert würden. Außerdem werde die Regierung entsprechend der Haushaltsgröße so lange finanzielle Unterstützung leisten, bis die Flutopfer wieder auf eigenen Beinen stünden.
Nepal steht vor enormen Wiederaufbaukosten
Eine Bewertung der nepalesischen Zivilschutzbehörde (RDNA) beziffert den Gesamtbedarf für den langfristigen Wiederaufbau auf 4,1 Milliarden Euro. Fast zwei Drittel der Mittel sollen in Energie- und Verkehrsnetze sowie Schulen investiert werden. Dies entspricht etwa einem Zehntel des jährlichen Bruttoinlandsprodukts von Nepal.
Bisher war die Wasserkraft die wichtigste Einnahmequelle für den Staatshaushalt in Nepal. Der erzeugte Strom wird in der Regenzeit an das energiehungrige Nachbarland Indien exportiert. Nun bestehen große Sorgen, wie Nepal den kostspieligen Wiederaufbau ohne diese Einnahmen finanzieren soll. Am Montag genehmigte Indien den Stromexport nach Nepal für 18 Stunden pro Tag bis mindestens zum Jahresende. "Wir werden versuchen, alle verfügbaren inländischen Ressourcen zu nutzen und internationale Unterstützung zu suchen, um die Finanzierungslücken zu schließen", sagt Kommunikationsminister Timilsina.
Nepal will widerstandsfähiger werden
Nepal hat sich offiziell an die UN-Klimarahmenkonvention (UNFCCC) mit Sitz in der deutschen Stadt Bonn gewandt. Die Behörde soll bei der Bewältigung von Auswirkungen des Klimawandels helfen, hat jedoch noch nicht mit der Verteilung ihrer begrenzten Mittel begonnen.
"Angesichts unserer bisherigen Erfahrungen im Katastrophenmanagement kommt es vor allem darauf an, wie effektiv wir die Mittel einsetzen, um das Leben und die Lebensgrundlagen der Menschen wiederherzustellen und eine katastrophenresiliente Infrastruktur aufzubauen", erklärt Roshee Lamichhane, Professorin an der Universität Kathmandu, im DW-Interview.
Über die Finanzierung des Wiederaufbaus hinaus plädiert Nepal auf der internationalen Bühne für mehr Klimagerechtigkeit. Nepals Premierminister Balendra Shah wird Ende September vor der Generalversammlung der Vereinten Nationen in New York sprechen. Dort dürfte er zu einer größeren globalen Verantwortung für die Eindämmung der Klimaauswirkungen aufrufen.
Obwohl Nepal weniger als 0,1 Prozent zu den weltweiten Treibhausgasemissionen beiträgt, ist das Land äußerst anfällig für klimabedingte Gefahren. "Der Wiederaufbau muss als Chance genutzt werden, um eine klimaresiliente Infrastruktur zu errichten", erläutert Maheshwar Dhakal, Leiter der Abteilung für Klimawandelmanagement im nepalesischen Ministerium für Forstwirtschaft und Umwelt, gegenüber der DW. Sein Ministerium werde einen Leitfaden entwickeln.
Klimaforscher warnen zwar davor, einzelne Extremereignisse ohne detaillierte Studien ausschließlich der globalen Erwärmung zuzuschreiben. Sie sind sich jedoch einig, dass steigende Temperaturen das Abschmelzen der Gletscher im gesamten Himalaya beschleunigen. Manjeet Dhakal, Direktor von Climate Analytics South Asia, betont, das Ausmaß der Katastrophe verdeutliche die zunehmenden Folgen der Erderwärmung. Nun habe die Welt allen Grund, sich für eine Senkung der weltweiten CO₂-Emissionen einzusetzen. "Auf wie viele weitere Katastrophen müssen wir noch warten, bevor es eine globale Reaktion gibt, um die Auswirkungen des Klimawandels anzugehen?", fragt er. Die Industriestaaten und andere führende Länder sollten gemeinsam mehr Verantwortung übernehmen.
Aus dem Englischen adaptiert von Dang Yuan
description: Bestattungen ohne Leichnam, Dörfer ohne Häuser - Wochen nach der Flut suchen Familien noch immer nach Vermissten. Erste Schätzungen beziffern die Kosten für den Wiederaufbau auf mindestens 4,8 Milliarden US-Dollar.

title: Five takeaways from Burnham's Commons debut as PM
content_c:
Five takeaways from Burnham's Commons debut as PM
- Published
Andy Burnham has taken questions from MPs in the House of Commons for the first time since taking over as prime minister.
The statement on his future plans for power comes six weeks after he took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July, just before Parliament's summer recess.
Here are the main points from what he said.
He plans to give away power
Burnham told MPs his time as mayor of Greater Manchester had given him a "clear theory of growth" that further devolution of power away from Westminster would help boost the UK's economic prospects.
But he said he wanted to avoid a "two-tier England" - where areas that have already been given greater powers pull away from those that have not.
He announced that work was under way with Cornwall council and its six MPs on a devolution deal, "with or without" an elected mayor, to help the rural economy.
Burnham's move to grant the county greater powers, without requiring it to team up with councils in neighbouring areas, could open the door to more devolution for other single counties.
Burnham also said he would meet leaders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to explore more local powers there.
He was pressed on defence spending
The statement was the first chance for Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to grill Burnham on defence spending following headlines on the issue over the summer.
Chancellor John Healey was appointed by Burnham after quitting as defence secretary under Sir Keir Starmer, calling for the UK to spend 3% of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence by 2030.
However, since entering the Treasury, Healey is yet to attach a date to this spending target, and has faced pressure to do so in recent days.
Healey has said a target date for increasing spending to 3% of GDP will be set out at the next government spending review, expected in spring next year.
But in a potential signal of his intentions in this area, Burham said the arguments Healey had made about defence spending in his former role were a key reason why he had put him in charge of the Treasury.
He will go to the UN's climate summit
Burnham confirmed he would attend the COP31 climate summit in November, as he vowed to "meet the climate challenge".
The annual UN climate change conference will take place in Antalya, Turkey, allowing Burnham to come face to face with many world leaders and senior officials.
While Sir Keir attended COP summits when he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak was criticised in 2022 for not going because he had "other pressing domestic commitments".
Burnham's pledge to attend the summit comes as he faces a looming decision about whether to allow drilling to start in the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield, in the North Sea, which have been in legal limbo for a year.
He wants to continue leasehold reform
Labour's 2024 election manifesto promised to "finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end", after campaigners said it was unfair that flat owners had little control over spiralling property costs.
A draft Leasehold and Commonhold Reform Bill published by Starmer's government earlier this year included plans to cap ground rent at £250, ban the sale of new leasehold flats and give homeowners greater control over how their buildings are managed.
Under the bill, leasehold would be banned "except in limited cases", and developers would no longer be allowed to sell new flats as leasehold.
That bill is yet to be introduced to Parliament, but Burnham confirmed he intended to "bring forward" a Commonhold and Leasehold Bill during the current session of Parliament, which began in May and would normally last around a year.
He paid tribute to Starmer
Burnham kicked off his Commons statement by paying tribute to his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, who had announced he was resigning as MP for Holborn and St Pancras just hours earlier.
Sir Keir had given the UK "a lifetime of service", Burnham said, including delivering the Hillsborough Law which demands more accountability from public officials during official inquiries, as well as work to achieve peace in Ukraine.
He also praised Sir Keir for leading Labour to one of its "best victories" in the 2024 election.
He said Sir Keir had "created a platform to change this country for the better" which the new government would "use well".
- Burnham to tell MPs optimism at heart of his vision for UK 
  - Published1 September

title: Early voting begins in midterms as campaign shifts focus to cost of living and Iran war – US politics live
content_c:
Early voting begins in midterms as cost of living and Iran war loom large
Good morning, and welcome to our US politics live blog. The midterm elections are less than two months away, but some states begin early voting today, marking the start of a crucial stretch of campaigning for control of Congress.
Virginia begins early in-person voting, while voters in Minnesota, Idaho and South Dakota can cast absentee ballots in person, as the campaign turns increasingly on the cost of living and the continuing war in Iran.
High gas prices and low approval ratings are adding to the challenges facing president Donald Trump as Republicans head into the 3 November elections with their control of the House and Senate at risk. In its analysis of the US economy, the Wall Street Journal reports that mortgage rates are nearing 7%, consumer prices rose 3.4% in the year to August and gas prices are close to their highest levels since 2022.
“We are seeing what happens when a president launches a war of choice without anticipating the unintended consequences,” Aaron David Miller, a former adviser on Middle East policy to Republican and Democratic administrations, told Reuters.
Trump will take his case to the UN on Tuesday, where he is likely to present the Iran war as a victory despite having initially promised the military campaign would be over within weeks. The conflict has instead entered its seventh month, with Iran still able to disrupt regional shipping and the war putting further pressure on global energy prices.
In other developments:
The Trump administration has approved a potential sale of 48 advanced F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, worth an estimated $24.3b. The Department of State said the propose sale “will improve Saudi Arabia’s capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense”. The move comes despite concerns from intelligence agencies that China could potentially gain access to, or steal, sensitive F-35 technology through Saudi Arabia, according to the New York Times. The newspaper reported:
One detailed report, issued months ago by the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency, raised questions about whether the Americans and Saudis would be able to secure sites with F-35 technology. It also raised concerns about the access that Chinese military personnel have to Saudi bases and the prevalent use by Saudi Arabia of Chinese technology in telecommunications infrastructure and defense installations.
Former staff members of the US Institute of Peace have asked a federal appeals court to prevent the Trump administration from carving the president’s name into the facade of its headquarters in Washington, which was renamed the ‘“Donald J. Trump United States Institute of Peace” last year. Lawyers for the institute’s ousted board members argued that engraving Trump’s name on the building would cause “irreparable harm” by undermining the organization’s independent mission.
The USIP dispute comes as another Washington cultural institution faces a court battle over changes under Trump. A federal judge has ordered the Kennedy Center to give 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition as Trump has threatened. The president said the centre could be “ripped down” amid a dispute over plans to put his name on the building and a proposed $257m renovation. The center is currently closed due to what its Trump-backed leadership described as safety issues caused by age and structural deficiencies.
JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon will attend Donald Trump’s state dinner for Chinese president Xi Jinping, Reuters has reported.
Trump will host the Chinese leader at the White House next week for their second meeting this year, as the two leaders seek stability in a relationship under pressure over issues ranging from trade to Taiwan and Iran as well as global worries about artificial intelligence.
Dimon joins other top executives, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who are also planning to attend the meeting, Politico reported earlier.
The meeting comes as concerns about the dangers of AI are at an all time high after insiders at Anthropic voiced fears that the technology they are building could become so advanced and dangerous as to cause human extinction within the decade, and they asserted many of their colleagues feel the same but have not said so publicly.
Majority of Michigan voters dislike Trump's Canada tariffs, new poll finds
Ove 60 percent of prospective voters in Michigan, a border state both heavily dependent on trade with Canada and key to control of Congress in 2026, dislike the Trump administration’s tariffs on the US’s northern neighbor, according to a new poll.
The poll by the The Washington Post and Schar School found that most likely voters it surveyed in Michigan, including a majority of independents, weren’t a fan of the tariffs on Canada. Support largely broke down along party lines, with 89 percent of Democrats against them, but only a slim majority – 56 percent – of Republicans in favor.
Michigan hosts one of this year’s most closely-watched Senates races, between Republican congressman Mike Rogers, a Republican, and his progressive Democrat challenger Abdul El-Sayed. Unlike other Republicans in northern border states, who have spoken out against the escalating US/Canada trade war, Rogers has largely voiced support for Trump’s tariffs.
The latest round of US tariffs against Canada snapped into effect in late August, after negotiations between the two countries broke down in the eleventh hour. Canada retaliated with new tariffs on US goods, disrupting a flow of trade vital to the economies of border states like Michigan.
Shapiro and Newsom aren’t the only governors making moves on AI lately.
Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, announced at a news conference today plans for tighter rules on data center development in order to address transparency, energy use and environmental concerns. And Nevada’s governor, Joe Lombardo, a Republican, signed an executive order aimed at tackling similar issues.
While concerns over an AI doomsday remain abstract, the impacts of the physical infrastructure needed to support the technology have manifested in a very real way. And outrage over massive data center projects bulldozing over local opposition and transforming communities has become a rallying point in state and local races across the country.
Josh Shapiro, Gavin Newsom stake positions on AI regulation
As the threat of an AI apocalypse becomes a growing issue ahead of the midterm elections – and as both parties are struggling to form an identity around the subject – two prospective 2028 presidential candidates are going public with their positions: Josh Shapiro and Gavin Newsom.
First at an event on Thursday in Pittsburgh, and later in an interview with NBC News, Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro made an appeal for guardrails on AI technology.
Shapiro’s take landed somewhere between President Trump’s all-out support of AI development and the doomsaying of high-profile opponents like Bernie Sanders. Steering a middle course, Shapiro called for comprehensive regulations on AI development without putting a halt to it altogether.
“We’ve got to regulate this, we have to have real guardrails, we have to understand this technology better,” Shapiro said in an interview with NBC News.
“You have to have third parties in the room with these companies, understanding what they’re doing,” Shapiro continued. “When the CEO says ‘I can’t control what I’ve built, and what I’m building could destroy humanity,’ that’s not a time to kick the can down the road.”
Once a cheerleader of data center development in his state, Shapiro began to take a more skeptical position toward AI as pushback began to grow.
He isn’t the only 2028 hopeful seriously mulling AI policy; Gavin Newsom, governor of California (home of the AI industry’s biggest players), also told POLITICO that he’s considering taking further action on the tech before his term expires.
On Friday, Newsom also issued an executive order aimed at increasing third-party oversight of AI development.
Republican-aligned groups are pouring millions of dollars into Ohio to try to shore up an imperiled GOP Senate seat in the state, as the party’s incumbent has fallen behind a democratic challenger in the polls, Reuters reported on Friday.
Super PACs friendly to President Trump and backed by major Republican donors like Elon Musk have fueled the surge in advertising spending, which the outlet found amounted to $14 million in the past week alone.
Ohio’s Senate race has pitted Jon Husted, a former Ohio lieutenant governor who was appointed to finish out JD Vance’s Senate term, against Sherrod Brown, a former Democratic Senator eying a return to office.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive standard-bearer and potential 2028 presidential hopeful, is planning to campaign for Democrats across New York state ahead of the midterms, according to a new interview with The New York Times. During the trip, she will reportedly venture far from her home district in the Bronx to make stops in Buffalo, Syracuse and Ithaca, among other sites.
AOC is backing up the campaign blitz with financial support, the Times wrote, contributing to a pot of money overseen by New York governor Kathy Hochul to support Democratic candidates around the state.
She embarks on the trip as speculation continues to swirl about her future ambitions – either for a Senate seat or for the presidency.
Head of Postal Service tells AP work has stopped on Trump-backed mail voting system
Earlier this week, the Supreme Court struck a final blow at President Trump’s audacious plan to centralize authority over mail-in voting under the federal government, which would’ve given his administration a say in who does and doesn’t get to vote by mail.
By Thursday, the behind-the-scenes efforts in the Postal Service to bring that system to life had ground to a halt, David Steiner, Trump’s postmaster general, told the Associated Press in a new interview.
Steiner and his agency had been caught in the middle of a legal and political whirlwind since March, when Trump signed an executive order seeking to position the USPS as an arbiter of mail-in voting. Under the terms of the order, states – which typically oversee their own elections – would’ve been required to turn over lists of eligible voters to the federal government for approval, and adopt a uniform design for mail-in ballot envelopes. The USPS could’ve refused to deliver ballots for states that declined to go along.
The whole project was the latest manifestation of Trump’s fixation with mail-in ballots and illegal voting by noncitizens, a largely debunked issue which has nonetheless formed a cornerstone of Trump’s domestic policy agenda in his second term.
In the same interview, Steiner dismissed rumors that the strain of being torn between Trump and the courts had prompted him to consider resigning.
JD Vance is back on the midterm campaign trail today, slated to head to Iowa to speak at a rally in Council Bluffs.
Republicans in the state are fighting to hold on to a Senate seat and the governorship, both of which appear too close for comfort. Vance will be joined at the rally by the Republican candidate for governor, Zach Lahn. The GOP’s Senate nominee, Ashley Hinson, has said she will not attend due to a previously scheduled commitment.
Analysis: What Trump’s attacks on mail-in voting mean for the midterms
George Zornick
For the millions of Americans who vote by mail – almost a third of the country – the week began with significant uncertainty that they would be able to easily submit their ballot this fall, thanks to a March executive order from Donald Trump that aimed to restrict mail-in ballots. By Monday night, the supreme court restored a measure of order by rebuking the president and rejecting his plan – but Trump’s frothing response portends more danger for the rapidly approaching midterms.
Trump’s March order forbade the US Postal Service from delivering mailed ballots to anyone the administration deemed ineligible. The Department of Homeland Security, working with the Social Security Administration, would have devised that list of supposedly ineligible, noncitizen voters. On its face, the move appeared plainly illegal. One expert told the Guardian’s Sam Levine, “This is a wholly unconstitutional EO,” because ultimately the federal government cannot set election rules; only states can.
The plan was full of logistical problems, too. A whistleblower told Congress earlier this month that the Postal Service simply didn’t have the ability to implement the system safely, and that the whole plan was “perilously rushed and potentially unlawful”, according to Richard Blumenthal, the senator who handled the whistleblower complaint. State election officials also complained they would be unable to implement Trump’s restrictions this close to an election, even if they were deemed lawful. Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin had already begun mailing out ballots before the supreme court ruled, and chaos would have reigned there and across the country had the court blessed Trump’s plan.
Early voting in Virginia begins amid a legal dispute over voting by mail.
The Trump administration had sought to restrict mail ballots for the midterm elections, but on Monday the US supreme court declined to lift a lower court ruling blocking the new requirements. The decision means states can continue using the same mail-voting procedures they have used in previous elections.
The dispute stems from an executive order signed by Trump in March directing the US Postal Service (USPS) to introduce new rules for handling mail-in ballots. The rules would require states to provide the USPS with lists of voters receiving mail ballots and use specially marked envelopes.
Trump argued that tighter controls are needed to prevent election fraud and strengthen confidence in mail voting. Writing on Truth Social after the supreme court ruling, he said the US was “the only country that has to endure such a Nation Destroying SCAM”.
George Chidi, a politics and democracy reporter for Guardian US, provides more background on Trump’s efforts to change mail-in voting rules in this explainer:
The dispute could have an impact on how Virginians choose to vote, said Stephen Farnsworth, professor emeritus of political science at the University of Mary Washington
“President Trump’s continuing efforts to make voting harder, and the possibility of mayhem on election day, should really energize early voting in Virginia and around the country this fall,” he told the Virginia Mercury.
“Virginians have already demonstrated a great willingness to vote early and this year may see even more interest.”
Trump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
Alexandra Villarreal
The Trump administration has started sending a majority of undocumented children who came to the US alone and have new immigration court cases to Texas, where government facilities for them are unlicensed, their chances of getting a lawyer are low and advocates fear that “a deportation churn-out factory” awaits them, the Guardian has learned.
Almost 80% of children in federal custody who arrived unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian and who were placed in immigration court proceedings in July – and over 90% in August – have been funneled into shelter networks somewhere in Texas, a dramatic upswing from the months prior, according to analysis shared exclusively with the Guardian from researchers at the immigration data insights platform bklg.org.
This is understood to amount to a total of 925 children in the care of the Health and Human Services (HHS) department’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR) and in open immigration court proceedings based in Texas, with 651 sent there in July and August alone.
