title: Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'
content_c:
WEF report: Progress on gender equality remains 'fragile'
September 16, 2026
The Global Gender Gap Report 2026, published by the World Economic Forum (WEF) on Wednesday, reveals that gender parity worldwide is closer than ever — standing at 69.2%.
However, the Geneva-based nonprofit warned that full parity may still be 120 years away and that the progress made so far remains "fragile."
The report, which looked at gender parity across workforce participation, education, health and politics in 145 economies, found that women now occupy senior leadership positions in government and business at levels that were rare globally when the index began in 2006.
Yet, while women's presence at the top of politics has grown since the first report, the past decade has seen that trend reverse. The percentage of countries led by women peaked in 2022 and has now fallen back to 2016 levels.
WEF Managing Director Saadia Zahidi warned that while parity is a foundation for growth and competitiveness, it is "not inevitable."
"To accelerate, governments and employers need to learn from the policies that work and apply them faster. A new economy demands a new approach to talent," Zahidi said in a press release to accompany the report.
Women still missing in top power roles
The WEF found that women remain underrepresented in roles with the largest economic and political influence. They still hold fewer than a fifth of chief executive officer (CEO) positions, while only one in 10 ministerial roles held by women is considered high influence.
While the number of ministerial roles led by women has risen 26% since 2008, only one in 10 was considered weighty then — a share the WEF report said was "virtually unchanged today."
Despite nearly $1 trillion (€866 billion) being invested globally to develop artificial intelligence (AI), the report also revealed that fewer than one in five AI engineers are women, and they are underrepresented at every level of AI firms.
For the 17th consecutive year, Iceland leads the ranking with 93% of the gender gap closed, followed by its Nordic neighbors Finland and Norway. The three nations have made the Top 10, along with Sweden, every year since 2006.
Namibia ranked fourth globally, higher than Germany (9th), the United Kingdom (5th) and Australia (8th).
US falls in gender gap ranking
The United States dropped five places in the rankings to 47th, with 74.9% of its gender gap closed.
The country achieved full parity in education for a second year, ranking first in the world in that area.
In the US, women have long matched men in professional and technical jobs, but parity in senior management has fallen by almost 11 points since 2006, the WEF calculated.
The political score fell 4.1 points from last year after the share of women ministers dropped from two-thirds parity to one-half. The decline coincided with a lower share of women serving as Cabinet secretaries in President Donald Trump's second administration.
The WEF kept the head-of-state indicator for the US at zero as the world's largest economy has never had a female president.
India stuck while China moves up
India, the world's most populous country, remains at 131st in the rankings, with 64.5% gender parity closed.
The report noted India's overall gains amount to a 4.3 percentage-point rise since 2006, which the authors said was mostly due to educational achievement. Women's labor-market participation has barely moved over 20 years, the WEF noted.
India's economic parity score has varied significantly since the first report. Parity among professional and technical workers has almost doubled since 2006, to 49.9%. Among legislators, senior officials and managers, however, it is still only 13.1%.
In parliament, India has closed 16.1% of the gender gap, up seven points since 2006, while the share of women in long-serving Prime Minister Narendra Modi's cabinet has fallen recently, with parity slipping to 5.9% from a 30% peak in 2019.
China, meanwhile, rose seven places to 96th, closing 69.9% of its gender gap. Economic parity is its strongest pillar, at 72.3%, but politics has barely moved in 20 years, with women still accounting for only a fraction of ministers.
Large jumps for Namibia, Kenya and Ghana
Reaching 84.5% parity in the latest report, Namibia leads the way in Sub-Saharan Africa, climbing four places to No. 4 in the ranking.
Namibia has long been well represented by women on the political stage. Last year, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah became its first female president. The country also has a female vice-president and the parliament speaker is a woman, too.
Other African countries were among the biggest climbers in the 2026 rankings, with Kenya rising 33 places in a year to 65th, Ghana up 32 places to 56th and Angola climbing 30 places to 87th.
However, Africa shows the widest range of outcomes for women, the report found, with Chad recording the lowest score of 57.8% parity closed.
Other large climbers in the 2026 report were Guatemala, which rose 31 points to 50th place, and the Czech Republic, which climbed 25 points to 77th.
The WEF also ranked the countries that have progressed the most since 2006 in closing gender gaps, namely Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador, France, Guatemala, Iceland, Mexico, Namibia and Nepal.
Edited by: Tim Rooks
description: Two decades of progress toward gender parity is at risk as women's political representation declines, according to a new World Economic Forum report. At the current pace, the remaining gap could take 120 years to close.

title: Verschleppt und ausgebeutet: Afrikaner in Kambodscha
content_c:
Verschleppt und ausgebeutet: Afrikaner in Kambodscha
15. September 2026
Die Geschichte von Emmanuel David steht exemplarisch für viele andere Schicksale von Afrikanern in Südostasien: Der 28-jährige Liberianer kam 2025 nach Kambodscha, nachdem er eine gefährliche irreguläre Reise aus Vietnam hinter sich gebracht hatte. Ein Freund habe ihm von einem Job erzählt. "Er hat mir aber nicht gesagt, dass es sich um Betrugsarbeit handelt", erzählt David.
Das Unternehmen versprach ihm rund 800 US-Dollar im Monat, mehr als doppelt so viel wie das durchschnittliche Einkommen qualifizierter Arbeitskräfte in Liberia. Doch die Realität sah anders aus. Nach seiner Ankunft musste David 14 Stunden täglich arbeiten. Seine Aufgabe: Frauen über Dating-Apps zu täuschen und sie dazu zu bringen, Geld zu überweisen.
Erst konnte, dann wollte er die vorgegebene Zahl an Betrugsfällen pro Tag nicht mehr erfüllen. Daraufhin zog die kriminelle Gruppe ihm Geld für Essen und Unterkunft vom Lohn ab. Schließlich nahm sie ihm persönliche Gegenstände ab, auch seinen Reisepass. Vier Monate lang sei er immer wieder geschlagen worden, berichtet David. Schließlich floh er "ohne Dokumente und ohne Geld". Seitdem hofft er, irgendwann einmal nach Liberia zurückkehren zu können.
Seine Geschichte ist kein Einzelfall. Ein weiterer Betroffener möchte aus Angst vor Vergeltung anonym bleiben. Er berichtet, wie er "geschlagen und Elektroschocks ausgesetzt" worden sei. Nach den Misshandlungen habe er drei Wochen im Krankenhaus behandelt werden müssen. Die Arztrechnungen könne er nicht bezahlen.
Afrikaner in der Schuldenfalle
Pia Oberoi, Leiterin der Abteilung für das Recht auf Entwicklung beim UN-Menschenrechtsbüro, sagt: "Trotz des Versprechens eines guten Gehalts kommen die meisten nur mit Schulden wieder heraus." Immer mehr Opfer von Menschenhandel in Südostasien stammen aus afrikanischen Ländern, bestätigt Oberoi. "Es gibt ganz offensichtlich eine auf Afrika ausgerichtete Rekrutierungsindustrie, die gezielt afrikanische Staatsangehörige ins Visier nimmt."
Andere Betroffene berichten von Hunderten Afrikanern, die in schwer bewachten und befestigten Anlagen zusammengepfercht werden. "Sobald man drin ist, gibt es keinen Weg mehr hinaus", sagt ein Informant, der ebenfalls anonym bleiben möchte. Die Anlagen hätten ihre eigenen Gesetze. Sexueller Missbrauch und psychische Gewalt gehörten zum System. Die Polizei sehe weg, berichtet er.
Südostasien: Afrikaner im Visier von Betrugsnetzwerken
Südostasien ist zu einem Zentrum hochorganisierter Online-Betrugsnetzwerke geworden. Sie nehmen Menschen auf der ganzen Welt ins Visier und erwirtschaften nach Angaben der Vereinten Nationen jährlich Einnahmen in zweistelliger Milliardenhöhe. Der Betrug habe damit den illegalen Drogenhandel als lukrativstes Geschäft krimineller Netzwerke überholt, berichtet das United States Institute of Peace.
Doch nicht nur die Betrogenen sind Opfer dieser Netzwerke. Allein in Südostasien werden mindestens 300.000 Menschen aus 66 Ländern in der sogenannten "Betrugsindustrie" ausgebeutet. Sie werden gefoltert, sexuell missbraucht und zur Zwangsarbeit gezwungen, heißt es in einem aktuellen UN-Menschenrechtsbericht. Staatsangehörige afrikanischer Länder bilden inzwischen die größte Gruppe der Menschen, die nach Myanmar und Kambodscha verschleppt werden und dort stranden, sagt die Nichtregierungsorganisation Freedom Collaborative.
In Kambodscha wird ihre Rückkehr zusätzlich dadurch erschwert, dass Länder wie Uganda, Liberia, Ghana und Nigeria dort keine konsularische Vertretung haben. Doch das ist nicht der einzige Grund. "Einige Länder haben überhaupt kein Interesse daran", sagt Montse Ferrer, Co-Regionaldirektorin von Amnesty International. Die Herkunftsländer würden ihre Verantwortung nicht wahrnehmen. "Sie gehen nicht einmal ans Telefon, geschweige denn, dass sie die nötigen Papiere beschaffen oder das Geld für die Rückreise bereitstellen."
Kambodschas zögerliches Vorgehen
Auch die kambodschanische Regierung habe ein Interesse daran, Opfer des Menschenhandels im Land festzuhalten, sagt Ferrer. Viele Betroffene hätten hohe Geldstrafen wegen überzogener Visa angehäuft, in manchen Fällen mehrere tausend Dollar. "Sie erlauben NGOs nicht, den Menschen die notwendige Unterstützung zukommen zu lassen. Stattdessen versucht man, sie festzunehmen und zu bedrohen", sagt Ferrer.
Erst nach massivem internationalen Druck - unter anderem durch die Androhung von Finanzsanktionen der USA, Großbritanniens, Kanadas und der Europäischen Union - begann Kambodscha Anfang dieses Jahres, gegen die Betrugsindustrie vorzugehen. Nach Angaben des kambodschanischen Informationsministeriums führte die Kampagne zu zahlreichen Festnahmen und einer Massenflucht mutmaßlicher Betrüger aus den Zentren.
Für die verschleppten Arbeitskräfte entstand dadurch jedoch eine neue Krise: Tausende sitzen weiterhin ohne gültige Dokumente oder legalen Aufenthaltsstatus im Land fest. Vielen fehlen inzwischen auch Unterkunft und Geld, berichten NGOs. Wer Hilfe sucht, landet den Angaben zufolge teilweise in Abschiebehaft. Andere schlafen auf der Straße und betteln um Essen. Statt Schutz zu erhalten, werden die Opfer in der Hauptstadt Phnom Penh und anderenorts häufig stigmatisiert und misshandelt.
Keine staatliche Hilfe, von keiner Seite
Amnesty International spricht von einer sich zuspitzenden humanitären Krise. Wer den Menschenhändlern entkomme, werde häufig wie ein Krimineller behandelt, und nicht wie ein Mensch, der selbst zum Opfer geworden sei. Auch die Vereinten Nationen teilen diese Einschätzung. "Sie sollten nicht für Verbrechen bestraft werden, zu denen sie gezwungen wurden", betont auch Pia Oberoi vom UN-Menschenrechtsbüro.
Mehrere von der DW kontaktierte Opfer berichten, ihre Regierungen reagierten auffallend "langsam" auf die Bemühungen um ihre Rückführung. Anfragen der DW an mehrere afrikanische Außenministerien blieben unbeantwortet. Nach Angaben der kambodschanische Regierung wurden im vergangenen Jahr mehr als 700 überwiegend von chinesischen Staatsangehörigen betriebene Anlagen durchsucht. 58.266 ausländische Staatsangehörige sind demnach abgeschoben und fast 30.000 Verdächtige festgenommen worden. Auf eine direkte Anfrage der DW nach weiteren Informationen reagierte die Regierung nicht.
Angst, Schuldgefühle und Stigmatisierung
Die Internationale Organisation für Migration (IOM) erklärte, sie wolle die Betroffenen unterstützen. Wegen erheblicher finanzieller Engpässe könne sie jedoch nur "begrenzte, priorisierte Unterstützung" leisten. Hilfsorganisationen warnen zudem vor der Gefahr, dass die Betroffenen erneut in die Fänge von Menschenhändlern geraten können. Das gelte auch für diejenigen, die es schafften, in ihre Heimat zurückzukehren. Manche Rückkehrer würden dort als Versager stigmatisiert. "Eine Situation, die wirklich unerträglich ist", sagt Ferrer.
Auch Emmanuel David kennt dieses Gefühl. Er glaubt, sich bei seiner Familie dafür entschuldigen zu müssen, dass er nicht als erfolgreicher Mann zurückgekehrt ist. Auf seine kleine Tochter angesprochen, sagt er nur: "Für Daddy ist es nicht leicht, ohne Geld nach Hause kommen."
Dieser Artikel ist im Original auf Englisch erschienen.
description: Mit falschen Versprechen werden Afrikaner nach Kambodscha gelockt und landen in Scam-Zentren und Zwangsarbeit. Warum immer mehr Menschen in Südostasien festsitzen und vielen die Rückkehr nach Hause verwehrt bleibt.

title: Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?
content_c:
Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?
- Published
The prime minister's announcement that he will keep hundreds of criminals behind bars who would otherwise have been released early is one he has wanted to make for weeks.
Andy Burnham had already expanded the list of people ineligible for early release and had consistently said he wanted to go further.
What is not clear is exactly what has changed to allow him to do so.
Earlier this month, the Ministry of Justice warned that exempting any more prisoners risked "prisons reaching capacity and collapsing".
The prime minister himself previously said he had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".
In his exclusive interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham picked out the release of people on controversial indefinite sentences and the deportation of foreign criminals as measures that had made his latest intervention possible.
It is understood extra capacity will also be created by immediately beginning work to create new cells in existing prisons.
But none of these are short-term solutions.
Ending indefinite sentences will require new legislation, meaning it could be years before space is freed up.
Previous governments have struggled to quickly deport foreign offenders and there are not thought to be any new returns agreements with other countries. The case of grooming gang ringleader Shabir Ahmed, who Pakistan has resisted attempts to deport, is one example.
Retrofitting prisons to create more cells is also expected to take months.
People in government concede that in the short-term, Burnham will only be able to follow through on today's announcement by making prisons even more full.
With the adult male prison estate already running at 98% capacity, it is a move that could worry some in the sector.
But in the end, the prime minister believed he simply had to act.
The extra exemptions Burnham has announced are being described within government as a "political decision".
That is not surprising given the intense pressure that had built up, especially around the potential for PC Andrew Harper's killers to be released early.
Burnham's inner circle are mindful that political misjudgements at the start of Sir Keir Starmer's premiership caused long-lasting damage.
They believe Sir Keir never recovered from early rows over freebies and winter fuel payments, and point to a lack of major mishaps in Burnham's first six weeks in office as evidence of a more slick political operation.
There was some surprise in Downing Street about how much media attention the issue of early release received over the summer.
That is one reason why the prime minister's aides are relishing the new parliamentary term, when news stories come along at a faster rate and so are less likely to linger in the headlines.
After the initial flip-flopping on whether the government would be able to exempt more prisoners, the mother of PC Harper told BBC Breakfast that the handling of the situation had been a "hash".
Government officials working on the plans have spoken to the families of victims, who made it clear they did not want the new measures to be dripped out in leaks to the media.
Instead it was decided one big announcement would be the neatest option.
It had seemed likely that would come in the form of a parliamentary statement on Tuesday from the justice secretary.
Instead, the prime minister decided to make the announcement himself in an interview with BBC Breakfast.
It is understood Burnham was mindful of mounting speculation and wanted to give victims and the public as much certainty at the earliest possible opportunity.
In doing so, he may have risked the ire of the Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle, who is generally disdainful of governments that make major announcements outside of Parliament.
He may also have offered up ammunition to the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who has already accused Burnham of being a "people pleaser" who finds it difficult to say no to people.
That characterisation is likely to be tested again when more stories inevitably appear about the victims of prisoners who will still be released early.
It already started on Sunday morning, when the domestic abuse commissioner said she remained "deeply concerned about the number of abusers" still set to be freed.
While this is not the first time Burnham has said he has pushed the system to the limit, Whitehall sources are now adamant there will be no more additional exemptions.

title: Lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy murder trial speaks out
content_c:
The lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial is speaking out, saying that he “didn’t have any doubts” during the jury’s deliberations of the case which ended in a mistrial.
“I didn’t have any doubts. As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present,” the 48-year-old male juror, Michael P Desronvil, said in a statement to NewsNation on Thursday.
“Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she (Clancy) knew exactly what she was doing and planned,” he added.
Desronvil’s public statement follows widespread debate online over the controversial case about whether Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse who fatally strangled her three children in Massachusetts in 2023, should be held criminally responsible.
Clancy has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder charges by reason of insanity, with her defense team arguing that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time.
The trial, which brought nationwide attention to systemic gaps in maternal mental health care, lasted nearly six weeks and culminated in a mistrial after nearly 40 hours of deliberation over seven days.
Several members of the 11-1 deadlocked jury, which comprised nine women and three men, have since publicly commented on the case.
Speaking to NBC10 earlier this month, Roni Carlson, the jury’s foreperson, said the single holdout juror “admitted he had reasonable doubt, and I started filling out the forms, I was so excited”.
“There were three forms I had to fill out and I started filling them out, I wrote my signature on each one, and then he said, ‘But I’m still not going to say that she’s not guilty by reason of insanity,’” she added.
Another juror, Kellie Farina, said: “He had the hardest time getting off the fact that Lindsay viciously killed her children … Every one of us in the hours of our frustration would get up and walk the room because you just couldn’t sit anymore.”
Meanwhile, juror Paula Devlin said: “He was very arrogant,” adding: “He really did not take anything that anybody said.”
Desronvil’s lawyer, Edward Andrew Paltzik, has publicly defended his client, describing Desronvil as an “American hero and champion of justice” who will “not be giving any interviews at this time”.
In a Friday statement on X, Paltzik said: “Any attempts to contact our Heroic Lone Holdout Juror will not be well-taken. Please respect his dignity, humanity, and privacy. Stay away from his home, stop calling him, and don’t even think about deciphering his location.”
Since the mistrial, Desronvil’s personal legal issues have come to light, raising questions over the jury selection process.
Numerous outlets, including NBC10 and the Boston Globe, report that he has a past domestic violence charge from 2021 and an active civil restraining order for allegedly assaulting his nephew, and was facing eviction proceedings while deliberating the Clancy case.
Plymouth district attorney Timothy Cruz has not yet publicly stated whether he will retry Clancy while Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he will ask for the jury to be sequestered in a new trial.
Judge William F Sullivan has set a hearing for 29 September to determine next steps.

title: Kosovo ex-president Thaci sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
content_c:
Kosovo ex-president Thaci convicted of war crimes
Published September 16, 2026last updated September 16, 2026
A Kosovo war crimes tribunal on Wednesday found former President Hashim Thaci guilty of war crimes committed during the 1998-1999 war for independence from Serbia.
Thaci, a former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) commander, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes including murder, torture and illegal detention.
He was tried along with three other former KLA guerrilla leaders in The Hague.
What did the tribunal rule?
The tribunal said Thaci was guilty of the murder of of 96 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces at the hands of the KLA during the conflict. He was also convicted for the illegal detention of 385 people and torturing more than 300 people
The court added Thaci had "actively participated in and encouraged crimes."
Prosecutors alleged KLA forces killed more than 100 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces during and just after the Kosovo war.
This included prisoners held at KLA facilities in Kosovo and Albania, along with politically motivated murders of Serb, Albanian and Roma civilians.
The defense argued that the senior KLA figures could not control or be held responsible for such acts, as the group lacked a strict command structure.
Lawyers had argued there was no direct evidence linking Thaci's command to any of the alleged crimes.
Seen as heroes in Kosovo
The accused are revered as national heroes in Kosovo, and the KLA and Thaci are seen as symbols of the independence movement. Thaci remained a central political figure after the war and was instrumental in Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence from Serbia.
The verdict in The Hague was livestreamed in the Kosovo capital, Pristina, where thousands of Thaci and KLA supporters gathered.
This follows rallies over the weekend that drew tens of thousands calling for the men's acquittal.
Foreign embassies warned of the possibility of unrest after the verdict.
"Our war was just, a war of liberation," Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti said ahead of the verdict.
"We believe and hope … that the KLA leaders will return free to their country and to their families," he added.
After being indicted in 2020,Thaci resigned as president and has been detained in The Hague since then.
The Kosovo War left 13,000 people dead, of which some 9,000 ethnic Albanian Kosovars who were subjected to a campaign of ethnic cleansing at the hands of Serbian forces. The conflict ended after NATO intervened in 1999, pushing Serbian forces out.
Serbia still does not officially recognize its former province Kosovo as an independent state.
Tribunal deeply unpopular in Kosovo
Throughout the proceedings, prosecutors tried to distinguish between Kosovo's struggle for independence from Serbia and the alleged crimes committed by the men on trial.
During the verdict, the presiding judge, Charles Smith, emphasized that the trial was "not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army" or its goal of Kosovo independence.
The tribunal responsible for prosecuting the case, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC), was set up in 2016 after earlier cases in Kosovo failed due to alleged political interference and witness intimidation.
Although based in The Hague, and staffed by international judges, the KSC was established under Kosovo law specifically to prosecute alleged KLA war crimes.
Nevertheless, the KSC remains deeply unpopular in Kosovo. Out of 15 people indicted so far by the KSC, three are serving sentences.
"Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice," Thaci told judges in February as the proceedings concluded.
Edited by: Natalie Muller

title: Kein frittiertes Essen in Schulen - warum die Idee gut ist
content_c:
Kein frittiertes Essen in Schulen - warum die Idee gut ist
14. September 2026
Das britische Bildungsministerium hat neue Regeln für Schulmahlzeiten erlassen. Unter anderem gehört die Idee dazu, Kindern kein frittiertes Essen mehr vorzusetzen. "Das ist eine sehr richtige Idee", findet Stefan Kabisch, Studienarzt und Ernährungsforscher an der Charité in Berlin und am Deutschen Zentrum für Diabetesforschung.
Frittiert bedeutet, dass Nahrungsmittel wie Pommes, Fleisch oder auch Donuts in einer mit heißem Fett gefüllten Friteuse zubereitet werden. Das geht nicht nur schnell, es schmeckt auch ziemlich lecker.
Gesundheitsrisiko durch gesättigte Fettsäuren im Frittierfett
Das Problem beginnt schon beim Fett: Theoretisch könne es sich dabei um ein gesundes Pflanzenfett handeln, sagt Kabisch. "Da aber mit sehr hohen Temperaturen gearbeitet wird, nimmt man in der Regel ein raffiniertes Pflanzenfett, das also so stark weiterverarbeitet ist, dass es die hohen Temperaturen aushält, dass es nicht zu rauchen anfängt und dass es sich nicht geschmacklich verändert."
Raffiniertes Pflanzenfett enthalte allerdings eher gesättigte Fettsäuren. "Gesättigte Fette sind ein Problem, weil sie in unserem Körper Entzündungsprozesse stimulieren, weil sie die Insulinresistenz mit antreiben und auf die Weise einerseits zu Adipositas, aber eben auch zu Typ-2-Diabetes beitragen", so Kabisch.
Des Weiteren erhöhen gesättigten Fettsäuren das Risiko für Arteriosklerose, also die Verstopfung von Arterien, die wiederum zu Herzinfarkten und Schlaganfällen führen kann. Dazu trägt außerdem der hohe Salzgehalt in frittierten Speisen bei: Salz erhöht den Blutdruck und damit das Risiko für Herz-Kreislauferkrankungen.
Krebs und Depressionen durch frittiertes Essen?
Beim Frittieren stärkehaltiger Lebensmittel wie Kartoffeln kann es passieren, dass sich Acrylamid bildet - ein Stoff, der als potenziell krebserregend gilt. Erhöhte Acrylamid-Gehalte finden sich unter anderem in Chips, Pommes Frites, Bratkartoffeln oder Kroketten.
Forschende haben außerdem einen statistischen Zusammenhang zwischen Depressionen und dem Verzehr frittierter Lebensmittel festgestellt. An dieser Stelle ist Stefan Kabisch allerdings vorsichtig. Ein solcher Zusammenhang sage noch nichts über die Kausalität aus.
Es könne auch umgekehrt sein: Menschen mit Depressionen neigen möglicherweise eher dazu, zu schnellen, frittierten Speisen zu greifen, als sich eine gesunde Mahlzeit zuzubereiten, die mehr Aufwand bedeute.
Da das Darmmikrobiom allerdings durch unsere Ernährung beeinflusst wird und der Darm wiederum Einfluss auf Gehirn und Psyche nimmt, schließt Kabisch einen kausalen Zusammenhang zwischen Frittiertem und mentaler Gesundheit auch nicht komplett aus.
Die frittierte Dosis macht das Gift
Wer Frittiertes weglässt, hat mehr Platz für andere, gesündere Alternativen. Die Menge frittierter Lebensmittel ist letztlich das Entscheidende und da gilt: so wenig wie möglich.
"Man kann jetzt nicht mit voller Überzeugung sagen, dass die Dosis null sein muss", sagt Ernährungsforscher Kabisch. Aber man sollte den Verzehr von Frittiertem so weit wie möglich reduzieren. Kabisch hält deshalb einen solchen Eingriff in die Schulernährung für "völlig gerechtfertigt".
description: In Englands Schulen könnte Kindern zukünftig kein frittiertes Essen mehr serviert werden. Zu viel Pommes, Chicken Nuggets und Co. verursachen nicht nur Übergewicht, sondern machen krank.

title: We helped create UK emergency alert system - but question how government is using it
content_c:
We helped create UK emergency alert system - but question how government is using it
- Published
As the Conservative minister who launched the UK's emergency alert system, Oliver Dowden was more than familiar with the loud bleeping sound coming from his phone earlier this month.
What took him by a surprise was the message on the screen.
Like millions of people across England and Wales, the "severe alert" on 14 August warned him of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" and against doing anything that could start a fire, including lighting disposable barbecues.
It was the biggest use of the system to date - but Dowden has now weighed in to question whether it was strictly necessary.
Dowden and two officials who helped create the government's emergency alert system are calling for Labour ministers to be up front with the public on what it could be used for in future.
"I was surprised at the decision to issue this nationwide alert and it raises some serious questions," Dowden, who served as deputy prime minister under Rishi Sunak, tells BBC News.
"The government needs to clarify the criteria for its use and why this alert met those criteria."
'People will ignore it'
When he fronted the launch of the alert system in April 2023, he says it was intended for as narrow a geographic area as possible where the threat to life is imminent.
The government's own webpage, external for emergency alerts says they are only sent for "life-threatening emergencies", listing wildfires, severe flooding and extreme storms.
Two national tests of the system took place in 2023 and 2025, while 10 local alerts have been sent since its launch, all related to weather or flooding bar one in Plymouth for a World War Two bomb removal.
The day before the alert was sent earlier this month, 19 homes burned down in the west Midlands town of Stourbridge after a wildfire. The day of the alert, ministers say they were asked directly by fire chiefs to send one as crews dealt with 43 wildfires and 11 major incidents across the country.
The government's Cobra emergency committee met to discuss how to respond. After sign off from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy Louise Haigh, the alert was sent at 19:00 on 14 August.
It triggered a backlash on social media with some vowing to opt out of further alerts in their phone settings, domestic abuse charities and survivors saying victims with hidden phones were put at risk, and confusion about alerts sent multiple times.
Dowden's worry is that the wildfire alert was more like a public information campaign than an imminent threat to life across all of England and Wales.
"People need to know that when they receive an alert, it is a genuine imminent emergency," the Conservative MP says. "If that confidence is lost, people will simply ignore it."
A Cabinet Office report during trials in 2014 warned of this "cry wolf" effect, while pointing out there was strong support among the public for the alerts.
"Alerts should not be issued just because the government wants to be seen to be doing something," Dowden adds.
The National Fire Chiefs Council said the alert heightened people's awareness and public behaviour, while government insiders point out wildfire alerts are commonplace in many European countries.
"By following the guidance that was issued, people were able to take the necessary steps to keep themselves safe and front line services recorded a significant decrease in incidents in the following days," a government spokesperson said.
But Frazer Rhodes, who worked in government across a decade to help build the technology and devise high thresholds for the alerts, feels a review is now necessary to avoid future ones backfiring.
He was in a bar in Halifax, West Yorkshire, with his wife when the sound of pinging phones began echoing around.
"Everybody around was just going, 'what's this?' What's this?'" he tells us. "Then my wife shouted, 'he did that'."
His wife's joke aside, he said his "immediate thought" was whether it met the threshold for sending one. He explains: "At its heart are three criteria: urgency, severity and certainty. So, in simple terms, how bad, how soon, and how sure?"
Rhodes thinks the wildfire alert arguably met the bar for urgency and severity, but perhaps not for certainty of a threat to life.
"It should be very rare to get an alert," he points out.
He thinks ministers should accept there has been a divided response and launch a review to ask themselves: "How do we do this differently?"
Rhodes, a service delivery specialist, adds: "The national protocol should be a public document… I think that document is almost like a contract with us to say 'this is when we're going to use it, these are the parameters, this is who can use it'."
The emergency alerts we may get in future
Back in 2021 when designing the alerts, he says these were the scenarios considered valid for future alerts:
- Pandemics
- Severe weather and environmental alerts such as flood risk
- Counter-terrorism
- Bomb disposal evacuation
- Major hazards such as the Buncefield oil depot fire in 2005
- Wildfires
- Coal tip landslides
When building the UK alert system, which cost up to £25.3m in its first three years, officials looked to Australia, external and New Zealand, external where emergency alerts have no "opt out" option for the public, unlike in the UK. They also considered minor types of public safety alerts which are sent in the US for issues such as missing children.
The alert targets individual cell towers with a radiowave-like signal, allowing all mobile phones in the area to pick it up without needing to know people's mobile numbers. This cell broadcast technology is used instead of SMS texts or an app.
It comes as the Cabinet Office plans to launch a separate campaign in the autumn about how people can make themselves and their homes more prepared for extreme weather and cyber-attacks.
Another one of those involved in creating the alert system, Nick Corney, thinks the government "missed a trick" with the wildfire alert by sending it nationally rather than targeted at specific postcodes with the highest risk.
Corney, who worked in the Cabinet Office between 2018 and 2021 and says he was in weekly and then daily meetings about designing alerts, wants a "thorough review".
He says this would look at making future alert wording more specific, such as explaining the threat to life with a link to a webpage. "An extra level of consideration needs to be put in place" for national alert versus a local one, he adds.
"You've really got to take yourself out of the Cobra room," he says.
"There's a level of scaring the public that needs to be taken into consideration."
- Wildfire phone alert was 'entirely appropriate', government says 
  - Published17 August

description: Millions across England and Wales received a wildfire alert on their phones earlier this month, but it partly backfired.

title: Oxford United apologise for launching ‘United 93’ clothing range around 9/11 anniversary
content_c:
Oxford United have abandoned a new range of American style-sportswear after it inadvertently referenced the tragedy of September 11.
The League One club launched their new “Campus Collection” on Friday morning but had removed it from sale by lunchtime, after clothing designs were revealed to bear the slogan “United 93”. The U’s immediately published an apology that admitted to a lack of understanding of “the historical context and associations” related to the branding and made “sincere apologies for this error and any offence caused”.
“Inspired by the style and culture of American sports,” the club originally trailed the Campus Collection as launching on 11 September of this year, the 25th anniversary of the atrocity that killed nearly 3,000 people. Concerns over sensitivity saw the launch then delayed, but when the online collection was finally made available for sale on Friday, images showed models wearing an NFL-style shirt with “United 93” on the chest, in recognition of Oxford being founded in 1893.
United 93 was one of four domestic passenger jets seized by al-Qaida terrorists on 11 September 2001. A mutiny by passengers prevented hijackers from using the plane to destroy a government building in Washington DC, and it ultimately crashed into a field, killing all 44 people on board. A film titled “United 93” was also made about the tragedy.
The Campus Collection was live for approximately two hours on Friday before the webpage was deleted by the club after they realised the meaning of the phrase. “The range was released without understanding of the historical context and associations,” the club statement read. “It should not have reached the point of sale and we take full responsibility for not undertaking proper due diligence.
“We have removed the collection with immediate effect and are reviewing our approval processes to ensure nothing like this happens again. Once again, we would like to put on record our sincere apologies for this error and any offence caused.”
Opinion was mixed among Oxford fans, with many outraged but others inclined to forgive the error. One user of the Yellows Forum called it a “monumental cock-up that I would expect to be sacked for if I’d signed off on it”. Another wrote: “Whilst not ideal … everyone who sees this realises there’s no malicious intent. Ultimately there was just no consideration to it at all.”

title: German drama 'Blindspot Berlin' revisits 2016 Christmas market attack
content_c:
'Blindspot Berlin' revisits 2016 Christmas market attack
September 16, 2026
A decade after the deadliest jihadist attack in Germany's history, a new six-part TV series looks at the institutional failures that allowed it to happen.
"Blindspot Berlin," which had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, follows the year-long police investigation that failed to stop Anis Amri — a Tunisian whose asylum applications had been rejected, and who was already known to German security services — from driving a hijacked truck into a crowded Christmas market at Berlin's Breitscheidplatz on December 19, 2016.
Twelve people died, including Lukasz Urban, the Polish driver Amri shot before seizing his vehicle. Dozens more were injured; a 13th victim died of their injuries in 2021. Amri fled the scene and made his way across Europe before being shot dead four days later by Italian police, near Milan, during a routine identity check.
"What happened behind the scenes of that attack is in many ways just as disturbing," says "Blindspot Berlin" director David Nawrath . "[It's] a picture of overwhelmed institutions, systemic failure and a staggering blindness to the threat that was developing right in front of our eyes."
Inside the Salafist network
Set in the year before the attack, the series follows police investigator Frank Laudin (Albrecht Schuch, of "System Crasher" and "All Quiet on the Western Front") and Isra Al-Husseini (Bayan Layla), a young officer and Arabic-language translator, as they try to infiltrate the Salafist network around Abu Walaa, the Iraqi preacher based in Hildesheim who recruited for extremist group "Islamic State" (IS). Frank recruits Murat (Tamer Trasoglu), who risks his life as an undercover informant. Inside the network, they find Amri: volatile, and getting more dangerous.
But despite repeated warnings, their bosses refuse to take the threat seriously. They dismiss Amri as a possible terrorist, in part because he is also a drug dealer, something the authorities see as incompatible with being a radical Islamist.
Fiction built on the parliamentary record
The series writers and production team closely based "Blindspot Berlin" on the facts of the Amri case, and the years-long parliamentary investigation into the institutional failures that made the attack possible. The main characters in the series — Frank, Isra and Murat — are fictionalized, but the events play out as they did in real life.
"We tried to keep as close as possible to what is known about the attack and what led to it," producer Simon Amberger told DW. "There is still a lot that isn't known, that is speculation. There we tried to leave things open."
Border authorities stopped Amri from leaving Germany before Berlin attack
The facts of the case are damning enough.
The parliamentary inquiry committee found that the criminal division investigating Amri and other suspects was grossly understaffed, that judicial and security agencies failed to coordinate the exchange of information, and that officials made serious errors of judgment. Amri's asylum claims were rejected, but he was never deported.
At one point the bureaucracy tipped into farce. Amri tried to leave Germany to rejoin his family and was stopped at the border. Since he only had forged documents that Germany could use to establish where he came from, they couldn't let him leave the country. The German government was forced to issue him a temporary residence permit pending his deportation.
Not only a German story
The producers knew from the start that the story reached beyond Germany.
The Breitscheidplatz attack came at the end of a run of assaults across Europe: the Bataclan and coordinated shootings in Paris in 2015, the suicide bombings at Brussels airport and Maelbeek metro station, and a similar truck attack in Nice, in 2016.
Despite the lessons learned in the past decade, threat levels remain high. On July 25, 2026, a man drove a van into the crowds of Christopher Street Day Pride celebrations in Berlin, killing one and injuring dozens.
The Breitscheidplatz attack also continues to resonate today, as it raises questions on "how far a free democratic society is willing to go, how much of its freedom it is willing to sacrifice for security," says Amberger.
Fears of political misuse
He's aware, however, that a story of Islamic extremism, and the failure of the German state to protect its citizens, lands differently now, in the wake of recent elections that have seen a surge of support for the anti-immigrant, Islamophobic far-right AfD party.
"There is a danger that this story, this series, could be misused to support a simplistic, populist political agenda," Amberger admits. "But it isn't that simple. [In the series] we show how extremism arises in marginalized groups that feel isolated, unseen and powerless. The solution isn't 'stop immigration.'"
"Blindspot Berlin" premieres in Germany on public broadcaster ARD in October; international distribution is also planned.
Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier
description: A decade after the terrorist attack on a Berlin Christmas market, a new German miniseries looks into the institutional failures that allowed the deadly truck rampage to happen.

title: Frauen-Basketball: Kann Deutschland den WM-Boom verarbeiten?
content_c:
Frauen-Basketball: Kann Deutschland den WM-Boom verarbeiten?
14. September 2026
Volle Hallen, begeisternde Stimmung und herausragender Sport - bei der Basketball-Weltmeisterschaft der Frauen in Berlin haben die besten Spielerinnen der Welt echte Werbung für ihren Sport gemacht.
Entscheidend daran beteiligt, dass der Frauen-Basketball in den zehn Tagen der WM einen solchen Hype auslöste, war die deutsche Mannschaft um ihre Stars Leonie Fiebich, Nyara Sabally und Co.
Das Team steigerte sich in der Vor- und Zwischenrunde von Spiel zu Spiel. Im Viertelfinale besiegte Deutschland den amtierenden Europameister Belgien und lieferte das wohl beste Spiel einer deutschen Frauen-Nationalmannschaft bisher.
Am Finalwochenende, als es um die Medaillen ging, zeigte sich zwar, dass dem Team noch ein wenig fehlt, um auch gegen die besten der Welt über ein gesamtes Spiel mitzuhalten. Deutschland unterlag im Halbfinale Frankreich und verlor auch das Spiel um Platz drei gegen Spanien. Weltmeister wurden am Ende erneut die USA. Trotz Platz vier war die WM für die DBB-Frauen sportlich ein Riesenerfolg - bei aller verständlichen Enttäuschung.
"Wir sind einfach nicht gut genug", sagte Leonie Fiebich direkt nach der letzten Partie gegen die Spanierinnen. "Wir haben das Turnier mit ganz viel Euphorie gespielt, haben mit Belgien den Europameister geschlagen. Aber es ist einfach schwer, dann noch mehr overzuperformen. Aber wir werden besser werden."
Die WM war der bisherige Höhepunkt der guten Entwicklung im deutschen Frauen-Basketball der vergangenen Jahre. 2024 hatte sich die Mannschaft erstmals für Olympische Spiele qualifizieren können, bei der EM 2025 wurde sie Fünfte. Im kommenden Jahr steht die nächste Europameisterschaft an. Sollten die Deutschen die Qualifikation schaffen, gehören sie dort zu den Medaillenkandidatinnen.
"Ich denke, dass es wichtig ist, den Schmerz, den die Spielerinnen gerade fühlen, zu kultivieren", sagte Bundestrainer Olaf Lange. "Weil in der täglichen Arbeit in den nächsten Monaten und Jahren müssen wir individuell noch besser werden. Und da braucht man starke Motivation. Und das ist Treibstoff, um besser zu werden."
Der Zuspruch der deutschen Fans könnte jetzt schon größer kaum sein. Für die WM wurden insgesamt rund 230.000 Tickets verkauft. Bei den vier Spielen der Finalrunde am abschließenden Wochenende feuerten jeweils rund 13.000 Zuschauer die Teams an. Zwar waren auch einige Fans aus den USA, Frankreich und Spanien vor Ort, in der Hauptsache waren es aber deutsche Basketball-Anhänger.
Nur drei Spielerinnen aus WM-Kader in Deutschland
Allerdings: Während der Nationalmannschaft der Frauen noch die letzten zwei bis drei Schritte fehlen, um sich in der Weltspitze zu etablieren, hinkt die deutsche Frauen-Basketball-Bundesliga (DBBL) der internationalen Konkurrenz meilenweit hinterher. Die Liga ist, was sportlichen Wert, Budget und Professionalisierung angeht, klein. Europäische Top-Spielerinnen verirren sich eher nicht dorthin.
Auch die meisten Spielerinnen aus dem deutschen WM-Kader haben ihre Heimat bereits verlassen. Die Topstars Fiebich, Nyara und ihrer verletzt fehlende Schwester Satou Sabally sowie Luisa Geiselsöder und Frieda Bühner spielen in der WNBA in den USA. Team-Kapitänin Marie Gülich wechselt nach der WM zu einem Klub in Australien und war zuvor in Taiwan. Emily Bessoir, Lina Sontag und Alexis Peterson-Smalls spielen in Spanien. Die erst 19-jährige Clara Bielefeld ist derzeit in den USA auf dem College.
Mit Alexandra Wilke, Emma Eichmeyer und Britta Daub sind aktuell nur drei Nationalspielerinnen in der deutschen Bundesliga aktiv, wobei Eichmeyer und Daub zwischenzeitlich auch schon im Ausland gespielt haben.
In Deutschland fristen sie das Dasein von Halbprofis und können vom Basketball alleine nicht leben. Wilke, die in den vergangenen Jahren mit den Rutronik Stars Keltern mehrfach die deutsche Meisterschaft gewann, hat nebenher ein Lehramtsstudium abgeschlossen und unterrichtet an einem Gymnasium.
Bundestrainer beklagt Strukturen in der DBBL
Nach Ansicht von Basketball-Bundestrainer Olaf Lange, der seit vielen Jahren als Coach in den USA arbeitet, ist der Zustand der DBBL sogar schlechter als früher. Die Bedingungen bei den Vereinen seien "halbprofessionell". "Medizinisch sind die Situationen katastrophal", so Lange, der von 1995 bis 2002 selbst in der Bundesliga gearbeitet hat.
"Damals hatten wir in den Top-Vereinen bessere Strukturen als heute - und wir sind in 2026. Das sagt schon alles. Es ist sehr rückläufig", beklagte er in der Pressekonferenz zum WM-Abschluss. "Ich muss dafür Sorge tragen, dass unsere Top-Spielerinnen ins Ausland gehen. Solange sich da in der Liga nichts tut, wird es schwierig, diesen Erfolg zu halten."
Maßnahmen zur Professionalisierung
Allerdings soll sich etwas ändern und verbessern, um den Erfolg des Nationalteams auch künftig zu garantieren. Seit März ist Ireti Amojo neue Ligapräsidentin. Die ehemalige Nationalspielerin ist in der deutschen Basketball-Bubble durch ihre Arbeit als TV-Expertin und Podcasterin bekannt. Zuletzt war sie außerdem jahrelang für den Frauen- und Mädchen-Basketball bei ALBA Berlin tätig. Sie hat mit dem Verband und in Zusammenarbeit mit den zehn DBBL-Klubs bereits einige Maßnahmen in die Wege geleitet.
"Es soll auf Parkettböden gespielt werden, auf denen nur Basketballlinien zu sehen sind, die Vereine sollen LED-Banden um den Spielfeldrand herum aufstellen", sagte Amojo vor der WM in einem Interview mit der Tageszeitung "taz".
"Im Nachwuchsbereich sollen Trainer und Trainerinnen hauptamtlich eingestellt werden. Auch die Hallenkapazitäten wollen wir steigern. In einigen Hallen finden aktuell maximal 600 Zuschauende Platz. Wenn das Interesse steigt - was zurzeit der Fall ist - brauchen wir größere Hallen an unseren Erstligastandorten."
DBBL-Chefin Amojo: "Zu spät, um WM-Boom zu nutzen"
Jedoch gibt es nicht nur in der höchsten Spielklasse viel zu tun, sondern auch im Unterbau, bei den kleineren Vereinen und in der Jugendarbeit. Denn sollte die Basketball-WM zu einem Ansturm junger Mädchen auf die Basketballvereine führen, wären diese darauf eher nicht vorbereitet.
Zum einen, weil Trainerinnen und Trainer fehlen, zum anderen aber auch - was in Deutschland ein großes Problem ist - weil eine ausreichende Anzahl vorhandener und intakter Turn- und Sporthallen fehlt und sich die Jugendlichen mit den Erwachsenen quasi um die Hallenzeiten streiten müssen.
"Man hätte vor fünf Jahren anfangen müssen, damit man jetzt sagen kann: Wir nutzen das Momentum der WM und sehen zu, dass all diese Kids, die jetzt Basketball-Fans sind, irgendwo in Vereinen in ganz Deutschland Basketball spielen können", sagte Amojo nach dem WM-Finale bei Magenta Sport.
"Wir sind zu spät. Wir haben die Strukturen nicht, um dieses Interesse aufzufangen und allen Basketball faszinierten Kindern unter perfekten Trainingsbedingungen die Möglichkeit zu geben, zur neuen Leonie Fiebich oder Nyara Sabally heranzuwachsen."
Dennoch sieht Amojo die WM als Erfolg und eine Art notwendigen Startschuss für die Entwicklung. "Das war so ein bisschen der Beweis, den wir alle brauchten, weil es wird ja schnell immer abgetan und gesagt: Frauen-Basketball interessiert ja niemanden in Deutschland. Jetzt haben wir gesehen, dass der Frauen-Basketball Leute in Deutschland interessiert", sagte sie. "Wir haben schon ein paar Hebel, wie wir an den Strukturen arbeiten wollen. Und auch das darf nicht das Ende sein."
description: Nach der Basketball-WM wollen viele Mädchen Stars wie Leonie Fiebich, Nyara Sabally oder Caitlin Clark nacheifern. Doch sind die Strukturen in Deutschlands Frauen-Basketball ausbaufähig und nicht bereit für einen Boom.

title: How one man gets new laws passed - again and again
content_c:
How one man gets new laws passed - again and again
- Published
Ron Bailey has been called many things in his 40 years of political campaigning, not all of them printable.
"The UK's most successful parliamentary campaigner," by a former Friends of the Earth director.
"The most effective and relentless lobbyist that it has been my misfortune to encounter during the last two decades," according to ex-minister Sir Oliver Letwin.
"A bit of a pain in the arse at times," by Lib Dem peer (and friend) Lord Foster.
Over the years Bailey has worked for groups including the Green Party, the Community Rights Project and the Sustainable Energy Association.
In that time he estimates he has been involved in getting 16 bills into law and has had a hand in a further 25 law changes.
Surprising stats for someone who used to have a poster that read "Don't vote, it only encourages them".
In his younger days Bailey was less interested in parliamentary process, preferring direct action.
His folk-singer brother first awakened his interest in politics while being "asked to leave" grammar school for "messing about" deepened his dislike of authority.
He cut his campaigning teeth in the 1960s, joining protests against harsh homelessness laws that split up families and getting involved in the squatting movement.
Activities included occupying hostels, moving homeless families into empty houses, and battling with bailiffs.
The campaigns were infused with the revolutionary spirit of the time but underpinned by Bailey's forensic understanding of the law.
He recalls spending hours in the British Library researching property laws going back to the 14th Century, so that when challenged he was armed with the facts.
More than a decade later, Bailey began trying to change the law, rather than just reading about it. One of his early victories was a freedom of information campaign.
In 1983, the Greater London Council Grants Committee awarded one of his projects enough money to rent an office and employ staff.
Happy to bite the hand that feeds, Bailey used the cash to launch a campaign demanding that they make their meetings public.
Next, he pushed for a Local Government (Access to Information) Bill, which expanded the public's access to council meetings and documents.
To build support for the bill, Bailey and his team contacted hundreds of local groups sending them the "secret files" which detailed activities councils were getting up to behind closed doors.
One of Bailey's favourite examples, he recalls, was a council that voted for a motion supporting freedom of information - in private.
He knew the campaign was paying off when he overheard MPs in a parliamentary bar complaining about the flood of letters they were receiving on the subject.
"I don't call myself a lobbyist," Bailey says.
"I call myself a community mobiliser. That's what's crucial. You don't win these campaigns in Parliament, you win them outside Parliament."
The then Conservative government had a big majority and had opposed the bill, but in the face of public pressure, relented.
Bailey says he and his team were careful to allow ministers to "save face", altering the wording of their proposal so the government didn't look like it had climbed down.
'Capitalists and anarchist nutters'
"Giving your opponent a way out" is one of his golden rules of campaigning - his full list can be found in his new book Institutionalised Deceit: Taking the Lid off Westminster Governance.
Another is to avoid party tribalism. Despite voting Green, Bailey has rarely been picky about who he works with.
In the 1980s, he teamed up with the Association for the Conservation of Energy, a body governed by directors and CEOs.
In a goodbye speech at the end of his time with them, Bailey said: "Perhaps we have both learnt something.
"I have learnt that not all capitalist bastards are capitalist bastards and you have learnt that not all anarchist nutters are anarchist nutters."
Another mantra is to always appear "ultra reasonable". In his book he writes: "Make it as difficult as possible for people to oppose you."
Among his success, he counts:
- the Home Energy Conservation Act, which put a duty on councils to set out how they were improving home energy efficiency
- the Private Hire Vehicles Act, which regulated minicabs
- the Road Traffic Reduction Act, which required local councils to produce traffic reduction plans
One of Bailey's key methods of getting laws passed is the private members' bills process - the parliamentary procedure which begins with the deputy speaker, wearing white gloves and picking small numbered balls out of a goldfish bowl.
The lucky MPs, whose numbers are drawn, get crucial parliamentary time to introduce their own bill.
As soon as the numbers were drawn, Bailey would move fast - immediately lobbying the seven MPs on the list, presenting them with bills, oven-ready for presentation.
He became a master of the tricky process of turning private members' bills into law.
That put him on a collision course with Conservative MP Eric Forth.
Forth was a dedicated parliamentarian and one of the most vehement opponents of the private members' bill process. He would regularly try to block bills by talking them out.
The Bromley and Chiselhurst MP argued that such bills represented the "dreams of this or that group and the proper aspirations of good minded-people" but were "not necessarily very well-thought through".
Forth was so prolific at "filibustering" backbenchers bills that the Friday sessions in the House of Commons, where the bills are debated, gained the nickname "Eric Forth's killing fields".
In his book, Bailey described Forth as "uncrackable" - but he was able to claim victories against the MP.
In an (ultimately successful) effort to save his Private Hire Vehicles Bill, Bailey organised an intense local campaign, which saw leaflets sent to every one of Forth's 50,000 constituents.
Bailey was also not above returning to the direct action tactics of his youth.
He once locked the Liberal Democrat chief whip in his office, in a bid to prevent him from being lobbied by rival campaigners.
Now in his 80s, Bailey is recovering from his sixth stroke, while insomnia and restless leg syndrome keep him up at night.
But his friend Lib Dem peer Lord Don Foster says he is "still at it".
"Still chasing, still writing parliamentary questions.
"Above everything, Ron Bailey has probably got more pieces of legislation through Parliament than the vast majority of cabinet ministers."

title: US veterans have greater levels of Pfas in their blood than civilians, new study finds
content_c:
Many US military veterans have much higher levels of Pfas “forever chemicals” in their blood than non-veterans, new peer-reviewed research finds, raising more questions about health risks the nation’s service members face after serving at polluted bases.
Ground water, surface water and soil around military bases show among the highest levels of Pfas pollution in the US because the chemicals are used in firefighting foam deployed during training and emergencies. While the problem has been clear for over a decade, the new Brown University-led study is the first to compare levels in veterans’ blood with those in civilians.
The analysis of federal health data found the problem to be concentrated among younger veterans. It estimated that 23 million veterans ages 20–39 have levels of Pfas in blood that are between 13% and 24% higher than non-veterans, depending on the specific compound being measured.
The younger veterans were also more likely to have dangerous levels of Pfas in their blood – they were 18% more likely than young non-veterans to exceed the threshold at which experts suggest people seek medical monitoring.
About 13 million, or 58%, of all veterans in this age group are above the threshold, set by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine.
“There is some amount of urgency here, and my hope is that this might accelerate the conversations that the government might have about providing [Pfas health monitoring] to all veterans,” said Christian Hoover , a study co-author and a pre-doctoral fellow in epidemiology at Brown’s School of Public Health.
Pfas are a class of at least 16,000 compounds often used to help products resist water, stains and heat. They are called “forever chemicals” because they do not naturally break down and accumulate in the environment, and they are linked to serious health problems such as cancer, kidney disease, liver problems, immune disorders and birth defects.
The military is in the process of phasing out Pfas firefighting foam because the highly toxic substance has widely contaminated water and the environment around more than 720 bases nationwide. The chemicals are also released by burn pits in which the military open burns or incinerates munitions and waste, dispersing a toxic cocktail of chemicals, including Pfas, in the process.
Levels detected in groundwater around bases have been as high as 1.1m parts per trillion (ppt). The EPA has found one of the most widely present compounds increases cancer risk at .004ppt. Despite the clear health risks, blood levels of service members are not regularly tracked. Previous research has found people living near a contaminated base in New Mexico to have elevated levels in their blood compared with the general population.
Brown’s researchers analyzed data from 2003 to 2018 from the US Centers for Disease Control’s National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), a national program that monitors US residents’ health.
It did not find a similar elevation among older veterans. Hoover said that is likely because the chemicals are slowly excreted from the body via blood or urine over months and years, depending on the specific compound.
Older veterans’ bodies have likely expelled the chemicals to a level that is more in line with the civilian population, Hoover said. Disease from Pfas exposure can take many years to manifest, so older veterans who were exposed may be at more immediate risk for developing health issues.
The study’s limitations include not knowing the service members’ occupations, or how or when they were exposed to Pfas. But Hoover said it strongly shows broad level exposures. He said there was a social contract between the government and service members that the government should take care of those who choose to serve the nation after their service is complete.
“If they still believe in that social contract then I would hope they would feel like this may be incumbent upon them to fix in some capacity,” Hoover said.
author: Tom Perkins
