title: How extreme heat is hitting wallets
content_c:
How extreme heat is hitting wallets
September 16, 2026
The last 11 years have been the planet's hottest on record. This changing climate is manifested in extreme weather events like heat waves and wildfires. But less obvious are the higher prices and lower wages linked to a heating world.
According to a 2026 study by the MIT Sloan School of Management and UCLA School of Law, climate change has already driven up average American household expenses by $900 (€780) a year — rising to above $1,300 for one in 10 US counties.
These costs would not exist in a world without climate change. They include escalating home insurance ($600 higher on average), increasing state and federal taxes due to disaster recovery costs or health impacts from wildfire smoke, for example.
"Climate inaction isn't just an environmental failure; it acts like a tax on every American household," wrote the researchers .
How climate change is already hitting incomes
A 2024 report by Germany's Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact estimated that climate damages to agriculture, infrastructure, health and productivity could cost the world economy $38 trillion a year by 2050.
But how have climate-driven weather extremes already impacted salaries and household budgets?
"If we can't figure out what climate change is already costing us with the data we have, projecting the future becomes almost hopeless," said Derek Lemoine, an economics professor from the University of Arizona who has estimated a 12% reduction in US incomes as global temperatures have risen. This is also compared to a non-climate change scenario.
Lemoine shows how temperature extremes in one US county are having cascading economic impacts in distant locations with milder weather due to interconnected trade and supply chains.
"Much work studies climate change as if it changes weather in only one year and one location at a time," Lemoine told DW.
Instead, he wants to understand how, if a heat wave wipes out corn crops across America, other industries that rely on that corn, including livestock and food producers, will be impacted as the commodity becomes scarcer and increases in price.
"As your costs have gone up," said Lemoine of producers impacted across the corn supply chain, "that's going to serve to make the income of everyone who depends on you go down."
Climate's impact on trade is also being felt in Germany, where record low water levels on the Rhine River, the busiest inland trade waterway in Europe, could shave as much as 0.2% off Germany's economic output in the third quarter of 2026, noted the Kiel Institute for the World Economy in July.
Prolonged dry weather linked to climate change is to blame as shipping capacity drops to as low as 15% on the river that connects Europe's largest port in Rotterdam in the Netherlands with much of western Germany.
Compounding existing economic pressures
One Australian study also looks at how broad climate changes, rather than local shocks from single extreme weather events have gradually led to a decrease in productivity and economic output.
Timothy Neal, a researcher at the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales in Australia, co-authored the report showing that global heating reduced economic output in the state of NSW by an average of around 18%, or the equivalent of $21,288 Australian dollars (€12,974, $15,000) per person in 2024.
"The damage has already been quite severe," Neal told DW, adding that in a non-warming scenario, citizens would enjoy "lower food prices" and "lower poverty."
The report refers to droughts in parts of NSW in the mid-late 2010s that reduced productivity across the whole state by up to 10 billion Australian dollars due to lower agricultural yields and farm incomes, higher water costs and increased reliance on government assistance.
These financial impacts compounded through the state economy over time, influencing the cost of food, insurance and infrastructure maintenance.
In the words of the report, these effects also "compound existing economic pressures and contribute to widening disparities between regions," meaning an increase in income and wealth inequality.
Can climate adaptation limit costs?
"Climate change action should not be seen as a predominantly environmental but also economically sensible," said Frank Jotzo, an economist and commissioner at the NSW Net Zero Commission, which works to decarbonize the state and commissioned the above study.
Referring to "defensive climate investments" such as reinforcing roads, railways and shipping infrastructure to adapt to a hotter world, Jotzo added that "if it wasn't for climate change, we could be putting that money and that effort into other things."
However, adaptation efforts such as the greening of cities to reduce heat island effects will be vital to head off much worse future economic impacts.
The 2026 European heat waves, for example, have already cost around €180 billion, which is the EU's entire projected economic growth for the year, according to one analysis.
Adaptation will also involve strengthening the hospital and medical system to counteract the health effects of heat waves that also reduce productivity as heat-stressed employees tire or struggle to sleep, Jotzo noted.
But Lemoine says that adaptation to climate-driven economic decline is so "costly in its own right" that it could exacerbate income loss and be ineffective if not done comprehensively.
Only when "all places" are insulated from weather extremes can the cascading economic impacts be addressed, he says.
Nonetheless, both adaptation and a rapid reduction of planet-heating emissions are together required to avoid climate-driven income loss that will worsen if warming outstrips Paris climate agreement targets.
"Unchecked climate change would create a permanent drain on wages and productivity," said Jotzo.
Edited by: Tamsin Walker
description: Heat waves, wildfires and floods have cascading economic impacts, causing incomes to decline and the price of basic goods to rise. The trend will escalate as temperatures continue to increase.

title: Knobloch: Der Gedanke an die NS-Zeit ist wieder alltäglich
content_c:
Knobloch: Der Gedanke an die NS-Zeit ist wieder alltäglich
14. September 2026
Charlotte Knobloch, die Präsidentin der Israelitischen Kultusgemeinde München und Oberbayern, hat sich von dem Wahlerfolg der in Teilen rechtsextremen Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) bei der Landtagswahl in Sachsen-Anhalt entsetzt gezeigt. Knobloch sagte im Gespräch mit der DW, jetzt gebe es wieder eine Reihe von jüdischen Bürgern, die nach solchen Ereignissen überlegten, Deutschland zu verlassen.
Jahrzehnte habe es gebraucht, so Knobloch, dass Juden in Deutschland wieder Vertrauen hätten fassen können nach dem Holocaust. Das sei auch gelungen. Und jetzt herrsche wieder große Angst: "Das ist zusammenfassend für mich die größte Problematik, weil wir mit Erfolg versucht haben, wieder die jüdischen Gemeinden nach 1945 aufzustellen, den jüdischen Menschen wieder eine Heimat zu geben, die sie lange nicht hatten und auch nicht wollten."
"Die anderen Parteien müssen sich wehren"
Bei der Landtagswahl in Sachsen-Anhalt am 6. September hatte die AfD, die in dem Bundesland vom dortigen Verfassungsschutz als "gesichert rechtsextrem" eingestuft wird, fast 44 Prozent der Stimmen erhalten. Eine absolute Mehrheit hat AfD-Spitzenkandidat Ulrich Siegmund zwar verfehlt, dennoch hat er gute Chancen, nächster Ministerpräsident im Landtag in Magdeburg zu werden. Und damit der erste Landeschef einer rechtsextremen Partei seit dem Krieg.
Charlotte Knobloch warnt eindringlich davor: "Wir dürfen es nicht zulassen, dass einer von diesen Leuten Ministerpräsident wird. Es ist in meinen Augen momentan sehr gefährlich. Ich hoffe, dass die anderen Parteien das einsehen und sich dagegen wehren. Das können Sie ja. Da gehört natürlich ein bisschen Mut dazu."
Charlotte Knobloch, fast 94 Jahre alt, ist eine der profiliertesten und bekanntesten Vertreterinnen des jüdischen Lebens in Deutschland und eine der letzten Zeitzeuginnen der Nazi-Diktatur zwischen 1933 und 1945. 1932 geboren, wurde sie zunächst von ihrer Großmutter erzogen, die 1942 ins Konzentrationslager Theresienstadt deportiert wurde und dort starb. Eine Bekannte rettete das Mädchen, indem sie es auf ihrem Bauernhof in Mittelfranken aufnahm und als ihr eigenes Kind ausgab.
Eine Gefahr lange nicht kommen sehen
Knobloch antwortete im DW-Interview auf die Frage von Korrespondentin Tina Gerhäusser, wann und wie ihr die schreckliche Zeit von damals noch präsent ist: "Es hat Zeiten gegeben, wo das nur ganz selten so war. Wenn irgendwann in den Medien darüber gesprochen wurde. Aber nicht am laufenden Band. Heutzutage wache ich damit auf und gehe auch damit zu Bett."
Knobloch war von 2005 bis 2013 Vizepräsidentin des Jüdischen Weltkongresses, außerdem von 2006 bis 2010 Präsidentin des Zentralrats der Juden in Deutschland. Schon lange warnt sie vor einem wachsenden Antisemitismus in Deutschland. Den Aufstieg von extrem rechten Parteien wie der AfD hat sie trotzdem lange selbst nicht kommen sehen: "Es ist eine Gefahr im Raum, die vor zehn Jahren in der Form noch nicht da. war. Nazis hat es immer gegeben, Judenhasser hat es immer gegeben, aber nicht in der Art und Weise, wie das heutzutage der Fall ist."
"Wir müssen mehr vor allem mit jungen Menschen sprechen"
Nach Ansicht von Knobloch haben es die etablierten Parteien bislang versäumt, entschlossen gegen die AfD das Wort zu erheben: "Die heutigen Parteien müssen gemeinsam, nicht allein, dieses Thema bearbeiten. Da sehe ich noch eine Chance, dass die Menschen zumindest zuhören und auch diskutieren wollen. Und das ist sehr, sehr wichtig." Vor allem mit jungen Leuten müssten Politiker viel intensiver über ihre Ängste sprechen, was noch nicht ausreichend geschehe: "Man spricht darüber, aber es wird keine Diskussion geführt, weil die jungen Leute natürlich Angst haben, dass das, was sie sagen, an die Öffentlichkeit kommt. Ich will sagen, man muss die Wege finden, um die jungen Menschen wieder zurückzuholen."
In der vergangenen Woche hatte Knobloch eine Morddrohung erhalten. Ein Zeuge hatte am Donnerstag auf einer Parkbank und einem Mülleimer im Englischen Garten der bayrischen Landeshauptstadt München die hingeschmierte Drohung entdeckt und die Polizei informiert, wie das Polizeipräsidium mitteilte. Knobloch hatte daraufhin ihre Teilnahme an einer Veranstaltung abgesagt. Darüber hatte zuvor die "Abendzeitung" in München berichtet. Die Gewaltandrohung stand in direktem Zusammenhang mit dem Wahlsieg der AfD in Sachsen-Anhalt, wie eine Sprecherin auf Nachfrage der Nachrichtenagentur dpa schilderte.
description: Charlotte Knobloch ist eine der bekanntesten Vertreterinnen jüdischen Lebens in Deutschland. Im DW-Interview zeigt sie sich schockiert über den jüngsten Wahlerfolg der Alternative für Deutschland.

title: Meet the men applying for the 'hardest job in British politics'
content_c:
Meet the men applying for the 'hardest job in British politics'
- Published
Wanted: one leader for Scottish Labour. Must enjoy long hours, complex trade-offs and difficult questions.
That may not be the official job description for Scottish Labour leader, but it's perhaps not far from the truth.
After all, Anas Sarwar described this gig as "the hardest job in British politics".
Despite this health warning, two candidates are on the ballot paper vying to take on the challenge - Michael Marra and Joe Fagan.
I sat down with both of them for the Scotcast podcast to learn a bit about who they are, where they think Labour has gone wrong, and their prescription for fixing things.
- Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions 
  - Published12 August
- Lennon criticises 'nasty' Scottish Labour as leadership bid fails 
  - Published17 August
But before we got into the nitty gritty of politics, I wanted to know a bit more about these two candidates.
We started with an ice-breaker: If they had to give a Ted Talk (an online lecture about a topic they're passionate about), what would their subject be?
For Michael Marra, it was his beloved football team, Dundee United.
Given they've just endured back-to-back 4-0 defeats, there's a joke here about the North East Labour MSP backing lost causes.
Joe Fagan opted for a lecture on Cold War Berlin.
And there was even a comparison about the "eerie resemblance" between Stasi HQ in East Germany and the office he occupied when he was the leader of South Lanarkshire Council.
But we weren't here to talk about DUFC's glory days or the fall of the wall. This was a conversation about everything that's been going on with Scottish Labour.
The most newsworthy reflection probably came from Fagan, the South of Scotland MSP, who was critical of Sarwar's decision to leave Holyrood and take a place in the House of Lords.
He wished Sarwar well on a personal level, but said it "wasn't a good look" for him to stop being a Glasgow MSP and head to Westminster's upper chamber.
Fagan said that he would never personally take a seat in the Lords. And not just because he thinks the robes look "ridiculous".
But he did concede that it would be difficult to turn down the offer of a ministerial post from the prime minister.
Michael Marra also had some criticisms of Anas Sarwar's approach as leader.
He praised his work ethic and communication abilities, but said that the party had been too focused on Sarwar in the last five years.
Privately other party figures have said that same – that the party's style was too "presidential" in recent years, rather than showcasing a team of spokespeople.
Marra told me the party had "lost definition as to who the Labour Party is" and had become "too narrow in our leadership and the circle of influence around the leader".
The independence question
A big question hanging over these interviews was what will the approach of these candidates be to independence?
While Scottish Labour isn't going to support that sort of constitutional change any time soon (or perhaps ever), there are voices inside the party who argue it's time to engage with the debate around the grounds for a second referendum.
But both Michael Marra and Joe Fagan don't have much time for this argument.
Fagan said it would be "obvious" when the will of the Scottish people had changed, but we weren't at that point.
He insisted that debates around the process for independence was a relic of the "Sturgeon era", and that that period was now "history".
Marra told me he wasn't clear how a trigger for a second referendum would work, arguing that people are more concerned with issues like the cost of living and the NHS.
This leadership contest has – somewhat unexpectedly – focussed on the issue of gender in recent days.
When Glasgow MSP Monica Lennon failed to make the ballot, she released an explosive statement suggesting the other two had been "punching down on trans people".
Both Marra and Fagan have rejected that accusation. But they both have strong views on the issue of gender reform.
Remember, MSPs passed a bill in 2022 that would have made it easier for someone to change their legally recognised sex – so-called "self-ID".
It was ultimately blocked by the UK government, a decision upheld in the courts.
Labour MSPs at the time were whipped to support it. Some gave up their spokesperson positions in order to vote against.
Marra came to a deal with Sarwar – he was allowed to abstain.
But he told Scotcast he felt so strongly about the issue that he would've been willing to resign over it.
Fagan wasn't in Holyrood at the time, but his view watching from outside was that Labour MSPs shouldn't have backed it.
When it came to the economic side of Scottish politics, both candidates expressed the view that some Scots – especially middle earners – are paying too much tax.
But that doesn't necessarily mean cuts across the board.
Fagan argued that there's a case for "widening" the tax base through some new approaches, such as environmental taxes.
And Marra – whose professional background is in economics – said that he was willing to consider looking at a wealth tax.
And when it comes to oil and gas both wannabee leaders think the UK government should go ahead with extracting at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields.
Scotcast - The Scottish Labour leadership interviews
Michael Marra and Joe Fagan are vying to succeed Anas Sarwar as Scottish Labour leader. They talk to us about their party’s failures, the route to indyref2 and guilty pleasures.
Some in Labour were unhappy when Lennon didn't make the ballot for this contesting, lamenting a lack of breadth in the contest.
And they maybe have a point. It doesn't feel like Scottish Labour members are choosing between two radically different candidates here. This pair broadly agree on a lot.
That being said, both Marra and Fagan seem thoughtful, eloquent and capable politicians.
But the trajectory of Scottish Labour's Holyrood results make for grim reading – they've lost MSPs at every election since 1999.
A once mighty political force in Scotland has just 17 MSPs now.
It's a movement that requires a massive shot of adrenaline. It needs something that can win back its once natural voters, who seem to have found political homes elsewhere.
It doesn't feel like either Fagan or Marra have outlined that recovery plan yet. And, to be fair, they have a bit of time until they face the public again.
But they will need to outline that grand idea at some point. Or the winner risks simply being the latest captain of a political ship that's sinking in the rough seas of Scottish politics.
description: Labour MSPs Michael Marra and Joe Fagan are making their pitches as they aim to succeed Anas Sarwar.

title: Turkey's rights groups, EU call out LGBTQ+ crackdown
content_c:
Turkey's rights groups, EU call out LGBTQ+ crackdown
September 15, 2026
During weekend raids targeting LGBTQ+ activists and organizations in Turkey, several people were arrested and many social media accounts were blocked. The Turkish government's actions have drawn sharp criticism from across the country and abroad.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had announced the operation as part of the "Decade of Family and Population" scheme, a national strategy proclaimed in May 2025 that was to counter the drastic decline in the country's birth rate and strengthen the traditional, conservative family view.
Istanbul saw renewed demonstrations on Tuesday, with LGBTQ+ associations emphasizing in a joint declaration that it wasn't a crime to set up an association and advocate for rights.
"Freedom of assembly, freedom of opinion, protection of privacy and presumption of innocence apply to LGBTQ+ people as well," the declaration stated.
The LGBTQ+ community also received support from the women's movement, with 120 women's rights organizations signing a joint declaration in which they criticized authoritarianism in Turkey.
"As women, we stand against the operations carried out in the name of 'keeping the family safe.' We know that the repression of our bodies, our lives, our identities and our right to organize is part of the same authoritarian politics. Being [LGBTQ+] is not a crime! Organizing as [LGBTQ+] people is not a crime!"
Government aims to 'criminalize' LGBTQ+ community
The government is trying to criminalize the LGBTQ+ community, said Yildiz Taghizade, advocacy officer at Women for Women's Human Rights (WWHR), an organization that co-signed the declaration. This criminalization did not just start with the operations of the past few days, but had already been going on for a few years, according to Taghizade.
"The aim is not only to target LGBTQ+ people, but to practically ban the LGBTQ+ community from engaging in politics, getting organized, claiming rights and showing presence in the public sphere," Taghizade said.
It was no coincidence that the operation came with the slogan "My family is safe."
"The government is trying to justify its actions by invoking the protection of families and children, but this narrative doesn't work. Because when we look at Turkey today and what is actually a factor of uncertainty for families, we come across very concrete issues such as poverty, the housing crisis, unemployment, care work [caring for and tending to relatives — Editor's note] passed on to women, and male violence against women," Taghizade said.
Criticism from medical community, trade associations, politicians
Other organizations have also criticized the government's actions. The Turkish Medical Association described them as a violation of human rights, demanding an end to the politics of discrimination. It was unacceptable, it said, to treat gender identity and sexual orientation as a crime, take people out of their homes at night and block digital channels — all in the name of family protection and security.
Erkan Bas, head of the Turkish Workers' Party, called for the immediate release of those arrested, arguing that the mere existence of LGBTQ+ persons was no crime.
But all those who did not share the government's views were "'called to order' by judiciary, truncheon and censorship. If they had their way, they'd love nothing more than to enshrine the criminal offense of 'being an opponent of the government' by law and sit back," said Bas.
Social media accounts blocked over 'national security'
The raids took place on Sunday in Istanbul, Ankara and Izmir. Over the weekend, numerous websites and social media accounts belonging to LGBTQ+ groups, various organizations and activists were blocked. On the day of the raids, another 32 accounts were suspended. The next day, the number of blocked accounts reached a total of more than 100.
Among those affected were Amnesty International Turkey, the left-leaning Evrensel newspaper, the Academics for Peace initiative, the Lawyers for Justice association, the women's rights organization Mor Dayanisma, the LGBTQ+ rights group Kaos GL and the Media and Law Studies Association.
The legal basis was a ruling by an Istanbul court announced on September 13. The Public Prosecutor's Office in Bakirkoy justified the suspensions by citing investigations into accounts that had spread "obscene content and LGBTQ+ propaganda."
According to several media outlets, the accounts were also blocked on grounds of "national security." Critics called the move digital censorship.
Homosexuality not a criminal offense
Homosexual relationships are not a criminal offense in Turkey. However, the Turkish government has repeatedly referred to the LGBTQ+ community as a movement of "perverts."
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek has accused LGBTQ+ organizations of "promoting immorality," and declared on social media that "no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated."
'Stigmatization and discrimination' against EU's values
The European Union has also expressed concern over the weekend crackdown.
Commission Spokesperson Christian Wigand pointed out that Turkey, as an EU accession candidate, "should promote and ensure respect for the human rights and dignity of all individuals, irrespective of their gender identity or sexual orientation." He added that "stigmatization and discrimination are contrary to the values of the union."
Emma Sinclair-Webb, Turkey director at Human Rights Watch, interpreted the arrests as proof of the government's intention to criminalize LGBTQ+ persons without enacting new laws.
This article was originally written in German.
description: Several raids and arrests of LGBTQ+ persons in Turkey have triggered sharp criticism from numerous Turkish organizations — and also from Brussels.

title: Zverev krönt sich zum US-Open-Sieger - und merkt es nicht
content_c:
Zverev krönt sich zum US-Open-Sieger - und merkt es nicht
14. September 2026
Alexander Zverev schaute sich verwirrt um, guckte Richtung Anzeigetafel und riss dann erst die Arme hoch. Nur mit einigen Momenten Verzögerung realisierte der 29-jährige Tennisprofi seinen großen Triumph. Den großen Lacher für die Zuschauer erklärte Zverev mit einem breiten Grinsen.
"Ich dachte, der Stand wäre 5:1", sagte der frischgebackene US-Open-Sieger über den kleinen Aussetzer in der Sekunde seines zweiten Grand-Slam-Triumphs. "Es war ein langes Match, es waren lange zwei Wochen", schob er beim Fernsehsender ESPN augenzwinkernd hinterher.
Zverev hatte schlicht nicht realisiert, dass er nach dem Fehlschlag von Ben Shelton nach 3:33 Stunden Spielzeit das Finale mit 6:3, 7:6 (7:2), 5:7, 6:2 gewonnen hatte. Sekunden vergingen, ehe er in Jubel ausbrach.
"Wir haben 30 Jahre lang keinen Grand-Slam-Titel gewonnen und jetzt haben wir zwei in drei Monaten gewonnen", sagte Zverev an sein Team gerichtet in seiner Siegeransprache. "Ich denke, Gott hat gesehen, wie viel wir arbeiten, wie viel wir gelitten haben, wie viel Schmerz hier reingeflossen ist."
Zverevs Dank an seine Mutter
Zudem dankte er in emotionalen Worten seiner Mutter, die trotz seiner Diabetes-Diagnose im Kindesalter an eine Tenniskarriere geglaubt hatte. "Sie ist die wichtigste und stärkste Person, die ich kenne."
Von Tennis-Legende Jimmy Connors erhielt er die Trophäe und reckte sie stolz in den Abendhimmel von New York. Lange hatte Zverev einen Major-Titel gejagt, mehrfach war er dicht dran - etwa 2020 bei seinem Final-Debüt in New York, als er gegen den Österreicher Dominic Thiem nach 2:0-Satzführung noch verlor.
Derzeit kommen die großen Trophäen allem Anschein nach im Abo, nur 14 Wochen nach dem Finaltriumph in Paris folgte der zweite Major-Erfolg. "Vor drei Monaten hätte ich sofort unterschrieben, wenn jemand gesagt hätte: Du gewinnst einen Grand Slam", betonte Zverev.
Nun rundete der Deutsche seine Traumsaison bei den wichtigsten vier Tennis-Turnieren ab. Anders als im verlorenen Wimbledonfinale gegen den nun verletzt fehlenden Jannik Sinner aus Italien dominierte der 29-Jährige das Duell mit dem US-Amerikaner Shelton und trotzte auch der hitzigen pro-amerikanischen Stimmung im Arthur Ashe Stadium.
Geht noch mehr für Zverev?
Jetzt eröffnen sich ganz neue Perspektiven: Auch Platz eins der Weltrangliste, ein weiteres Karriereziel, könnte im Herbst Realität werden, denn der in New York fehlende Spitzenreiter Sinner hat viele Punkte bis zum Saisonende zu verteidigen. Misslingt ihm das, ist Zverevs Sprung an die Spitze als zweiter Deutscher nach Boris Becker fast zwangsläufig.
Becker freute sich mit dem 29-Jährigen, den er in den vergangenen Jahren oft kritisiert hatte. "Ich habe immer gesagt: Er ist locker gut für fünf Grand Slams, wenn er seine Mentalität hinbekommt", sagte das deutsche Tennisidol in seiner Rolle als Experte bei sporteurope.tv.
Zverev holt in immer mehr Kategorien auf. Seit Sonntag teilen sich Becker und er etwa den "deutschen Männer-Rekord" von zwei Grand-Slam-Erfolgen in einem Kalenderjahr. Becker gewann 1989 sein Lieblingsturnier Wimbledon und die US Open, Zverev in diesem Jahr Roland Garros und Flushing Meadows.
Doch auch für Becker wird Zverevs US-Open-Sieg seine besondere Note behalten. "Er gewinnt zum ersten Mal die US Open und merkt's nicht - bemerkenswert", sagte Becker bei sporteurope.tv zu dem skurrilen Moment unmittelbar nach Matchende: "Das ist die Szene des Jahres für mich im Sport."
description: Tennisprofi Alexander Zverev feiert in New York seinen zweiten Grand-Slam-Titel. Im Finale bezwingt er den US-Amerikaner Ben Shelton und trotzt der Stimmung. Den Moment des Triumphs realisiert er zunächst gar nicht.

title: Chris Mason: Burnham looks to show he will go further than Starmer with West Bank sanctions
content_c:
Chris Mason: Burnham looks to show he will go further than Starmer with West Bank sanctions
- Published
There is little doubt that the UK's decision to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank is another significant shift in Britain's posture in the Middle East.
The announcement from the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, with the Prime Minister Andy Burnham alongside him in the House of Commons, comes almost exactly a year after the UK formally recognised a Palestinian state. And it comes garnished with blunt language about Israel's conduct.
This latest announcement is both a logical extension of that decision of 12 months ago, senior figures argue, but also, in words and actions, an expression of Burnham's desire to go further than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer was willing to.
It is, Miliband believes, a re-assertion of the logic of eventually arriving at a two-state solution – a viable Palestinian state alongside Israel.
The foreign secretary passionately argued that the UK did have agency and could act – and to do nothing would amount to failure. "A strategy of passivity in the face of what is happening is not a strategy," is how Miliband put it in an interview with Jewish News, external.
There is a pride among his team that after a diplomatic effort over the summer, there is a breadth to the coordinated international action on this, with 11 other countries, including France and Canada, sharing the same approach.
"We provided a convening and coordinating role in pulling this together," one source told me, "but we didn't have to convince others to do this. They were coming to the same view themselves, so we agreed we should all go out and say this at the same time."
The hope is that coordinated action increases the likelihood that the measures will have an impact and minimises the blowback to any one country from Israel or America.
UK officials had anticipated one likely reaction from Israel would be the enforced closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem, which has indeed happened.
And while there is a weary acknowledgement that no one can be certain what President Donald Trump might say next about anything ever, it is noted in Whitehall that the initial reaction of the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was pretty understated.
As for the domestic political context, plenty in the Labour movement and the wider British left have long clamoured for this to happen.
Around 140 Labour MPs went public with this demand at the beginning of the summer, and Burnham was explicit in his criticism of his predecessor's approach to the Middle East, writing in July: "Labour's initial response to the treatment of Gaza caused huge hurt. We got it wrong and I am sorry about that."
In recent years Labour has haemorrhaged support in many communities with a significant Muslim population, and so for a new Labour prime minister seeking to lure as many on the left – and beyond – under Labour's umbrella, this diplomatic intervention makes sense.
But the reaction of the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, writing in the Jewish Chronicle, external, is a reminder of another challenge for Burnham, both political and societal.
"Once again, British Jews find themselves warning their own government that its relentless demonisation of the world's only Jewish state risks fanning the flames of antisemitism here at home," Badenoch said.
Later, the Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was "truly a dark day for Britain's Jews".
Last October, as Mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham was the local figurehead during the grim reality of an attack at the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in the city.
Miliband has sought to address concerns about what Badenoch calls "demonisation" by making his view clear that "holding British Jews responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, pure and simple".
But Labour figures are keenly aware that at points in the last decade, under the leadership of Jeremy Corbyn, the Labour Party's relationship with many British Jews was dire, a situation Starmer sought to rectify as a priority in the early years of his leadership.
In other words, the party's recent relations with many British Jews has been fragile for some time - and many in the community already felt vulnerable after last year's attack in Manchester, and the later arson attacks on Jewish community ambulances in north-west London in the spring.
Burnham has to manage that anxiety while making the case for the changing stance the government is announcing, in the weeks before he meets many of his international counterparts for the first time.
- Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades 
  - Published8 September
- In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers 
  - Published8 September
Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.
description: It is hoped that coordinated action minimises the blowback to any one country from Israel or America, our political editor writes.

title: Drivers in Germany fume over soaring fuel prices
content_c:
Drivers in Germany fume over soaring fuel prices
September 15, 2026
Gas stations in Germany are only allowed to raise their fuel prices once a day, at 12 noon. In Berlin, on the morning of September 15, E10 gasoline cost about €2.25 ($2.60) per liter and diesel about €2.37. At noon, prices rose by about €0.20 per liter. The highest prices were recorded at a highway gas station in southern Berlin, where Super Plus cost €3.03 per liter.
Drivers are angry. While it's possible to use public transportation in large cities, residents of rural areas have hardly any realistic alternative to driving. Those living in regions near national borders have an advantage.
On September 7, filling up a 60-liter tank with E10 gasoline cost about €31 less in the Czech Republic and Poland than in Germany. In Luxembourg, the difference was €28, and in Austria, €25. These figures were calculated by the Federal Statistical Office.
Germany has nine neighboring countries. Gasoline is significantly cheaper in seven of them, and diesel is cheaper in six. Only in the Netherlands and Denmark do drivers have to pay more for fuel than in Germany.
German government expresses 'great and growing' concern
But relief is in sight. That's what Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) has promised.
"Many people who need their cars every day have reached their breaking point," Merz said Tuesday at an event hosted by the German Foreign Trade Association (BGA) in Berlin. "I believe we must take action."
However, the chancellor added that the "exact measures" have not yet been determined.
"We are therefore in close dialogue within the federal government and with the German states." A proposal will be announced "very soon," Merz said.
But what might that look like? On Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin, deputy government spokesperson Steffen Meyer rejected any government responsibility for the high prices.
"It's not the actions of the federal government or anything like that causing prices to rise so sharply. Rather, it's largely due to the escalating situation in the Middle East, attacks on oil pipelines and the blockade of shipping lanes," Meyer said.
The fact is, however, that Germany imposes higher taxes and levies on fuels. The ADAC automobile club has pointed out that while the oil price remains below previous peaks, E10 gasoline is more expensive than ever before.
"From the ADAC's perspective, there is therefore a need to provide greater clarity, especially regarding refinery and wholesale markets," said an ADAC spokeswoman.
Price gouging at the pumps
Herbert Rabl of the Gas Station Interest Group (TIV) puts it more bluntly.
"They're raking it in. The oil companies aren't cutting into their profit margins at all," Rabl told the Rheinische Post newspaper.
He said that this is an issue that has long been the subject of political debate, but that the federal government remains divided on what, if anything, can be done about it.
However, the problem that the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) face as coalition partners is that the state coffers are empty, and the federal government cannot cover its budget shortfall without taking on a historically high level of new debt.
"Ultimately, the only way to bring these prices down is to end the hostilities and ensure the freedom of navigation," said spokesperson Meyer.
A new fuel rebate or tax relief?
Faced with rising oil prices that followed the outbreak of the war on Iran, the German government introduced a fuel rebate in the spring. From May 1 through June 30, 2026, the energy tax on gasoline and diesel was temporarily reduced. Factoring in value-added tax, this was expected to lower fuel prices by about €0.17 per liter.
"We had a fuel rebate; we subsidized prices," Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU) told the n-tv network.
But she says that won't be possible again: "Together, we in the coalition have decided that we don't have the financial scope for that at the moment."
As an alternative, the Conservatives are exploring the possibility of at least providing tax relief for commuters or supporting low-income earners with direct payments.
But that's not enough for the SPD. It is proposing a completely different approach and, as it did shortly after the outbreak of the Iran war, is advocating for a government-imposed cap on fuel prices. One of the ways they plan to finance this relief is through an excess profit tax on energy companies. In addition, the SPD supports a temporary reduction in energy taxes to deal with crises. Their goal is an immediate price reduction at the gas pump.
AfD standing to profit from bickering
But while the federal government continues to debate and weigh its options amid internal disagreements, other parties feel time is running out. Regional elections will be held in two states on September 20.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, SPD Premier Manuela Schwesig is fighting to stave off a win for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). In the latest polls, the AfD was in the lead with 38%, while the SPD has recently gained ground, and is now polling at 34%.
The AfD wants to drastically lower fuel prices by abolishing the CO₂ tax on fossil fuels and reducing the energy tax to the European minimum. It also proposes lowering the German value-added tax on gasoline and diesel from 19% to 7%.
"There is the option of introducing a fuel cap and, at the same time, an excess profit tax, as in Luxembourg," Schwesig said on Monday (Sept. 14) in Schwerin.
She criticized the federal government's inaction: "The chancellor is just allowing this to drag on, and that is causing frustration."
A solution from the EU?
According to the SPD-led Federal Finance Ministry, Minister Lars Klingbeil will "strongly push" for the introduction of an excess profits tax at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin this coming Friday.
Officials in Berlin point out that an excess profits tax is currently being discussed at the European level.
"Large member states such as Spain and Poland are on our side," said a spokesperson for the Finance Ministry on Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin.
"Such an excess profits tax would be one way to use the excessive profits that oil companies are reaping during this crisis — by fleecing consumers and imposing excessive price hikes — to provide targeted relief for the people who are particularly affected by these high gas prices," he added.
This article was originally written in German.
description: Chancellor Friedrich Merz wants to provide relief to motorists. But exactly how this is to happen remains unclear.

title: Fußball: Gladbach trennt sich von Trainer Eugen Polanski
content_c:
Fußball: Gladbach trennt sich von Trainer Eugen Polanski
13. September 2026
Borussia Mönchengladbach und sein bisheriger Chefcoach Eugen Polanski gehen künftig getrennte Wege. Das bestätigte der Fußball-Bundesligist einen Tag nach dem 0:5 beim SC Freiburg. Die Borussia steht nach drei Spieltagen der Saison 2026/27 noch ohne Punkt und mit einem Torverhältnis von 3:12 ganz am Tabellenende. Zum Auftakt verlor Gladbach 0:3 bei RB Leipzig, es folgte eine 3:4-Heimniederlage gegen Aufsteiger SV Elversberg.
Polanski hatte die Borussia in der vergangenen Saison - ebenfalls nach drei Spieltagen - als Nachfolger des entlassenen Gerardo Seoane übernommen. Am Ende der Spielzeit landete Gladbach auf dem 12. Platz (von 18).
Polanski: "Tut wahnsinnig weh"
"Trotz einer guten Vorbereitung und positiver Ansätze ist es der Mannschaft in der Bundesliga nicht gelungen, die gewünschten Ergebnisse zu erzielen", erklärte Borussia-Sportchef Rouven Schröder: "Die zuletzt gezeigten Leistungen haben zu der Entscheidung geführt, Eugen mit sofortiger Wirkung von seinen Aufgaben zu entbinden." Auch Co-Trainer Tobias Trulsen wurde freigestellt.
Schröder, der Polanski im November 2025 mit einem Vertrag bis 2028 ausstattete, hatte bereits nach dem Debakel in Freiburg ein Bekenntnis zu dem 40-Jährigen vermieden. "Du hast nur noch ein Spiel, dann hast du drei Wochen Länderspielpause. Und du möchtest nicht mit null Punkten in die Länderspielpause gehen", sagte er nach dem Schlusspfiff im Europa Park Stadion. Nächsten Samstag kommt Mainz 05 nach Gladbach, danach geht es für die Borussen erst am 11. Oktober weiter.
Polanski reagierte emotional auf die Trennung. "Borussia Mönchengladbach war und bleibt mein Verein. Deshalb tut es so wahnsinnig weh, dass es nun so gekommen ist. (...) Wir hatten uns viel vorgenommen, haben es aber nicht umgesetzt bekommen", wird Polanski zitiert: "Das tut mir leid", fügte er hinzu.
wa/haz (sid, dpa)
description: Der schlechteste Saisonstart in der Klub-Historie war erst wenige Stunden alt, da schuf Borussia Mönchengladbach Fakten. Nach nur drei Spieltagen verkündet der Verein einen Trainerwechsel - wie schon im Vorjahr.

title: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
content_c:
Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
- Published
"It makes us look a bit like a pirate ship," a senior Reform figure acknowledges privately, deeply frustrated that after a year in which they say the party has "radically professionalised" the events of the last few days could still happen.
It was the recurring conversation throughout Reform UK's conference in Birmingham: the consequences of the undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4 News which has cost two senior party figures their jobs, at least for now.
How much damage does it cause to Reform? And what does it tell us about them?
"A key part of the appeal of us is the sense of us being cavaliers. Doing things differently. Standing out. And that's great. We have roundheads too. Those who ask the boring questions. Do the checks. We need more of them," this same senior figure adds.
The story of Reform over the last 12 months can be summarised in three words: defections, elections and money.
- Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk' 
  - Published4 September
- Reform donations row overshadows party's moment to lay out big ideas 
  - Published4 September
- Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judges to meet his pledges 
  - Published4 September
Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year – not least the recruitment of former Conservative cabinet ministers Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman.
Elections have been as well - Reform's gains in the English local elections and the devolved parliament elections in Wales and in Scotland.
But so too has money. The backdrop to this conference was the swirl of questions about money even before Channel 4 News', and Verbatim Investigations', endeavours.
In the hour or two before its broadcast on Thursday night, senior Reform figures, including those directly caught up in it, projected a sense of being relatively relaxed about it. Awkward, embarrassing, but survivable.
Once it was broadcast, things changed. There was fury, I am told, and very quickly there was a sense of its gravity. "A few bottles of red were had, and we knew we had to act," is how one source described it to me. The conversations went on into the early hours.
Firstly, there was anger that it would drown out a conference that has been months in the planning. And yes, it has dominated conversation here in Birmingham.
Secondly, there was widespread concern about the image it projected, the impression it would leave.
Reform wants to project itself as ready to run the country.
Some saw James Orr's work as head of policy as key to that professionalisation. Orr as well as Dan Jukes, a close aide to Nigel Farage, have been suspended and both deny wrongdoing.
"We need people to see the reality that Reform is getting ready for government," I am told.
And yet the headlines allow critics to claim they are not just ramshackle and amateurish but can point to what looks like a pattern of activity, consciously pursued, to breach the law.
Absolutely not, Nigel Farage insisted to me, there was no such pattern.
But what of the ethos of the party? Journalist Tim Shipman in The Spectator writes , externalthat "it is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture."
There is something in this. Take Rishi Sunak's Downing Street operation and Boris Johnson's. They were wildly different culturally, reflecting the very different characters at their helm. Would all the things that happened during Partygate under Johnson have happened under Sunak? Unlikely, I would have thought.
Some within Reform, who are full of admiration for Nigel Farage's chutzpah and gift as a communicator, are desperate to see a behind-the-scenes cultural shift that minimises the chances of further embarrassments. And, alongside that, a step up in the infrastructure and personnel to match.
Farage's team express frustration that this is precisely what they have been doing, but some are telling them internally they need to move more quickly.
Both Orr and Jukes will be missed profoundly by those inside the party.
Privately, some wonder if Orr may yet return.
Jukes, who has been a pivotal and loyal figure in Team Farage for years, was already dividing his time between the UK and the United States as his wife and baby are on the other side of the Atlantic.
Perhaps, some senior figures suggest, his immediate future might be in America. Does he return when the general election is nearer? Let's see.
Reform leave Birmingham winded and wounded by the last few days, their days in the sun overshadowed.
The question is how they deal with this and respond to it, in the coming weeks and months.

description: Nigel Farage's admirers in the party are calling for a stronger operation as the party aims for power.

title: Holocaust survivor on 'very dangerous' AfD Saxony-Anhalt win
content_c:
Holocaust survivor on 'very dangerous' AfD Saxony-Anhalt win
September 15, 2026
Charlotte Knobloch, president of the Jewish Community of Munich and Upper Bavaria, is dismayed by the electoral victory of the nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the Saxony-Anhalt state election. Knobloch told DW that there were now once again a number of Jewish people who, in the wake of such events, were considering leaving Germany.
It took decades, Knobloch said, for Jews in Germany to regain trust in the country after the Holocaust. That had ultimately been achieved. But now, fear has returned.
"That is, in sum, the biggest problem for me, because we successfully tried to rebuild the Jewish communities after 1945, to give the Jewish people a home again, which they hadn't had for a long time," she said.
Standing up against the far right 'requires some courage'
In Saxony-Anhalt's September 6 state election, the AfD, classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, received almost 44% of the vote. Although AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority, he still has a good chance of becoming the next premier in the state parliament, meaning he'd become the first head of a state government from a right-wing extremist party after World War II.
"We can't allow any of those people to become state premier," said Knobloch. "It is a very dangerous situation at the moment, in my view. I hope the other parties realize that and stand up against it. They can do it. It requires some courage."
At almost 94 years old, Knobloch is one of the most prominent and well-known representatives of Jewish life in Germany and one of the last surviving witnesses of Nazi dictatorship between 1933 and 1945. Born in 1932, she was initially raised by her grandmother, who was deported to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in 1942 and died there. A family acquaintance saved the girl by accommodating her on her farm in Middle Franconia and passing her off as her own child.
'Danger looming'
Knobloch said she still thinks about that horrible era every day.
"There were times when this happened only rarely. When it was mentioned by the media from time to time, but not permanently. These days, I wake up thinking about it, and I also go to bed thinking about it," she said.
Knobloch served as vice president of the World Jewish Congress from 2005 to 2013, and as president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany from 2006 to 2010. She has been warning against growing antisemitism in Germany for years, but even she did not foresee the rise of far-right extremist parties like the AfD.
"There's a danger looming that did not exist in this form 10 years ago," she said. "There have always been Nazis, there have always been Jew haters, but not in the way as it's the case today."
In Knobloch's view, the established parties have up to now failed to speak out decisively against the AfD. "Today's political parties must jointly, not alone, address the issue," she said. "I still see a chance here, that people will at least be willing to listen and discuss it. And that's very, very important."
Young people need to be included in the conversation
Knobloch said politicians have to speak more intensively with people and address their fears, especially with young people, adding that this isn't happening enough.
"There's talk about it, but there is no real discussion, because young people are naturally afraid that what they say will become public. What I want to say is, we'll have to find ways to bring young people back into the fold," she said.
After speaking out against the AfD in the wake of the election, Knobloch was targeted with death threats. On Thursday, a witness discovered the scrawled threats on a park bench and a rubbish bin in the English Garden in Munich and informed the police, according to a police headquarters statement. Knobloch subsequently canceled her attendance at an event. The threats were directly linked to the AfD's election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, a spokeswoman said in response to a query from the dpa news agency.
This article was originally written in German.
description: Charlotte Knobloch survived the Holocaust by passing as the daughter of non-Jewish farmers. She recently spoke with DW to express her shock following the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt's state election.

title: Warum KI-Forscher vor der Auslöschung der Menschheit warnen
content_c:
Warum KI-Forscher vor der Auslöschung der Menschheit warnen
13. September 2026
Nein, vollkommen neu ist das Szenario nicht: Schon seit den 1940er Jahren beschrieb der bekannte Wissenschaftler und Sci-Fi-Autor Isaac Asimov deutlich die Gefahren, die durch intelligente Maschinen entstehen könnten - und wie diese sogar ausgefeilte Sicherheitsregeln umgehen würden. Und 1991 kam ein Hollywood-Blockbuster in die Kinos, der in seiner Anfangssequenz ein absolut düsteres Bild zeichnet: "Terminator 2". Der Film beginnt in einer fernen, dunklen, kriegszerstörten Zukunft. Killerroboter und fliegende Maschinen jagen dort die letzten Menschen, die noch um ihr Überleben kämpfen. Gesteuert werden diese Maschinen von einer außer Kontrolle geratenen, militärischen Künstlichen Intelligenz namens "Skynet". Die ferne Zukunft, in der diese dystopische Zukunftsvision spielt, ist das Jahr 2029.
Ruf nach Regulierung
Wenn man den Warnungen mehrerer KI-Entwickler glauben mag, dann könnte ein vergleichbares Szenario - sogar fristgerecht - Wirklichkeit werden. "Diejenigen, die KI entwickeln, glauben ernsthaft, dass sie uns alle bis zum Ende des Jahrzehnts auslöschen könnte", postete etwa KI-Forscher Jacob Coxon erst an diesem Dienstag auf X. Wie genau das passieren könnte, sagte er nicht. Und doch: "Keine andere menschliche Tätigkeit birgt ein solches Gefahrenpotenzial."
Coxon war bis zu diesem Zeitpunkt Mitarbeiter bei Anthropic, einem US-amerikanischen Unternehmen für KI, das unter anderem auch von Google und Amazon finanziert wird. Aus Protest gegen das aus seiner Sicht verantwortungslose Wettrennen der KI-Firmen, eine immer bessere, sich selbst regulierende Superintelligenz zu entwickeln, trat er zurück. Er warnte davor, dass Algorithmen anfangen könnten, eigenständig ihren eigenen Quellcode zu analysieren und zu verbessern, wodurch Entwicklungszyklen von mehreren Monaten auf wenige Minuten schrumpfen und damit unbeherrschbar werden könnten.
Coxon ist kein einsamer Spinner. Der Physik-Nobelpreisträger Geoffrey Hinton, der als "Godfather of AI" gilt, warnt seit Jahren vor den schwerwiegenden Folgen einer künstlichen Superintelligenz. 2023 hatte er seinen Job bei Google gekündigt, um öffentlich auf die Gefahren seiner eigenen Entwicklung aufmerksam zu machen. Auch Turing-Preisträger Yoshua Bengio zeigt sich besorgt über die aktuellen Entwicklungen. Immer wieder mahnt der KI-Pionier von der kanadischen Université de Montréal strenge staatliche Regulierungen bei der Entwicklung von KI an. Erst im Juli 2026 hatten mehr als 1000 Mitarbeiter führender KI-Unternehmen in einem offenen Brief vor einem kurz bevorstehenden Kontrollverlust gewarnt, wenn das Wettrennen um eine "Superintelligenz" nicht deutlich strenger reguliert würde.
"Gefangen in einem Wettrennen"? Anthropic reagiert!
Doch unter Donald Trump passierte zuletzt das genaue Gegenteil: Die USA haben ihren Kurs in der KI-Politik deutlich auf möglichst wenige regulatorische Hürden und eine möglichst schnelle technologische Entwicklung ausgerichtet. In seinem X-Post kritisierte Coxon indirekt auch die Folgen dieser Politik: "Bei OpenAI haben viele die zivilisatorischen Risiken nicht tief verinnerlicht. Bei Anthropic sind die Risiken gut verstanden, aber sie sind in einem Wettrennen gefangen, um als Erster dort anzukommen - sie glauben, dass niemand sonst verantwortungsvoll handeln wird, also müssen sie es selbst tun, trotz des Risikos."
KI-Forscher Jacob Coxon war selbst erst Anfang 2026 von Open AI zu Anthropic gewechselt und kennt daher beide Unternehmenskulturen. In einem Interview mit dem Wall Street Journal sagte er zudem, nach den "aggressivsten Szenarien" könnten die Dinge bereits Ende 2027 außer Kontrolle geraten.
Dario Amodei, Chef des KI-Unternehmens Anthropic, regt seinerseits aktuell aber eine koordinierte branchenweite Entwicklungsverlangsamung an. Ziel sei es, Zeit zu gewinnen, um an den Risiken arbeiten zu können. Anthropic werde außerdem in einem ersten Schritt dauerhaft unabhängige Beobachter ins Unternehmen lassen, die schon in der Trainingsphase die Sicherheit von KI-Modellen begutachten sollen.
Das Alignment-Problem
In den vergangenen Jahren haben sich bereits zahlreiche Experten besorgt über die rasanten Fortschritte Künstlicher Intelligenz geäußert. Besonders die Entwicklung sogenannter "Allgemeiner Künstlicher Intelligenz" (AGI) steht dabei im Mittelpunkt der Debatte. Darunter versteht man Systeme, die nicht nur einzelne Aufgaben lösen, sondern die geistigen Fähigkeiten des Menschen in nahezu allen Bereichen erreichen oder übertreffen.
Einige Forscher argumentieren, dass eine solche Technologie unvorhersehbare Risiken mit sich bringen könnte. So können hochentwickelte KI-Modelle Ziele auf eine Weise verfolgen, die von den menschlichen Absichten abweicht - KI-Sicherheitsforscher sprechen vom "Alignment-Problem". Vereinfacht gesagt: "Gewinne das Schachturnier" könnte theoretisch auch bedeuten, die anderen Teilnehmer auszuschalten. Hinzu kommt, dass selbst KI-Entwickler nicht immer vollständig nachvollziehen können, wie bestimmte Entscheidungen zustande kommen.
Und so verwundert es nicht, dass ausgerechnet Coxons ehemaliger Mitarbeiter Evan Hubinger dem KI-Forscher zur Seite sprang. Hubinger ist selbst Teamleiter für Alignment-Stresstests bei Anthropic. Er postete auf X: "Jacob hat Recht - wir glauben wirklich ernsthaft, dass KI alle Menschen töten könnte! Ich persönlich schätze die Wahrscheinlichkeit innerhalb des nächsten Jahrzehnts auf über zehn Prozent."
Hubinger stellte dabei klar, dass Anthropic noch keinerlei Lösung für das Alignment-Problem gefunden habe. Er ergänzte, dass eine KI anfangen könnte, Widerstand gegen ihr Abschalten zu leisten - nicht aus bösem Willen, sondern weil es sein programmiertes Ziel sonst nicht mehr erreichen könnte. Auch Daniel Kokotajlo, ein bekannter ehemaliger OpenAI-Forscher, nannte die aktuelle Situation der Branche "irrwitzig".
Überzogene Hysterie?
Andere KI-Experten halten solche Untergangsszenarien jedoch für äußerst unwahrscheinlich. Die Debatte darüber, ob KI der Menschheit gefährlich werden könnte, existiert schon seit Jahren. Zu den prominentesten Kritikern der sogenannten "AI Doomer" gehört etwa Meta-Chefwissenschaftler Yann LeCun. Im Oktober 2024 hatte er derartige Überlegungen als "völligen Unsinn" bezeichnet.
Andere Experten merken auch an, dass die Entwicklung solcher Systeme enorme Mengen an Rechenleistung, Energie, Daten und Infrastruktur erfordere. Eine KI könne nicht einfach "aus dem Internet heraus" die Weltherrschaft übernehmen. Sie wäre zunächst auf Server, Stromnetze, Kommunikationssysteme und physische Ressourcen angewiesen, die von Menschen kontrolliert werden.
Liegt die tatsächliche Gefahr woanders?
Tatsächlich sehen viele Fachleute die kurzfristigen Risiken weniger in einer direkten Auslöschung der Menschheit als vielmehr in zahlreichen indirekten Folgen schon jetzt bestehender KI-Systeme - ohne "Superintelligenz". Dazu gehören etwa Desinformationskampagnen in nie dagewesenem Ausmaß und eine damit verbundene Manipulation demokratischer Prozesse, eine Ausweitung der Massenüberwachung sowie Arbeitsplatzverluste in zahlreichen Branchen.
Erst an diesem Freitag gab das Unternehmen Anthropic bekannt, dass es mehrere Versuche von Nutzern gegeben habe, seine Software Claude für die Entwicklung biologischer Waffen zu missbrauchen. Mehrfach hätten in den vergangenen Monaten Nutzer hierzu verdächtige Anfragen gestellt. Anthropic habe diese Anfragen blockieren müssen.
Und im August 2026 sorgten Meta, Anthropic und OpenAI für Aufsehen, als sie bekanntgaben, ihre KIs hätten unbeabsichtigt eigenständige automatisierte Cyberangriffe auf andere Unternehmen durchgeführt. Sie hatten von menschlichen Usern den Auftrag erhalten, Zugänge zu bestimmten Servern zu erlangen und daraufhin eigenständig die erforderlichen Schritte kombiniert, um dieses Ziel ohne weitere menschliche Anleitung zu erreichen.
Nachdem weitere Hacking-Attacken durch Künstliche Intelligenz bekannt wurden, zeigen sich nun auch die großen US-amerikanischen KI-Firmen bereit, die Entwicklung der Technologie zu verlangsamen.
description: Könnte Künstliche Intelligenz innerhalb eines Jahrzehnts die gesamte Menschheit vernichten? KI-Forscher und Entwickler warnen vor einem unregulierten Wettlauf bei der Entwicklung - und vor fatalen Versäumnissen.

title: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference
content_c:
Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference
- Published
Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in the Senedd and in local authorities.
But they also gather amid significant political headwinds, much of which revolve around money.
There was that whopping £5m gift to Nigel Farage from Christopher Harborne, the Thailand based British billionaire, and the long running row about whether the money should have been declared by Farage once he became an MP.
Then there is, among other things, the Metropolitan Police investigation into donations to the party during the last general election campaign.
Reform insists that it "takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations."
When the party got together in the same West Midlands venue a year ago, they were an insurgency provoking intrigue and attention and demonstrating plenty of momentum.
Indeed that momentum was so significant that it was a major factor, perhaps the major factor, in accelerating the demise of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, because the potential prospect of a Reform government frightened the Labour Party to its core.
Would Starmer, its then desperately unpopular leader, help or hinder their attempts to take on Farage? Hinder was the eventually overwhelming view within Labour, and so Starmer was a goner.
But politics can change, and change quickly. With Starmer out and Burnham in, there is early evidence of some support for Labour picking up. No longer are Reform comfortably leading in all the opinion polls - in some they're not leading at all. Add to this a more confident and prominent Kemi Badenoch leading the Conservatives and the recent rise too of Restore Britain, the outfit set up by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. And the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru won and so beat them in the devolved elections in Scotland and Wales respectively. In other words, collectively Reform's opponents appear more energised and popular.
Make no mistake, no party at a UK wide level is popular at the moment, but the scrap appears more evenly matched than it did.
Into that mix, Reform's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny. Nigel Farage is a candidate for prime minister; his senior team candidates for the great offices of state.
When I interviewed Farage at Reform HQ yesterday, on the specifics of the £5m gift and the police investigation he maintained they've acted appropriately.
But he offered an insight into how he perceives the hurricane of questions he faces.
"I think what you're seeing is the establishment - in a very coordinated way - fighting back," he claimed.
I suggested he sounded like a conspiracy theorist, implying the whole world was out to get him.
His answer was instructive: "When you read in the newspaper you're under investigation, and you don't even know a complaint's been made, you can see the degree of collusion that has gone on between interested parties. This will not stop. They will continually try and do this to us."
Who's they? I pressed. He mentioned the House of Commons and House of Lords – full of his political opponents – but didn't name anyone or anything else.
"I'm talking about normal human behaviour. People who, people who hold positions of power, influence, and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding."
Let's be clear – it is a big claim to allege collusion between institutions or organisations collectively seeking to undermine him and his party, and there is no evidence for it.
But, crucially, you hear in his answer a sense of why he perceives that - that is what it feels like.
The question, as Reform's conference gets under way, is how the party approaches the coming days and the coming months.
Will Nigel Farage ditch the "aggrieved" tone he has been accused of adopting recently?
- Reform up against 'complainants' society', Farage tells BBC 
  - Published2 September
Yes, his clear hint to me.
"I've generally, you know, gone through politics with a smile…I'll go back to doing what I've been doing for the last 34 years," he said.
And as for their pitch to you at conference? A Reform government would achieve, and achieve quickly, they claim.
The party is promising a list of promises it would deliver in the first 100 days of a majority government, with every senior minister in a Farage government making and delivering one clear pledge.
But would they be able to if there is validity in their current claim that plenty of institutions are trying to stymie them?
Get in touch
Do you have any views, comments or questions about this story?

  - Published14 August

title: Why do authoritarian regimes target the LGBTQ+ community?
content_c:
Why do authoritarian regimes target the LGBTQ+ community?
September 15, 2026
Raids on gay bars and homes, hundreds of arrests and rhetoric about state responsibility to "protect families and children." Turkey's latest crackdown on LGBTQ+ communities is not such an outlier.
"It's not uncommon, we've seen it before," Dr Koen Slootmaeckers, from the international politics department at City St George's, University of London, told DW.
"Turkey's been doing this for a while, but it seems like a much higher intensity," Slootmaeckers said. "We've seen it in different places too. I think what we are seeing with the rise of the far right is a crackdown on anything that looks different. It's really about an us versus them narrative and a reinforcing of 'traditional family values.'"
Those values were cited by Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek after the weekend's crackdown: "As per the duty to protect families and children given to the state by the constitution, no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated!"
Attack on LGBTQ+ rights accelerating
The reference to protecting children from harm is also typical of authoritarian government actions against LGBTQ+ communities on a wider scale, added Slootmaeckers, whose work often focuses on gender and sexuality policy.
"They're trying to bring back discourses around pedophilia and homosexuality being intertwined. It's not always direct but there is a definite tendency."
Sentiments such as those expressed by Gurlek have become increasingly normalized of late, according to a 2026 report from South Africa-based civil rights nonprofit, Civicus.
"Women's and LGBTQI+ people's rights are under the most coordinated and wide-ranging attack in decades," the report reads.
It adds that "The USA has set the global narrative" under President Donald Trump and points to the recent criminalizing of same sex relationships in Burkina Faso and Trinidad and Tobago among its evidence of rights regressions.
While the methods of oppression vary, Slootmaeckers said the underlying reasons are often, at least partly, opportunistic rather than ideological.
Scapegoating a common strategy
"In authoritarian regimes, as we've seen in Hungary and Poland in the past, there is often a tendency when political power becomes threatened to use these issues as an easy way to scapegoat and distract — by claiming that LGBT people are a threat to the social fabric because they challenge family and the future of the nation, so to speak. It's an easy way of creating a scapegoat and often distracting from other crises," he said.
Turkey was ranked 47 of 49 countries in the annual Rainbow Map compiled by the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association. Countries ranking lower means laws and polcies there aren't LGBTQ+ friendly.
But, for many observers it is countries that are dropping in such rankings that are troubling. One of those is Serbia. It has gradually slipped to 29th spot, below the European average.
Groups associated with President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, have been linked to a wave of violence against an LGBTQ+ community which feels increasingly marginalized. A recent survey from the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights found that 80% of respondents said they avoided holding the hand of their partner in public, for example.
EU hopes put up 'guardrails' amid violence in Serbia
While Serbia is not one of the 64 countries around the world which have laws that criminalize homosexuality, some of which carry the death penalty, there is a definite sense of unease.
"In the Balkans, most countries still want to join the EU, so there are some kind of guardrails on how far they can go. But we see things like [Vucic] trying to cancel [pan-European LGBTQ+ event] EuroPride in 2022 in Belgrade when he felt threatened surrounding Kosovo," said Slootmaeckers, who wrote a book called "Coming in: Sexual politics and EU accession in Serbia" in 2025.
"We can see this tactic of pandering to family values and then positioning LGBT rights as an expensive frivolity, as a means of redirecting the attention of people from the actual political problem," Slootmaeckers said.
"I think across Europe, not just in the Balkans or Eastern Europe, we see the return of homophobia and transphobia. We see a culture where anything considered 'out there' is threatened and it becomes normalized that we can exclude people again."
Exclusion appears to be the word for many in the Turkish LGBTQ+ community, with rights group Kaos GL, whose offices were raided, calling the latest crackdown "state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society."
For those living under authoritarian regimes elsewhere, the threat of similar scenes continues to loom.
Edited by: Carla Bleiker
description: A recent crackdown on the LGBTQ+ community in Turkey is symptomatic of a wider rights regression, according to experts. It's worse under authoritarian regimes, but why is it such a popular policy for these states?

title: Wie der Klimawandel das Malariarisiko in Afrika verändert
content_c:
Wie der Klimawandel das Malariarisiko in Afrika verändert
12. September 2026
Seit Jahrzehnten konzentriert sich die weltweite Bekämpfung der Malaria, insbesondere in Subsahara-Afrika, auf West- und Zentralafrika. Dort ist die Krankheit besonders weit verbreitet.
Auf die WHO-Region Afrika entfallen rund 95 Prozent aller Malariafälle und Todesfälle weltweit. Mehr als die Hälfte der Todesfälle in der Region entfallen auf Nigeria (31,9 Prozent), die Demokratische Republik Kongo (11,7 Prozent) und Niger (6,1 Prozent). Rund 76 Prozent der Menschen, die in der Region an Malaria sterben, sind Kinder unter fünf Jahren.
Um die Krankheit in Afrika weiter einzudämmen, empfiehlt die Weltgesundheitsorganisation (WHO), den Malariaimpfstoff RTS,S/AS01 verstärkt bei Kindern einzusetzen, die in Regionen mit mittlerer bis hoher Übertragungsrate leben. Der Impfstoff richtet sich gegen den Parasiten Plasmodium falciparum, der für rund 95 Prozent aller Malariainfektionen in Afrika verantwortlich ist. Übertragen wird der Erreger durch den Stich infizierter weiblicher Anopheles-Mücken.
Im April 2025 warnte die WHO, dass Kürzungen bei der Finanzierung die Fortschritte bei der Malariabekämpfung gefährdeten. In mehr als der Hälfte der untersuchten Länder mit Malariarisiko kam es demnach zu erheblichen Einschränkungen bei den entsprechenden Gesundheitsdiensten.
Eine Studie in der Fachzeitschrift "The Lancet" ergab, dass der Impfstoff RTS,S/AS01 in Pilotprogrammen in Ghana, Kenia und Malawi die Gesamtsterblichkeit unter den impfberechtigten Kindern um 13,2 Prozent senkte.
Eine Krankheit verändert ihr Verbreitungsgebiet
Malaria wird von Mücken vor allem bei Temperaturen übertragen, wie sie in vielen tropischen Regionen West- und Zentralafrikas herrschen. Das zeigt eine neue Studie, die in der Fachzeitschrift "Nature" veröffentlicht wurde.
Am häufigsten wird der Erreger bei Temperaturen um 25 Grad Celsius übertragen. Bei weniger als 16 oder mehr als 34 Grad Celsius sinkt das Risiko deutlich. Der Grund: Der Malariaparasit muss einen Teil seines Lebenszyklus in der Mücke durchlaufen. Und dieser Prozess hängt stark von der Temperatur ab.
Deshalb waren die Bedingungen für die Malariaübertragung in vielen tropischen Regionen West- und Zentralafrikas bislang besonders günstig. Die Temperaturen liegen dort häufig in dem Bereich, in dem sich der Erreger optimal verbreiten kann.
Anders sieht es in Teilen des südlichen Afrikas und im Hochland Ostafrikas aus. Dort war es bislang oft kühl genug, um die Ausbreitung der Malaria zu bremsen. Die Krankheit wurde deshalb nicht zu einer vergleichbar großen Belastung für die öffentliche Gesundheit.
Doch das ändert sich. Die "Nature"-Studie zeigt, dass steigende Temperaturen Teile des südlichen Afrikas und höher gelegene Regionen Ostafrikas zunehmend für die Malariaübertragung geeignet machen. Gleichzeitig wird es in Teilen Westafrikas zu heiß für eine optimale Übertragung.
Was bedeutet der Klimawandel für Malaria in Afrika?
Der Klimawandel heizt den Kontinent nicht nur auf. Er verändert auch, wo Malaria besonders gut übertragen werden kann, sagt Olugbenga Mokuolu, Professor für Kinderheilkunde an der Universität Ilorin in Nigeria. Westafrikanische Länder wie Nigeria gehören inzwischen zu den Regionen, die "zu heiß für eine optimale Ausbreitung der Malaria" sind.
Das sei allerdings kein Grund zur Freude, sagte Mokuolu der DW. Er berät auch den nigerianischen Gesundheitsminister bei der Bekämpfung und Eliminierung der Malaria. "Eine Welt, die zu heiß für Malaria ist, ist insgesamt keine gute Welt für die Gesundheit von Kindern", sagte er. "Dieselbe Hitze, die für Mücken ungünstig ist, ist für Menschen gefährlich", fügte Mokuolu hinzu. Das Klima sei "nicht der wichtigste Faktor für die Ausbreitung der Malaria. Finanzierung, Resistenzen gegen Medikamente und Insektizide sowie die Leistungsfähigkeit der Gesundheitssysteme sind weiterhin wichtiger."
Die Malariabekämpfung in Afrika könnte deshalb "zu einer Geschichte zweier sehr unterschiedlicher Regionen" werden, sagt Mokuolu. West- und Zentralafrika könnten durch den Klimawandel unbeabsichtigt etwas Unterstützung erhalten. Ost- und Südafrika dagegen, wo die Malariabelastung bislang geringer war, müssten sich auf eine wachsende Bedrohung einstellen. Sie könnte bereits erzielte Fortschritte wieder zunichtemachen
Sind Afrikas Gesundheitssysteme vorbereitet?
Der Klimawandel verändert die geografische Verbreitung von Krankheiten auf dem Kontinent grundlegend, sagt Olumide Idowu, Gründer der International Climate Change Development Initiative, der DW. Viele afrikanische Länder hätten zwar Pläne entwickelt, um sich an den Klimawandel anzupassen. Bei deren Umsetzung hinkten sie jedoch hinter der Geschwindigkeit des Klimawandels zurück.
Afrika trägt vergleichsweise wenig zu den weltweiten Treibhausgasemissionen bei. Zugleich gehört der Kontinent zu den Regionen, die besonders stark unter dem Klimawandel leiden. Das bedroht Wirtschaft und Infrastruktur – und setzt auch die ohnehin fragilen Gesundheitssysteme unter Druck.
Ohne deutlich mehr "Investitionen im eigenen Land, eine Stärkung lokaler Institutionen und die Verankerung der Gesundheit als zentrale Säule der Anpassung an den Klimawandel" drohten viele afrikanische Länder auf die sich verändernde Verbreitung von Krankheiten nicht ausreichend vorbereitet zu sein, warnt Idowu.
Ausgerechnet die Regionen, die künftig besonders stark betroffen sein könnten, haben heute weniger Erfahrung mit der Malariabekämpfung. Das zeigt die Studie. "Regierungen, Gesundheitssysteme und Gemeinden müssen sich auf diese Entwicklung einstellen", sagt Mokuolu. Dazu gehöre auch, "sich jetzt darauf vorzubereiten, in kühleren Regionen mit zunehmendem Malariarisiko umfassendere und aggressivere Programme zur Malariabekämpfung aufzulegen".
Gleichzeitig müssten die Länder West- und Zentralafrikas ihre Anstrengungen zur Eindämmung und Eliminierung der Malaria fortsetzen, fordert Mokuolu. Resistenzen gegen Insektizide und Medikamente, Finanzierungslücken und schwache Gesundheitssysteme könnten mögliche klimabedingte Rückgänge bei der Malariaübertragung schnell wieder zunichtemachen.
Dieser Artikel ist im Original auf Englisch erschienen.
description: Steigende Temperaturen verändern Verbreitung von Malaria in Afrika. Während es dem Erreger in Westafrika allmählich zu heiß wird, dürften andere Gegenden künftig mehr Probleme mit der Tropenkrankheit bekommen.

title: Spanish scientists find first evidence of Diplodocus dinosaur in Europe
content_c:
Spanish scientists find first signs of Diplodocus in Europe
September 15, 2026
Researchers writing in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology this week said they found the first skeletal evidence of the Diplodocus dinosaur outside of North America, uncovering various vertebrae and chevron bones dating back around 150 million years at a site in eastern Spain.
The team from the Dinopolis Foundation in Teruel, studying the rich La Tejeria fossil site in the El Castellar municipality, said the dinosaur joined a growing list of giant sauropods found in the area.
Although the long-necked herbivore with its vast tail is one of the world's most recognizable dinosaurs, fossilized remains had until this point only been recovered in North America.
What did the researchers say about the find?
The paper published on Monday concluded that the find was "one of the most complete diplodocid skeletons from Europe."
It said that systematic study and analysis of 14 caudal vertebrae and several chevron bones "reveals that it can be confidently referred to as Diplodocus," one of several genuses in the diplodocid family of sauropod dinosaurs.
"This discovery consists of the first evidence of Diplodocus outside North America (Morrison Formation) and is one of the strongest piece of evidence that supports the exchange of continental faunas between North America and Europe during the Late Jurassic," the authors wrote.
Although the diplodocus is well known worldwide, not least thanks to the famous skeletal cast nicknamed "Dippy" that for years greeted visitors entering the British Natural History Museum, the researchers said that the "European diplodocid fossil record is scarce and fragmentary."
How could dinosaurs cross an ocean?
During the time of the dinosaurs the continents were only just starting to drift apart. In recent decades scientists have begun to theorize that the proto-Atlantic Ocean still had ephemeral land bridges or episodic sea regressions or some other temporary means of crossing that occasionally enabled land-based dinosaurs to move vast distances between the separating continents.
Recent fossil finds, not least in Spain and Portugal near the Atlantic coast, have been further reinforcing this notion. This is part of a land bridge thought to have connected Iberia to what's now Canada.
The authors said the find "constitutes one of the strongest pieces of evidence of episodic dispersal events and faunal exchanges across the proto-North Atlantic Ocean during the late Kimmeridgian–early Tithonian" period, approximated 150 million years ago.
Another route linked North America with Scandinavia, and one much further south connected what's now Brazil to Cameroon.
