description: Paleontologists in Spain say they have found the first evidence of the long-necked Diplodocus genus of dinosaur outside of North America. They found bones at the rich La Tejeria fossil site in Teruel in eastern Spain.

title: Roma-Künstler Norbert Olah: Zwischen Orban und Aliens
content_c:
Roma-Künstler Norbert Olah: Zwischen Orban und Aliens
11. September 2026
Auf der bemalten Leinwand spielt ein Mann gegen einen Roboter Schach. Sein Gesicht aus Ölfarbe glänzt noch feucht. Norbert Olah hat bis in die frühen Morgenstunden in der Bura-Galerie gearbeitet, die er den Sommer über als Atelier nutzt. Nachts, wenn Ungarns Hauptstadt Budapest langsam zur Ruhe findet, kann er sich am besten konzentrieren.
Im hinteren Teil der Galerie hat Olah den Fliesenboden mit Folie und Pappe abgeklebt. Über den Raum verteilt stehen Pinselbecher und Farbtuben, Bleistift-Skizzen und immer wieder Bilder mit der blau-grünen Roma-Fahne.
Norbert Olah ist Künstler - und Rom. Lange klammerte er diesen Teil seiner Identität aus seiner Kunst aus. Nicht, weil seine Herkunft für ihn unwichtig gewesen wäre, sondern aus Angst vor dem Etikett, das damit hätte einhergehen können: das Etikett des "Roma-Künstlers". "Es gibt so viele Vorurteile über Roma-Kultur und Roma-Kunst", sagt Olah. "Die Kunstszene sieht sie als naiv an, als unprofessionell, unbedarft und kitschig."
Doch je älter Olah wurde, desto schwerer ließ sich die eigene Geschichte künstlerisch ausblenden. Erst recht nicht in einem Land, in dem Roma-Sein nicht nur eine Frage der Herkunft, sondern auch der politischen Realität ist.
Eine Jugend unter Orban
Als Viktor Orbans Fidesz-Partei 2010 zum ersten Mal mit absoluter Mehrheit die Parlamentswahl gewinnt, hat Olah gerade die Schule abgeschlossen und beginnt sein Studium der Malerei an der Ungarischen Universität der Bildenden Künste in Budapest. In einer Zeit im Leben, in der die Welt eigentlich größer wird, hat er das Gefühl, dass sich immer mehr Grenzen auftun.
Als Künstler und als Rom bekommt Olah die Folgen der politischen Neuausrichtung Ungarns unmittelbar zu spüren: Die Kulturszene wird politisch vereinnahmt und auf Linie gebracht, die Roma werden rhetorisch zur Zielscheibe. Auch durch Orban selbst. Er fällt immer wieder mit rassistischen Bemerkungen über Roma auf.
Für die etwa 700.000 Roma in Ungarn bedeutete die Orban-Herrschaft 16 Jahre zwischen offiziellen Integrationsversprechen und anhaltender Ausgrenzung. Orbans Regierung führte zwar ein staatliches Beschäftigungsprogramm ein, in dem vor allem Roma arbeiten - statt ihnen dabei zu helfen, auf dem Arbeitsmarkt Fuß zu fassen, hält es viele Roma jedoch nur in prekären, schlecht bezahlten Aushilfsjobs fest. Für tatsächliche Veränderungen tat die Regierung wenig. Roma sind in Ungarn bis heute überproportional häufig von Armut und sozialer Ausgrenzung betroffen.
Irgendwann kann und möchte Norbert Olah nicht länger zusehen.
Die Grenzen der Anderen
Bei der Off-Biennale in Budapest, der größten unabhängigen Veranstaltung für zeitgenössische Kunst in Ungarn, mauert Olah 2021 gemeinsam mit seinem Vater eine Wand aus Backsteinen, direkt vor dem Eingang des sogenannten Roma-Parlaments, ein Roma-Kulturzentrum mit Kunstsammlung, Archiv, Bibliothek und Veranstaltungen. Das ließ die Orban-Regierung 2016 räumen, angeblich aufgrund von baulichen Sicherheitsbedenken - verbunden mit dem Versprechen, dort ein nationales Roma-Kulturzentrum zu errichten. Das Gebäude steht bis heute leer.
"Die Ängste des Roma-Künstlers" nennt Olah sein Werk, in die Backsteine hat der Künstler Wörter wie "Integration", "Assimilation" und "Segregation" gemeißelt. Einige Wochen später schlägt Olah bei einer Performance mit einem Vorschlaghammer so lange auf sein Kunstwerk ein, bis es in sich zusammenbricht.
In einem Begleittext zu dem Kunstwerk schreibt Olah zum ersten Mal öffentlich über die Ängste, Vorurteile und Erwartungen, denen er als Künstler mit Roma-Wurzeln begegnet. Es ist ein Text voller Fragen. Sollte sich die Kunst eines Roma-Künstlers um Roma-bezogene Themen drehen? Was hat Herkunft mit Ästhetik zu tun? Würde man einen Künstler mit Roma-Wurzeln nur anfragen, wenn ein Roma-Künstler gesucht - oder auch, wenn ein ungarischer Künstler gebraucht werde?
"Natürlich suchen wir alle immer nach Antworten. Aber manchmal ist es interessanter, die Frage selbst zu betrachten", sagt Olah und zupft ein Stück Kreppklebeband vom Boden. "Wenn sie sich unangenehm anfühlt, ist sie eine gute Frage."
So erschafft Olah ein neues Etikett für Roma-Künstler - abseits aller äußeren Zuschreibungen. Die 2021 von Roma-Aktivisten ins Leben gerufene Bura-Galerie im 8. Budapester Bezirk wird unter seiner künstlerischen Leitung zu einem Ort dafür, zu einer Plattform für zeitgenössische Roma-Kunst. "Wir bitten nicht um Akzeptanz in der Kunstszene. Wir öffnen die Tür und bitten andere herein", sagt Olah.
Offener Antiziganismus
Identität und Ausgrenzung, Macht und Machtmissbrauch - diese Themen werden für Olah zentral für sein künstlerisches Schaffen. An Inspiration wird es ihm während der Orban-Jahre nicht fehlen.
Obwohl Fidesz kaum Politik für die Roma machte, konnte die Partei von Viktor Orban bei Wahlen lange auf die Stimme der Minderheit zählen - etwa, weil Lokalpolitiker über die kommunalen Beschäftigungsprogramme die Möglichkeit hatten, Druck auf sozial schwächere Wähler auszuüben. Außerdem wurden immer wieder Fälle von Stimmenkauf dokumentiert. Tatsächlich war Fidesz sich so sicher, dass ein Großteil der Roma weiterhin für sie stimmen würde, dass sie den immer noch weit verbreiteten Antiziganismus in der Gesellschaft offen schürte.
So sprach sich kurz vor der Wahl im April 2026 der damals noch amtierende Fidesz-Verkehrsminister Janos Lazar öffentlich gegen Arbeitsmigration aus mit dem Hinweis, dass es noch "interne Reserven" wie die Roma gebe, die die "vollgeschissenen Toiletten" in den Intercitys reinigen könnten. Auch diese Szene hat Olah künstlerisch aufgegriffen, in einem fingierten Wahlplakat, auf dem ein Mann in Sturmhaube auf einer goldenen Toilette sitzt und eine Klobürste schwenkt, darunter der Schriftzug "Gypsy Criminals for President".
Chance auf echten Wandel?
"Gypsy Criminals", das ist der Name des Künstlerkollektivs, das Olah 2024 zusammen mit einem Freund und dessen Zwergpinscher gegründet hat. Der einschlägige Begriff stammt eigentlich aus der ungarischen Kriminalstatistik und wird seit den 2000er Jahren von rechten Politikern verwendet, um Roma pauschal kriminelles Verhalten zu unterstellen. Der Name des Kollektivs ist ironisch gebrochen, wie vieles in Olahs Arbeiten.
Analysen der Roma for Democracy Stiftung zeigen, dass bei der Parlamentswahl im April 2026 viele Roma nicht mehr für Orbans Fidesz stimmten. Der neue Premier Peter Magyar schlug schon im Wahlkampf einen anderen Ton an gegenüber Roma an: Er traf sich mit Vertretern der Minderheit, im Wahlprogramm gab es einen eigenen Abschnitt zur Roma-Chancengleichheit. Vier der neuen Abgeordneten der Tisza-Partei im Parlament sind Roma, einer von ihnen wurde zum stellvertretenden Parlamentspräsidenten gewählt.
Seit der Wahl herrscht so etwas wie vorsichtiger Optimismus, dass sich nun tatsächlich etwas an der prekären Situation vieler Roma im Land ändern könnte. Gleichzeitig hat sich in den vier Monaten seit der Wahl außer dem Tonfall gegenüber der Minderheit noch nichts Grundlegendes geändert. "Ich sehe aktuell vor allem viele symbolische Gesten", sagt Olah.
Roma auf dem Mars
Während einige seiner Freunde aus der eher liberalen Kunstszene langsam ungeduldig würden, weil sie sich eine deutlich liberalere Politik von Magyar wünschen, bleibt Olah Realist: "Er ist ein konservativer Politiker. Wir haben ihn gewählt, damit er das Orban-System abschafft. Mehr hat er nicht versprochen." Die Wahl im April böte aber die Chance für einen politischen Neuanfang. "Ich denke, wir werden langfristig wieder in einer normalen Gesellschaft leben, die von einer normalen Regierung geführt wird, die manches gut machen wird und anderes nicht so gut. Als Künstler wird es meine Aufgabe sein, das zu kritisieren", sagt er.
Auch in seinen Werken beschäftigt sich Olah mit der Zukunft. Die ersten Bilder für sein nächstes Projekt hängen bereits im Atelier. Es geht um Roma-Futurismus: ein Roma-Paar beim Mars-Spaziergang, die blau-grüne Roma-Fahne auf dem Mond, ein schwereloser Astronaut mit einer traditionellen Cegled-Kanne, wie sie Roma-Musiker verwenden, außerdem ist eine zwei Meter große Raumstation in Form des Roma-Speichenrads geplant.
Die Raumfahrt ist für Olah auch eine Metapher für sozialen Aufstieg - für den Wunsch von Menschen und Gemeinschaften, die Grenzen zu überwinden, die ihnen Herkunft, Armut oder das Leben als Minderheit setzen. Was wäre, fragt er, wenn man eine Gesellschaft noch einmal von vorn denken könnte? Würden Aliens Roma vorurteilsfrei begegnen? Was bleibt von einer Identität, wenn sich alles an ihr wandelt?
Olah zerrupft das Klebeband zwischen den Fingern. Wieder so viele Fragen ohne Antwort. Aber genau das macht sie ja so interessant.
description: Norbert Olah ist Künstler - und Rom. Lange mied er seine Herkunft als künstlerisches Thema, aus Angst, darauf reduziert zu werden. Dann begann er, genau damit zu arbeiten. Über die Kunst, sich nicht festlegen zu lassen.

title: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land 'gobsmacking' donations
content_c:
Look closely at the posters, placards and online posts. Your eyes aren't deceiving you if Labour's red seems a little deeper and the Conservatives' blue a little truer.
Politics seems to have found a new rhythm, one that feels a little familiar, despite Reform's jaw-dropping new donations putting it back in the headlines today.
For the avoidance of doubt, the scale of that initial £36m gift to Nigel Farage's party alone is like something from a different political universe.
"It's a gobsmacking sum," a senior figure involved in running successive election campaigns for one of the big parties tells me.
That was even before another Reform donor pledged to match that astonishing sum with another £36m, saying the first donation had provoked his "competitive spirit".
But one cabinet minister is enjoying what they see as a newly obvious difference between Labour and the Tories. "It's clarifying," they say, a clear gap between Labour and the Tories' "sense of purpose and values".
A member of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's top team tells me, "normal jogging is reasserting itself", hopeful they're at the start of a more straightforward, routine moment in politics after years of craziness, with smaller parties vying to shove the traditional tribes out of the way.
The standout moment was at the despatch box this week when Prime Minister Andy Burnham declared that national security couldn't come at the expense of social security - a phrase immediately seized on by the Tories, interpreting it as the PM saying he'd never cut welfare spending to pay for defence.
One senior conservative said: "It was a real line in the sand, we could never have imagined Sir Keir Starmer saying that."
The party seems cock-a-hoop at a line they can use again and again, asserting the prime minister cares more about welfare than guarding against war.
But there is a positive atmosphere in No 10 too, one source telling me that the face-offs between Badenoch and Burnham have "breathed new life into the Labour versus Tory dynamic".
How can they both be happy, when ultimately politics is a contest and there can only be one winner in the end?
Well, on the security spat, Burnham's backers are adamant he does want to cut welfare spending, and find more money for defence. How does that stack up with his words this week?
I'm told No 10 will explain in more detail his belief that security also means secure communities, which aren't created by slashing benefits.
Crucially, they reckon while cutting welfare might appeal to some voters, "once you dig into the 'who' and the 'how' of doing that, public support wavers, and when Kemi talks about housing benefit cuts, public opinion goes all over the shop".
They even cite that moment as evidence that the prime minister is "happy to grab thorny issues and put himself at the centre of them", as he did with the early release of prisoners.
He'll give a grabby-sounding view before the government has found a solution to a problem, stake part of his reputation on it, and make the case, hoping it will work out.
The choices are only going to get harder and harder though. "Hope" as a slogan and a strategy could never be enough.
But when politics is fundamentally a contest, how can both the traditional political tribes be buoyant?
For Labour, it's not just the obvious change of leader to a more effective politician who is much more at ease talking to the public, whether that's an eight-second TikTok or his long explanations of his positions expressed in a newspaper opinion piece and posted on Facebook.
It's that Burnham is making arguments that are more appealing to Labour's psychology – build council houses, take stronger action against the worst excesses of the Israeli government, stand up for those who need to rely on benefits from the state.
Labour believes, for now, they have a leader who is simply a better politician, who is making arguments many of them find instinctively more appealing.
The party knows what its leader believes, broadly at least. As one senior figure said: "He has a worldview which the last one didn't - he's clear what he wants and he's grabbed the reins of power."
Another who has worked under Starmer and now Burnham said: "It's just chalk and cheese."
And don't underestimate the importance of keeping backbenchers content, feeling understood. A government source joked the whips, the party managers, are becoming a bit "like an HR department" listening to concerns rather than driving the troops forward.
But as Starmer found to his cost, backbenchers weren't prepared to be loyal to him when many felt he hadn't shown much care or loyalty to them.
But Badenoch's tribe also seems more chipper because, as she has told friends, there is now a sharper ideological divide between the two parties saying, "it's much clearer to have those arguments rather than a process discussion with Starmer".
Shadow ministers reckon it's easier to make classic Conservative arguments because in the words of one, "Andy Burnham is a classic old leftie and we're the obvious answer to that".
Shock, horror, Labour sources I put that to dispute that is the case, one close ally calling him "a pragmatist", another denying he's further to the left than Starmer, because, "Keir was so hard to place".
But one conservative source also pointedly wonders how long Labour's happiness with their new leader will last, given Burnham's rapid return to Parliament saying, "looking at the benches opposite there is a vision of somebody who has turned up to a Tinder date and doesn't quite look like his profile pic".
Ouch.
Will this newly refreshed red-blue battle prove to be the real deal?
Rhetorical lines have been drawn this week, but real choices and arguments loom, and the bouncy feeling around the place may not last, especially when it comes to finding cash for the prime minister's big promises.
Downing Street sources acknowledge privately that bringing down the welfare bill in the way that Alan Milburn envisages, with his report expected, but not confirmed, to come before the Budget, will need billions spent up front, money the government might struggle to find.
Similarly, to build the council houses Burnham desires to cut the housing benefits bill will need big cheques.
It's one thing promising those Labour friendly dreams. It's another, perhaps at the party conference, to answer the much harder question of how the government plans to pay.
It won't be easy for a mid-term prime minister to find money in the short term that might only produce savings in the years to come.
But Burnham's Labour are happy to talk about the economy and how they want to help hard-up families, still citing the chaos of Liz Truss and keen to underline the early steps the prime minister has taken to ease the pressure.
With borrowing costs and the country's debt seriously sky high, the Conservatives are pleased to sketch out a classic left-right argument too.
It's also true they have both been enjoying the moment of real pressure on their opponents in Reform, who have slipped back in the polls, besieged by claims and counter claims about party funding.
Although this weekend's mega donations illustrate that Nigel Farage still has the capacity to bust political conventions, the money from the crypto billionaire, Ben Delo, and cryptocurrency investor, Christopher Harborne, is completely off the charts for our politics.
Talking about the initial donation, a senior figure told me: "To put £36 m in context, one man has donated a sum bigger than Labour's entire 2024 election budget, bigger than the Conservatives', and about six times what Reform actually spent.
"It's the kind of donation that could change how politics is funded in the UK."
During the last general election campaign Labour raised about £9m, the Tories, Reform and the Lib Dems all less than £2m.
These extra millions give Farage enormous and immediate spending power, and there might be more to come. Although you can bet the other parties will cry foul over the scale of this big money coming from men with deep pockets, not least because Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over violating the Bank Secrecy Act.
It would be daft for either of the two main parties to assume this apparent return to traditional two-party politics is here to stay. But it is strangely new to be in a moment when both Labour and the Conservatives are broadly content.
As the new prime minister's universe settles, a key Labour figure observed: "We've had the amuse–bouche and it was very tasty. What happens next?"

title: Why the era of cheap government debt is over
content_c:
Why the era of cheap government debt is over
September 15, 2026
When the world's largest pension fund changes its investment strategy, the financial world pays close attention, especially when it plans to drastically reduce its holdings of US government bonds.
According to Reuters, Norway's sovereign wealth fund wants to cut its US bond holdings — which totaled about $215 billion (€186 billion) at the end of June — by $80 billion.
Global investors are increasingly viewing the debt binge with suspicion, especially as the US's national debt passed $40 trillion in August. This week, the yield on 30-year US Treasury bonds climbed to nearly 5.4%, the highest level since 2007.
How much debt is too much?
For highly indebted countries such as Japan, where debt exceeds 200% of economic output, borrowing money on capital markets is getting increasingly expensive. The same applies to Italy, France and the UK.
Germany is in a much better position. At around 65% of gross domestic product (GDP), its debt-to-GDP ratio is only about half that of the US.
Borrowing to modernize its armed forces and infrastructure, however, means that ratio is set to move toward 80% over the coming years.
Why US debt keeps rising
The US now spends over $1 trillion annually on interest payments — more than $3 billion per day — according to calculations by the Congressional Budget Office. Since 2024, Washington has spent more annually on servicing its debt than on its entire military.
The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis calculated that the US national debt has risen by around 650% over the past 30 years from $5.2 trillion in 1996.
The US budget deficit is on course to reach nearly 6% in 2026. Yet, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent aims to cut it by half — a goal seen as unrealistic given the huge cost of the Iran war plus a shortfall in revenue due to corporate tax cuts and the tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court.
"That is a very difficult path," Carsten Roemheld, a capital market strategist at Fidelity International, told DW. "Nervousness is also rising sharply within the US administration — that is clearly evident. If this trajectory continues, it will be very difficult to sustain."
This is particularly striking when you consider how rapidly US debt is rising.
The $10 trillion mark was passed during the 2008 financial crisis; $20 trillion was reached in 2017. By early 2022, the figure had already hit $30 trillion. It took just four and a half years to reach the next record high of $40 trillion this summer.
Why bond investors are worried
Bessent has resorted to a special measure to drive down US bond yields.
On September 9, he announced that he would triple the volume of long-term US government bond buybacks from the previous $2 billion to as much as $6 billion.
"The measure is, of course, far too small on its own to truly keep yields in check over the long term," Roemheld said.
"The bond market [now] demands discipline," Kim Crawford, global fixed income portfolio manager at JPMorgan Asset Management, told the Financial Times.
That discipline is, however, sorely lacking and many analysts say governments have shown little appetite for spending cuts.
US still dominates capital markets
Despite all the problems, most economists agree that there is currently no way for investors to bypass the United States.
"The European capital market is not yet an alternative to the US market," Carsten Brzeski, chief economist at ING Bank, told DW. He noted that China and other emerging markets are neither able nor willing to take over this role.
"That is why I believe investors — even though they currently fear higher inflation and question the sustainability of US sovereign debt — will not turn away from the US," Brzeski said. "At least not as long as the US economy is growing."
Fidelity's Roemheld also sees no immediate danger for the United States, which he says is unlikely to default and can simply print money to pay off the debt.
"But this course of action will undermine confidence," Roemheld said. "And one outlet for this is the dollar exchange rate, which suffers when international investors become less willing to continue providing dollars to the US."
AI investment drives up interest rates
However long the US war against Iran drags on — driving up military spending and energy prices — there are strong indications that the United States will have to pay higher interest rates on capital markets
Robert Sockin, chief US economist at asset manager PGIM, said this was partly because of artificial intelligence or "AI-related corporate bonds increasingly crowding out government bonds."
Roemheld agrees that, as major tech companies issue bonds to finance AI infrastructure, they are creating competition for government debt.
"The four major 'hyperscalers' alone — the companies building platforms for the US AI industry — have already raised over $800 billion in debt this year, a figure expected to rise further over the next year or two," Roemheld said.
This is an attractive alternative for many investors who previously held US Treasuries for safety, Roemheld said, only to see their outlook deteriorate in recent years.
If an investor can now get "long-term bonds from high-quality companies like Alphabet or Microsoft, sometimes with spreads of 100 basis points over Treasuries, then that represents genuine competition," Roemheld said.
This article was originally published in German.
description: US debt has topped $40 trillion. How risky is the country's growing debt burden. And will investors keep funding Washington's deficits?

title: Irans Kalkül vor den US-Zwischenwahlen
content_c:
Irans Kalkül vor den US-Zwischenwahlen
11. September 2026
"Der Krieg wird unmittelbar nach den Zwischenwahlen enden, weil der Iran nicht länger durchhalten kann", sagte US-Präsident Donald Trump am 9. September vor Journalisten. Trump bezeichnete die bevorstehende Abstimmung als "eine der wichtigsten Wahlen in der Geschichte unseres Landes" und verteidigte erneut den Krieg gegen den Iran. Er habe die Angriffe angeordnet, um die Entwicklung einer iranischen Atomwaffe zu verhindern. Zugleich versprach er, die Ölpreise würden sinken, sobald die Vereinigten Staaten den Krieg gewonnen hätten.
Die US-Zwischenwahlen finden am 3. November 2026 statt. Steigende Benzin- und Energiepreise in den USA könnten für die Republikaner um Präsident Trump zu einem politischen Problem werden. Viele Amerikaner sind von den höheren Kosten an der Zapfsäule betroffen. Eine weitere Verteuerung von Energie dürfte daher die Stimmung der Wähler belasten.
Am Mittwoch (09.09.2026) stieg der Preis für Rohöl der Referenzsorte Brent erneut auf mehr als 100 US-Dollar pro Barrel (159 Liter). Hintergrund sind die jüngsten Eskalationen zwischen dem Iran und den USA rund um die strategisch wichtige Straße von Hormus. Am Freitag (11.09.2026) hieß es, dass die mit dem Iran verbündeten Huthis im Jemen die Meerenge Bab al-Mandeb zwischen dem Roten Meer und dem Golf von Aden kontrollierten. Dies dürfte den globalen Energiemarkt weiter unter Druck setzen.
Nach Angaben der US-Regierung zerstörten amerikanische Streitkräfte am 8. September fünf iranische Rohöltanker. Die Aktion erfolgte als Reaktion auf zwei Angriffe der iranischen Revolutionsgarden (IRGC), die mit ballistischen Raketen ein Kriegsschiff der US-Marine attackiert haben sollen.
"Der Iran betrachtet Eskalation offenbar nach wie vor als kontrolliertes Instrument für Verhandlungen unter Zwangsdruck, und nicht als Selbstzweck", sagt der Nahost-Experte Mohammad Ghaedi im Gespräch mit der Deutschen Welle. Der Professor am Department of Political Science der George Washington University beschreibt die iranische Strategie als eine Form kontrollierter Eskalation. "Der Iran versucht, den USA vor den Zwischenwahlen Kosten aufzubürden. Zugleich soll der Druck nicht so groß werden, dass sich Washington zu einem umfassenden Krieg gezwungen sieht. Das erklärt, warum die Zahl der auf US-Marineschiffe abgefeuerten Raketen vergleichsweise gering war."
Der Iran wolle zwar demonstrieren, dass das Land in der Lage sei, US-Streitkräfte zu bedrohen und den Schiffsverkehr in der Region zu stören. Gleichzeitig solle die Konfrontation unterhalb einer Schwelle bleiben, die eine deutlich massivere amerikanische Reaktion auslösen könnte.
Rückkehr zum Memorandum?
Aus iranischer Sicht wäre eine Rückkehr zum Islamabad-Memorandum vom Juni offenbar die bevorzugte Option. Das betonte Präsident Massud Peseschkian Ende August auf dem Gipfel der Shanghaier Organisation für Zusammenarbeit in Bischkek. Der Iran werde zum Memorandum zurückkehren, wenn auch die Vereinigten Staaten ihre Verpflichtungen wieder erfüllten.
In Teheran scheint jedoch das Bewusstsein zu wachsen, dass eine rasche Rückkehr der USA zu dem Abkommen unwahrscheinlich ist. Ghaedi verweist dabei auf ein wesentliches Hindernis: "Das stellt die erste Bestimmung des Abkommens dar, die einen israelischen Rückzug aus dem Libanon voraussetzt, ein Schritt, den Teheran vor den israelischen Wahlen für unwahrscheinlich hält."
Die Wahl zur 26. Knesset, dem Parlament in Israel, findet am 27. Oktober 2026 statt, knapp eine Woche vor den US-Zwischenwahlen. In Teheran rechnen viele Beobachter offenbar damit, dass die entscheidende Weichenstellung im Konflikt erst nach dieser Wahlperiode erfolgt.
Am 2. September berichtete die Nachrichtenagentur Reuters, dass hochrangige Berater von Präsident Trump auf eine Begrenzung der Eskalation vor den Wahlen im November drängen. Sie fürchten demnach politische Nachteile für die Republikaner. Zugleich werde im Weißen Haus erwogen, militärische Maßnahmen nach der Wahl auszuweiten. Ob es tatsächlich zu einer erneuten Zuspitzung kommt, bleibt jedoch offen. Der wirtschaftliche Druck auf Iran dürfte unterdessen weiter zunehmen.
Wirtschaftlicher Druck und politische Zugeständnisse
Der iranische Wirtschaftswissenschaftler Ahmad Alavi, der in Schweden lebt, warnt im Gespräch mit der DW davor, wirtschaftlichen Druck automatisch mit politischen Zugeständnissen gleichzusetzen.
"Wenn die Führung der Islamischen Republik zu dem Schluss kommt, dass das Ziel des Drucks nicht darin besteht, ihr Verhalten zu ändern, sondern sie zu schwächen oder zu stürzen, könnte sie Zugeständnisse als eine größere Bedrohung für ihr Überleben ansehen und stattdessen auf eine Eskalation der militärischen Aktionen zurückgreifen", sagt Alavi. Teheran werde eher dann zu Zugeständnissen bereit sein, wenn eine tatsächliche Verringerung des Drucks möglich sei und ein verlässlicher Verhandlungskanal bestehe.
Oman und mehrere Golfstaaten bemühen sich inzwischen erneut um eine diplomatische Lösung. Nach Angaben der Financial Times planen die Außenminister der Golfstaaten in der kommenden Woche ein Treffen mit ihrem iranischen Amtskollegen im omanischen Salala. Ziel der von Oman initiierten Gespräche ist ein Abkommen, das die kommerzielle Schifffahrt durch die strategisch wichtige Meerenge vorübergehend sichern soll. Ein solches Abkommen dürfte allerdings die Zustimmung Washingtons benötigen, da die USA ihre Seeblockade gegen Iran aufrechterhalten.
Gleichzeitig signalisiert die Führung in Teheran öffentlich weiterhin Härte. "Wir werden den Krieg bis zum endgültigen Sieg fortsetzen", erklärte Ali Nikzad, stellvertretender Parlamentspräsident, am 9. September am Rande einer Veranstaltung vor Journalisten.
Auch Hossein Mohebbi, Sprecher der Revolutionsgarden, erklärte am 8. September, die USA müssten "den Krieg vollständig einstellen" und auf weitere Drohungen verzichten, wenn sie die aktuelle Situation beenden wollten. Zugleich drohte er mit einer umfassenderen Reaktion der Revolutionsgarden, sollten die Angriffe andauern.
Am 10. September veröffentlichten die Revolutionsgarden ein Video, das nach iranischen Angaben die Festsetzung eines unbemannten US-Unterwasserfahrzeugs vom Typ Anduril Dive-LD in der Straße von Hormus zeigt. Das Fahrzeug soll demnach bei einer verdeckten Mission zur Minenräumung eingesetzt worden sein.
Was passiert nach den US-Zwischenwahlen?
Nach Einschätzung Ghaedis wird die weitere Entwicklung maßgeblich vom Wahlausgang in den Vereinigten Staaten abhängen. Unabhängig davon habe der Iran jedoch wenig Interesse daran, den Konflikt auf eine deutlich höhere Eskalationsstufe zu heben.
Sollten die Demokraten die Kontrolle über den Kongress gewinnen und versuchen, Trumps Kriegsführung einzuschränken, könnte Teheran sogar noch vorsichtiger agieren. Die iranische Führung dürfte alles vermeiden wollen, was in den USA zu einem parteiübergreifenden Schulterschluss, der sogenannten Stunde der Exekutive, führen könnte.
description: Mit Blick auf die US-Zwischenwahlen im November steigt der Iran vorsichtig die Eskalationsleiter hinauf. Teheran versucht offenbar, den Druck auf Washington zu erhöhen, ohne dabei einen umfassenden Krieg zu provozieren.

title: The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough
content_c:
In early 2015, flower crowns started appearing on Ed Miliband's head. Petals and hearts were photoshopped on to the then-Labour leader by the "Milifandom", a movement of young, mostly female, voters sharing romanticised images on Twitter to protest against Miliband's "distorted media portrayal".
It was the brainchild of Abby Tomlinson, a 17-year-old sixth-form student, who came to the defence of the man she called "Milibae". The hashtag #Milifandom trended. Then Labour lost the 2015 election.
This prompted David Cameron, whose Conservatives increased their number of seats, to boast: "Britain and Twitter are not the same thing." Tomlinson later told me that having her hopes of Milibae in No10 dashed had made her a "political pessimist", after realising winning over voters online "doesn't happen in a day, a week or even months, it's going to take years".
More than a decade on and she is again using social media to big up a Labour leader, but this time in the heart of government. She sits in the press office in No 12 Downing Street as head of content for Andy Burnham. The government has spent the last few weeks recruiting producers, videographers and strategists, working out of both Whitehall and No 10 North in Manchester.
In his first month as PM, Burnham posted more than 50 times on Instagram, ranging from meetings with world leaders, campaigners, farmers and influencers, to meme-based content like ranking pub snacks with Chancellor John Healey as part of an announcement on business rates. Strategists believe Instagram and TikTok can play to Burnham's communication strengths and sense of humour.
They're all at it, of course. Videos of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch tearing into the budget or mocking ex-PM Sir Keir Starmer have gone viral. Reform UK's Nigel Farage has by far the biggest online audience of any UK party leader, with 7.6 million followers across Facebook, Instagram, X, TikTok and YouTube.
In Scotland, the SNP have long mobilised their online army to campaign for independence, building a following larger than that of the Lib Dems, which campaigns across Britain, whose leader Ed Davey has achieved some success with campaign stunts going viral.
Restore Britain, founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe, enjoys its highest level of support among users of X. The platform is owned by Elon Musk who has publicly endorsed the party, expanding its reach.
Plaid Cymru, newly installed in government in Wales, is still experimenting with its approach, using First Minister Rhun Ap Iorweth in "fun" memes while also posting more serious interview excerpts. The Greens' Zack Polanski has made much of running his own accounts, though as he has found in recent weeks, this comes with risks too.
So how much is enough? In a world where reputations can be made (or broken) with one comment or collaboration, getting the balance right is tricky – being accessible, authentic and approachable, without being cringe. And does it make any difference to elections?
Bring on the hashtag coffee
Cameron's successor, Theresa May, was similarly doubtful about the merits of social media. When she took office she rebuffed aides who suggested she start tweeting: "People don't say 'pass me the hashtag newspaper, or I'd like a hashtag coffee'." Announcements were to be made formally. When cabinet ministers were appointed in May's first reshuffle, it was heralded in press statements beneath the UK government coat of arms.
By contrast, this summer, presenting my 5 Live show from Downing Street during Burnham's first reshuffle, I could predict the appearance of another new minister because the two-person social media team from No 10 would move into position to capture the new arrivals on their cameras.
Of course, prime ministers (and wannabes) have long adapted to new technology. Winston Churchill harnessed the power of radio, but thought television a vulgar diversion. In the 1960s, Labour's Harold Wilson modelled his TV campaigning on JFK in America. In the 1990s, and 2000s leaders like Tony Blair were just as likely to be found on the chatshow sofa as on the Today programme.
Now, podcasts give long-form - and less combative - opportunities to connect with voters, while social media gives a quick hit of direct democratic dopamine.
Peter Hyman, a former adviser to both Tony Blair and Keir Starmer when in Downing Street, said the success of Burnham's early digital output was about "quantity as well as quality".
"You have to narrate the story of what you are doing three or four or five times a day so that you are out there regularly," Hyman said. "Keir Starmer wasn't out there enough and therefore it wasn't landing."
There is a causality dilemma here. Is Burnham more popular in the polls because he is racking up the likes on social media, or is he doing better online because people like him?
Not everyone is convinced. Cody Dahler, a comedian who posts sweary political explainers to his two million followers, warns voters will become cynical if they sense politicians are just using social media simply "as a comms tool". Burnham, Dahler told me on Newsnight, comes across like a "cool substitute teacher".
And after Burnham released a video discussing what a bread roll is called in different parts of the country – barm, cob or bap - to promote his plans for devolution, broadcaster Piers Morgan asked him to "stop wasting your time and ours with these cringe videos".
And therein lies the difficulty of striking a balance. Bea Timpson, a former press secretary to Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak who says she prefers "trad media" like broadcast and print, added: "I have to accept that it's now non-negotiable to be online a bit, but you definitely can be too much."
The arms race for audiences
TV and online websites remain the most used sources for news, but more and more of us say we also get news from social media, according to media watchdog Ofcom. While this is highest among 16-24 year olds at 78%, a majority of adults in every age group use social media to access news, apart from the over-65s. Even among over 75s, 22% find out what is happening in the world from social media. For politicians, this is no longer just about reaching young people – this is all voters.
Some platforms are more important than others. Even after Elon Musk's conversion of Twitter into X, you will still see MPs, spin doctors and journalists in the Westminster village scrolling through the platform, but digital strategists say "real voters" are found on other platforms. The main parties have far more followers on Facebook (four million combined), which is much more widely used overall, than X (where they have a combined 3.2 million).
Politicians have always looked abroad for policy and campaigning ideas, and social media is no different.
Those on the right seek to emulate the impact Donald Trump has on TruthSocial, while left-wing politicians look to the success of Zohran Mamdani becoming mayor of New York.
Some have even imported social media experts from overseas. In 2019 Boris Johnson hired New Zealand duo Ben Guerin and Sean Topham to run the digital campaign for the general election. They imported into UK politics the concept of "shitposting", releasing deliberately bad images in order to generate a reaction. This included posting a tweet featuring the slogan "Get Brexit Done" in Comic Sans, a font loathed by graphic designers.
There was a method in the madness. "People are more likely to engage with something if they feel like it's been written by a human, not by a committee of design experts," Guerin told me. "It's pretty easy to go viral for doing something weird and wacky, but that doesn't always advance the objectives of your campaign."
This seems to be borne out by some recent hits. Burnham's TikTok post rating pub snacks attracted a million views. Yet a less gimmicky video, straightforwardly listing the five things he said he had done in his first week as PM, got five million.
Spoiling the magic?
There is an inherent tension in political social media. Authenticity is key. Yet who really expects the prime minister to be shooting and uploading his own content?
Back in 2013 I wrote a story about how Cameron's Twitter account had favourited a tweet mocking William Hague from an account handle that made a crude joke about former Tory MP Norman Tebbit being injured in the Brighton bombing.
The prime minister's director of communications called me to complain about my "slapdash and crappy" reporting. My crime? Including a sentence which allowed for the possibility that someone other than Cameron had clicked on the like button by mistake. This would, apparently, spoil the magic for those that thought the prime minister was running his own account for his 500,000 followers.
We now know that Zack Polanski does indeed have his own log-ins. The leader of the Green Party in England and Wales faced criticism in May for sharing a post condemning police actions in the Golders Green attack, for which he apologised. Then in July he accepted an Instagram collaboration which included a man wearing a T-shirt featuring a cartoon guillotine and the song lyrics "we're only making plans for Nigel". Reform UK said it amounted to incitement of violence against Farage. "I'm accepting my responsibility in that I shouldn't have accepted that collaboration," Polanski said, but refused to apologise.
Reform UK's Gawain Towler, a long-time media adviser to Nigel Farage, says: " My big takeaway is: don't be a berk on social media, which I think was Zack Polanski's big takeaway too."
Dov Forman, who helped Tory-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick grow his following from 20,000 to more than half a million with viral clips including confronting fare dodgers on the London Underground, says it is "risky" for a leader to run their own social media. But sometimes it can be a risk worth taking.
Badenoch has taken to directing her own videos, telling aides what she wants to post. She has attracted backing on X from American rappers Nicki Minaj and Azealia Banks. Those are the sort of authentic third-party endorsements politicians crave.
Up the ladder
On the day he became prime minister, a video was released of Burnham being interviewed on the Career Ladder, a series run by Ukrainian TikToker Max Klymenko who interviews guests about their career, while standing on a ladder. "If they personally haven't seen the channel it's sometimes quite difficult to make sense for them," Klymenko says. Burnham had seen the show, and did use the ladder.
Which leads us to the big question: Does any of this actually work? Emma Connolly, an academic who has researched this at the Digital Speech Lab at UCL, isn't sure. "We don't necessarily have really strong evidence or convincing evidence that it could really persuade or transform the opinion of opponent voters or even those that are undecided," she says.
More from InDepth
- Why phones on loudspeaker may become just another noise 
  - Published6 August
And this in turn raises the question of how long the Burnham digital honeymoon might last. Can a prime minister TikTok his way through a war, terror attack or controversial court case? Announcing a new giveaway may go viral, but what about the details of the cuts to pay for it?
The truth is none of this is new, as Hyman explains: "The politicians who get this wrong think that social media is now the only place to be, and a substitute for doing the hard work and the heavy lifting of actually getting the right policy, getting the right narrative, and telling that story properly," he says. "Politics is about winning arguments."
After all, politicians have always wanted to be liked. It's just these days they can see it instantly if you hit that heart button on your feed.
Listen to Matt Chorley live from Westminster, weekdays from 14:00 on BBC Radio 5 Live.

title: Socialist Left Party holds slim lead in polarized Berlin polls
content_c:
Socialist Left holds slim lead in polarized Berlin polls
September 15, 2026
Berlin, a city-state of 3.9 million people, is famously diverse, but it's also very atomized — a city of villages, where people often don't stray beyond their district, or Kiez, as Berliners like to call them.
That atomization extends to its political landscape: While the central districts of Berlin have recently voted Green or for the socialist Left Party, the outskirts — where in fact most Berliners live — is dominated by the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), and, in certain districts, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). That makes it notoriously difficult to predict Berlin's elections, particularly in the past few years, when more parties have crowded onto the city's lampposts at election time.
Ahead of Berlin's state election on September 20 (when Berliners will elect the state parliament, which decides who is the next mayor) three parties are neck and neck: The Left Party, the CDU and the AfD. In the latest infratest dimap poll, the Left Party has a slim lead: They're at 21%, with the CDU at 20% and the AfD at 18%. Not far behind are the Greens, with 16%, while the center-left Social Democrats, for so long a party of government in Berlin, is currently mustering just 12%.
The AfD's relative weakness in Berlin means the situation is not as dramatic as it was in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, where the scale of the far-right victory likely means it will be impossible to keep them out of government.
Nevertheless, a victory for the Left Party — and yet another defeat for Friedrich Merz's CDU — would both transform the politics of Berlin, where the CDU are currently in government, and increase the pressure on the chancellor.
How to fight for election victory in a polarized city
The capital's disparate political scene makes running an election campaign in Berlin tricky, especially for a conservative party like the CDU.
"Berlin is indeed particularly challenging," Lukas Krieger, the CDU's general secretary in Berlin, told DW.
Krieger is in a perfect position to understand the national implications of regional elections, as he is also a member of the federal parliament, where the CDU is still digesting the result in Saxony-Anhalt.
But, he insists, "Berlin isn't comparable to the country as a whole or to Saxony-Anhalt."
Dressed in a neat suit and about to enter a post-mortem meeting of CDU parliamentarians, Krieger remained bullish about the fight in Berlin, and said it was clear who the main opponent was.
"It's crystallizing more and more as a duel between the CDU and the Left Party," he said. "The AfD in Berlin has no option to negotiate a government. There's no one who wants to work with them. We have a very radical Left Party in Berlin, and that's why we say: Berlin will stay stable, and the CDU is the only party that guarantees that Berlin will stay in the middle of the political spectrum."
Another challenge for the Berlin CDU is dealing with the loss of their incumbent mayor, Kai Wegner, who is still in office but is not running again thanks to his decision to play tennis in the middle of Berlin's biggest power outage since World War II.
Instead, the party was forced to hastily present a new candidate, Wegner's Finance Minister Stefan Evers, who now has to navigate a course between two very different political threats: The super-confident AfD and the surging Left Party, both of whom look set to make significant gains on their 2023 election results in the city.
Evers' main opponent is another new face: Elif Eralp, a lawyer born in Munich in 1980 just weeks after her parents fled a military putsch in Turkey. But Berliners are used to mayoral candidates not being natives of the city: Evers was born in North Rhine-Westphalia. In fact, polls show that none of the leading mayoral candidates are particularly well-known: In one recent poll, around half of Berliners said they didn't have any strong opinion on any of them.
Be credible and make offers
The CDU's problem is that German politics is increasingly radical — as the Saxony-Anhalt election showed — and observers say this is partly because of the perceived failure of the centrist parties of government to present new solutions to the electorate.
"The question is: Do you have your own political offers? Are you trying to unlock new groups?" said Julia Reuschenbach, political scientist at Hamburg University.
She thinks that the Left Party has established itself in Berlin as the most "credible" opposition to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). That's partly, she says, because it's the only one of the left-of-center parties not willing to support the CDU (nor is the CDU willing to collaborate with the Left).
But the Left Party has its own disadvantage: The party has been pursued by accusations of antisemitism after a rapper performing at a campaign event in Neukölln, where many of Berlin's large Palestinian community live, chanted "Death to the IDF," referring to the Israeli military. Eralp condemned the performance and promised an internal investigation, but Gaza has become vital to the Left Party's supporters: In June, the party officially resolved to consider Israel's military action in Gaza a genocide.
Nevertheless, Reuschenbach thinks the Left Party's strength is that it is able to make tangible political offers.
"Of course, they're populist," she said. "They formulate maximalist positions: 'We want to socialize. we want to expropriate.' But it's straight. I'd say that for many people, the Left have more clarity, more of their own proposals."
The pundit was referring specifically to what many consider the Left's most radical demand, an idea that has been at the heart of Berlin's politics for at least half a decade: The Left Party is the only one of the major parties that promises to implement the result of a referendum carried out in 2021, when 59% of Berliners voted to expropriate real estate companies that own more than 3,000 units in the city and transfer their property to public ownership.
Since then, successive Berlin governments, led by center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and then the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), have dragged their feet on the implementation, by setting up commissions on the question.
It's the rents, stupid
Kerstin Wolter, co-leader of the socialist Left Party in Berlin and candidate in the upcoming state election, rejects the idea that expropriating landlords should be considered "populist." After all, she said, the idea was written into the German constitution, or Basic Law, at the founding of West Germany in 1949 — though the expropriation article has never actually been invoked.
As far as Wolter is concerned, there's one reason why the Berlin population became so "radicalized," and made her party so strong.
"All the polls, all the surveys, all the conversations we have with voters ourselves, it's always the same: The rent situation is catastrophic," she told DW. "People can't find an apartment, people are scared of rent increases, people are losing their apartments because the landlords are claiming them for their own use."
Housing, according to a recent Berlin Trend poll, is indeed by far the most important issue in this election: Some 32% of Berliners said it was the city's most important problem — way more than the 10% who said immigration and asylum, or the 9% who said security/crime/terrorism.
Perhaps adding to this taste for revolutionary ideas is that this is the first election in Berlin's history where the voting age has been lowered to 16, and young Germans have become increasingly politicized in the last few years.
"I think a lot of young people — much more than when I was young — are concerned with questions like climate change, will I still get a job," said Wolter. "Even pensions: At an info-stand I had a girl, she seemed about 14, asking me about our pensions policy."
Berlin, which has always been its own mix of conservatism and radicalism, is now also becoming more and more economically diverse, according to Wolter: "We have an increasing number of millionaires in Berlin, as well as an increasing number of people living in poverty."
That contributes to making the city a unique political challenge.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg
description: The results of the Berlin election are as hard to predict as ever. Three parties are vying for first place, including the socialist Left Party and the far-right AfD. But one issue is most important to Berliners.

title: Einst lebten hier Juden: Wenn Häuser Geschichten erzählen
content_c:
Einst lebten hier Juden: Wenn Häuser Geschichten erzählen
11. September 2026
Schon viele Menschen sind über die Türschwelle der Berliner Altbauwohnung im vierten Stock getreten. Hier, in der Rosenheimer Straße 40, saßen sie auf dem Sofa und am Küchentisch, hier schauten sie aus dem Fenster, hier hingen sie ihren Träumen nach.
Seit 2007 wohnt Marie Rolshoven mit ihrer Familie hier. "Das Gefühl, über die Schwelle zu gehen, über die auch die früheren Bewohner zum letzten Mal gegangen sind, lässt einen nicht los", sagt sie. Denn sie weiß: Hier lebten einst Juden - und keiner hat die Nazi-Zeit überlebt.
Aus dem Zuhause vertrieben
Nach der Machtübernahme der Nationalsozialisten im Januar 1933 wurde schnell klar, dass Juden in Hitlers Deutschland als "Bürger zweiter Klasse" galten. Auch das Wohnrecht war keine Selbstverständlichkeit mehr.
"Einem rassebewussten Volksgenossen ist eine Hausgemeinschaft mit einem Juden" nicht zuzumuten, daher sei eine fristlose Kündigung rechtens, schrieb am 18. September 1938 das Parteiorgan der Nazis, der "Völkische Beobachter". Am 30. April 1939 wird das Gesetz dazu erlassen: Jüdische Mieter und Eigentümer werden gezwungen, ihre Wohnungen zu verlassen und in behördlich bestimmte Gebäude, im NS-Jargon "Judenhäuser" genannt, umzuziehen.
In Henny und Carl Möllers Wohnung in der Rosenheimer Straße 40 werden mehrere Menschen zwangsweise einquartiert. Am Ende sind sie zu neunt. Im Herbst 1941 beginnen die Deportationen in die Vernichtungslager.
Hitlers Propagandaminister Joseph Goebbels notiert in seinem Tagebuch: "Hauptsache ist, dass die Reichshauptstadt judenrein gemacht wird; und ich werde nicht eher ruhen und rasten, bis dieses Ziel vollkommen erreicht ist." Auch die Bewohner der Rosenheimer Straße werden abtransportiert.
Erinnern an einem realen Ort
Es sind diese Menschen, an deren Schicksal Marie Rolshoven erinnern möchte. Zusammen mit ihrer mittlerweile verstorbenen Mutter und einem Freund gründete sie deshalb 2016 die Initiative Denk Mal Am Ort (DMAO), inspiriert von dem Amsterdamer Projekt "Open Jewish Homes".
Die Idee dahinter: Dorthin einladen, wo sich damals der Alltag abspielte. "Man kommt den Menschen einfach sehr nah über den realen Ort", so Rolshoven. "Es ist anders, als wenn ich in eine Gedenkstätte gehe."
"Hier stand mal das Bett meines Bruders"
Diese Erfahrung machten auch ihre Nachbarn zwei Stockwerke tiefer. "Denk Mal Am Ort" hatte herausgefunden, dass einst die jüdische Familie Katzenellenbogen die Wohnung gemietet hatte.
Die Familie verließ Nazi-Deutschland 1939 gerade noch rechtzeitig. "2018 kam dann wirklich der 92-jährige Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen mit Tochter, Schwiegersohn und Enkel auf unsere Einladung hin an diesen Ort zurück", erzählt Rolshoven der DW.
Gefunden hatte ihn die DMAO-Initiative über Facebook. Rolshoven erzählt, wie beeindruckend es für die Besucher und Besucherinnen war, als der ehemalige Bewohner hereinkam und sagte: "Ja, ich kann mich genau erinnern. Hier stand das Bett meines Bruders. Er war zehn, als wir das Land verlassen mussten."
Bald keine Zeitzeugen mehr
Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen ist mittlerweile verstorben. Wie so viele Zeitzeugen. Umso wichtiger sei das generationenübergreifende Erinnern, sagt Rolshoven. Sie selbst hat schon eine Nachfahrin einer ehemaligen Bewohnerin bei sich zu Hause empfangen.
Claudia Samters Mutter konnte einst aus Berlin nach Argentinien fliehen, ihre Tante nicht. Sie bat "Denk Mal Am Ort" um Hilfe bei der Spurensuche - und es stellte sich heraus, dass die Tante früher in Rolshovens Wohnung einquartiert worden war.
Claudia Samter war schon zwei Mal zu Gast. "Es gibt ja auch kein Grab auf einem Friedhof, wo sie hingehen kann", sagt Rolshoven. "Wir saßen am Küchentisch und haben über das Leben heute und morgen gesprochen und haben viel gelacht und auch geweint. Es war gut, diesen Raum noch mal so neu zu bespielen."
2026 hat "Denk Mal Am Ort" 90 Erinnerungsveranstaltungen in acht Städten organisiert. Es seien viele sehr junge Nachfahren gekommen, so Rolshoven. "Zu wissen, dass diese in diesem Treppenhaus gestanden und dieselbe Klinke berührt haben, das habe ihnen geholfen.
Ein Schweizer auf Spurensuche nach den Vorfahren
Auch der 19-jährige Adam Ethan Klein aus der Schweiz wollte mehr über die Geschichte seiner Vorfahren erfahren. "Ich wusste schon immer, dass da eine Fluchtgeschichte war, aber zu Hause war das nie ein großes Thema", erzählt er.
"Es hieß dann: 'Ja, deine Urgroßeltern verließen 1938 Deutschland. Gerade noch rechtzeitig. Zum Glück, sonst gäbe es dich heute nicht'."
Dass Adam tiefer nachzubohren begann, habe mit dem um sich greifenden Antisemitismus zu tun, sagt er - und dem allgegenwärtigen Slogan "Never again is now". ("Nie wieder ist jetzt": ein Aufruf, sich in der Gegenwart aktiv gegen Antisemitismus, Hass und Angriffe auf die Demokratie zu stellen, Anmerkung d. Red.)
Auf dem Dachboden, das wusste die ganze Familie, lag ein Koffer seines Urgroßvaters mütterlicherseits. "Aber nie hat jemand irgendwie gewagt zu sagen: 'Schauen wir mal hinein'."
Bis Adam das Gepäckstück öffnete. Er findet Dutzende Dokumente und stößt auch auf ein Schreiben des Amtsgerichts Hannover vom 12. Juni 1933 an den Rechtsanwalt Max Haas, seinen Urgroßvater.
"Sie waren vor allem eins: Juden"
Darin heißt es: "Sie sind heute auf Grund des Erlasses des Herrn Justizministers in der Liste der zugelassenen Rechtsanwälte gelöscht."
Adam ist zutiefst betroffen: "Mit diesem einen Satz wurde den Familien auf unmissverständliche Weise klar gemacht, dass sie genau das nicht waren, was sie seit Generationen angestrebt hatten: eine durchschnittliche deutsche Familie. Ab diesem Zeitpunkt waren sie vor allem eines: Juden."
Für Adam eine verstörende Erkenntnis. Ebenso wie die Nachricht, dass jemand einen ultraorthodoxen Juden in Zürich erstach und dabei antisemitische Parolen rief.
Der Angriff ereignete sich unweit der Synagoge, in der er kurz zuvor die Bar Mizwa eines Cousins gefeiert hatte. (Bar Mizwa bezeichnet im Judentum die Feier für Jugendliche zum Eintritt in die Religionsmündigkeit, Anm. d. Red.)
"Ich dachte, in der Schweiz passiert so was nicht"
"Zum ersten Mal in meinem Leben hatte ich das mulmige Gefühl, nicht ganz hierher zu gehören. Dabei ist Zürich meine Heimat, die Stadt, in der ich von Geburt an als jüdischer Schweizer unbeschwert lebe", wird Adam später notieren.
"Das war für mich schon ein neues Territorium. Ich dachte eigentlich immer, in der Schweiz passiert so was nicht. Das war vielleicht ein bisschen ignorant von mir", sagt er.
Das Thema lässt ihn nicht los. Adam forscht weiter, er will seine Abschlussarbeit am Gymnasium über seine Verwandten schreiben. Und er fährt im Frühjahr 2024 mit seinen Eltern, seiner Schwester, der Großmutter, Onkels, Tanten sowie mehreren Cousins los, um die Herkunftsorte ihre Vorfahren zu kennenzulernen.
Eine "magische" Begegnung
Irgendwann stehen auch sie vor einem fünfstöckigen Gebäude in der Hölderlinstraße 55. Da kommt plötzlich ein Mann mit dem Fahrrad aus der Hofeinfahrt.
"Na, machen Sie eine Stadtführung oder wollen Sie hier einziehen?", fragt er scherzhaft. Es ist Thomas Koch, der schon länger recherchiert, wer mal in seinem Haus gewohnt hat. Als die Antwort lautet: "Nein, wir gucken uns an, wo unsere Vorfahren gelebt haben", ist er elektrisiert.
Koch hat bereits herausgefunden: Die ehemaligen Hausbesitzer, die Brüder Merzbacher, verkauften das Haus 1936 für 75.000 Reichsmark. Davon mussten sie 70.000 Reichsmark an Vermögensabgaben und Reichsfluchtsteuer zahlen. Der Rest reichte gerade für die Schiffspassagen nach Brasilien und in die USA. Im Erdgeschoss lebte 1937 und '38 eine Familie Hirschheimer, tätig im Sperrholzhandel, bevor sie in ein "Judenhaus" zwangsumgesiedelt wurde. Ab 1939 verlor sich ihre Spur, Koch fand keine weiteren Unterlagen. Also fragt er: "Sind Sie die Familie Hirschheimer?"
Sie sind es. "Magisch" sei diese Begegnung gewesen, sagt Koch. Adolf und Auguste Hirschheimer waren Adams Ururgroßeltern. Ihre Tochter Ilse war mit Max Haas verheiratet.
Adam Klein und Thomas Koch bleiben in Kontakt. Als der junge Mann das nächste Mal in Stuttgart ist, laden ihn die Kochs zu Kaffee und Kuchen ein.
"Eine schöne Wohnung", findet Adam. "Und es war spannend, sich vorzustellen, wie meine Vorfahren dort mal gelebt haben und dass es wahrscheinlich gar nicht so viel anders war. Damals gab es wahrscheinlich auch Kaffee und Kuchen."
Adam zeigt dem Stuttgarter Fotos seiner Großmutter Ilse, die in der Synagoge in Stuttgart geheiratet hatte, und im Hochzeitsornat im Wohnzimmer stand. "Vor der Tür, die wir immer noch haben", sagt Koch.
"Das war schon berührend, neue Mitbewohner im zeitversetzten geschichtlichen Kontext gefunden zu haben. Und ich glaube, dieses Erleben, dieses Nachvollziehen, ist ein hoch empathischer Prozess, der verbindet einen einfach über diese Wohnung."
Gebrochene Identitäten
Ilse und Max Haas finden Zuflucht in England, das Ehepaar Hirschheimer reist 1939 in die Schweiz aus. Adolf Hirschheimer stirbt 1940 an einem Herzleiden, aber "sicher auch an einem gebrochenen Herzen", glaubt Adam, sein Ururenkel.
Auguste wird von ihrem Schwiegersohn Max nach England geholt. Die Familie hat Heimweh: "Dort waren wir die Juden, hier sind wir die Deutschen. Da soll sich ein Mensch zurechtfinden", schreibt Ilse Haas an eine Freundin. Es sind diese Zeilen, die Adam als Titel für seine Abschlussarbeit wählt.
Denn seine Urgroßeltern kommen nicht zur Ruhe, nachdem ihnen die Heimat genommen wurde. Von England gehen sie schließlich nach Israel und irgendwann zurück nach Europa, in die Schweiz.
"Meine Urgroßeltern ließen sich am Ende ihres Lebens nur gerade zwei Autostunden von der alten Heimat nieder", schreibt Adam. "Wenn ich ihre Biografien aus der Distanz des Urenkels betrachte, wird klar, dass es ihnen nach dem Bruch mit Deutschland nie mehr gelungen ist, irgendwo Wurzeln zu schlagen."
"Erinnern ist wichtig, weil man schlussendlich aus der Geschichte lernen muss," sagt Adam. Und ich denke, jeder einzelne ist in der Pflicht und kann bewirken, aktiv zu erinnern. Und so geht es dann hoffentlich auch ohne Zeitzeugen." Zum Beispiel in der ehemaligen Wohnung seiner Vorfahren.
Korrekturhinweis: Im Text wurde ursprünglich einmal einer der Namen verwechselt, am Tag nach Veröffentlichung wurde dieser in Thomas Koch geändert, wie es korrekt lauten musste.
description: Wer lebte früher in meiner Wohnung? Immer wieder stoßen heutige Bewohner bei der Suche nach ihren Vorgängern auf geflohene oder deportierte Juden - und erinnern an deren Leidensgeschichte.

title: Burnham's 'Manchesterism' got him to No 10 - but will it work for the UK?
content_c:
It was just five months ago when Andy Burnham retreated to his mayor's office in Manchester, having been blocked by Labour's ruling executive from standing for parliament.
When I met him there a few weeks later, he told me he planned to deal with his disappointment with some ambitious plans for his city region.
Burnham told me he wanted to appeal directly to Fifa to host the final of the women's football World Cup in 2035 Manchester instead of Wembley. "Imagine how electrifying that is for any girl growing up in the north of England," he said.
He said he was also joining forces with other mayors for a "Great Northern" Olympic bid across the north of England, and a plan was also afoot to host the Ryder Cup in Bolton. Sports bodies needed "re-educating" about the rest of the country, he said.
Manchester has already poached the Brit Awards from London after half a century in the capital.
Big, bold gestures like these tell part of the story of what has happened in the city. Burnham's civic ambition is a byproduct of Manchester's status as the fastest-growing city economy in the country. As Burnham prepares to become prime minister, will he be able to apply the same model to the whole of the nation?
Manchester's rise
Even before Burnham returned to parliament in June, there has been talk of Manchesterism as a political-economic philosophy that offers a programme for national transformation, rooted in a critique of a currently unresponsive, over-centralised British state.
The city has a long history of blending the freest of free markets with a strong social spirit. Manchester's cotton traders championed free trade and liberal economics, at the same time as the emergence of the co-operative movement, the trade unions and the Suffragettes. Even the Manchester Ship Canal, the emblem of monopoly-breaking free trade, required local government intervention backed by the workers.
But for an understanding of contemporary Manchester, you need to go back to the summer of 1996.
Andy Burnham had left the north-west of England by then. He told me how when he first looked for a local media job after graduating in the early 1990s, all he could get was a role as an unpaid reporter on the Middleton Guardian.
"I had to do what so many people of my generation, born in the 60s or 70s in the north-west of England had to do to get on in life," he said. "We had to go south."
By 1996, Burnham was an MP's researcher. That year, back in Manchester, the IRA detonated the largest bomb in the UK since World War Two, devastating the city centre,
The reconstruction in the aftermath of the attack marked the start of Manchester's ascent from the doldrums of de-industrialisation. The essential idea provided by a group of local political, cultural and business leaders, and an architect called Ian Simpson, was that the city centre should be reshaped by demolishing, not repairing, many of the damaged buildings.
From disaster could then arise a great opportunity to reshape the city's geography and economy. Council leader Sir Richard Leese and his top civil servant, the late Sir Howard Bernstein set the tone for a variety of bold centrally driven strategic plans that were actually largely delivered by private capital and then significant international investment.
The council leadership was ruthlessly focused on transforming brownfield industrial sites. The private sector would go nowhere near them, but the council de-risked those investments with public money. It also sometimes stepped in to tide projects over during financial crises.
At the end of this process, private capital poured in, lining up the cranes and the hard hats. The council offered a flexible interpretation of requirements to build a proportion of "affordable housing", sometimes effectively waived, sometimes met by funding building in cheaper areas of the city.
Paul Thwaite, the chief executive of NatWest, which has funded some of these projects, and who is on the board of the University of Manchester, says Manchester's success story over the past 20 years was "built on there being a clear plan the private sector can get behind".
Why hanging on to students matters
Such a shift would have been unthinkable a generation ago. The model of Manchester's city centre development has succeeded in creating a critical mass of population, housing, jobs and service sector activity that has allowed it to turn its significant undergraduate population into a goldmine.
According to the mayor, more people from London had moved to Manchester (13,000) than the other way round (11,800) in the latest set of internal migration figures.
He put this down to a flow of young workers into the Manchester city centre service economy.
In a reverse from the 1990s, "no-one here has to leave to get on in life", Burnham told me. "And in fact, there's a net inflow of young people from London."
Manchester now retains over half its graduates, more than any other city apart from London, according to the Centre for Cities, and Manchester also attracts almost as many young graduates as it produces.
Tom Beahon, the CEO of Manchester-based sports brand Castore, who has not been shy about criticising some of the government's business policies, told our Big Boss podcast earlier this year that the mayor had helped "attract inbound investment, making it a place that students want to stay after they graduate from the fantastic universities". That in turn means more businesses want to launch in the city, he added.
It is a case study in agglomeration effects - the economic power of locating similar types of jobs close together. And if its infrastructure can keep up, Manchester's economy will continue to fly.
Burnham's Manchester
Andy Burnham is a product of this Greater Manchester and spent his decade as its first mayor trying to shape it. As Andy Spinoza, the foremost chronicler of Manchester's turnaround, puts it: "Burnham jumped into a moving car, and by the end he was driving it."
But what else is there to Burnham beyond driving that moving car?
While he has managed to ascend to the Labour leadership and the cusp of No 10 without revealing his wider policy plans, there is a fairly recent text already out there. In 2024 with his fellow north-west regional mayor, Merseyside's Steve Rotherham, he published a book called Head North: A Rallying Cry for a More Equal Britain.
It was the basis for Burnham's speech earlier this month on Manchesterism and remains his national political-economic-constitutional prospectus. The 10-point plan to "rewire" the country argues that better "homes, transport and jobs" across the country can only come from "a new set of principles and rules for the running of the British state".
What underpins this is a determination to tear up two formulas that have long formed the backbone of how UK governments allocate money. The first is the Treasury's Green Book, which decides infrastructure spending and which has traditionally valued existing areas of high growth and land value the most. In Burnham's view, this drags investment in transport to the south of England.
The tangible example of all of this can be found on Platforms 13 and 14 of Piccadilly station in central Manchester. The only east-west train link for both the city centre and the North's main international airport is here, and it is often jam-packed with trains and 40,000 daily passengers attempting to cross the Pennines, or get to the airport, or to Merseyside. Burnham has long advocated for an underground four-platform "Kings Cross of the North" with a northern version of London's Elizabeth Line.
He relays a story about his time as chief secretary to the Treasury in 2007 when he was told: "No project in the north passed the Green Book, Minister." He told me the same in 2020 when there were murmurings of reform to the formula. Chancellor Rachel Reeves pursued pilot projects to change the approach that could favour local investment.
In the book, Burnham also advocates tearing up the Barnett formula, which allocates public spending, topping up spend for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland so they do not lose out to England as a whole. The effect, Burnham argues, is that the north of England is left squeezed in a "pincer".
In Head North and his recent speech, Burnham points to Germany's "Basic Law", with its duty of "equivalent living standards" across the regions. Such a law, he argued, would protect local government and give regions a right to be consulted on long-term decisions.
Burnham also advocates significant constitutional change, including a form of proportional representation and the replacement of the House of Lords with a "Senate of the Nations and the Regions", alongside devolution of powers over large swathes of public services to regional level.
On Net Zero he proposes a "Northern Way", which subsidises the transition, retrofits, cutting bills, and building exportable locally owned industry. He contrasts this with a "Whitehall way", which he characterises as bans, charges and taxes that hit the poorest.
The actual policy consequence of this will have to reckon with rising global energy prices, pressure on household budgets, and some impatience from North Sea energy interests to pump more oil and gas. There are some contradictions in for example, full tax and spend devolution for every region. Would the south-east get to keep the taxes it raises? Some aides recently played down any changes to the Barnett formula amid concerns from Scottish politicians.
The national stage
The fundamental difference between running a city region and a country is the need to raise the entire spectrum of tax revenues to fund spending. Or to borrow more money. The picture is rather constrained on both right now. Manchester has been agile in attracting private capital to build infrastructure, especially housing, partly because it had to. Can that stretch across the whole country?
With Manchester's cotton traders in mind, I asked Burnham back in February if he considered the Manchester model to be politically left or right - an example of statism, perhaps?
"When it comes to right versus left, well, we've always been very pro-business, pro-enterprise here. We want people to succeed individually and businesses to succeed, but give back at the same time," he said.
Some campaigners say that the dash for the gleaming towers and spires in the centre has left behind much of the rest of the region, and that the centre of Manchester is becoming a mini-London. While Burnham has criticised decades of "neoliberalism" and the "trickle-down effect", the reality is it has been core to the Manchester model.
At the same time, Margaret Thatcher's 1985 bus deregulation has been reversed and over the years public money from central and local government, from the EU, as well as from the partly council-owned airport, has been spent on trams - a nod to the importance of spreading the proceeds of growth in the centre around the region.
To greater or lesser degrees Burnham has floated more "public control", cost of living support, small business rates relief, and higher infrastructure investment and higher defence spending. They sound difficult to reconcile with sticking to promises to limit borrowing and not raise major taxes.
For example, the Defence Investment Plan is "funded" by cuts to capital investment in transport, energy and elsewhere. These are precisely the areas that Manchesterism would suggest might get more central capital investment.
Burnham the mayor has beaten the drum for the new Liverpool-Manchester Northern Powerhouse Rail and the high speed Manchester-Birmingham line he worked up with former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street. But what will Prime Minister Burnham do?
More from InDepth
And what about the paused Brexit reset? There was a deal ready to go for closer relations at a UK-EU summit originally planned for next week. The government had started to explore different red lines for the next Labour manifesto and a turn back towards Europe's single market. Does he go with Remainy Manchester? Or do the feelings of his Leave constituency, Makerfield, trump all?
NatWest's Paul Thwaite says there could be a "powerful recipe for sustained growth" from the private capital that flows from "long-term certainty and genuine collaboration". There isn't, however, a "single blueprint" from Manchester or anywhere, he says. For devolution to work "the institutions, the leadership and the commercial capability matter as much as the powers themselves".
Burnham in his speech quoted the famous line attributed to Tony Wilson in the film 24 Hour Party People: "It's Manchester, we do things differently here." Now it's time to reveal what exactly it means for the nation.
Clarification 31 July: We have amended a passage in this article to make clear that Manchester Piccadilly station is Greater Manchester's only link for trains going from east to west across the Pennines, and that Platforms 13 and 14 are for services to the east coast, to Merseyside and the city's airport.
