title: Germany news: Merz to cancel UN trip amid party infighting
content_c:
Germany news: Merz to cancel UN trip amid party infighting
Published September 15, 2026last updated September 16, 2026
What you need to know
These updates have been closed. Thank you for joining us.
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany from Tuesday, September 15, 2026:
- Sources say Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz canceled a planned trip to the UN General Assembly
- Germany and US agree to deal to boost cooperation on new arms projects
- Police have found a large depot of firearms and ammunition in Rhineland-Palatinate
- A Berlin woman is facing charges of supporting the 'Islamic State' terror group
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Germany deports 13 men to Afghanistan
Germany's Interior Ministry said it deported 13 Afghan men on Tuesday.
An Interior Ministry statement said the men, who had been convicted of crimes including assault, drug trafficking and sexual abuse while in Germany, were flown to Kabul in a chartered plane.
That brings the number of Afghans — most of them criminals — repatriated since Germany's current ruling coalition came to power last year to 263.
The organization Pro Asyl put the number of Afghans "obliged to leave" Germany at around 13,000 in late 2025, though about 10,000 have "tolerated" status, meaning they cannot be immediately deported.
Prior administrations were loath to deport individuals to Afghanistan due to the political situation under the Taliban.
Now the radical Islamists have begun to send representatives to Germany to help facilitate deportations.
Critics say, firstly, that it is not safe for many Afghans to return and secondly, that Berlin is making concessions to the hardline Taliban, even though the group is not internationally recognized — foremost, due to its gruesome human rights record.
Germany and US to boost arms projects cooperation
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said he had a "good discussion" with US counterpart Pete Hegseth on Tuesday and that the two had signed a declaration of intent for cooperation on future arms projects.
"Germany and the United States agree that the current security challenges require a robust and mutually beneficial, closely interlinked defense industrial base on both sides of the Atlantic," said Pistorius.
He said Washington and Berlin were keen to complement one another in producing state-of-the-art weapons systems, components and complex munitions.
The declaration covers the development, production, licensed production and maintenance of defense equipment, setting a political framework for future projects.
Pistorius said the agreement also aims to strengthen supply chains, review technology transfer rules and expand research and development cooperation.
High demand for defense equipment, he added, requires increased production capacity, quick delivery and reliable supply on both sides of the Atlantic to ensure supply security and operational readiness.
German foreign minister pledges solidarity with Jews after community leader gets death threat
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Tuesday reaffirmed government solidarity with Jews in Germany in the wake of death threats against Charlotte Knobloch — a 93-year-old Holocaust survivor and a leading member of the Jewish community.
"Jews must never again be forced to live in fear in Germany," exclaimed Wadephul in remarks delivered at a press conference with Bavarian State Premier Markus Söder.
Wadephul said he had been deeply moved when speaking with Knobloch earlier in the day and called the threat against her life after the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt state elections abhorrent.
Wadephul said that during their meeting, he pledged Knobolch — now the president of Israelite Religious Community of Munich and Upper Bavaria — his and the government's solidarity.
Police are currently investigating threats leveled in Knobloch's hometown of Munich last week after she called for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to be banned.
The threat, scrawled on a park bench and a garbage bin in Munich's English Garden, directly referenced the vote and Knobloch, causing the former president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany to cancel attendance at an upcoming event.
Knobloch had called the AfDs victory a sign that democracy in Germany was breaking down, adding, "it scares me."
2 more malaria cases identified near Frankfurt Airport
Two people living close to Frankfurt Airport have contracted malaria, accoridng to the city's Public Health Authority.
This follows the identification of six cases in total among airport staff, with two of the patients dying, between July and the end of August.
The two patients were receiving medical treatment.
"The infected individuals have not traveled abroad," said Peter Tinnemann, head of Frankfurt's Public Health Authority. He said they were not staff at the airport as with past cases.
However, Tinnemann said the patients lived in such close proximity to Germany's busiest hub — in the Schwanheim district just north of the airport — that they could still be considered cases of so-called "airport malaria."
He said there was no cause for public concern, but said people in the Frankfurt area should consult a doctor if they experirence unusual symptoms like chills, headaches, aching limbs and gastrointestinal complaints.
While "very rare," according to Germany's Robert Koch Institute, the phenomenon of "airport malaria" is well documented: a small concentration of cases in or around an airport after an infectious mosquito was brought in via an aeroplane or luggage.
As with the previous cases, Tinnemann said, the patients had contracted Malaria Tropic, the most dangerous form of the disease. He said that to his knowledge, it was the first case in recent decades when a German resident living near an airport caught malaria.
Merz cancels UN trip over party infighting — reports
Government sources have told dpa and Reuters that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will not travel to New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) next week, saying, "Contrary to original plans, he will not travel to New York, since his presence is required in Berlin."
The U-turn comes as pressure is piled on the chancellor over his party's poor showings in state elections.
The CDU got shellacked by Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6 — leading the far-right outfit to style the vote in the east German state of only 1.7 million voters as the beginning of the end of Merz's conservative CDU, with Alice Weidel claiming the CDU is dead and demanding new federal elections.
Now the CDU is gripped by fear that it may not even make it over the 5% hurdle to enter the state parliament of eastern Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, which votes this Sunday, alongside Berlin.
Internal party sources say faith in Merz is fading with some saying he should step down, yet Cabinet members and state premiers have stepped up to offer support.
Merz has scheduled a party leadership meeting on Sunday in hopes of shoring up further support among state leaders, and on Tuesday he will sit down with the CDU/CSU's parliamentary caucus in Berlin.
Brandenburg BSW state lawmaker quits the leftist party, becoming the 6th to do so in 10 months
The left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) contingent of lawmakers in Brandenburg continues to shrink.
Oliver Skopec announced on Tuesday he was quitting the party, becoming the 6th of what was once 15 BSW parliamentarians to do so since November last year.
The first four left last November. When the former party leader at the state level, Robert Crumbach, quit in January, the state coalition between the BSW and senior partners the Social Democrats lost its majority and fell apart.
Skopec, a 41-year-old businessman said he wanted to retain his place in the state parliament and operate as an independent, at least at first.
He linked his decision to quit with the BSW's character as what he termed a party of protest. "For me personally, that is not enough," he said.
Tensions are high in the party as it wrangles with questions like how, or whether, to deal with the far-right AfD — particularly in Saxony-Anhalt after the recent election.
A senior BSW politician at the federal level, Niels-Olaf Lüders, said it was "regrettable" that Skopec was leaving, "but of course it doesn't topple us either."
The party's chairwoman in Brandenburg, Friederike Benda expressed anything but regret at seeing Skopec go, saying it was "not a loss."
"Separating the chaff from the wheat will help us," Benda said, accusing Skopec of using his seat in parliament "as a comfortable, state-financed pillow" to rest on at the taxpayer's expense.
In another eastern state, Thurinigia, the BSW group of parliamentarians has dissolved itself altogether and set up a rival group at the state level.
In Brandenburg, two of the six defectors left for the more centrist Social Democrats (SPD), and four set up a group they call "We for Brandenburg."
Skopec did not say he planned to join them, but said "we will surely speak to each other."
The BSW surfed a brief wave of popularity fairly soon after its foundation — and enjoyed big state election results in Thuringia and Brandeburg in 2024 as a result. But it has since lost almost all of its momentum and is fighting to survive, in large part because of the relative resurgence of the more traditional socialist Left Party in the run-up to last year's federal elections.
Actor Ralf Richter, revered for roles related to his native Ruhr region, dies aged 69
German actor Ralf Richter has died at the age of 69, his children Aline and Maxwell Richter said in a joint statement on Facebook on Tuesday. Richter was known to have been living with heart problems.
"For us a world has just stood still," his children wrote in the notice, saying that for many fans their father was an actor, cult character and a face who had accompanied them for many years.
Born in Essen in the industrialized but declining Ruhr region, and later a resident of Cologne, Richter's first big break was a role in the 1981 German World War II submarine epic "Das Boot," which immediately introduced him to a wide audience in Germany and even beyond.
He played Petty Officer Frenssen, a young and rather crude sailor who loved to trade dirty jokes with his best friend Petty Officer Pilgrim.
Richter's later roles often played on his roots in the Ruhr; the films might not have traveled like "Das Boot" but were successful at home.
He starred as a stressed out coal miner from Gelsenkirchen in the film "Superstau" (Super Traffic Jam) trying to drive to his Corsica holiday in his Audi 100 with his wife and child.
In particular he achieved cult status for his comedic starring role in the 1999 film "Bang Boom Bang — Ein Todsicheres Ding" (roughly: Bang Boom Bang — A Dead Certain Deal) as a choleric, feared but also fundamentally likeable mobster from the Ruhr called Karlheinz "Kalle" Grabowski.
Richter also made headlines prior to the film's premiere when he was himself arrested and later given a jail sentence for cocaine offenses.
Richter released one album as a vocalist, called One Heart, parallel to his acting career.
A Cologne resident in later life and a passionate football fan, with VfL Bochum his club, Richter became known in North Rhine-Westphalia for his efforts to help the club in the south of the city, SC Fortuna Köln, avoid bankruptcy in 2003.
Police detain two suspected of belonging to Eritrean terror group
Police on Tuesday detained two men — an Eritrean and a German — accused of using violence at two German community festivals.
The German Federal Prosecutors Office in the southwestern city of Karlsruhe accuse the two of membership in Brigade N'Hamedu Germany, a domestic terror organization bent on overthrowing Eritrea's authoritarian government.
The men will now appear before the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe, which will rule on terms of their pre-trial detention.
Brigade N'Hamedu Germany is accused of orchestrating violence at three community events organized by perceived supporters of Eritrea's government — twice in the city of Giessen in 2022 and 2023, as well as in Stuttgart in 2023.
"In doing so, the members of the organization regarded violence against German state institutions and representatives of state authority — for example, police officers deployed to protect the events — as a legitimate means," prosecutors said.
Both men are accused of helping establish the group's presence in Germany, with one said to have actively participated in mass brawls in Giessen, where attendees and police were violently attacked.
Police say the terrorists threw objects at and beat the heads of those they attacked, with the intent of potentially killing them.
Several people were injured during the respective attacks, some seriously. In all, 39 police officers were injured and some 230 arrests made.
Similar incidents have occurred in the Netherlands and Sweden.
Large-scale raids were carried out across Germany and Denmark in connection with the group in 2025, though no arrests were made at the time.
Eritrea, a country of 4 million, became independent of Ethiopia in 1993 and has been ruled with an iron fist by President Isaias Afwerki ever since.
Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and other rights groups say Afwerki's government suppresses the population through forced labor, compulsory military service and restrictions on freedom of expression, religion and the press.
AfD rejects claim it might give NATO plans to Russia, says CDU playing politics
A dispute over Germany's classified defense plan intensified Tuesday as the far-right AfD rejected calls to strip Saxony-Anhalt of the document.
Germany's operational plan, or OPLAN, contains key defense measures and planned NATO movements across Europe in the event of a Russia attack, which German and NATO military assessments indicate Moscow could be ready to carry out by 2029.
In such a scenario, Germany would become NATO's central logistics hub and a prime target for attacks and sabotage.
All 16 German states currently have copies of the 1,000-page document.
Following the AfD's landslide victory in Saxony-Anhalt, Bastian Ernst, a CDU politician and president of Germany's Reservist Association, demanded it be withdrawn from the state before the AfD could potentially form a government.
The AfD has faced scrutiny for years over its Russia-friendly stance. It's members routinely call for ending German military aid to Ukraine and a negotiated settlement to the war, claiming Moscow simply wants peace and is acting in self-defense.
"If they [AfD] were to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, the OPLAN would almost certainly be leaked to Russia," Ernst said. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has privately backed the move, German media reported.
The AfD's response was immediate and combative.
Jan Nolte, the party's defense policy spokesperson in the Bundestag, told DW that withdrawing the document would create a security breach. "Whoever removes this state from defense planning tears a hole in national defense and endangers citizens across all of Germany," Nolte said.
He argued that Saxony-Anhalt sits at the crossroads of NATO's eastern logistics network, making it indispensable to wartime coordination.
Nolte dismissed Ernst's approach as party politics at the expense of security, asking what would happen if the AfD were to win majorities in more states.
The AfD, Nolte declared, remains, "unwaveringly committed to the defense of the country and its alliances."
Munich to host 2031 World Athletics Championships
The World Athletics Championships will be held in Munich in 2031, the third time Germany will host the event.
World Athletics, the governing body of the championship, made the announcement in Budapest on Tuesday.
It also revealed that the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, would host the event in 2029, a first for Africa.
"They offer very different, but equally exciting, opportunities for our sport, and I am glad that we can now start working with both cities to host two world-class championships," said Sebastian Coe, president of World Athletics.
"The Olympic Park in Munich is one of the iconic venues of world sport. We know that Munich can host major championships, that Germany has an audience for athletics, and we believe that Munich 2031 has all the ingredients to be a spectacular World Athletics Championships," he added.
Germany hosted the World Championships in 1993 in Stuttgart and in 2009 in Berlin. The Olympic Stadium in Munich also hosted the European Athletics Championships in 2022.
Wadephul to seek German seat on UN Human Rights Council
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is set to arrive in Geneva on Tuesday to campaign for a seat for Germany on the UN Human Rights Council.
He was expected to meet with Mirjana Spoljaric, president of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk.
A meeting with the director-general of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Ghebreyesus, is also planned, according to the German minister's office.
Germany and Ireland are competing for the two seats allocated to Western European countries. According to the Foreign Ministry, Germany has been an elected voting member of the council five times since its founding 20 years ago.
It last served on the body from 2023 to 2025.
The Human Rights Council will be elected in October at the UN headquarters in New York.
Germany's bid for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council in early June was unsuccessful, with Portugal and Austria elected instead. This sparked a debate about the value of Germany's contributions to the UN.
Wadephul and Söder back Merz
Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has received public backing from two senior conservative allies, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul (CDU) and Bavarian state premier Markus Söder (CSU), ahead of a key party meeting in Berlin on Sunday.
"We have been elected for a full parliament, we will fulfill our responsibility in this parliament, and we will do it under this chancellor," insisted Wadephul after taking part in a meeting of the Bavarian state parliament in Munich on Tuesday.
"That's what he was elected for," he said of Merz. "I voted for him. We voted for him. I enjoy working in his cabinet and I am determined to continue doing so."
Bavarian state premier Söder, who chaired the cabinet meeting, also called for "togetherness" and "strength" in support of the chancellor, saying:
"It would be a real problem if, amid all the complications of these times in which we are living, with hybrid attacks on our democracy, Germany were to falter."
CDU calls crisis meeting as pressure mounts on Merz
The leadership of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is to hold a crisis meeting in Berlin on election night amid mounting speculation over the chancellor's political future.
The CDU's executive committee will meet under Merz's leadership on Sunday evening to assess the party's latest state election results and discuss its next steps, a party spokeswoman said. A meeting of the wider federal party leadership is due to follow on Monday.
Merz is expected to seek a clear show of support from senior CDU figures as criticism of his leadership intensifies.
Could Merz seek a confidence vote?
One option reportedly under consideration is for Merz to seek an explicit declaration of confidence from the party leadership.
There has been speculation that influential CDU politicians at state level could seek to oust the increasingly unpopular chancellor. A declaration of support could help Merz head off such a challenge.
The CDU executive committee is the party's most senior inner leadership body and includes all CDU state premiers.
Political scientist Oliver Lembcke of Ruhr University Bochum said preparations at CDU headquarters suggested Merz himself now regarded an early end to his chancellorship as a realistic possibility.
"That is why Merz is trying to rally the influential state premiers behind him in particular," Lembcke told the AFP news agency.
"If they do not demonstratively express their confidence in him after the elections, his situation will become very difficult."
Merz determined to continue despite plummeting ratings
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he is is determined to serve out his full four-year term despite sinking ratings and growing pressure following his Christian Democratic Union (CDU)'s recent electoral defeat in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
"I was elected for four years and I want to use this time to solve problems," he said on Tuesday, insisting: "We have to prove that this can be achieved with this coalition."
Merz said he intended to pursue further reforms alongside the CDU's coalition partner, the Social Democrats (SPD). "This is not possible with other majorities in parliament," he said.
Nationally, the conservative CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), are polling at between 18% and 20%, far below their result in last year's federal election and significantly behind the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).
This week, a new INSA poll found that a majority of CDU supporters and 78% of the wider public no longer believe Merz is the right person for the job.
Merz: Government will act to combat fuel prices
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday that his government would take action to protect consumers from rising fuel prices (seen entry below).
"We will respond to profiteering," he told a meeting of business leaders in Berlin, without specifying precisely how.
"I am of the opinion that we must act," he said, adding that discussions between the federal government and state governments had already taken place. "You can rest assured that we will be making suggestions soon."
Gas prices in Germany continue to rise with standard unleaded Super E10 currently costing an average of €2.286 per liter and diesel at €2.412 per liter – only a few cents below the all-time record.
description: Germany's chancellor nixxed his trip over doubts about his leadership after party losses to the AfD in state elections. Meanwhile, Defense Minister Pistorius is in Washington for talks with his US counterpart.

title: 25 Jahre 9/11: Al-Kaida ist nicht verschwunden
content_c:
25 Jahre 9/11: Al-Kaida ist nicht verschwunden
10. September 2026
Um US-Sanktionen muss sich Abdullah al-Muhaysini keine Gedanken mehr machen. Ende August 2026 strich das US-Finanzministerium den ehemaligen dschihadistischen Prediger von der SDN-Liste. Diese umfasst Personen und Organisationen, deren Vermögen in den USA eingefroren wird und mit denen US-Personen grundsätzlich keine Geschäfte machen dürfen.
Abdullah al-Muhaysini hatte der aus Al-Kaida hervorgegangenen Al-Nusrah-Front während des Bürgerkriegs in Syrien unter anderem als religiöser Berater gedient, Kämpfer rekrutiert und beim Aufbau einer von Al-Nusrah geprägten Herrschaftsstruktur mitgewirkt. Die Streichung steht im Zusammenhang mit der neuen Syrien-Politik der US-Regierung. Washington hob zugleich die Einstufung von Al-Nusrah beziehungsweise Hajat Tahrir al-Sham als terroristische Organisation auf und strich HTS von der SDN-Liste.
25 Jahre nach den Anschlägen vom 11. September ist das eine bemerkenswerte Momentaufnahme. Denn Al-Kaida ist weder verschwunden, noch dieselbe Organisation wie damals. Ihr Kern ist schwach, ihre regionalen Ableger sind dagegen in Teilen Afrikas und Asiens weiterhin schlagkräftig. Zentrum und Außenstellen haben sich zunehmend voneinander entfernt.
Regionale Ableger
"Wir müssen uns im Grunde von der eurozentrischen Sicht verabschieden", sagt der emeritierte Islamwissenschaftler Rüdiger Lohlker. Al-Kaida und andere dschihadistische Organisationen seien außerhalb Europas und den USA immer sehr viel präsenter gewesen als es aus westlicher Sicht geschienen habe.
Heute gilt das besonders für Afrika: Im Sahel ist mit der "Dschamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin" (Gemeinschaft zur Unterstützung des Islam und der Muslime, JNIM) ein mächtiger Al-Kaida-Verbund entstanden, in Somalia ist die Al-Kaida eng verbundene Gruppe Al-Shabaab stark, im Jemen hält sich Al-Kaida auf der Arabischen Halbinsel (AQAP). Auch Afghanistan bleibt ein Rückzugsraum der Organisation.
Al-Kaida selbst firmiert immer weniger unter eigenem Namen. Das liege wesentlich an der erfolgreichen Terrorismusbekämpfung nach 2001, sagt Lars Berger, Professor für Terrorismusforschung an der Hochschule des Bundes. Das militärische Vorgehen in Afghanistan sowie die Zusammenarbeit von Geheimdiensten und Polizei hätten die Gruppe erheblich geschwächt.
"So gesehen waren die Anschläge vom 11. September ein großer strategischer Misserfolg Al-Kaidas", sagt Berger. Die erhoffte Radikalisierung der arabischen Welt und der Sturz der dortigen Regime blieben aus. Rund zehn Jahre nach den Anschlägen von New York und Washington, D.C. wurde im Mai 2011 das bekannteste Gesicht Al-Kaidas, Osama bin Laden, getötet.
In der Folge organisierte sich Al-Kaida neu. "Die Miliz suchte Gebiete, in denen sie dauerhaft Fuß fassen konnte - etwa in Teilen Afrikas oder auch im Jemen", sagt Berger. Besonders günstig seien Staaten mit schwacher staatlicher Ordnung, überforderten Sicherheitskräften und ungelösten lokalen Konflikten.
Dies gilt etwa für die Sahel-Zone. Dort konnten dschihadistische Gruppen ihre Rückzugsräume ausweiten. Eine Analyse des Thinktanks Critical Threats Project zeigt am Beispiel Niger, wie JNIM und die Sahel-Provinz des Islamischen Staates (ISSP) um Territorium, Kämpfer und Ressourcen konkurrieren. JNIM griff im Juni 2026 den internationalen Flughafen von Niamey an.
Ökonomie der Gewalt
Diese Erfolge seien nicht allein durch die dschihadistische Ideologie erklärbar, sagt Lohlker. Vielmehr fielen sie vielfach mit einer Art Gewaltwirtschaft zusammen. "Gewalt ist für den Terrorismus längst ein Wirtschaftsfaktor." Entführungen, Schmuggel und Plünderungen bildeten eine "Plünderungs"- oder "Schmuggelökonomie". Es existierten regelrechte "Gewaltmärkte", so Lohlker: Wo sich mit Gewalt Geld verdienen lasse, könnten dschihadistische Organisationen auch Menschen an sich binden.
Hinzu kommt die Schwäche des Staates. "Wenn eine relativ schwache Staatsmacht vorhanden ist oder ein Staat praktisch nicht existiert, sind das natürlich günstige Umweltbedingungen", sagt Lohlker. Al-Kaida kann dort überleben, wo sie auf lokale Konflikte und Machtvakuen trifft.
Regionales Engagement
Über die Jahre hat sich auch ihre Strategie verändert. Berger beobachtet einen "strategischen Schwenk": weg vom unmittelbaren Angriff auf den "fernen Feind", hin zum Aufbau lokaler Strukturen. "Nun sehen wir den Versuch, alternativ und inkrementell vorzugehen: keine von höchster Ebene angeordnete spektakuläre Gewaltanwendungen, sondern kleinere, eher von unten." Im Sahel bedeutet das, lokale Bündnisse zu schließen, Einfluss auf Gemeinden zu gewinnen und Territorien zu kontrollieren. Das Critical Threats Project beschreibt diese Entwicklung als "lokale Anpassung" ("localization").
Al-Kaida überlebt damit gerade durch ihre Ausdifferenzierung. JNIM greift ethnische und soziale Konflikte im Sahel auf, Al-Shabaab Konflikte innerhalb der somalischen Clanstrukturen. Das globale dschihadistische Ziel bleibt als ideologischer Rahmen bestehen, der konkrete Kampf wird jedoch vor Ort geführt.
Konkurrenz zum "Islamischen Staat"
Im Wettbewerb um Aufmerksamkeit hat Al-Kaida allerdings einen Konkurrenten, der ihr überlegen ist: den "Islamischen Staat" (IS). "Letztlich ist es so, dass sich jüngere Dschihadisten eher vom Islamischen Staat angezogen fühlen", sagt der Terrorismusexperte Behnam Heidenreuter-Said von der Akademie der Polizei Hamburg.
Der IS habe sich "spektakulärere" und medial erfolgreichere Terrorschläge geleistet. Doch Al-Kaida habe langfristiger kalkuliert, so Heidenreuter-Said, der vor einigen Jahren eine umfassende Geschichte Al-Kaidas veröffentlichte: "Der IS wollte sich inszenieren und möglichst schnell Erfolge vorweisen, um explosionsartig zu wachsen." Auf die Expansion des IS folgte allerdings dessen Zusammenbruch. Al-Kaida hingegen besteht - wenngleich unter veränderten Vorzeichen - weiter.
Allerdings stellt sich für die Gruppe heute die Frage, ob sie die alternde Generation ersetzen kann. Das sei zwar denkbar, sagt Heidenreuter-Said, weist aber darauf hin, dass Al-Kaida als Marke zusehends verblasse. Gerade in Europa sei der militante Dschihadismus weniger attraktiv geworden. Dschihadistische Ideen seien damit jedoch nicht verschwunden - Al-Kaida habe nur ihre frühere Fähigkeit verloren, junge Menschen in großer Zahl zu mobilisieren.
Das Zentrum von Al-Kaida ist schwach, ihre regionalen Ableger sind es nicht. Besonders JNIM, Al-Shabaab und AQAP können in fragilen Staaten erheblichen Einfluss entfalten.
Dünne Informationslage
Wie gefährlich die Organisation tatsächlich noch ist, lässt sich deshalb schwer beantworten. Behnam Heidenreuter-Said weist auf einen entscheidenden blinden Fleck hin: "Alle betonen unisono, dass es derzeit so gut wie keine Informationen über Al-Kaida gibt. Man weiß schlicht nicht, was sie derzeit tut." Seit den Hamas-Anschlägen in Israel am 7. Oktober 2023 sei zudem auffällig gewesen, wie wenig Al-Kaida in den großen regionalen Konflikten sichtbar geworden sei. Hamas, Hisbollah, Huthi und Iran hätten die politische und militärische Bühne dominiert.
25 Jahre nach 9/11 ist Al-Kaida damit weder verschwunden, noch dieselbe Organisation wie damals. Sie hat ihre globale Bühne weitgehend verloren. Dafür hat sie gelernt, lokal zu überleben. Es ist nicht ausgeschlossen, dass sie in schwachen Staaten so lange Fuß fasst, dass aus einer Terrororganisation eine dauerhafte politische und militärische Macht wird.
description: 25 Jahre nach 9/11 ist Al-Kaida nicht mehr die globale Terrororganisation von einst. Ihr Zentrum ist geschwächt, doch regionale Ableger sind in Afrika und Asien stark. Ihre Strategie: lokal Fuß fassen.

title: Sir John Curtice: The 'Burnham bounce' is real but it's not massive
content_c:
The consistent message of the opinion polls since the new prime minister walked into Downing Street almost a fortnight ago is that Labour is enjoying a "Burnham bounce". And this has now been confirmed by the party's convincing victory in Thursday's Greater Manchester mayoral by-election.
Polls conducted in the last week put Labour on average in the mid 20s. It is the party's highest standing since the beginning of last year and compares to their rating of 19% in late June when Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down.
But with Reform polling only narrowly behind Labour, Burnham's party still has a long way to go before it can face the prospect of fighting a general election with confidence.
The new PM effect
The Burnham boost is far from unprecedented.
All but one of the recent mid-term changes of prime minister have been followed by an increase in the popularity of the incumbent government. Support for Labour rose by seven points after Gordon Brown replaced Tony Blair in 2007, while the Conservatives enjoyed a six-point bounce when Boris Johnson took over from Theresa May in 2019. Only Liz Truss' arrival in Downing Street in 2022 – which was overshadowed by the death shortly thereafter of Queen Elizabeth II – failed to give her party a boost.
We should also bear in mind the depth of the electoral hole that Burnham has inherited as Labour leader. The 19% at which Labour stood when Sir Keir resigned was the lowest poll rating passed on by any prime minister departing mid-term – even lower than the 23% bequeathed by Liz Truss when she resigned after just 45 days in office.
Against that backdrop, it would have been very surprising indeed if the replacement of the deeply unpopular Sir Keir by the relatively popular Burnham had not given Labour a short-term boost. However, even after Burnham's bounce, his party's poll average is still the lowest for any newly minted mid-term PM, while the party is still well adrift in the polls of the (relatively low) 35% it won at the 2024 general election.
That said, Labour's victory in Thursday's Manchester mayoral by-election was convincing. True, Labour's 47% share of the first preference vote was well down on the 63% that Burnham secured in the last mayoral contest shortly before the 2024 general election. However, not only did it represent a near doubling of the 24% that Labour registered across the region in May's local elections, but also it was even four points up on Labour's tally locally in the 2024 general election – and thus a much better performance than would have been anticipated from even the latest national polling.
Reform's difficulties
But with still no more than a narrow lead over Reform, it is unsurprising Burnham has ruled out an early election. In any event, Reform's displacement from first place in the polls for the first time in over a year appears to owe more to its own difficulties than it does to Labour's new-found popularity.
Reform has been dogged in recent weeks by questions about the legality of the source of some of its funding and about whether Farage should have declared to the Commons authorities some of the funding he received before being elected an MP. Following these allegations, Farage announced on 7 July that he was standing down and putting himself again before the voters of his Clacton constituency in a by-election now scheduled for 13 August.
This move appears to have backfired. Immediately before Farage's announcement, Reform's average poll rating stood at 27%. In the polls conducted immediately after Farage's announcement, it fell by three points to 24%, the level at which it still stands now, and the lowest it has been for 15 months. At the same time, Farage's personal poll ratings are now the worst they have been since he returned as Reform's leader during the 2024 election campaign.
In the Manchester by-election, Reform's share of the first preference vote was nine point down on its tally across the region in May's local elections. As in the Makerfield by-election, the party seemingly suffered from the advance made by Rupert Lowe's breakaway from Reform, Restore Britain, which won nearly 9% of the Manchester vote, outpolling the Conservatives in the process.
But for Reform's difficulties, the "Burnham bounce" would probably have been insufficient to put Labour in the lead in the national polls.
Greens suffering
The principal source of that bounce has been clawing voters back from the Greens and the Liberal Democrats, both of whom have suffered a two-point drop since Burnham's uncontested victory in the Labour leadership contest. For the Greens – much of whose increased support in recent months came from disappointed 2024 Labour voters – the change of prime minister has proven particularly damaging. The Greens' current 11% tally is as much as four points adrift of where it was when Sir Keir announced he was leaving.
When he resigned, 14% of Labour's 2024 election voters said they would now back the Greens. That figure is now 9%.
Winning back former Labour voters has generally been a key component of the Burnham bounce. Overall, 67% of those who voted Labour in 2024 now say they would vote for the party, compared to 57% when Sir Keir indicated he was leaving Downing Street.
Following Farage's difficulties, Labour is also now losing fewer of its 2024 voters to Reform. But the same is true of the Conservatives, whose loss of support to Reform in the polls during this Parliament has always been much greater than that suffered by Labour. Far from suffering from a Burnham bounce, Kemi Badenoch's party has edged up to 20% in the polls for the first time since last spring.
Burnham's arrival has given Labour new hope. But despite having overtaken Reform in the polls, the new Labour leader still has to prove he can win back the working class pro-Brexit voters that Labour once regarded as its core vote but who now form the heart of support for Reform.
To do this – and put Labour on course for victory in 2029 - Burnham needs to deliver on the policy challenges facing his government, which remain as formidable as those that beset Sir Keir. Labour's prospects at the next election will ultimately depend on whether voters have come to believe that what he has said he will do is actually happening.
John Curtice is a professor of politics at Strathclyde University and senior fellow at the National Centre for Social Research and The UK in a Changing Europe

title: Can popular state premier Schwesig hold off the far-right AfD?
content_c:
Can popular premier Schwesig hold off the far-right AfD?
September 15, 2026
The late-summer warmth is lingering in the countryside of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Lavender-infused cocktails and savory onion cakes are being served on the spacious terrace of Hasenwinkel Castle, an old country house turned conference hotel not far from the Baltic coast. The largest business association in this northeastern German state has invited members and guests from the political world to a convivial gathering. State Premier Manuela Schwesig, of the Social Democratic Party (SPD), is also in attendance.
It could be a relaxed evening, were it not for the upcoming state election on September 20. "We live in politically turbulent times," says association president Lars Schwarz in his welcoming remarks. But the evening is also meant to serve as an opportunity to "recharge," he says. Days before the election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading in the polls with around 37%. But the SPD is not far behind, with 33%, and has narrowed the gap in recent weeks. The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which leads the federal government with the SPD under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is far behind and hoping to remain above the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
Economy needs immigration to offset labor shortages
The term "remigration" is playing a major role in the AfD's campaign. But as far as the state's business leaders are concerned, sending people of immigrant background out of Germany would be a disaster for the economy.
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has a significantly older population than most other German states. It's also less densely populated and more severely affected by demographic change. "International skilled workers and laborers have long been an important part of our economic future," said Schwarz. "Openness to the world is not an abstract political formula, but a concrete prerequisite for ensuring that businesses in our state can continue to produce, offer services, train employees, and grow."
In a brief speech at the event, Schwesig recounted encounters she had during the election campaign. She speaks of a conversation with a baker who is concerned not only about high energy prices but also about her employees. "She said, 'Ms. Schwesig, I have employees with immigrant backgrounds working here, and I'm very worried that I'll lose them — because I value them, and because I care about them as people.'"
The head of a planning firm approached the state premier and explained that his Moroccan employee wanted to leave the country. "Because when he goes to the café at the market in Stralsund and waits for his German friends, the people sitting near him either make snide remarks or move to another table." Who, Schwesig asks, would want to live in such a climate?
Fear of social division
Preventing the AfD's victory — that is what the 52-year-old Schwesig has made her stated goal. In the final stretch of the campaign, her posters feature just her face on a red background — no name — above the slogan "The Woman Against Blue" — a reference to the AfD's party color.
"The situation is serious," Schwesig told DW. "The AfD would harm our economy; they would harm our social cohesion. Their crude way of speaking, their hate and incitement, is tearing our society apart; there's a renewed propensity for violence, and that will affect us women in particular."
Anyone who doesn't want those things must support her, she says. "To do that, you have to go to the polls and vote for the SPD — and that's why I'm the woman against blue."
Perhaps tellingly, the SPD isn't mentioned on most of her campaign posters, however. Only Schwesig herself is visible, dressed in red. The SPD's party color must suffice as a reference. Schwesig is the driving force: She represents the political comeback of the past twelve months. In September 2025, the SPD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania was languishing at just 19% in opinion polls, while the AfD stood at 38%.
A grassroots approach
Manuela Schwesig managed to close the gap, in part, by trying to stay closely connected to the people of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, seeking direct dialogue with voters as often as possible. She is friendly and approachable, yet also firm. Schwesig listens, answers questions with confidence, marshals the facts, and engages in discussions where she attempts to demonstrate that she is well-informed about everything happening in the state.
Above all, however, she scored points by maintaining maximum distance from the federal government — and thus from her own party too. In Berlin, the SPD governs as the junior partner in a coalition with the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) parties, and the government is more unpopular than any before it. As Schwesig has gained ground, the SPD's support at the federal level has plummeted to 12%.
Fierce criticism of Chancellor Merz
Schwesig believes much of what is decided in Berlin is wrong — and she says so. "I expect the chancellor and the entire federal government to chart a new political course,” she demanded following the AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt in early September.
She has long believed that the reform of the social welfare systems planned by the CDU/CSU and the SPD is heading in the wrong direction. "I expect that the reforms will ensure that those who have worked their entire lives and made contributions are not the ones who bear the heaviest burdens," she says regarding the plans to eliminate the retirement age of 63 for people who have contributed to the pension fund for a particularly long time. "And I'm glad that my criticism is now receiving a lot of support."
Could Schwesig take over as SPD party leader?
She also receives support from within her own party. Discontent is growing within the federal SPD over the two co-chairs, Lars Klingbeil and Bärbel Bas. There is open speculation about whether Manuela Schwesig should replace them at the party's helm. Amid the SPD's crisis, there are strong arguments for making one of the last Social Democrats who is popular with voters the party leader.
A woman who entered politics relatively late in life. Born in Brandenburg, she was already nearly 30 years old when she joined the SPD in 2003. Prior to that, she had studied public finance and worked as a tax official.
Underestimated by her rivals?
Her political rise was rapid: Local politics in the state capital of Schwerin, Social Affairs Minister in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and finally, in 2013, Federal Family Affairs Minister under former Chancellor Angela Merkel. By then, she had become well-known nationwide.
Her opponents often underestimated her, especially men. A CDU politician once derisively called her the "coastal Barbie." "Young, blonde, East German" was the headline when she became a federal minister.
Perhaps this was also because Schwesig never came across as a classic power-seeking politician. Her strengths, say her supporters, lie in her calm perseverance, fighting spirit, and pragmatism.
Nord Stream 2
This tenacity nearly proved to be her undoing in the dispute over the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline. In 2017, Schwesig returned to Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania to succeed State Premier Erwin Sellering, who was seriously ill at the time. Sellering had maintained very good relations with Russia, and Schwesig continued his policies.
This included defending the construction of the Baltic Sea pipeline — which was intended to transport even more Russian gas to Germany — in the face of criticism from Eastern Europe, the US, and some in Germany. When the US threatened sanctions in 2021, Schwesig even attempted to secure the completion of Nord Stream 2 by establishing a "climate foundation" funded by Moscow.
Strong approval ratings
After the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, her stance became a political liability. Schwesig made a political about-face and admitted to mistakes. To this day, however, she defends the logic behind her decisions at the time.
This has not caused her any lasting damage. Currently, in a direct election, 60% of voters in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania would vote for Schwesig as head of government.
The current state government, made up of the SPD and the socialist Left Party, is also performing well in polls. But it remains to be seen whether this will be enough to secure another term.
This article was translated from German.
description: Manuela Schwesig has led Germany’s northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania since 2017. Will the center-left premier be able to stop the far-right AfD from emerging as the strongest force in Sunday’s election?

title: Iran: Cafés im Visier der Sicherheitsapparate
content_c:
Iran: Cafés im Visier der Sicherheitsapparate
10. September 2026
In den letzten Monaten sind die iranischen Behörden in der Hauptstadt Teheran rigoros gegen die Cafés vorgegangen, die sie für Treffpunkte von regimekritischen Aktivisten halten. Nach Angaben der Menschenrechtsorganisation HRANA wurden im Juli mindestens sieben Kaffeehäuser geschlossen, weil dort Besucherinnen die Hidschab-Regel nicht eingehalten haben sollen. Im Iran ist für Frauen das Tragen vom Kopftuch in der Öffentlichkeit eine Pflicht.
Zuvor hatten einige Medien wie die Zeitung "Javan", die der Islamischen Revolutionsgarden (IRGC) nahe steht, Stimmung gegen die Cafés gemacht und sie als "Treffpunkte der Wutbürger" bezeichnet. Diese seien eine Gefahr für die "nationale Sicherheit". Die Behörden vermuten, dass Cafés eine Rolle bei der Organisation von Massenprotesten spielen könnten.
Cafés sind hip
Die Cafés sind sehr beliebt unter der relativ jungen Bevölkerung mit einem durchschnittlichen Alter von 34,5 Jahren. Immer wieder kam es im Iran zu Massenprotesten. Zuletzt fanden sie zum Jahreswechsel 2025/2026 statt, weil die Preise aufgrund schlechter Konjunktur explosiv gestiegen sind.
Zuletzt wurden zum Beispiel die Cafés im "Vanak Park" in Teheran geschlossen. Mindestens 200 Menschen verloren ihre Arbeitsplätze. An diesen Tagen musste auch die beliebte Café-Kette Saediniya ihre zehn Filialen im Iran nach einem Gerichtsbeschluss schließen. Sie steht in der Kritik der "staatsfeindlichen Propaganda". Ihren Eigentümer, den Unternehmer Sadegh Saedinia, hat der Oberste Gerichtshof zu zwölf Jahren und sechs Monaten Haft sowie zur Einziehung seines Vermögens verurteilt. Er soll die regierungsfeindlichen Proteste unterstützt haben.
Auch andere Cafés wie "Lamiz" und "Voria" mussten ihren Betrieb einstellen. Beide wurden wegen des Vorwurfs der indirekten Unterstützung von Protestaufrufen auf gerichtliche Anordnung hin versiegelt.
Veränderter Lebensstil
In Teheran hat die Zahl der Cafés in den letzten zehn Jahren stark zugenommen - von etwa 300 Anfang der 2010er Jahre auf mittlerweile bis zu 4000, wie verschiedene Schätzungen zeigen. Einige Experten führen diesen Anstieg auf Veränderungen im städtischen Lebensstil zurück. Sie sehen darin mehr als rein eine geschäftliche Ausweitung und deuten dies als Zeichen umfassender sozialer und kultureller Veränderungen innerhalb der Gesellschaft.
"Das explosive Wachstum der Cafés kann bis zu einem gewissen Grad als gesellschaftliche Reaktion auf das Leben in der chronischen Krise verstanden werden", sagt Saba Alaleh, Psychologin und Psychoanalytikerin mit Schwerpunkt auf politischen und sozialen Themen, im DW-Interview. "Unter solchen Umständen suchen Menschen nicht nur nach Konsum oder Unterhaltung, sondern nach einem Ort, an dem sie vorübergehend Abstand vom Alltagsdruck gewinnen können."
Ein Café wäre dann ein sozialer Raum neben dem Zuhause und dem Arbeitsplatz. "Es ist ein Ort dazwischen, an dem Menschen kurzfristig ihren alltäglichen Rollen und dem Stress entfliehen, Kontakt zu anderen herstellen und das Gefühl bewahren können, dass das Leben noch einigermaßen überschaubar und geordnet ist."
Das Café ist besonders bei der Generation Z beliebt, die im Iran stark unter galoppierender Inflation und hohen Lebenshaltungskosten leidet. "Die jungen Menschen, die sich in diesen Cafés treffen, stammen nicht unbedingt aus wohlhabenden Verhältnissen", sagt Nasser, Ex-Cafébesitzer in Teheran, gegenüber der DW. "In vielen Teilen Teherans versammeln sich auch junge Menschen aus der Mittelschicht in Cafés, und viele unserer Gäste gehören zu dieser Gruppe."
Regime fürchtet Kontrollverlust
Bereits vor der jüngsten Protestwelle Ende 2025 war die Schließung von Cafés für die iranische Regierung gängige Praxis. Die meisten Razzien und Schließungen wurden jedoch unter dem Vorwand der Durchsetzung der Hidschab-Pflicht durchgeführt. "Unser Café wurde unter dem Vorwand geschlossen, wir hätten Kundinnen ohne Kopftuch bedient, doch das ist nur eine Ausrede", sagt Nasser.
"Draußen, auf den Straßen Teherans, haben Frauen und Mädchen die Kopftuch-Pflicht faktisch abgeschafft. Doch die Regierung erwartet von uns, dass wir sie nicht ins Café lassen", ergänzt er.
Alaleh erklärt, es gehe nicht mehr nur um die Kontrolle von Frauen, die keinen Hidschab tragen. "Autoritäre Regierungen versuchen im Allgemeinen, den Informationsfluss, soziale Interaktionen und die Organisation der Zivilgesellschaft zu kontrollieren", betont sie. "Jeder Raum außerhalb der direkten Aufsicht der Machthaber, in dem Vertrauen, Dialog und soziale Bindungen entstehen können, schwächt das Monopol der Regierung."
Das harte Vorgehen gegen Cafés und ihre Gäste sei Teil der Bemühungen der Regierung, ihr Monopol über soziale Räume zu bewahren, so Alaleh. "Bereits eine Gruppe junger Menschen, die ungezwungen und zufällig zusammenkommt, ist für den Sicherheitsapparat die Bildung eines unabhängigen sozialen Netzwerks außerhalb formaler Machtstrukturen. Je breiter und tiefer diese unabhängigen Netzwerke verwurzelt sind, desto schwieriger wird es für die Regierung, ihre ausschließliche Kontrolle über den öffentlichen Raum aufrechtzuerhalten."
Aus dem Englischen adaptiert von Dang Yuan
description: Für viele junge Menschen im Iran sind Cafés soziale Orte, an denen sie zusammenkommen können. Genau deshalb geraten sie zunehmend in den Fokus der Behörden. Warum das Regime viele Kaffeehäuser schließt.

title: Our exclusive behind-the-scenes access at No 10 as Andy Burnham became PM
content_c:
"You can clap now," a Downing Street official with a clipboard instructed the staff eagerly lining the halls of No 10 in the moments before the new prime minister walked in.
The applause duly began before the famous door opened, so the first sight and sound to greet Andy Burnham and his wife were crowds of clapping staff, crammed into the Downing Street hall. They stretched up the long corridor all the way to the door of the Cabinet Room - left ajar for him to walk straight in and get down to work.
I've seen plenty of prime ministers come and go from outside No 10. But I'd never been allowed inside at that moment before, able to hover outside the Cabinet Room and grab a quick word with the country's new leader at such an intense, symbolic time.
I have rarely seen a politician look as thoroughly delighted as Burnham, pride bursting out of his buttoned-up suit - that's right, the T-shirt and bomber jacket didn't make it to No 10 - or a leader who has wanted to stop and shake as many hands.
Andy Burnham: The Laura Kuenssberg Interview
Panorama
What kind of prime minister will Andy Burnham be? In his first major broadcast interview since taking office, Laura Kuenssberg asks about his plans - and the challenges ahead.
No 10 staff are already wondering if they'll ever be able to stick to a regular prime minister's schedule, normally designed with military precision. If Andy Burnham was able to take the time to stop and speak to everyone in the country, I suspect he probably would.
It's a sign of his different style that our team was given permission to be behind the scenes at three key moments in the 59th prime minister's first week in charge - when he became Labour leader, when he walked into No 10, and on day one at his new Manchester outpost, No 10 North.
Most important by far was our half-hour interview in that shiny new office, after weeks during which Burnham was chased by accusations he'd avoided tough questions. But the extra glimpses we were given, alongside Burnham's own voracious appetite for social media, display a prime minister that's not just at ease in front of the cameras, but a leader who wants to bring you along for the ride.
They included revealing moments that are normally hidden - his first steps into the Cabinet Room to appoint his team, rating pub snacks with his Chancellor, John Healey, in an Instagram post, external, and sharing pictures with us of the family dog, Axel, whom he describes as having "angry little man energy".
"Comms" - how politicians communicate and explain themselves and talk to the public - is not the be-all and end-all.
Burnham's exploits online have already brought mockery and launched a thousand memes. But if a leader can't get your attention to make their arguments - as Keir Starmer found so challenging - ultimately, they are not going to get very far at all.
And the biggest difference of the Labour reboot so far is how the government looks and sounds. They've put an obvious priority on punter-friendly announcements such as cutting VAT from energy bills and tax breaks for pubs - although it is important to note the details on how to pay for all of that are not yet clear.
For Burnham though, telling his story is the easy part. Joking about the unique stink that accompanies Scampi Fries, or showing me his gold disc on loan from The Smiths' guitarist Johnny Marr, won't help him deal with US President Donald Trump, find money for defence, or create a new service to care for the elderly and vulnerable in England. Nor will it be any use as he grapples with the country's huge debts, changing demographics or public concerns about immigration.
Listening carefully during our interview, it seemed Burnham had distinct gears. He was fluent and passionate on his familiar ground: his desire to sort out social care, his track record in Manchester, his desire to run a government that feels relevant and effective where you live, local leaders eager to make many more decisions and able to spend taxpayers' money more freely without permission from Whitehall.
Those are his core beliefs, arguments he's made hundreds, if not thousands of times.
But when it comes to how he'll apply what he thinks in principle to what he does in practice, that was not always so clear. On social care for example, he's long believed there ought to be a National Care Service, like the NHS. But in a speech on Wednesday, that's not likely to be what he unveils.
Instead, he told me he'd "brought it straight forward", understood to mean speeding up the government review by Baroness Louise Casey of what ought to be done, not saying, "here's the plan".
When it came to questions that are on his desk for the first time, there was a contradiction. Burnham told us all many times that he will stick to the manifesto the country voted for in 2024.
But he's also vowed his arrival in office will usher in the biggest change in four decades. You don't have to be a student of political history to find a mismatch there - he's going to stick broadly to Sir Keir's plan, yet shift the government more fundamentally than leaving the EU, or the financial crash? Really?
And beyond the rhetorical tension in several areas, Burnham gave clear indications that he will apply "new eyes". Will he stick to the home secretary's plans to make migrants wait 10 years or more before they can permanently stay in the UK? He's looking at that again he told me, and hinted that care workers could possibly be exempt.
What about welfare? Remember Sir Keir ditched most significant reforms in the face of resistance on the back benches. While seeking not to "blame" anyone receiving benefits, Burnham said the country had to "get serious" about getting the welfare bill down, and suggested he might make it harder for some people to claim, by imposing extra conditions.
He didn't want to give much away about where he was going to find extra billions for defence, or pay for public services. He repeated that he'd stick to the promises on income tax, VAT and National Insurance made in 2024. But the prime minister clearly pointed to a possible shake-up of the council tax system, where those with the most expensive properties might have to pay considerably more. Changes like that to council tax, or to welfare, would be huge political moves that would put him on a collision course with some of his party, and some political opponents too.
Then, when it comes to matters of war and peace, which for Burnham are genuinely new, it felt we could see him thinking in real time how to answer the question, perhaps trying to balance giving a flavour of who he is, without creating a political accident.
Does he trust Trump? Twice he wouldn't say.
"It's a changing world," his second answer.
Would he take a call from Russian President, Vladimir Putin?
A pause, then: "I'd have to know the circumstances".
As mayor, Burnham evidently spent years thinking hard about how to use power, and how he wants to shift the balance in the UK away from Westminster. The impact of that stance could be profound, way beyond some admirably shiny No 10 signs emblazoned all over one floor of a government building in Manchester.
Mayors are expected to get power to spend nationally collected income tax, and crucially to spend billions without strings.
Burnham spent time too as mayor absorbing people's experiences, their hardships and frustrations.
"My strength always is in remaining close to people, close to the public, that will not change because I am prime minister," Burnham told me.
Although don't be in any doubt, he also spent time thinking and planning about how to make a return to the political heart of this country, the Westminster he believes is so flawed.
But when it comes to the gravest matters that prime ministers have to deal with - security, power around the world, or the country's long-term economic stability, we're perhaps yet to see if Burnham's ambition for No 10 is accompanied by truly new big ideas that match the scale of his rhetoric.
There are worries on the right of the Labour Party that Burnham has not absorbed the reality of the country's economic position - years of stuttering growth, and sky-high levels of debt that leave the UK incredibly vulnerable to the financial markets' judgements, whether he likes it or not.
And concerns on the left, that he's tickled their bellies with promises of "authentic Labour", flirting with the ideas of increasing state control of vital industries, but which might not come through. And like most incoming prime ministers, he has precious little experience of handling international events. The moments in our interview where he was least sure-footed were answering questions about how he'd manage relationships with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin.
One minister said he'd "vibe left, but govern from the centre". Perhaps, as he's tried to give firms and families a "breathing space" when it comes to the cost of living, he'll ask for "breathing space" from the public before his complete programme becomes clear.
Burnham has long been unusual as a politician - a leader who has managed to be popular in a time when politicians often disappoint and are sometimes despised. He knows he's walking into a job that's been marked by failure for a decade. As he told me, "the onus is on me not to be another one who just doesn't change things". He's part of a political generation he proclaims to be "just not good enough".
Remember, his own career has had plenty of failure too. It took Burnham three goes to become the leader of his party. As he arrived, straightening his tie, to be confirmed in the top job in central London 10 days ago, I asked him why he'd taken so long.
He laughed and told me, "I like to make an entrance".
Andy Burnham has now truly arrived. But he knows all too well, there won't be applause everywhere he goes.

title: Netherlands: Suspected sabotage disrupts train services
content_c:
Netherlands: Suspected sabotage disrupts train services
September 15, 2026
Train services in various parts of the Netherlands have been severely disrupted, with ProRail, the company that maintains the nation's rail infrastructure, saying that sabotage was possibly at play.
National railway company NS said that train services around the central cities of Zwolle, Deventer and Amersfoort have been affected since the morning rush hour.
What do we know about the causes of the disruption?
In a statement, rail authority ProRail said that "[m]aterials deliberately placed on the tracks have been found at several locations. This is causing track-circuit failures. It appears to be a case of sabotage."
The objects caused failures across the network, affecting several level crossings, which disrupted road traffic, Pro Rail said.
ProRail workers were clearing the objects and working to restore safe conditions, it added.
Though the company itself did not say what the "materials" were, a ProRail spokesperson told the daily de Volkskrant that "pipes had been found attached to the line" in several places.
This caused the disruptions, as the railway security systems can register a train's presence on a line because of an object placed on it and thus block access for other trains.
The spokesperson told the paper that one train had even collided with one of the pipes laid on the tracks, but that no accident or injuries had occurred.
Important event in The Hague
It remains unknown whether the incident has to do with so-called Prinsjesdag, the day the Dutch government presents its annual budget to parliament, where the reigning monarch gives a speech.
On the day, thousands of people go to The Hague to watch the royal family ride through the city in horse-drawn carriages.
Edited by: Natalie Muller

description: A major outage has hit parts of the Dutch railway system after objects were found placed across lines, authorities say. The company responsible for rail infrastructure says it suspects deliberate wrongdoing.

title: Beethovens Porträt: Warhols letzte Ikone
content_c:
Beethovens Porträt: Warhols letzte Ikone
10. September 2026
Der Künstler Andy Warhol prägte ein neues Bild von Ludwig van Beethoven. Sein Siebdruck aus dem Jahr 1987 zeigt nicht den grimmigen Mann historischer Porträts und Denkmäler. Warhols Darstellung zeigt einen präsenten Beethoven, bunt und verfremdet in Pop-Art Manier. So wirkt Beethoven eher wie ein Zeitgenosse.
Die Arbeit des Pop-Art-Gurus für seine New Yorker Studios "The Factory" erschien in einer limitierten Auflage von 60 Exemplaren und erwies sich als eine der innovativsten künstlerischen Auseinandersetzungen mit Ludwig van Beethoven im 20. Jahrhundert. Andy Warhol produzierte die berühmte Siebdruckserie "Beethoven" nur wenige Wochen vor seinem plötzlichen Tod am 22. Februar 1987. Die Serie gehört zu seinen letzten druckgrafischen Arbeiten.
Wie sich Warhol Beethoven genähert hat, und in welchem Kontext die Arbeit in ihren zahlreichen farblichen Variationen entstanden ist, zeigt die Sonderausstellung "Beethoven by Warhol" im Bonner Beethovenhaus. Das Haus ist das original erhaltene Geburtshaus von Ludwig van Beethoven.
Zwei Genies auf Augenhöhe
Die Ausstellung zeigt Raritäten, die Besucher sonst nie zu sehen bekommen. Das Kuratoren-Team des Beethovenhauses und des Bonner Archivs unter der Leitung von Direktor Malte Boecker hat sich drei Jahre lang mit dem Thema beschäftigt. Die Ausstellungsstücke haben sie aus den Untiefen der Archive und aus privaten Sammlungen zutage gefördert.
Neben der ikonischen Darstellung von Beethoven sind auch Zeichnungen von Warhol zu sehen, die er bei der Suche nach seinem Beethoven-Motiv in Bonn anfertigte. Darüber hinaus gibt es Probedrucke, die seine Auseinandersetzung mit der farblichen Gestaltung der Serie dokumentieren. Besonders stolz sind die Kuratoren auf einen aufwendig gestalteten Beethoven-Druck auf Leinwand. Das Werk ist Eigentum eines anonymen Sammlers aus dem Rheinland.
Beim Anblick des Bildes kommt die Kuratorin Silke Bettermann ins Schwärmen: "Warhol sagt uns: 'Schaut her! Dieser Mann, Beethoven, er ist ganz modern! Er ist ein Superstar!'"
Warhols Beethoven und andere Protagonisten
Wenn etwas leicht und locker aussieht oder klingt, steckt bekannterweise fast immer viel Arbeit dahinter. Dieses Grundprinzip gilt auch für Andy Warhols Werke, insbesondere für seine Beethoven-Serie. Auf der Suche nach seinem Beethoven hat Warhol zahlreiche Motive verglichen. Er hat auch selbst Zeichnungen von Beethoven-Darstellungen angefertigt, etwa von dem Beethoven-Denkmal auf dem Münsterplatz in Bonn. Dabei kommt einmal mehr zum Vorschein, was für ein großartiger Zeichner der Pop-Art-Künstler war.
Letztendlich hat sich Warhol für das ikonische Porträt von Joseph Karl Stieler entschieden, entstanden 1820 im Auftrag des Frankfurter Ehepaars Franz und Antonie Brentano. Eine Kaufmannsfamilie und Mäzene, die mit Beethoven befreundet waren. Das Porträt hatte den Anspruch, nicht nur die äußere Erscheinung Beethovens, sondern auch seine rebellische Persönlichkeit wiederzugeben.
Warhol übernimmt die grafische und verfremdet die farbliche Gestaltung des Stieler-Werks. Er überschreibt es mit einer handschriftlichen Partitur Beethovens. Allerdings nicht mit den Noten aus dem "Credo" der "Missa Solemnis" wie bei Stieler, sondern aus der "Mondscheinsonate", dem wohl berühmtesten Werk Beethovens. "Warhols Beethoven spricht zu uns regelrecht über und durch seine Musik", sagt die Kuratorin Silke Bettermann im DW-Gespräch.
Fußballlegende im Beethovenhaus
Eine Schlüsselrolle bei der Entstehung der Beethoven-Arbeiten spielte der Bonner Warhol-Galerist Hermann Wünsche, der den Künstler nicht nur in New York besuchte, sondern auch mehrfach ins Rheinland holte. Wünsche haben wir zahlreiche "deutsche" Werke Warhols zu verdanken – etwa die Porträts von Bundeskanzler Willy Brandt aus dem Jahr 1976 oder von Toni Schumacher. Den deutschen Nationaltorhüter porträtierte Warhol 1983.
Die Ausstellungsmacher ließen sich den Spaß nicht nehmen, das Meisterwerk und das Modell nach Bonn zu holen, zumal das Warhol-Werk sich heute im Privatbesitz von Toni Schumacher befindet.
"Damals, Mitte der 80er Jahre, war ich in aller Bescheidenheit auch schon ein Star", erinnert sich Toni Schumacher schmunzelnd an die Begegnung mit Andy Warhol. "Aber dann kam er, Andy Warhol. Als wir dann zusammen in einem Raum waren, hatte ich das Gefühl, dass ich zu einem Superstar rüber schaue und habe mich dann ein bisschen hintenangestellt". 1983 saß der heute 72-jährige Schumacher Model für Warhol: "Das war schon ein Gänsehautgefühl!"
Warhol und Musik: eine jahrzehntelange Beziehung
Auch ein einmaliges Konvolut der von Warhol gestalteten Plattencover, zusammengetragen vom belgischen Sammler und Warhol-Experten Guy Minnebach, ist erstmalig im Beethovenhaus zu sehen.
In drei Jahrzehnten hat Andy Warhol über 50 Schallplatten mit auffallend schönen und individuellen Covern ausgestattet. Die Bandbreite reicht von einer noch recht klassisch, aber bereits launig verspielt gestalteten Mendelssohn-Platte - mit Vladimir Horowitz, den Warhol auch persönlich kannte - bis hin zum legendären Jeans-Cover mit echtem Reißverschluss für "The Rolling Stones", oder das berühmte Bananen-Cover für "The Velvet Underground & Nico".
Da in Warhols "Factory" laut Augenzeugenberichten ununterbrochen Musik erklang, kann man anhand der von ihm gestalteten Plattencover auch den Musikgeschmack des Künstlers zumindest teilweise ablesen. Beethoven ist allerdings nicht dabei.
Wolfram Weimer: "Wir brauchen mehr Beethoven"
Mit der Warhol-Ausstellung greift das Beethovenhaus auf das anstehende große Jubiläum vor: Im März 2027 wird in der ganzen Welt an den 200. Todestag des Musikgenies gedacht. In Beethovens Heimatstadt Bonn wird der große Tag mit einer Sonderausgabe des Beethovenfestes gefeiert.
"Diese Ausstellung ist ein wunderbarer Auftakt für das Beethoven-Gedenkjahr", sagt Wolfram Weimer, Staatsminister für Kultur und Medien. Als Schirmherr der Ausstellung sagt er bei seiner Festrede in Bonn: "Wir müssen heute mehr Beethoven wagen".
"Beethoven war nicht nur ein Musikgenie und hat die Welt beglückt mit den großartigsten musikalischen Kunstwerken, die man sich vorstellen kann“, sagte Wolfram Weimer anschließend im DW-Interview. Beethoven verkörperte auch die Idee der Freiheit. "Er war ein Rebell, er hat Normen gebrochen und er hat die Machtverhältnisse seiner Zeit hinterfragt. Er war ein Bote der Freiheit, und das ist für uns heute eine gute Botschaft. Denn wir brauchen auch heute mehr Freiheit."
description: Zwei rebellische Genies: Die Ausstellung "Beethoven by Warhol" im Beethovenhaus Bonn präsentiert Warhols spätes Meisterwerk, die Beethoven-Serie.
